pdf_index.anonymized_output_policy: No anonymization performed by this check_diff run. Preserve every original PDF.
pdf_index.is_anonymized_semantics: True only when a verified anonymized PDF and completed receipt are linked by this index; false means no verified copy is linked.

C1.justification: The abstract, four introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about global–local entanglement, nonlinear semantic compression, complementary alignment, and faster convergence. New experiments provide additional support without redefining these core contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds a substantive mechanism explanation linking high-frequency suppression to diffusability and interprets stronger KL regularization as damaging semantic content. It also discusses metric dependence, compute efficiency, and fusion tradeoffs. Appendix C narrows the outstanding high-resolution limitation to larger models and adds mixed preliminary results from jointly decoding semantic and VAE latents.

D1.justification: v2 specifies throughput measurement on one A100 with batch size 64 and clarifies inclusion of DINOv2 and the compressor in compute accounting. Compressor-size reporting is explicitly reframed around encoder counts in Table 6. Most architecture, optimization, hardware/training-time disclosures, and the code-access statement remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds focused food-image generation on Food-101 and higher-resolution ImageNet generation at 512×512 (Appendix A.7, Table 14). v1's generation experiments cover ImageNet at 256×256. Existing Cityscapes probing and reduced-data ImageNet experiments are retained.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds RAE and REPA-E to the retained comparison methods, flagging their different latent spaces and the class-balanced evaluation of the 800-epoch REPA-E result. Table 1 also adds PCA-based combinations with global tokens, alignment, and multi-layer features as explicit comparison controls.

E3.justification: The stated default CFG scale changes from 2.8 to 2.3, retaining the guidance interval and sampling steps. v2 substantially expands evaluation through CMMD, DINOv2-based FD/FD-infinity, inference throughput, total training compute, and additional compression/fusion/resampling controls. Existing main training budgets and the 50,000-sample evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds matched PCA combination controls, a frequency-profile diagnostic, alternative-metric checks, compute-efficiency analysis, and fusion/resampling ablations (Table 1, Figure 3, Tables 11 and 13–16). The KL study expands to multiple weights and probing accuracy, while the GAN-loss experiment is removed. The CFG sweep expands; earlier channel, layer, VFM, and limited-data analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point results without repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional metrics in v2 are presented as point estimates, without a newly described uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include Food-101 FID 4.6 versus REG's 7.6 and ImageNet-512 FID 14.4 versus 18.1, plus new metric, compute, and ablation entries. Table 4's 80/160-epoch REGLUE FIDs change from 1.61/1.53 to 1.59/1.46 alongside the changed CFG setting, so these are not identical-setting gains. At the retained CFG scale 2.7, FID changes from 1.53 to 1.52. Main unguided benchmark FIDs remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed compressor, global/local/VAE fusion, velocity and alignment objectives, and sampling procedure remain unchanged in Section 3 and Appendix B. Newly evaluated fusion, compression, and regularization variants are diagnostic ablations; they do not replace the proposed architecture or training objective.

P1.justification: Most abstract, introduction, method, and conclusion wording and section order are retained. Changes concentrate on local experimental explanations, revised captions and cross-references, renamed or added appendix subsections, and a supplementary title page and contents list.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout, extensively resizing and repositioning displays. The overview moves later, and the compressor diagram and convergence samples move into the supplement. v2 adds the frequency plot and several tables and expands existing table columns and rows. The final sample grids retain the same images.

R1.justification: v2 adds references concerning Food-101, alternative evaluation metrics, diffusability, encoder/tokenizer alignment, and representation autoencoders, while removing the EQ-VAE citation. The related-work narrative and central positioning relative to REPA, ReDi, and REG remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–11, interpolation assumptions, token definitions, and training objectives retain the same mathematical content. The new frequency analysis is empirical; no theorem, proof, or formal derivation is added.

improvement.justification: Matched PCA controls and the frequency diagnostic substantially strengthen evidence isolating the compressor's contribution. Total-compute accounting addresses the limits of v1's iteration-based efficiency evidence, while Food-101, ImageNet-512, and alternative metrics broaden validation. These additions strengthen central design and efficiency claims. Removing the GAN ablation narrows one analysis, and uncertainty reporting remains absent; the retuned CFG scores also require qualification. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REGLUE work and provide readable methods, equations, experiments, figures, tables, and appendices A–E. Content can be reliably matched despite substantial reformatting and movement between the main text and supplement.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds Food-101 and ImageNet-512 evaluations, frequency analysis, compute measurements, and further ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet generation experiments, compressor and guidance ablations, and Cityscapes semantic-preservation results in the main text and Appendix A.

results.title: REGLUE Your Latents with Global and Local Semantics for Entangled Diffusion

C1.justification: The central claim that affordance descriptions improve occluded hand reconstruction and enable controllable generation is retained. v2 extends the stated contribution to learned grasp classification and joint image/text conditioning, and claims advantages over context-conditioned diffusion baselines. These refine the contribution without replacing its central research claim.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands mechanism explanations, attributing gains to token-level conditioning, modality-specific encoders, and visible-joint guidance. It interprets grasp-classification errors as having limited downstream impact. New limitations address static single-hand reconstruction, absent explicit 3D object geometry, and unreliable descriptions for unusual interactions; supplementary failure cases qualify applicability beyond training conditions.

D1.justification: v1 provides relatively few implementation details. v2 discloses loss weights, attention dimensions and heads, token counts, conditional dropout, 80 training epochs, batch size 64, Adam learning rate, scheduling, and dataset-specific refinement settings. The supplement adds classifier architecture, exact caption prompts, and post-processing settings. These materially improve reproducibility documentation without establishing that every newly disclosed setting changed.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from HOGraspNet reconstruction and text-controlled generation to HO3D and unconstrained HInt images, including New Days, VISOR, and Ego4D. v2 also evaluates grasp classification as an auxiliary task. This substantially broadens the evaluated data, environments, and task coverage.

E2.justification: v1 Table 1 compares against HaMeR and unconditional InterHandGen. v2 Table 1 adds HandOccNet, MeshGraphormer, WiLoR, Hamba, and InterHandGen with full text/image conditioning. The main InterHandGen refinement comparisons now use WiLoR initialization, substantially revising the comparison set.

E3.justification: The reported HOGraspNet evaluation expands from 300 examples to 3,000 evaluation images, and the main refinement experiments switch from HaMeR to WiLoR and Hamba. v2 adds PA-MPVPE, PCK, and mesh F-scores, alongside new HO3D and HInt protocols. The HOGraspNet S1 split and occlusion-bin definitions remain. Newly disclosed training hyperparameters are documentation additions rather than established changes to earlier settings.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's qualitative refinement and object-size controllability examples, v2 adds systematic ablations of conditioning modalities, caption generation, grasp labels, masks, encoders, guidance, and affordance fields. Figure 9 and supplementary Sections A–C add object-property analysis, classifier errors, hyperparameter sensitivity, and failure cases. The original size-control example is retained as Figure 8.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v2's additional tables and sensitivity plots continue point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 reports HaMeR refinement from 8.51 to 8.28 mm PA-MPJPE. Under its revised evaluation, v2 reports WiLoR refinement from 8.22 to 7.53 mm on HOGraspNet and adds HO3D results of 7.37 mm with WiLoR and 7.29 mm with Hamba. These are different experimental settings, not direct version-to-version gains. Numerous ablation, classification, efficiency, and HInt results are added; HInt includes both improvements and degradations.

M1.justification: v1 uses supplied ground-truth grasp labels and a text-only, CLIP-conditioned diffusion prior. v2 introduces a learned grasp classifier and replaces global text conditioning with DistilBERT text tokens, ViT image tokens, and cross-attention in AffHandGen. These substantially change the description-generation pipeline and model architecture. Occlusion-aware refinement was already present in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and the method and experimental narrative are reorganized into more detailed subsections. v2 adds a standalone Related Work section, explicit limitations, and supplementary Sections A–C. These constitute substantial changes in exposition and document structure.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column formatting. Pipeline diagrams are redesigned and separated, refinement gains algorithm pseudocode, and the main results table becomes a multi-benchmark, multi-metric display. New ablation tables, heatmaps, classifier diagrams, prompts, sensitivity plots, and failure panels substantially expand visual presentation. v1 Figure 5 is retained as v2 Figure 8.

R1.justification: v2 adds an extensive Related Work section covering hand reconstruction, affordance reasoning, and diffusion, with new works including Hamba, Text2HOI, DiffH2O, and AffordPose. It develops substantive distinctions from object-level affordance methods and globally conditioned diffusion priors, considerably expanding v1's brief introductory positioning.

T1.justification: v2 newly defines the weighted pose, vertex, and joint training objective in Equation 3, whereas v1 provides only the pose-space and conditional-denoiser formulation. This is a limited addition to mathematical specification. No new assumptions, theorems, or proofs appear; the added standard DDPM equations are explanatory.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important practical weakness by replacing ground-truth grasp inputs with a learned classifier and testing predicted versus oracle labels in Table 2. Broader evaluation, a fully conditioned diffusion comparator, and component ablations substantially strengthen the evidence beyond v1's small comparison. Detailed settings and prompts also improve reproducibility. Mixed HInt outcomes and component-level timing still limit generalization and efficiency claims, but the gains in practical validity and evidential support are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching title, authors, and central objective. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v2 includes readable supplementary Sections A–C.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark comparisons, ablations, computational measurements, grasp-classification results, and supplementary HInt evaluations in Tables 1–4 and the accompanying figures.

before.justification: v1 reports original HOGraspNet refinement results on 300 examples in Table 1, plus qualitative reconstruction and controlled-generation results in Figures 4–5.

results.title: Affordance-Guided Diffusion Prior for 3D Hand Reconstruction

C1.justification: v2 elevates circular synchronization into a central technical contribution and claims structurally enforced seamless generation without fine-tuning. Its abstract also explicitly broadens the generality claim to geometry, lighting, and semantics. The unified framework, PanoX dataset, and graphics-ready scene contributions remain.

C2.justification: v1 tentatively attributes seams to positional-encoding topology. v2 develops an operator-level explanation based on missing circular translation equivariance and argues that latent blending distorts features while synchronization preserves fidelity. It also interprets the new pretraining and completion comparisons. The speed, geometry, and metallic-generalization limitations are unchanged and merely relocated.

D1.justification: Reported training/evaluation hardware changes from four Ascend 910B NPUs to four NVIDIA L40S GPUs, and v2 specifies batch size per GPU. It adds an explicit project-page address but drops the Blender 4.2 version and graphics deployment detail. Core optimizer, learning rate, resolution, and adapter-count disclosures remain.

E1.justification: Generation training changes from HDR360-UHD to a mixture of Pano360, Structured3D, Poly-Haven, Humus, and PanoX, notably adding synthetic scene data to that task. v2 also introduces generation evaluation on Laval Indoor and SUN360. The existing perception targets, completion task, and graphics applications remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds generation comparisons with OmniDreamer, PanoDiffusion, Diffusion360, and CubeDiff, plus completion comparison with Flux.1-Fill. Figure 10 additionally compares seam handling against unmodified Flux.1-dev, circular blending, and latent rotation. The original intrinsic and geometry comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: New generation and completion protocols compute FID, KID, and CLIP-FID on perspective crops and FAED on ERP panoramas; generation also evaluates text alignment using CLIP Score. Generation caption extraction changes from BLIP-2 to Florence-2. Existing PanoX splits and perception metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 5 adds a from-scratch versus pretrained initialization control. Figure 10 adds qualitative seam comparisons and tests attention masking and padding size. These examine previously untested dependencies on pretrained weights and circular synchronization. Earlier camera-ray and joint material/geometry ablations survive as Tables S2-S4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, uncertainty intervals, run-level variability, or formal significance tests. The added experiments continue reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds generation scores, Structured3D albedo scores, completion scores, and ablation results. Table 2 reports OmniX/CubeDiff FID of 7.4/9.5 on Laval Indoor but 39.4/25.5 on SUN360, showing mixed rankings. Table S1 reports completion FID of 16.14 versus Flux-Fill's 30.09. Matched original PanoX scores remain unchanged apart from rounding.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 replaces v1's horizontal blending approach with training-free circular synchronization: circular convolution padding and RoPE attention with padded key/value tokens and attention masking across the DiT and VAE. This changes spatial processing during inference. The Separate-Adapter architecture and flow-matching losses are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method narrative, and experimental organization are extensively revised. Task formulations move into Appendix A, experimental settings are organized by task, the camera-ray analysis moves into the appendix, and limitations move into the conclusion. The appendices are reordered and expanded beyond simple renumbering.

P2.justification: The document adopts a different typographic layout and extensively redesigns the teaser, pipeline, qualitative comparisons, and application figures. It adds circular-operator, seam-analysis, generation-comparison, and completion-comparison displays. Tables gain benchmark columns and controls, and the geometry table groups depth-only and geometry methods.

R1.justification: v2 substantially develops positioning against latent seam manipulation and overlapping-view approaches, adding discussion and citations involving Diffusion360, PanoDiffusion, CubeDiff, RoPE, and circular-padding work. This supports a new novelty argument about intrinsic boundary consistency. Meanwhile, the broad inverse-rendering background citation list is substantially shortened.

T1.justification: The flow-matching formulation and Equations (1)-(5) are retained. Circular translation equivariance is introduced as architectural rationale, without a new mathematical definition, formal proposition, derivation, or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 supports generation and completion primarily through qualitative examples. v2 supplies quantitative baseline comparisons for both capabilities, adds Structured3D validation, and directly tests the benefit of pretraining. These additions resolve a substantial gap in evidence for the advertised unified framework. The seamlessness guarantee still lacks formal proof and generation rankings are mixed, but the stronger empirical validation represents a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OmniX and PanoX. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds quantitative generation and completion comparisons, Structured3D albedo results, and further ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original perception benchmarks, adapter and camera-ray ablations, joint-modeling experiments, and qualitative generation, completion, and simulation results.

results.title: OmniX: From Unified Panoramic Generation and Perception To Graphics-Ready 3D Scenes

C1.justification: V3 removes the introduction's explicit 'for the first time' priority assertion. The principal contributions otherwise remain: activation-outlier suppression, integer-convolution support, avoidance of additional weight outliers, and the same 12.8%/467.73% headline IS improvements.

C2.justification: V3 newly interprets its component results as showing benefits independent of distillation adjustments and learnable LSQ scales. It extends applicability arguments beyond U-Net to Transformers and interprets comparable training times as evidence of negligible Hadamard overhead. These substantially expand the earlier interpretation, which focused on low-bit gains, weight stability, and Hadamard order.

D1.justification: V3 adds single-A100 hardware information and training/calibration costs, documents the DiT sampler, and explains the convolution fallback used in DHQ-DM. These improve documentation of the added experiments, but numerical learning rates, LoRA rank, and other referenced appendix details remain unavailable.

E1.justification: ImageNet conditional generation and LSUN-Bedrooms/Churches unconditional generation remain. V3 Table 4 adds ImageNet generation at 512×512, extending the resolution requirement beyond v1's 256×256 evaluations. The additional DiT architecture is an experimental configuration change.

E2.justification: V3 adds QuEST to the LSUN-Bedrooms comparisons at W3A4 and W2A4, whereas v1 evaluated it only on ImageNet. V3 Table 6 also introduces DHQ-DM as a direct competing transformation scheme across four bit configurations, substantially strengthening comparison of the central design choice.

E3.justification: V3 introduces DiT-XL evaluation with the Improved DDPM sampler and 50 denoising steps, component controls involving fixed versus learnable scales, and quality/latency comparisons against DHQ-DM with single-Hadamard convolution layers. It also changes the weight diagnostic's layer and measurements. The existing LDM sampling counts and 50,000-image evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V3 adds component ablations separating Hadamard, LoRA, and scale-learning effects, plus direct single-versus-double transformation and efficiency analyses. Its Figure 4 replaces v1's projection-weight channel plots with attention-key weight statistics. V1's order sweep and Section 7 visual analyses are absent from the supplied v3; their possible relocation to the referenced appendix cannot be verified.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V3's new kurtosis and outlier-ratio measurements characterize weight distributions rather than experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: V3 adds DiT, component-ablation, DHQ-DM, and timing results. Existing values also change: Table 1 reports HQ-DM W4A8 IS/FID as 355.59/10.07 instead of 350.22/9.85, and EfficientDM W8A8 IS as 362.34 instead of 363.71. Table 2 changes TFMQ-DM W3A4/W2A4 FID from 25.74/25.77 to 227.64/245.85 without explaining the revisions. Previously blank baseline cells are populated; the headline W4A4/W4A3 HQ-DM results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains LoRA-based distillation, timestep-dependent quantization scales, symmetric activation quantization, and activation-only Hadamard transformations with inverse transformations before linear or convolution operations. DiT evaluation and the new ablation variants do not establish a change to HQ-DM itself.

P1.justification: The introduction and background are tightened, contribution wording is softened, and experimental discussion gains separate LDM/DiT and component/transformation headings. The principal section order and most method exposition remain intact; much of the apparent document expansion comes from layout and added experiments.

P2.justification: V3 switches from two-column to single-column formatting, redraws the overview diagram, separates the transformation schematics from the revised weight diagnostic, and adds a timing panel and several tables. Existing tables are restructured, while v1's extensive supplementary plots and image grids are not included in the supplied v3.

R1.justification: V3 adds foundational LoRA/QLoRA, DiT, and quantization/optimization references, classifies QuEST alongside QAT methods, and more explicitly acknowledges EfficientDM's distillation contribution. Broad generation and alternative-compression citations are pruned, while the central positioning against EfficientDM, QuaRot, and Xi et al. remains.

T1.justification: The diffusion, quantization, LoRA/distillation, Hadamard, and linear/convolution derivations remain mathematically equivalent. Equations are combined or renumbered and a duplicate block-diagonal definition is removed, but no substantive formal result, proof, or correction is introduced.

improvement.justification: V1's ablation only varied Hadamard order; v3 Tables 5–6 directly test component contributions and the central single-versus-double transformation choice, including latency. Together with DiT evaluation, these address substantial gaps in validating the method and its applicability. These gains outweigh the unavailable order/visual analyses, although missing appendix details and unexplained large baseline-score revisions remain important transparency weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HQ-DM work, and all supplied pages are readable. However, both reference an appendix that is absent from the files. V3 additionally refers to unavailable ablations, preventing confirmation of whether v1's Hadamard-order study and supplementary visualizations were relocated.

after.justification: V3 reports original LDM and DiT evaluations, component ablations, weight-distribution diagnostics, and training-time and inference-latency measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original LDM quantization results on ImageNet and LSUN, a Hadamard-order ablation, training-loss curves, and activation and generated-image analyses.

results.title: HQ-DM: Single Hadamard Transformation-Based Quantization-Aware Training for Low-Bit Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract narrows its diagnosis of earlier approaches from lacking explicit geometry to lacking a persistent, explicit geometric representation. The principal contributions—mesh-guided multi-room synthesis, robust consistency, and linear scaling with room count—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 adds specific attribution of consistency gains to mesh initialization and depth loss, with smaller contributions from validation. Appendix F interprets backbone comparisons as supporting scaffold-driven gains and connectivity as supporting traversability. These refine the existing explanation; the single-story and occluded-object limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies arc-length camera spacing and 10-degree pruning, Canny thresholds of 0.1/0.3 with a 3×3 Sobel aperture, and the distilled Flux2-klein-9B configuration with four sampling steps. It also documents parallel API generation versus sequential local execution and associated timing. Interactive SAM3 annotation was already disclosed in v1 Appendix C.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate text-guided, single-story, multi-room indoor scene generation across varied layouts, themes, and viewpoints. The separate five-scene evaluation, room-count measurements, and occupancy analysis extend assessment within this coverage; they do not establish a new domain or distinct generation task.

E2.justification: The six end-to-end baselines in Table 1 and Figure 3 are unchanged. New Table A2 adds component-level comparisons of Haiku 4.5, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, and gpt-oss-20b against the original Opus 4.6 layout backend. Table A1 evaluates three retained scene-generation baselines on the additional evaluation set.

E3.justification: v3 adds a separate five-scene evaluation using scale-normalized cross-view depth MAE, AbsRel, and scaffold depth/normal alignment. It also introduces a 0.15 m occupancy-grid connectivity protocol, scaling measurements at 4–12 rooms, and alternative image/layout-model configurations. The original 31-participant protocol remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 2 extends conditioning ablations with tests removing edge-recall validation, mesh-based 3DGS initialization, depth loss, and initialization plus depth loss together. Automatic ablation evaluation now spans five scenes. Appendix F additionally examines backbone dependence, layout-backend behavior, scaling cost, and free-space connectivity.

E5.justification: Table A2 newly specifies 10 runs with varying scene sizes for mean layout-correction iterations and timing. This is newly reported run information, not evidence of increased repetitions for retained experiments. Neither version supplies confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the perceptual ablation ratings are unchanged. New Table A1 reports reprojection MAE-norm of 0.1615 for NB Pro, 0.2173 for local Flux2-klein, and 0.3221 for WorldExplorer; Table 2 reports 1.8804 after removing both mesh initialization and depth loss. Appendix F adds timing, layout-generation, and 96.7% average connectivity results. Earlier single-scene automatic ablation scores are replaced by five-scene results, so their numerical differences are not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The scaffold construction, object reconstruction, iterative appearance synthesis, edge verification, and depth-regularized 3DGS procedure remain intact. v3 clarifies joint wall-texture accumulation and interactive segmentation, both already supported by v1 Section 3.3 and Appendix C. The alternative backbones instantiate the existing pipeline.

P1.justification: v3 makes targeted revisions to the wall-texturing explanation, metrics paragraph, ablation discussion, and conclusion, and adds Appendix F. Terminology, grammar, author-contact information, and cross-references are refined. The overall narrative and section organization remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: Table 2 is substantially redesigned into separate automatic and perceptual panels, while Tables A1–A3 and the occupancy visualization in Figure A5 add new displays. Figure 2 corrects its example prompt, Table 1 moves, and Figure A4 is reduced and relocated beside the study description. The original qualitative result images are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for Haiku 4.5, Qwen2.5-Coder, and gpt-oss, and acknowledges that recent video models incorporate camera or point-cloud geometric priors. The broader research positioning remains intact; numerous venue and bibliographic updates concern the same previously cited works.

T1.justification: The quaternion similarity, depth-edge recall, projection expressions, and 3DGS loss remain unchanged. v3 adds empirical evaluation measures but no new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its central consistency and scalability claims mainly through image-quality scores, perceptual judgments, and conditioning ablations. v3 adds direct geometric measurements across five scenes, targeted reconstruction ablations, alternative-backbone tests, and measured scaling and connectivity. Table 2 and Appendix F therefore address substantial validation gaps while retaining the original comparisons. Metric implementation details and uncertainty reporting remain limited, but the added evidence materially strengthens the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WorldMesh, with matching authors, core method, and original experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison. v3 retains Appendices A–E and adds Appendix F.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds quantitative 3D-consistency evaluations, component and backbone comparisons, layout-generation measurements, scaling results, and navigability analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original generated scenes, baseline comparisons, conditioning ablations, automatic image-quality scores, and a perceptual study with 31 participants.

results.title: WorldMesh: Generating Navigable Multi-Room 3D Scenes via Mesh-Conditioned Image Diffusion

C1.justification: Exact extraction, expressive SDF learning and encoder-specific preconditioning remain the central claims. v2 explicitly elevates tensorized GPU construction to a contribution and qualifies the conclusion from surpassing grid-based encoders to matching or surpassing them, consistent with the existing abstract.

C2.justification: New discussions explain the six-tetrahedron design relative to five- and twelve-tetrahedron alternatives, why the preconditioner does not benefit HashGrid, and the tradeoff between exact field agreement and triangle regularity. v2 also interprets capacity and adaptive-extraction results and identifies downstream editing limitations absent from v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page link and identifies publicly released baseline implementations, CGAL implementations for sampling-based extractors, and McGrids' official defaults. These are additional access and implementation disclosures; the existing training and hardware details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate SDF learning and isosurface extraction on the same Stanford shapes, 100 ABC meshes and 500 closed Thingi10K meshes. The added metrics, model configurations and extraction algorithms do not introduce new data domains or task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 Appendix A.5.3/Table A4 adds evaluated comparisons against octree Marching Cubes, octree Dual Contouring and McGrids. Original comparators remain. The MC256-to-MT256 correction in v1 Table 6/v2 Table 5 fixes a mislabeled existing row rather than adding a comparator.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include SDF MAE at one million ground-truth surface samples, AM configurations with 15/150 and 20/200 hidden-layer/width settings, adaptive extraction from the same Large network, and the fraction of faces with minimum angle below 5 degrees. Existing training settings and original evaluation protocols are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds analysis separating field fitting from extraction error, AM capacity/runtime sensitivity, a depth-12 octree failure case, and triangle-regularity assessment. Existing preconditioner ablations and resolution studies remain; the original runtime breakdown and Dragon comparison are relocated, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, standard errors or significance tests. The added averages across shapes do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Original numerical results are retained, but substantial new results appear in Table 3 and Tables A3–A5. For example, Large/Stanford SDF MAE is 0.62 for TetraSDF versus 0.53 for HashGrid, in units of 10^-3. Newly reported skinny-face fractions are 11.83% for TetraSDF, 10.05% for AM and 10.94% for TropicalNeRF.

M1.justification: The tetrahedral encoder, input preconditioner, skeleton construction, region tracking, edge subdivision and face extraction remain unchanged. The new grid-design discussion and Algorithm 1 explain existing choices rather than introduce a different procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introductory motivation and conclusion receive targeted revisions; related-work subsections and experimental material are reordered. Appendix A.7 adds explanatory notation and pseudocode. Most method and proof exposition remains intact, so the language changes are limited rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column to single-column formatting, with extensive rearrangement of tables and figures. v2 adds a conceptual extraction schematic, four result tables and an algorithm display, revises overview annotations, and relocates the runtime table. Existing qualitative image content is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to CGAL, power-diagram isosurfacing, McGrids, Reach for the Spheres, Flexible Isosurface Extraction and Marching Neurons. Related work expands its discussion of finite-sample and adaptive extraction while retaining the original positioning around exact CPWA extraction.

T1.justification: Appendix A.6.2 adds a mathematical argument that HashGrid's cube-average interpolation metric is proportional to the identity, so volume-preserving isotropization admits the identity preconditioner. Existing affine-interpolation and convexity proofs, and the tetrahedral preconditioner derivation, are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps: Table 3 separates field accuracy from extraction error, while Tables A3–A4 test larger AM networks and adaptive extractors missing from v1. The quantified triangle-regularity limitation makes applicability clearer without representing a deterioration of the method. Together these additions substantially strengthen evidence and transparency, although adaptive-extractor settings remain sparsely documented.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TetraSDF, despite the revised subtitle and formatting. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds original field-accuracy, baseline-capacity, adaptive-extraction and triangle-quality results.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction, self-consistency, preconditioning and runtime experiments on Stanford, ABC and Thingi10K, with additional qualitative results in the appendix.

results.title: TetraSDF: Analytic Isosurface Extraction with Multi-resolution Tetrahedral Grid

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: RL-based scene editing using VGGT verification, preserved editing quality, generalization, backbone transfer and over 2× speedup. The new title and supporting evidence do not redefine those central claims.

C2.justification: Section 5 and S4.3 newly acknowledge failure under drastic non-rigid deformations such as bowing the head. v2 also explains using VIEScore alongside blur-sensitive Ph-Loss and interprets the added anchor, denoising and reward-weight comparisons. The central explanation of VGGT's resistance to reward hacking is retained.

D1.justification: The supplement supplies substantial missing implementation and evaluation information: AnySplat initialization, 3,000-step 3DGS refinement, adapted EditSplat guidance, metric/reward computation, scene-specific prompt lists and a 25-participant video-preference protocol. These largely document previously referenced procedures. The promise to release code and models remains unchanged.

E1.justification: The scene-editing datasets and GEdit-Bench-EN evaluation are retained, as are eight training scenes, 70 prompts and the 100-case evaluation partition. Tables S1–S3 identify previously described scenes and instructions. Additional examples and view-count handling remain within the existing editing coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains DGE, GaussCtrl, EditSplat and EditSplat with FLUX-Kontext; Table S4 reports the same comparator set by split. Table 2 retains the alternative verifiers and Qwen-Image-Edit variant. Section S2.4 explains the existing adapted EditSplat baseline rather than introducing another comparator.

E3.justification: The main split, metrics and default training configuration remain unchanged. Reported training and timing hardware changes from RTX A6000 to RTX Pro 6000, without establishing reruns. Table S5 adds fixed-anchor, 6/20-step and unequal-reward-weight controls within the retained face-scene protocol; S4.2 also describes four-view input handling.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component and verifier ablations, Table S5 quantitatively tests anchor selection, denoising-step count and reward-weight balance. Figure S2 adds confidence-map evidence for blurry, distorted and high-quality inputs. These additions substantially expand validation of design choices and verifier behavior.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added user-study percentages also lack uncertainty estimates. VGGT confidence maps and GRPO candidate-group sizes concern the algorithm rather than statistical uncertainty in reported performance.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 retain their numerical entries. Newly supplied Table S4 reports RL3DEdit VIEScores of 5.52/5.40 and user preferences of 71.4%/60.0% for in-distribution/zero-shot cases. Table S5 adds design-variant outcomes, including fixed-anchor VIEScore 4.54 versus random-anchor 5.26. Figures S1–S2 add qualitative evidence; these are additional results, not cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The FLUX-Kontext editor, GRPO optimization and four reward components remain unchanged. Section S4.2 adds a limited inference adaptation that duplicates fewer views, exemplified by four, into nine input slots. The newly specified AnySplat initialization and 3DGS refinement otherwise document the previously described reconstruction stage rather than establish its replacement.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, its running headers change, and localized prose and caption wording are refined. Keywords, acknowledgements and an indexed supplement are added. The main six-section narrative and most existing paragraphs remain intact rather than undergoing extensive rewriting or reorganization.

P2.justification: Tables S1–S5 and Figures S1–S2 substantially expand visual documentation of instructions, split results, ablations and verifier behavior. Main figures are largely retained, with Figure 6 relocated and some captions and diagram labels revised. The major change comes from the added displays rather than pagination alone.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including AnySplat, standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, InsertNeRF and Thinking with Camera, alongside other background references. The related-work taxonomy, comparisons with existing editing paradigms and claimed first application of RL to 3D editing remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Sections S2.1–S2.2 supply previously deferred formal definitions, including the flow-to-SDE equation, clipped GRPO surrogate and SfM reward. The main reward equations remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is introduced. The standard CLIP metric formula is explanatory rather than a theoretical contribution.

improvement.justification: v1 defers essential reconstruction, baseline and dataset information to an absent appendix. v2 supplies that material and adds controlled ablations, split-specific results and user preferences, substantially improving reproducibility and empirical support without changing headline scores. The explicit deformation limitation also clarifies applicability. The unexplained GPU revision and continued absence of statistical uncertainty remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both readable PDFs describe RL3DEdit, with matching core methods, experiments and main results despite the changed title. v1 ends after its references despite referring to an appendix; v2 includes supplementary Sections S1–S5. These support comparison of newly documented material without establishing when the underlying experiments were performed.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and additionally reports split-specific scores, user preferences, further ablations and qualitative analyses in its supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original scene-editing comparisons, reward ablations, backbone evaluations and VGGT confidence analysis in Tables 1–2 and Figures 3–8.

results.title: Edit in 2D, Verify in 3D: Reinforcement Learning for Multi-view Consistent Scene Editing

C1.justification: V2 reframes the contributions around systematic failure of existing Gaussian methods, a transient-flame formulation, and a combined appearance/depth/motion/video evaluation protocol. The introduction makes broader claims about existing methods being unable to reconstruct fire reliably. The abstract extends validation to simulated fire, and the conclusion emphasizes improved motion alignment and depth consistency.

C2.justification: V2 adds a causal account involving persistent primitives, geometric absorption, depth collapse and temporal drift, plus interpretations of masking and joint optimization as physical-versus-visual tradeoffs. Appendix B newly argues that explicit shutter modeling is unnecessary at the tested motion speeds. The main limitations remain largely unchanged. One new interpretation is inconsistent: page 9 says separating optimization improves simulation performance, whereas Table 2 slightly favors JointOpt.

D1.justification: V2 substantially revises implementation documentation, adding alpha-loss rendering details, scale constraints, camera orientation, simulation construction, and the unofficial FreeTimeGS implementation and initialization procedure. V1's background-sphere initialization and Yang baseline Gaussian-cap/checkpoint-selection descriptions disappear, without establishing that those settings were changed. Appendix I replaces bundled-example and future-release directions with an official repository link. Hardware and the proposed method's training budgets remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 retains the 17 real-world fire scenes and adds synthetic fire reconstruction in the classroom, junkshop and monk environments. These Mantaflow/Blender scenes introduce a simulated domain with known volumetric velocities, substantially extending coverage beyond real videos with estimated depth.

E2.justification: The real-world comparison expands from the Wu and Yang 4DGS methods to include Grid4D and FreeTimeGS (Table 1). FreeTimeGS was already cited as a methodological foundation in v1, but was not an evaluated comparator. All four baselines also participate in the new motion and video-quality comparisons.

E3.justification: The two 4DGS baselines change from reported random initialization to COLMAP initialization. V2 introduces density-weighted volumetric evaluation and full-video CGVQM with soft masking of synchronization hardware. Synthetic evaluation uses 50 frames per camera over two seconds and 640-cubed velocity grids. NoSync changes from v1's one-frame or up-to-one-frame offsets to half-frame offsets; the real-data every-eighth-frame holdout remains unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds the NoMask ablation, evaluates component effects on simulated motion, and introduces a RoMa matching-failure analysis (Figure 12). It removes the quantitative GlobalShutter ablation and detailed per-scene ablation tables, although Appendix B retains the finding that explicit shutter handling did not improve image metrics. These changes substantially revise the evidence about component roles and failure mechanisms.

E5.justification: V1 explicitly identifies Table 1 entries as means and standard deviations across scenes. V2 retains the plus-or-minus format but omits that explicit definition, including for its new motion and video metrics. Neither version documents repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or formal significance tests; additional result rows do not establish additional runs.

E6.justification: Real-world results are extensively replaced: the proposed method's flame PSNR changes from 27.46 to 26.93, full-image PSNR from 33.61 to 35.89, and depth RMSE from 0.0412 to 0.094. The full-image ranking changes from Yang 4DGS leading to the proposed method leading. Settings also change, preventing interpretation as controlled performance gains. New results include motion cosine similarity of 0.744 and CGVQM of 86.1; per-scene baseline and ablation results are removed.

M1.justification: The two-stage, flow-initialized Gaussian model retains its lifetime and constant-velocity equations. V2 adds a motion-mask opacity loss weighted by 0.1 and bounds dynamic Gaussian scales using a voxel-scaled sigmoid (Section 3.2; Appendix H). Rolling-shutter modeling is presented as an optional extension. These refine the existing procedure rather than replace its core representation.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten, with substantial revisions to results interpretation and methodological explanations. Rolling-shutter treatment moves from the main methodology to Appendix B. The supplement is reorganized from Sections 8–14 into thematic Appendices A–J, with reordered dataset, implementation, visualization and resource sections.

P2.justification: Comparison figures are redesigned for four baselines, and new motion visualizations, synthetic-scene montages and a RoMa matching illustration are added. Existing fire-removal and capture-setup images move to the appendix. Real-world comparisons and ablations merge into a color-highlighted table, with new motion and video tables. Six per-scene baseline/ablation tables and the rolling-shutter illustration are removed; retained dataset and per-scene tables are reformatted.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts from a FreeTimeGS-based reconstruction pipeline toward a transient-Gaussian formulation claimed to overcome general failures of existing Gaussian representations. V2 also introduces an efficiency-based rationale for excluding non-Gaussian comparisons. It adds references to RoMa, Grid4D, CGVQM+D and MotionGS and removes R3D3; the broad related-work survey is otherwise largely retained.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.4 adds mathematical definitions for density-weighted motion comparison: opacity-volume weights, expected ground-truth velocities approximated by Gauss-Hermite quadrature, and weighted relative L2 and cosine scores. It also removes duplicated depth-loss weighting from the displayed formulation. Existing flow-reconstruction and rolling-shutter derivations are substantially retained; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central motion-reconstruction claim. V1 relied on image metrics, monocular-depth proxies and qualitative evidence; v2 adds direct comparison with simulated ground-truth velocities, video-quality evaluation and two additional baselines with better-documented initialization. This addresses an important evidential gap rather than merely increasing reported performance. The gains outweigh the loss of detailed per-scene comparisons, less explicit uncertainty labeling, and remaining weaknesses in the broad baseline-failure claims and contradictory JointOpt interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Gaussians on Fire and contain readable main texts, equations, figures, tables and supplementary material. Content can be matched across the substantial reorganization, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original real-world reconstruction experiments, adds three simulated fire scenes with ground-truth velocity evaluation, and reports video-quality results.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction experiments on 17 captured fire scenes, including baseline comparisons, component ablations and per-scene results.

results.title: Gaussians on Fire: High-Frequency Reconstruction of Flames

C1.justification: The abstract replaces the blanket statement that Wid3R consistently outperforms prior methods with metric- and dataset-specific gains, and explicitly claims benefits from diverse-camera conditioning under sparse 360-degree supervision. The contribution bullets clarify multi-view novelty. The central reconstruction contributions and conclusion remain intact.

C2.justification: The supplement explains the attention choice through degradation with angular-radial cross-attention, expands the efficiency and calibration arguments against cubemap preprocessing, and proposes geometric guidance for scene generation while acknowledging that integration remains future work. The existing limitation concerning dynamic scenes is unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands reproducibility information with dataset counts, uniform dataset sampling, softmin pseudocode, token/attention wiring, and a project-page link. However, Table 4 replaces exact localization scene identifiers with generic labels. Supplementary Table 1 also implies approximately 4.1% spherical training images, conflicting with the retained main-text claim of less than 1%.

E1.justification: The training datasets and established evaluation benchmarks remain unchanged. Supplementary Section 1 and Figure 1 add a qualitative reconstruction test on synthesized images from panorama-based scene generation, extending the input domain without demonstrating an integrated generation system.

E2.justification: Tables 2, 3, and 5 add Ours (π3), fine-tuned on the paper's training data, substantially strengthening the central comparisons. Supplementary Figure 4 adds cubemap-to-π3 inference. Main Figure 4 removes SPSG+COLMAP from its qualitative comparison, although Table 4 retains it.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce a training-data-matched π3 control, attention variants, and a cubemap procedure converting 37 spherical images into 222 perspective images. Existing benchmark splits, metrics, image resolution, and alignment procedures remain unchanged. Supplementary dataset counts disclose settings rather than establish changed sample sizes.

E4.justification: V2 adds substantial tests of the architectural rationale: fine-tuned π3 examines benefits beyond training-data adaptation, and supplementary Table 3 compares cross-attention with self-attention. Cubemap reconstruction, predicted-ray visualizations, and additional reconstruction cases expand diagnostic evidence. The original Table 7 ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Table 7 retains the same standard-deviation reporting, and Stanford2D3D retains ten sampling repetitions per scene and twenty cases. No new seed information, repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: Existing main-table scores are retained, but substantial new results alter comparative rankings. In Table 2, fine-tuned π3 achieves FIORD AUC@30 of 72.56 versus Wid3R's 68.20, while Stanford2D3D scores are 62.14 versus 79.93. Supplementary Table 3 adds attention results, including Stanford2D3D mean accuracy error of 0.273 for cross-attention versus 0.197 for self-attention, alongside new qualitative findings.

M1.justification: The ray-based angular/radial architecture, camera tokens, pose prediction, and training losses remain unchanged. Supplementary Sections 3–5 disclose sampling and attention details, including radial self-attention; they do not establish a revision of v1's implemented method.

P1.justification: The abstract and selected introductory and related-work paragraphs are rewritten, method subsection titles are refined, and a separately organized supplement expands explanations. The main method–experiments–conclusion structure and much of its prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The supplement adds architecture, ray, generation, and cubemap diagrams, data and attention tables, pseudocode, and extensive qualitative panels. Main Table 1 is redesigned around distortion awareness, Figure 4 is redrawn with fewer comparator columns, and Tables 2, 3, and 5 accommodate the additional baseline.

R1.justification: V2 adds Depth Anything 3 and MapAnything to the ray-representation discussion, clarifies distinctions from calibration-token methods and UniK3D, and cites panorama/world-generation work for the supplementary application. These extend the context while retaining the central positioning around distortion-aware multi-view reconstruction.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations 1–12 remain unchanged. Supplementary sampling pseudocode elaborates the existing proximity-based sampler; no new theorem, proof, substantive derivation, or formal assumption is introduced.

improvement.justification: The training-data-matched π3 comparison addresses an important weakness in v1: separating architectural benefits from adaptation to wide-angle training data. Together with the attention ablation and detailed sampling/architecture disclosures, it substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility, including revealing FIORD exceptions to Wid3R's advantage. Lost localization scene identifiers and inconsistent spherical-data counts are reporting regressions, but their localized impact is outweighed by these substantive evidentiary gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Wid3R and provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures. V1 ends after its references; v2 adds a seven-page supplement. The supplied material supports comparison throughout.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds fine-tuned baseline results, an attention ablation, and qualitative cubemap and synthesized-scene evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original pose, localization, point-map, and monocular-depth experiments, plus training-data and camera-token ablations in Tables 2–7.

results.title: Wid3R: Wide Field-of-View 3D Reconstruction via Camera Model Conditioning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same three contributions: the large dataset, systematic ten-method benchmark and DI2FIX enhancement application. The claimed average improvements remain 0.96 dB PSNR and 0.057 LPIPS; additional supporting evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds the interpretation that distractor-removal benefits generally outweigh damage to view-dependent static appearance, and explains the complementary roles of natural long-tail data and the curated subset. Existing severe-corruption and confirmation-bias limitations receive fuller mechanism explanations. Its broad interpretation of ranking significance needs qualification given the large p-values for some pairs.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset and leaderboard access information, licensing, directory structure and annotation guidance. It also discloses 8× downsampling, configuration and instability-handling policies, and DI2FIX loss settings, batch size 1, two L40 GPUs and approximately 3–4 days of training. These substantially improve reproducibility documentation without establishing reruns.

E1.justification: Both use RobustNeRF, On-the-go, DF3DV-1K and DF3DV-41, retaining the same 1,048 scenes and 17 challenging scenarios. The added masked-region diagnostic selects existing DF3DV-41 scenes. Changes to the dataset catalogues in Tables 1–2 do not change evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: Table 3 retains 3DGS and the same nine distractor-free methods, including both T-3DGS variants. The enhancer comparison retains Vanilla, DIFIX, DIFIX+RobustNeRF and DI2FIX. Supplementary comparisons use these existing methods without introducing a new comparator.

E3.justification: Section S.2 adds a diagnostic evaluation using three images from each of 18 DF3DV-41 scenes, with human-annotated masks targeting view-dependent static regions. Preprocessing, configuration and cross-method training details disclosed elsewhere in the supplement do not establish changes to the existing experiments.

E4.justification: v2 supplies detailed scenario analyses, the complete cross-method ablation matrix and extensive qualitative and failure examples, substantially expanding inspectable evidence for analyses summarized or cited in v1. It also adds the distinct investigation of distractor removal versus preservation of view-dependent static objects in Table S.5 and Figure S.7.

E5.justification: v2 introduces paired t-tests across scenes for the top four methods on PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS, with p-values in Table S.1; v1 reports no corresponding statistical analysis. This adds substantial inferential reporting, without documenting increased runs or seeds. Table S.7 mentions error bars but supplies no uncertainty intervals.

E6.justification: Numerical results in Tables 3–6 remain unchanged. v2 adds substantial scenario-level, per-method enhancement and cross-method result entries. The new masked-region study reports, for example, 23.19 dB PSNR for AsymGS versus 21.35 dB for 3DGS in Table S.5; these are additional diagnostic results, not performance changes between versions.

M1.justification: Both versions describe the same DIFIX adaptation using rendered reference views and LPIPS-filtered training pairs. Section S.3 newly discloses disabling the Gram-matrix loss, but presents this as a detail of the existing adaptation; it does not establish a procedural revision from v1.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain largely intact, with localized wording, caption and cross-reference edits. v2 updates author contribution markings, adds acknowledgements and organizes supplementary explanations into Sections S.1–S.4. The added scientific material does not entail extensive rewriting of the main argument.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands visual presentation through Tables S.1–S.7 and Figures S.1–S.19, including significance displays, scenario matrices, comparison galleries, failure examples and distribution charts. Some panels repeat existing main-text examples. Tables 1–2 are also reorganized, while the main experimental displays are largely retained.

R1.justification: Six references are added, including OpenCV, Gram-matrix style-transfer, view-selection and clustering work. Tables 1–2 revise dataset descriptions and classify RealX3D and D-RE10K-iPhone as public. The central positioning around large-scale casual-capture benchmarking remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version presents substantive theoretical propositions, proofs or derivations. The LPIPS filtering condition is retained, and the supplement adds no new formal mathematical framework.

improvement.justification: v1 repeatedly cites supplementary evidence and experimental details absent from its PDF. v2 supplies that material, adds practical access and implementation information, and makes robustness and generalization claims substantially easier to assess. The static-region diagnostic and statistical comparisons provide useful additional scrutiny. Some significance wording overreaches the evidence, such as the RobustSplat–DeGauss SSIM comparison with p=0.82, but this limited weakness does not outweigh the substantial gains in completeness and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable and describe the same DF3DV-1K dataset, benchmark and DI2FIX enhancer. v1 ends after its references despite citing supplementary items; v2 includes Sections S.1–S.4. Their reported content can be compared reliably, without assuming what unseen earlier supplementary material contained.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and supplies detailed supplementary results, paired significance tests and a view-dependent-static-object evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of ten radiance-field methods in Table 3 and DI2FIX enhancement and ablation results in Tables 4–6.

results.title: DF3DV-1K: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Distractor-Free Novel View Synthesis

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes modularity, dual APIs, preservation of the original 3DGS algorithm, 3.4x acceleration and approximately 30% lower memory use. v2 replaces this emphasis with system-and-algorithm codesign, parameter efficiency, up to 13.4x acceleration and state-of-the-art reconstruction quality. The title additionally introduces a subminute-training claim.

C2.justification: v2 introduces substantive explanations distinguishing unconverged regions from under-reconstructed regions through gradient variance, and explains opacity decay as reducing reset instability. It discusses register-pressure tradeoffs, attributes weaker lightweight LPIPS to lost high-frequency detail, and identifies Morton sorting's neglect of primitive size and anisotropy as a limitation. v1's attribution of Adam acceleration primarily to fusion disappears.

D1.justification: v2 adds detailed FP16/half2 choices, integer warp-reduction steps, Morton quantization and sorting instructions, four-pixels-per-thread configuration, and explicit densification and opacity schedules. v1's dual-API/autograd documentation and disclosure of adjusted SfM processing are absent. Both versions retain the same code repository URL.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates reconstruction only on Mip-NeRF 360. v2 retains that dataset and adds actual evaluations on Tanks & Temples and Deep Blending, substantially broadening scene coverage.

E2.justification: v1 compares training times against 3DGS and its TamingGS-integrated variant, but reconstruction quality only against 3DGS. v2 Table 1 adds Mini-Splatting, Mini-Splatting v2, 3DGS-MCMC and SSS, and includes TamingGS variants in quality comparisons. Table 3 additionally evaluates the TC-GS tensor-core rasterizer.

E3.justification: v1 reports A100 and RTX3090 experiments; v2 uses RTX3090 only and introduces turbo, balance and quality model-budget regimes. These use 18K or 30K iterations, with a 40K Tanks & Temples comparison matching SSS. New rasterizer comparisons control Garden primitive counts at 500K, 2000K and 5728K.

E4.justification: v1's warp-stall profiling, cache-hit curves, patch-count analysis and tile-size comparison are no longer reported. v2 adds culling ablations measuring end-to-end time and quality, controlled rasterizer comparisons, and separate removal of opacity decay and the variance criterion, including their joint removal (Tables 2–4). These substantially change the component-level evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v2's opacity-gradient variance is an algorithmic criterion, not uncertainty reporting for experimental results.

E6.justification: v1's per-scene quality scores and two-GPU training times are replaced by dataset-level results for multiple budgets, with additional primitive counts and ablation outcomes. For example, v2 Table 1 reports Mip-NeRF 360 PSNR/time of 27.70 dB/145 s for turbo and 28.25 dB/515 s for quality. These are new results under revised settings, not established same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: v2 introduces a one-warp-per-tile rasterizer with scanline computation, mixed precision and integer-based reduction, substantially revising v1's shared-memory multibatch reduction. It also introduces opacity-gradient-variance densification and opacity decay. Morton-based clustering, culling and compaction are retained, rather than newly introduced.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method and evaluation are extensively rewritten. v1's separate Motivation section is absorbed into the new narrative, and v2 introduces contribution bullets, dedicated ablation discussion and a conclusion. The title, author list and terminology also change.

P2.justification: The layout changes from single-column to two-column. v1's positioning schematic and profiling charts are replaced by paired quality–budget/time plots and a pipeline illustration. Results are reorganized into a multidataset comparison and component-analysis tables, and the two original pseudocode displays are replaced by a scanline algorithm.

R1.justification: The research positioning shifts from a modular library supporting diverse 3DGS extensions toward acceleration and densification. v2 adds substantial discussion of error-guided and color-guided densification, Mini-Splatting, TC-GS and other acceleration approaches, while removing much of v1's blur, dynamic-scene, anti-aliasing and gsplat-usability discussion.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's compositing equation, v2 adds a scanline quadratic decomposition, explicit gradient formulation, and the new densification definition C_i times Var = S_i minus M_i squared divided by C_i. These substantially expand the mathematical specification of the method. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited validation: Tables 1–4 compare speed, quality and model size against broader alternatives and test component contributions across three datasets. This provides much stronger evidence for the framework's effectiveness. These gains outweigh the loss of A100 results and detailed profiling, although reporting weaknesses remain: Table 1's caption gives 0.780 SSIM where Table 2 gives 0.870 for the corresponding setting, and the subminute title is unsupported by the reported 108–145 s turbo training times.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LiteGS, with a shared framework and substantial revisions. All pages, equations, tables, algorithms and figures are readable and support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction and timing results across three datasets, model-budget comparisons, rasterizer benchmarks and component ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original Mip-NeRF 360 training-time and reconstruction-quality results, GPU profiling, and cache and tile-size analyses.

results.title: LiteGS: a high-performance framework to train 3dgs in subminutes via system and algorithm codesign

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: training-free generate-then-compose synthesis, two-stage collision-aware composition, an interactive dataset exceeding 8,000 examples, and VLM-based geometric refinement. Expanded evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of the ablations concerning ICP local minima, SDF collision control and agentic corrections, and discusses MIDI's generalization limitations. It also asserts robustness to the retained hyperparameters. Existing limitations involving fine-grained geometry, symmetry and unreliable 2D-derived spatial priors remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies inference on one NVIDIA H200 and describes nine dataset categories and approximately 10,000 candidate scenes. The abstract associates the dataset with the planned code repository. Conversely, v1's explicit 4K image-resolution specification disappears; this does not establish that the actual resolution changed.

E1.justification: Both versions cover everyday-object pairwise and multi-object composition and describe approximately 8,300 compositional scenes. The additional test cases enlarge the sample within retained coverage; the newly listed nine categories document the existing collection rather than establish a new dataset or task.

E2.justification: v2 adds MIDI to Table 2 and both qualitative comparison panels, introducing an image-conditioned scene-generation comparator. New Table 3 also evaluates ICP-only, RANSAC+ICP and GeoTransformer-only registration alternatives. Jigsaw, 2BY2, PartField and PartField+RANSAC remain represented.

E3.justification: Section 5.3 expands quantitative evaluation from 10 to 150 cases and adds human and Qwen3 assessments on a 1-to-10 scale. Appendix A.2 introduces registration-variant and refinement comparisons on 150 cases. The existing CLIP and intersection metrics, including one million Monte Carlo samples, are retained.

E4.justification: Unlike v1's illustrative refinement and failure examples, v2 adds quantitative ablations examining registration alternatives and the agentic loop in Appendix A.2/Table 3. Figure 7 also adds categorized failure analysis covering reconstruction holes, symmetry ambiguity and collision-induced divergence. Earlier case studies remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and averages without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The Monte Carlo intersection-estimation procedure is unchanged; additional averages and failure counts do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces the 10-case aggregates with 150-case aggregates: Interact3D image CLIP changes from 0.8248 to 0.8236 and volume intersection, in units of 10^-3, from 3.2467 to 3.8762. These are different-sample results, not demonstrated performance regressions. New results include MIDI, human/VLM ratings of 8.33/8.57 for Interact3D, Table 3 ablations, and Figure 7's 2 reconstruction-hole, 11 symmetry and 16 collision-divergence failures.

M1.justification: The generation and segmentation workflow, OBB/GeoTransformer/ICP alignment, SDF collision optimization, and VLM-driven regeneration loop remain unchanged. The new ablations evaluate existing components rather than introduce a revised method.

P1.justification: v2 corrects spelling and grammar, revises several experimental paragraphs, updates affiliation information and keywords, and inserts an ablation subsection in Appendix A. The main section sequence and most explanatory prose remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: The empirical displays are substantially expanded: Table 2 gains a MIDI column and two rating rows, Table 3 is added, and Figure 7 becomes a 140-case success/failure montage. Both qualitative comparison panels gain generated-image and MIDI columns. Earlier five-case examples remain represented in Figure 10, while existing workflow, failure and multi-view figures are resized or relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to MIDI, CAST, 3D-FRONT and CLIP, and sharpens its contrast with data-dependent feed-forward scene generation. The broader related-work organization and existing research positioning remain intact; CAST is cited rather than evaluated.

T1.justification: The task definitions, similarity-registration objective, SDF objective and intersection definitions in Equations (1)-(5) retain their mathematical substance. Equation (2) receives a parenthesis cleanup, but no new assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs appear.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support rests on ten quantitative cases without component ablations. v2 substantially strengthens that support through 150-case comparisons, an image-conditioned generation baseline, registration and agentic-refinement tests, and explicit failure reporting. Human-rating procedures remain underspecified, uncertainty estimates are absent, and Table 3 does not cleanly isolate SDF removal. Nevertheless, the broader comparative and diagnostic evidence resolves important weaknesses in the earlier evaluation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Interact3D and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices. Renumbered and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 reports original comparisons on 150 cases, human and VLM ratings, quantitative ablations in Table 3, and additional generated results and categorized failures.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative comparisons on 10 cases in Table 2, alongside generated compositions, refinement examples and failure cases.

results.title: Interact3D: Compositional 3D Generation of Interactive Objects

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a DINO-informed design applicable to implicit and explicit RGB-D SLAM. V2 makes overcoming DINO's missing geometry awareness the explicit abstract-level rationale, replacing the broader hierarchy and structural-relationship framing. It also expands the stated compatibility from 3D Gaussians to include 2D Gaussian surfels.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the new concatenation control as evidence that simply adding depth is insufficient, acknowledges vulnerability to depth noise while claiming partial robustness, and explicitly discusses the accuracy-versus-speed tradeoff against ESLAM. Its TUM discussion qualifies superiority as an average result rather than success on every sequence. The earlier interpretation supporting global bundle adjustment is removed.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies that the feature backbone is frozen, SGE is optimized online, and NeRF keyframes use k=4. It changes the reported GPU and adds a project-page link and computational breakdown. Loss weights, tri-plane resolutions and GS keyframe thresholds are retained. The PDFs alone do not establish code availability through the new link.

E1.justification: The eight Replica scenes, six ScanNet sequences and three TUM sequences remain the benchmark coverage. V2 adds a distinct corrupted-depth input scenario on Replica office1 in Table 4. Adding 2D-surface representations changes the evaluated models, not the underlying task coverage.

E2.justification: The actual comparator sets expand substantially. V2's main Replica comparison adds HS-SLAM, Mamba-SLAM, SNH-SLAM, QQ-SLAM and SNI-SLAM, plus numerous GS methods including GauS-SLAM, SEGS-SLAM and VSS-SLAM. SNI-SLAM previously appeared only in the generality study. Gaussian-SLAM is removed from the ScanNet and TUM comparisons while remaining in Replica.

E3.justification: Standard benchmark scene counts and metrics remain unchanged. The GS component study moves from ScanNet to Replica with GauS-SLAM, and new experiments specify Gaussian depth noise with mean 0 and standard deviation 0.1 and stage-level profiling. Reported hardware changes from A100 to RTX 3090Ti; this does not establish which existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a DINO-plus-depth concatenation control, extends the generality study to GauS-SLAM, tests depth-noise robustness, and provides detailed computational overhead and memory analyses. The earlier GS component study is replaced by a Replica study, and its global bundle-adjustment ablation is removed. These substantially revise the evidence about mechanism, robustness and computational cost.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Both mainly report individual sequence results and averages across scenes. The new Gaussian noise parameters specify an input corruption, not statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Numerous results change or are added. Between v1 Table 1 and v2 Table 3, reported Replica NeRF RMSE changes from 0.51 to 0.49 cm and SplaTAM PSNR from 33.97 to 34.11 dB. The replaced GS variant reports Replica PSNR of 41.42 rather than 39.12 dB, and TUM RMSE of 1.42 rather than 1.36 cm. Changed backbones prevent treating these as controlled inter-version gains. V2 also adds baseline, noise-test and computational results.

M1.justification: V1 specifies DINO ViT-small, whereas v2 specifies DINOv2 ViT-small. V2 also extends the framework to GauS-SLAM's 2D Gaussian surfels and adopts that system for its principal GS variant, replacing the earlier 3D-Gaussian implementation. These change important model components; the underlying attention-based fusion remains substantially unchanged under the SSE/EDINO to SGE/geoDINO renaming.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, research positioning and encoder explanation are extensively rewritten. SSE/EDINO become SGE/geoDINO throughout, and ablations move ahead of the state-of-the-art comparisons to organize the experimental narrative around generality and geometry awareness. Author affiliations and citation style also change.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. Figure 1 is redesigned with new qualitative panels and a performance plot; the combined pipeline diagram becomes separate NeRF and GS figures. The qualitative comparison is revised, benchmark tables are expanded and reorganized, and new depth-noise and computational-breakdown tables are added.

R1.justification: V2 adds a dedicated discussion of DINO-informed neural representations and prior DINO-based semantic and dynamic SLAM, including SNI-SLAM, LOSS-SLAM and D3 FlowSLAM. It replaces v1's broad assertion that existing systems overlook DINO with a distinction centered on geometry-aware enhancement. Related work also expands substantially to newer implicit, Gaussian and feed-forward systems.

T1.justification: The attention, volume-rendering, Gaussian projection/blending and feature-loss formulations retain their substance.
