Renamed variables, regrouped equations and explicit ray-batch notation clarify presentation without introducing a substantive derivation. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the justification of the contribution: it acknowledges earlier DINO-based SLAM, tests geometry-aware fusion against simple depth concatenation, and evaluates stronger comparators. The depth-noise experiment and computational breakdown make robustness and cost more assessable than in v1. The removed bundle-adjustment ablation and continuing absence of run-level uncertainty limit validation, and the changed GS backbone prevents attributing inter-version score differences solely to the encoder. Nevertheless, the clearer novelty positioning and better controlled evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DINO-SLAM, with matching methods and benchmark experiments despite substantial revision. All supplied pages, equations, tables and figures support comparison. Both PDFs end with references; neither contains an appendix section.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results, feature ablations, depth-noise experiments and computational measurements in Tables 1–8.

before.justification: V1 reports original tracking, reconstruction and rendering results on Replica, ScanNet and TUM, plus component ablations and resource measurements in Tables 1–6.

results.title: DINO-SLAM: DINO-Informed RGB-D SLAM for Neural Implicit and Explicit Representations

C1.justification: v1 identifies Stage II as the primary contribution; v2 explicitly positions integration of foundation-model priors with physically based representations across the framework as the core contribution. The abstract specifies competitiveness across 4–32 views. The central claims about complementary priors enabling sparse-view inverse rendering remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning ignored global illumination and wavy normals causing specular effects to enter albedo. It explains diffusion's artifact suppression and limited hallucination under late activation. The dense-view discussion replaces v1's segmentation-versus-fine-roughness tradeoff with an explanation involving Ref-Gaussian's appearance fitting and continued densification. These substantially revise mechanism explanations and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies diffusion guidance scale 100, KNN removal every 1,000 iterations, and fixed hyperparameters without scene-specific tuning or prior fine-tuning. Appendix B adds preprocessing times and distinguishes offline priors, intermediate semantic processing, and diffusion active during optimization. It also revises reported optimization time from approximately 1.5 hours to 1 hour 20 minutes.

E1.justification: v2 adds Shiny Blender evaluation on reflective synthetic objects, extended with ground-truth albedo and relighting and excluding the ball object. This expands the evaluated object coverage. Synthetic4Relight and Ref-Real remain, while TensoIR is retained in Appendix C rather than removed.

E2.justification: Synthetic4Relight Table 1 adds evaluated GShader, R3DG, MaterialRefGS, and SVG-IR comparators to Ref-GS and GI-GS. Ref-Real's quantitative comparison also adds GShader and R3DG. Ref-GS becomes Ref-Gaussian but cites the same work; GIR remains a qualitative comparator.

E3.justification: Reported loss weights change: BCE from 0.1 to 0.75, IID from 1 to 2, and lighting TV from 1 to 0.1. The new Shiny Blender view-count study includes 64 and 100 views, beyond v1's 4–32 range. v2 also introduces Stage I experimental controls, runtime comparisons, and controlled 90-degree lighting rotation. These are reported setting and design changes, without independently establishing reruns.

E4.justification: v2 adds Stage I ablations of depth, normals, SDS, and outlier removal in Table 3, directional-shading and relighting-error analysis in Figure 6, and MI-SDS difference images in Figure 7. View-count sensitivity is revised and extended on Shiny Blender. Conversely, v1's segmentation-lifting sensitivity study using 25, 50, and 100 views and its separate toycar view-count analysis disappear.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Variance terms in the method are regularizers, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Many reported values and result entries change. In Synthetic4Relight Table 1, GAINS NVS/albedo/relighting PSNR changes from 30.23/22.97/25.582 to 29.32/22.34/28.16; roughness MSE changes from 0.026 to 0.04, while newly evaluated SVG-IR reports 0.03. TensoIR and Ref-Real scores also change. New benchmark, comparator, and ablation results accompany removal of extensive appendix results. These revisions accompany changed method settings and do not establish controlled same-setting gains.

M1.justification: Sections 4–5 retain the two-stage framework but substantially revise its components. TV-only normal guidance becomes combined L1 and TV supervision, KNN floater removal supplements alpha-mask regularization, and Teamwork supplies IID albedo priors with RGB2X retained for outdoor scenes, replacing v1's exclusive RGB-X specification.

P1.justification: The seven-section main outline and much of the method exposition remain. Editorial changes include revised abstract and contribution framing, foundation-model terminology, clearer evaluation and ablation headings, baseline-name corrections, and condensed appendix discussion. Much of the added prose documents scientific changes assessed separately.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column layout to a single-column format and substantially reorganizes its displays. Tables gain comparator rows, runtime and normal columns; TensoIR moves from main Table 2 to appendix Table 4. v2 Figure 5 combines a new view-count chart with the gardenspheres comparison, and Figure 7 combines quantitative and qualitative ablations. New error/shading panels appear while most earlier appendix comparison panels are removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Relightable 3D Gaussian, Teamwork, SVG-IR, and MaterialRefGS, connecting them to evaluated baselines or the IID prior. The related-work narrative and sparse-view research gap remain largely intact. Ref-GS/Ref-Gaussian and RGB-X/RGB2X refer to retained cited works rather than new citations.

T1.justification: Section 4 mathematically redefines normal guidance from a TV term to a weighted combination of two L1 terms and TV. The principal BRDF, segmentation-consistency, and SDS formulations remain equivalent; neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation: broader comparator testing addresses v1's narrow comparisons, Shiny Blender tests reflective-object recovery, and Table 3 supplies previously missing evidence about Stage I components. Explicit limitations and computational details improve transparency. These benefits outweigh the loss of useful appendix sensitivity studies and examples. Some claims remain overstated: SVG-IR has lower roughness error in Table 1, and removing segmentation improves albedo PSNR in Figure 7 despite the blanket full-model superiority claim.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GAINS by the same authors and retain the same underlying research framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renamed content.

after.justification: v2 reports original results on the retained datasets and Shiny Blender, including new Stage I ablations and directional-relighting analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, view-count analyses, and qualitative reconstructions on Synthetic4Relight, TensoIR, and Ref-Real.

results.title: GAINS: Gaussian-based Inverse Rendering from Sparse Multi-View Captures

C1.justification: V2 withdraws InstanceMV-14K construction as a central contribution and reorganizes the contribution around dual-branch distillation and compact semantic representation. Its abstract, introduction, and conclusion add the concrete claim of comparable semantic fidelity using fewer than 5% of pixel-aligned embeddings and emphasize preventing input-view overfitting. Arbitrary-view reconstruction and multitask capabilities remain core claims.

C2.justification: V2 develops the interpretation that novel-view distillation mitigates input-view overfitting and qualifies semantic sparsity with observed degradation at excessive sparsity. Appendix I newly identifies dependence on VGGT geometry, generalization demonstrated primarily indoors, and memory difficulties with hundreds or thousands of images. These materially qualify applicability beyond v1's discussion.

D1.justification: V2 discloses eight H200 GPUs and approximately two training days, additional loss details, validation/frame sampling, pose alignment, float32 storage accounting, and a default semantic voxel size. Appendix A adds previously undocumented supervision details. Conversely, v1's AdamW, cosine schedule, peak learning rate, and backbone multiplier disappear. Reproducibility remains imperfect: Appendix C states a default voxel size of 0.016, while Figure 5 labels it 0.16.

E1.justification: V1 trains using InstanceMV-14K, assembled from ScanNet, ScanNet++, ARKitScenes, and RealEstate10K. V2 reports training only on ScanNet and ScanNet++. Appendices D–F add explicit camera-pose and depth-estimation tasks and evaluation on unseen Replica scenes. ScanNet++ itself is retained coverage, already used for v1 ablations.

E2.justification: V2 adds AnySplat and SAM2+CLIP to the main comparisons and VGGT to the new pose/depth comparisons. LSeg, LSM, Uni3R, LangSplat, and LangScene-X remain evaluated, but LSeg/LSM/Uni3R no longer have 32-view comparison rows. These changes substantially broaden and revise the evaluated comparator sets.

E3.justification: Fixed-view baseline evaluation changes from DUSt3R-style post-processing to selecting the two input views nearest each target. The training image pool changes from N=14 to N=12, and mask preparation changes from projected scan annotations to the described SAM2 pipeline. V2 revises view sweeps, drops runtime measurements, and introduces pose AUC and depth AbsRel/threshold-accuracy protocols.

E4.justification: V2 Table 3 expands the original distillation, contrastive-loss, and sparsification ablations with separate voxel/pixel embedding controls and an isolated novel-view-distillation ablation. Appendix C adds semantic voxel-size sensitivity and its storage–accuracy tradeoff. Appendix F explicitly tests cross-dataset generalization on unseen Replica, substantially extending robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2 Table 3 averages across input-view settings; this does not introduce repeated-run or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Benchmark values and result coverage are substantially revised. For example, ScanNet two-view FLEG mIoU/PSNR changes from 47.12/24.20 to 48.01/25.05 under the revised training/evaluation regime, not an established same-setting gain. V2 Table 3 reports 73.89K embeddings and 18.04 MB versus 2.012M and 491.3 MB for its pixel variant. Tables 4–6 add pose, depth, and Replica results; v1's runtime results are removed.

M1.justification: The transformer architecture, novel-view selection, instance contrastive learning, and isotropic semantic-Gaussian aggregation remain substantially the same; DGLE largely renames the earlier sparsification strategy. V2 explicitly adds LPIPS to the photometric objective and changes photometric/feature weights from 1/1 to 2/0.5. Appendix A newly documents depth consistency and supervision of both Gaussian representations, without establishing when these procedures were introduced.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around compact semantics. Method sections are reorganized into dual-branch distillation and a dedicated DGLE section, replacing the earlier dataset-centered exposition. Appendices A–I introduce a substantial new document structure.

P2.justification: V2 changes to a single-column layout, redraws the teaser and pipeline, and reorganizes qualitative comparisons by reconstruction versus segmentation. Tables 1–3 gain new structures, dataset groupings, metrics, and highlighting. New Tables 4–6 and Figures 5–13 display geometry evaluations, sparsity sensitivity, generalization, and additional scene visualizations.

R1.justification: The same broad research areas remain, with targeted additions including DF-3DGS's semantic sparsity, several pose-free/self-supervised reconstruction methods, and a formal IGGT citation. V2 removes the EA3D discussion and revises its distinction from IGGT. These refine prior-work positioning without replacing the overall literature framework.

T1.justification: The mathematical training objective is revised through the additional LPIPS term in Equation 4 and independently weighted loss terms in Equation 12. The projection, contrastive complexity, moment-matching, and isotropic-covariance derivations remain essentially unchanged. Neither version introduces a theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central method: Table 3 better isolates compactness and novel-view supervision, while Appendices C–F test sparsity limits, geometry, and unseen-scene generalization. Explicit limitations also make applicability easier to assess. These address important evidential gaps in v1. The gains outweigh lost optimizer/runtime information and reporting defects, including Figure 5's inconsistent voxel-size labels and Table 2's malformed SSIM entry. This assessment rests on stronger controls and clearer boundaries, not the revised performance values alone.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FLEG by the same authors, with identifiable correspondence between methods and experiments. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains readable Appendices A–I.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark comparisons and ablations, plus semantic-sparsity, camera-pose, depth-estimation, and unseen-Replica results in its appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction and segmentation experiments on ScanNet, comparisons with per-scene methods, and ScanNet++ ablations in Tables 1–3.

results.title: FLEG: Feed-Forward Language Embedded Gaussian Splatting from Any Views via Compact Semantic Representation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: tightly coupled visual-inertial estimation, robust initialization, time-varying biases, consistent loop-closure updates, robust real-time tracking and high-fidelity mapping. Expanding evaluation from four named benchmarks to five datasets supplies broader support rather than redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds specific explanations involving DBA-Fusion's linearization gap and VINGS-Mono's depth generalization and loop-closure failures. Its limitations paragraph replaces the multicamera/fisheye and high-end-GPU caveats with marginal gains from Gaussian-assisted pose refinement, attributed to insufficiently sharp online renderings. These refine mechanisms and applicability discussion without overturning the main interpretation.

D1.justification: v1 describes partially NumPy-based IMU processing and future CUDA optimization; v2 reports C++ preintegration, CUDA Jacobian/Hessian computation and TensorRT inference. It also adds baseline configuration details, smartphone-demo implementation, and Odin acquisition, calibration, undistortion and anonymization information. The project-page link is replaced by promises to release code and data, which do not establish current availability.

E1.justification: The four original benchmarks remain. Self-captured evaluation expands from one extreme-condition sequence to 18 indoor/outdoor sequences covering long trajectories, dynamic objects, glare, low light and reflective/transparent surfaces. Controlled motion-blur, overexposure and low-light variants of EuRoC introduce additional input conditions.

E2.justification: v2 adds DBA-Fusion and VINGS-Mono to tracking comparisons on the original benchmarks, increasing the stated baseline set from 13 to 15. VINGS-Mono also enters rendering comparisons, including Table 3 and Figure 3. It was discussed but not evaluated in v1; these additions directly address closely related visual-inertial competitors.

E3.justification: New protocols include controlled blur, exposure and noisy low-light transformations, success-curve AUC through 6 meters, and peak GPU-memory measurement. Newly evaluated baselines use specified adaptations: forced EuRoC keyframes, a reduced UTMM initialization threshold, and disabled monocular depth and loop closure for VINGS-Mono. The original ATE, recall and rendering metrics remain.

E4.justification: Table 6 expands from three tracking ablations to six, adding zero-bias, shared-global-bias and removal-of-inertial-only-initialization tests. v2 also adds controlled corruption sensitivity tests and broader trajectory/rendering case studies. Conversely, v1's appendix Tables 17–18 with per-sequence mapping and tracking ablations disappear, although their aggregate results remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v2's synthetic-noise parameters describe input corruption, not uncertainty in estimated performance.

E6.justification: Original benchmark accuracy/rendering results are largely retained, but v2 adds extensive baseline, self-capture, corruption and ablation results. Table 10 reports self-captured mean ATE of 0.588 m for VIGS-SLAM versus 1.850 m for DBA-Fusion. Runtime Table 9 changes mean tracking/full-system FPS from 16.40/7.09 to 39.83/12.02, while mean keyframes change from 491 to 366; this is not an isolated same-workload speedup. Some per-sequence ablation results are removed.

M1.justification: Both versions retain joint pose/disparity/velocity/bias optimization, three-stage IMU initialization, IMU-based keyframe initialization, pose-graph loop closure and consistent Gaussian updates. v2 adds solver and sampling details and reports implementation acceleration; these do not establish a different estimator, objective or core algorithm.

P1.justification: The main section order and much existing prose remain. v2 makes targeted introductory and related-work rewrites, expands optimization and ablation explanations, updates author/front matter, and adds dedicated supplementary sections for the demo and baselines. References move behind the supplementary narrative.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column to a single-column layout. Figure 2 is reorganized; Figure 3 adds VINGS-Mono and replaces the HKU example with Retail. New self-capture Figures 5–6 replace the earlier single-case display. Tables gain comparator, ablation and memory rows, new experimental tables appear, and two detailed appendix ablation tables are removed.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning around newly cited DBA-Fusion, acknowledging its earlier use of DROID-SLAM correspondences and contrasting its cascaded optimization with VIGS-SLAM's coupled solve. The existing VINGS-Mono discussion is recast around that relationship and specific weaknesses. Additional references support implementation and acquisition; KITTI and KITTI-360 citations are removed.

T1.justification: v2 adds the block normal equations and Schur-complement update in Section 3.1, Equation 4, including the argument that the depth block is diagonal. v1 states the residual objectives without this algebra. Other core mathematical formulations remain equivalent, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1: missing empirical comparisons with closely related dense visual-inertial systems and limited tests of staged initialization and bias modeling. The added comparisons, targeted ablations, controlled corruptions and diverse self-captured sequences substantially strengthen support for robustness. Implementation documentation also improves. Removed per-sequence ablation tables and less explicit hardware/camera caveats reduce transparency, while changed keyframe counts limit runtime comparability, but these losses do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VIGS-SLAM and contain readable main text and supplementary material. Text, equations, tables and figures support comparison across the substantial expansion and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds self-captured-dataset evaluations, baseline comparisons, visual-corruption experiments, additional ablations and memory measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original VIGS-SLAM tracking, rendering, robustness, ablation and runtime results in the main paper and appendix.

results.title: VIGS-SLAM: Visual Inertial Gaussian Splatting SLAM

C1.justification: The central contributions remain compact Gaussian initialization and gradient-free recurrent refinement. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend the generalization claim explicitly to unseen view counts, while the stated empirical scope expands to ACID and 32-view inputs.

C2.justification: v2 adds mechanism explanations concerning middle-view coordinate alignment, hidden-state features, weight-sharing regularization, and DINOv2's spatial limitations. It also discusses the narrowing advantage over optimization with more views. The limitations retain computational bottlenecks but remove v1's conjecture that fixed Gaussian counts cause iteration saturation.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies two-layer Gaussian and four-layer update heads, the middle-view coordinate reference, and details of additional baseline adaptations. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously unspecified implementations. Training budgets are relocated unchanged, and code release remains prospective. Table 1 removes the explicit single-GH200 timing-hardware statement.

E1.justification: v2 adds zero-shot RealEstate10K-to-ACID evaluation (Table 4) and generalization from eight training views to unseen input-view counts (Figure 5b). Appendix A also evaluates expanded scene coverage with up to 32 views. These substantially broaden the tested generalization scenarios beyond v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated SplatFormer (Table 10), 3DGS refinement initialized by ReSplat (Table 8), and depth-regularized 3DGS (Table 11), substantially expanding relevant alternatives. The cited sparse-view optimization papers motivate the depth-regularized comparator; their named methods are not separately reported as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Training samples one to four recurrent iterations instead of one to three. New experimental designs control initialization for refinement comparisons, vary weight sharing and network depth, and expand the sampling region and target-view coverage across view counts (Tables 7-9). Existing progressive training schedules and budgets are retained in Appendix B.

E4.justification: v2 expands rendering-error ablations to RGB, feature, and fusion alternatives, and adds coordinate-system, hidden-state, weight-sharing/depth, feature-extractor, and component-runtime analyses (Tables 6, 9, 12, and 13). View-count robustness and qualitative ablations are also added. The original compression and initialization ablations remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Additional result tables retain the same point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Reported recurrent results change substantially: Table 1's three-iteration PSNR changes from 26.82 to 27.65, with a new four-iteration result of 27.70. Table 2's two-iteration PSNR changes from 23.23 to 23.51, and Table 3 from 29.72 to 29.75. These accompany model/training revisions. ACID, new comparators, and expanded analyses add many results; compression and initialization-ablation values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 changes the feedback signal from ResNet-feature residuals alone to their sum with projected RGB residuals, using pixel unshuffle, a linear layer, and LayerNorm. This modifies one component while retaining compact initialization, attention-based recurrent updates, and the training losses.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the narrative remain intact. Local passages are rewritten, training details move to Appendix B, and the appendix gains separate evaluation, visualization, and LLM-use sections. The acknowledgments are removed; the expansion primarily documents added scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands tables and plots, rebuilds Figure 3 with rendering-error heatmaps and per-image PSNR, adds a view-count generalization panel, and introduces iteration and ablation visualizations. Existing compression and Gaussian-reconstruction images are retained and relocated: v1 Figures 6-8 become v2 Figures 7, 12, and 13.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for LayerNorm, COLMAP, ACID, and two sparse-view optimization works, and expands its discussion of SplatFormer's scene-level adaptation difficulties. The main related-work organization and positioning against single-step reconstruction and gradient-based refinement remain.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 5 revises the mathematical definition of rendering-error feedback to combine feature residuals with projected RGB residuals. The remaining update and loss mathematics is retained apart from notation and numbering; neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in evidence for recurrent refinement: Table 8 controls initialization, while Table 9 compares weight sharing against stacked and deeper alternatives. Expanded mechanism ablations and generalization tests substantially strengthen support for the central contribution. These gains outweigh limited reporting problems, including Table 8's 0.960 SSIM entry conflicting with its best-value highlighting and the removed timing-hardware disclosure.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReSplat with the same authors, core approach, and retained experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and all appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports revised original experiments and additional ACID evaluation, controlled refinement comparisons, architectural ablations, and runtime analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original view-synthesis experiments on DL3DV and RealEstate10K, generalization tests, ablations, and reconstructed-scene visualizations.

results.title: ReSplat: Learning Recurrent Gaussian Splatting

C1.justification: v1's abstract claims state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on both benchmarks; v2 instead emphasizes consistent pre-training gains across architectures, especially with limited labels. The methodological contribution is redefined around Gaussian rendering and prototype alignment, and the failure of naive pseudo-label supervision becomes a central claim. The Internet-video occupancy novelty claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 introduces geometric-scale and semantic-taxonomy mismatch as conjectured explanations for weak pseudo-label supervision, and interprets the new alignment mechanisms as addressing noisy supervision. Its limitations now include invisible/occluded voxels, extension to temporal or multi-view networks, and dependence on the wall-height assumption. v1 mainly emphasized object-level grouping and identified dynamic/static separation as future work.

D1.justification: v2 adds class-name prompting instructions, Gaussian parameterization details and the default prototype momentum of 0.999. It promises public code and data, whereas v1 withheld the dataset and promised code upon acceptance; actual release is not established. Conversely, v1's explicit YouTube train/validation counts and Occ-ScanNet scene-disjoint resplitting description are omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions use NYUv2, Occ-ScanNet and YouTube-Occ for indoor semantic occupancy prediction. The larger Internet-video collection, additional architectures and revised label fractions change experimental settings without establishing a new domain, population or task.

E2.justification: The NYUv2 comparison adds ISO and EmbodiedOcc; the Occ-ScanNet comparison adds EmbodiedOcc++ and RoboOcc. v2 Table 4 additionally evaluates HASSC, GaussRender and Pri3D against the proposed training strategy, substantially broadening v1's architecture and random-initialization comparisons.

E3.justification: YouTube-Occ grows from 14,592 to 100,372 frames, with a new 50K-subset comparison. Pre-training is evaluated on three architectures instead of only Symphonies. The stated pre-training learning rate changes from 8e-4 to 2e-4, and Occ-ScanNet/YouTube-Occ training changes from 30 to 10 epochs. v2 also adds pseudo-label and joint-training controls and revises the evaluated label fractions.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's annotation-efficiency and qualitative analyses, v2 adds pseudo-label quality and naive-supervision diagnostics, a 50K-versus-full-data scaling analysis, and component ablations. Tables 5–6 isolate the two losses and test projection choices, learnable Gaussian parameters, prototype momentum and semantic thresholding.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, uncertainty estimates or significance tests. v1 explicitly acknowledges 'No error bars' in its checklist; that acknowledgment disappears, but v2 retains the same point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: The main proposed-method NYUv2 result changes from 30.74/51.12 to 31.65/52.15 mIoU/IoU. Occ-ScanNet changes from 58.15/67.75 to 49.38/61.25, while its Symphonies baseline also changes from 57.85/67.50 to 47.71/59.89. Numerous architecture, scaling, strategy and ablation results are added, and the NYUv2 zero-shot result is removed. These are revised results under changed methods/settings, not controlled cross-version performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: v1 back-projects pixels into voxels and contrasts pooled superpixel/supervoxel features. v2 replaces this correspondence mechanism with voxel-anchored Gaussian rendering into the image plane and adds an online class-prototype memory bank and cross-scene contrastive loss. These substantially change the pre-training procedure and objective.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related work are extensively rewritten. The narrative now develops manual annotation, automated curation and pseudo-label failure before presenting the revised framework; experiments are reorganized around pipeline evaluation, pre-training and ablations. The checklist is removed, and authorship, affiliations and acknowledgments are updated.

P2.justification: The document adopts a different layout and substantially restructures its displays. Figures 1–2 are retained with resizing/relocation, and v1 Figure 4 becomes v2 Figure 5. The NYUv2 qualitative figure and radar plots disappear; new framework and pseudo-label figures appear. Benchmark and few-shot displays are consolidated, with new strategy and ablation tables.

R1.justification: New Section 4.3 explicitly distinguishes the approach from GaussTR, AGO, AutoOcc and other outdoor self-supervised methods through calibration assumptions and architectural coupling. References and discussion also expand to alternative training strategies and the manual occupancy-annotation pipeline, while v1's CrossPoint/MM-Point discussion disappears. This materially revises research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical definitions for class prototypes, the prototype contrastive loss and the combined objective in Equations 3–4. The region loss retains the earlier contrastive form. This is a limited extension of the formal objectives; no theorem, proof or theoretical guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidentiary weaknesses: multiple-architecture tests support model-agnostic applicability, Table 4 adds relevant competing training strategies, and Tables 5–6 test component contributions absent from v1. It also replaces the unsupported abstract claim of state-of-the-art zero-shot performance with claims centered on demonstrated pre-training benefits and states more specific limitations. Statistical uncertainty remains unreported, and omitted split documentation weakens reproducibility, but the new comparisons and diagnostic evidence substantially strengthen the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe YouTube-Occ, and their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison despite substantial revision. All pages were inspected, including v1's concluding NeurIPS checklist. Neither supplied PDF contains a separate scientific appendix.

after.justification: Section 5 reports original pseudo-label evaluations, experiments across multiple architectures, data-scaling comparisons and component ablations.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original pre-training, limited-annotation, cross-dataset and zero-shot experimental results for the proposed approach.

results.title: YouTube-Occ: Learning Indoor 3D Semantic Occupancy Prediction from YouTube Videos

C1.justification: v1 claims state-of-the-art performance across retrieval/localization and point-cloud understanding. v2’s abstract, contribution list, and conclusion reserve that claim for point-cloud understanding and describe retrieval/localization as competitive. The conclusion also adds a 90% total-processing-time reduction claim. Figure 1 and Appendix C retain broader state-of-the-art wording.

C2.justification: New Section 6 identifies limited upsampled-feature resolution, difficulty with small or crowded objects, and lack of real-time novel-view feature rendering. Sections 4.4–4.5 newly attribute advantages to dense registration beyond encoder choice and explain memory costs through mask-proposal caching. These materially expand the mechanism discussion and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 specifies chunking and FP16 for Dr. Splat’s previously mentioned memory optimization, discloses SAM-level and filtering choices, and gives image counts for memory measurements. Conversely, it removes v1’s explicit softmax and weighted vertex-score aggregation description from Section 4.3; this omission does not establish a changed implementation.

E1.justification: Appendix D/Table 10 adds 200-class ScanNet200 evaluation, extending semantic-category coverage within the existing indoor point-cloud understanding task. LERF retrieval/localization, ScanNet 10/15/19-class evaluation, and KITTI-360 segmentation/editing coverage are retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds LaGa to LERF 3D and ScanNet comparisons, Occam’s LGS to LERF 2D comparison, and both to the runtime comparison. Appendix Table 10 newly compares OpenVoxel on ScanNet19; its ScanNet200 entries are blank. The backbone ablation also newly evaluates Dr. Splat with AM-RADIO.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce a separate multi-level-SAM LaGa setting, representation-by-encoder controls, and per-scene peak-memory measurement. Existing benchmark metrics and feature-transfer settings are retained. Newly stated SAM-level and mean-filtering details clarify existing evaluations without establishing that those experiments were changed or rerun.

E4.justification: v1’s sequential LERF ablation is expanded into geometry ablations on LERF and ScanNet and a crossed representation/backbone comparison in v2 Tables 4–5. These test whether improvements arise from geometry, encoder choice, or their combination. Table 6 adds memory analysis. Existing upsampling and TSDF analyses remain in Appendices A–B.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Reported averages aggregate benchmark results; geometric confidence weights are not statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Existing LESV benchmark scores are retained, but substantial results are added for competitors, ablations, memory, and ScanNet200. Table 10 reports ScanNet200 mIoU/mAcc of 30.65/42.35 for LESV versus 17.88/25.96 for Dr. Splat. Table 6 reports average peak memory of 22.5 versus 131.75 GB. New ablation tables give Dr. Splat LERF mIoU as 52.76, inconsistent with the retained 52.67 in Table 1.

M1.justification: Equation 9 removes the +epsilon stabilizer from the sliding-window aggregation denominator, a small change to the specified normalization. The SVRaster backbone, geometric losses, TSDF confidence fusion, AM-RADIO features, SCRA/SCGA, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. An implementation change beyond this formula edit is not established.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites affect related work, evaluation explanations, ablation and efficiency discussions, and the conclusion. A limitations section and ScanNet200 appendix section are added, and the unresolved Figure ?? reference becomes Figure 5. The overall narrative organization and most method and existing appendix text remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 restructures the ablation display, adds backbone, memory, and ScanNet200 tables, and expands existing comparison tables. Figures 1–10 retain their visual content, with relocation and reflow. The page canvas and margins change, while the basic figure and table design is preserved.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning to multi-view consensus, contrastive grouping, and the closely related voxel-based OpenVoxel approach. It adds Beyond Averages, LaGa, Occam’s LGS, OpenVoxel, and Trace3D, with substantive discussion of their relationship to LESV. The J-NeuS reference and its attribution in the depth-confidence discussion are removed.

T1.justification: Equation 9’s mathematical definition changes by removing the denominator epsilon. Other mathematical formulations and the multi-level TSDF algorithm are retained, apart from notation and punctuation edits. No new theorem, proof, or formal assumption is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central contribution: Tables 4–5 address the representation-versus-encoder attribution gap in v1, while memory measurements and additional competitors better test its efficiency and accuracy claims. Narrowed headline claims and concrete limitations improve calibration. Some scoring documentation is lost, and numerical inconsistencies and overly broad claims remain, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the stronger experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LESV research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite reflow, renumbering, and additions.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds backbone controls, memory measurements, baseline comparisons, and ScanNet200 results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LERF retrieval, ScanNet segmentation, ablation, and runtime results, plus KITTI-360 demonstrations in the appendix.

results.title: LESV:Language Embedded Sparse Voxel Fusion for Open-Vocabulary 3D Scene Understanding

C1.justification: The central alignment, distillation, and boundary contributions remain. v3 narrows the blanket absence-of-2D-supervision claim to no pretrained 2D features or language supervision in the segmentation pipeline, drops the 'first approach' claim, and replaces overall state-of-the-art assertions with competitive-performance claims. Opacity's contribution is specified more precisely as visibility cues.

C2.justification: v3 develops opacity as structural/visibility confidence, explains why SH and rotation are excluded, and acknowledges texture-induced small-scale boundary noise. It adds interpretations of reconstruction-quality dependence and geometry-versus-appearance tradeoffs. Sections A and E explicitly discuss offline preparation costs, Gaussian availability, and outdoor scale variability, substantially extending v2's brief indoor-coverage qualification.

D1.justification: v3 supplies teacher batch size and learning rate, B–S channel dimensions and attention heads, boundary-head architecture, explicit training-only split usage, and the nearest-Gaussian fallback. It specifies the 0.06 m search radius and default k=20. Table 13 documents preparation costs, including 22 minutes per scene for GS optimization and 27.9 hours per dataset for teacher training. A project-page link replaces the future code-release statement, without establishing code availability from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: v3 adds actual ScanNet200 instance-segmentation evaluation, extending coverage from semantic classification to grouping individual objects (Table 5). ScanNet v2, ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D, and SceneSplat-7K remain represented. ScanNet200 hidden-test semantic evaluation was already present in v2.

E2.justification: For ScanNet v2, v3 Table 1 adds SPG and PT v3 + PPT and removes DeepViewAgg. For ScanNet200, v3 Table 2 adds PT v2, SPG, and PT v3 + PPT while removing OneFormer3D. Table 6 adds MinkUNet and OctFormer to the existing ScanNet++/Matterport3D comparisons. Table 5 adds instance-segmentation comparisons using MinkUNet, PT v2, and PT v3 backbones.

E3.justification: v3 introduces PointGroup-based instance evaluation with mAP25, mAP50, and mAP, plus new controlled protocols: boundary tests without distillation at fixed boundary-loss weight and attribute-distillation tests without the B–S block. Main semantic tables remove mAcc and several OA columns, although supplementary tables retain these metrics. Section 4.1 reports AdamW instead of v2's Adam; this reported setting revision does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond retained module and correspondence ablations, v3 tests semantic versus scale-based boundary supervision, appearance-encoder fine-tuning, individual Gaussian attributes and combinations, conventional-feature teachers, pruning ratios, loss weights, and class-group tradeoffs (Tables 8–9 and 14–17; Figure 11). Supplementary Sections B–D also add reconstruction-quality analysis, feature PCA visualizations, and boundary case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added scene-wise PSNR/mIoU comparison is descriptive analysis and does not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: G2P's core validation mIoUs remain 78.4, 36.6, 48.7, and 55.9 across the four semantic benchmarks. However, Table 4's hidden-test row changes from 35.5/55.3/28.6/18.7 to 35.7/54.3/28.7/20.2 for mIoU/Head/Common/Tail, making G2P highest on Tail. v3 adds instance results of 41.8 mAP25, 33.3 mAP50, and 23.2 mAP, plus extensive ablation and cost results. Several reproduced baseline scores are replaced by reference scores, and some secondary metric entries disappear; these replacements are not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Both versions retain Mahalanobis-weighted attribute aggregation, combined scale/semantic boundary labels, the Sonata teacher, PT v3 with the BFANet B–S block, and the same losses. Algorithm 1 and the clarified teacher inputs expand implementation documentation without establishing an algorithmic revision. The instance experiment uses G2P within a common PointGroup framework.

P1.justification: The main five-section organization and much of the prose remain. v3 revises the abstract, contribution wording, opacity terminology, method explanations, and ordering of experimental discussions. It also updates the title, authors, and affiliations and organizes the additional supplementary material into Sections A–E.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column formatting. v2's combined overview becomes separate preparation and training diagrams in v3 Figures 2 and 4, while Figure 3 is expanded. The existing qualitative comparison is retained as Figure 5. Tables are extensively restructured, including reduced metric columns and a transposed correspondence ablation, and numerous supplementary plots, tables, and qualitative panels are added.

R1.justification: The related-work organization and distinction from UniPre3D remain largely intact. v3 adds references including SPG, PT v2, PointGroup, Segment then Splat, DNGaussian, and Speedy-Splat, replaces the Bhattacharyya citation with Mahalanobis's distance paper, and removes the first-approach novelty wording. Publication and bibliographic updates to retained works are not additional research coverage.

T1.justification: The covariance, aggregation, boundary-selection, and loss definitions remain mathematically equivalent in Equations 1–9. Pruning-ratio notation is clarified, and pseudocode is supplied, but neither version introduces formal theorems or proofs, nor does v3 add a substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves the evidence supporting the individual Gaussian cues through boundary-source, teacher, and attribute controls that were absent from the supplied v2. Architecture, split, fallback, and preparation-cost disclosures make the approach more reproducible and its practical requirements assessable. More precise supervision claims and substantive limitations also improve credibility. These gains outweigh the loss of some secondary metric reporting; the assessment rests on stronger experimental support and documentation, rather than higher headline scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same G2P work, with matching core methods and experiments. All 11 pages of v2 and 33 pages of v3 were inspected, including rendered equations, tables, and figures. The supplied v2 ends with references; v3 additionally contains Supplementary Sections A–E.

after.justification: v3 retains original semantic-segmentation experiments and adds instance-segmentation results, attribute and boundary ablations, preparation-cost measurements, and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original G2P semantic-segmentation results, class-wise comparisons, ablations, and computational measurements in Tables 1–9.

results.title: G2P: Gaussian-to-Point Attribute Alignment for Boundary-Aware 3D Segmentation

C1.justification: v2 narrows 'first neural representation' to 'first flow-matching based representation,' replaces the zero-shot framing with composition requiring no further optimization and shared landmarks, and frames competitive accuracy around landmark-based matching. The central contribution of composing flows for correspondence across representations is retained.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the interpretation of embedding failures through smoothness and frequency, explains landmark priors, and explicitly identifies partial matching and non-bijective nearest-neighbor retrieval as limitations. The supplement adds explanations of inversion deviations and anchor instability. v1 mainly discusses map smoothness and unreliable point-cloud geodesics.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the six-layer, 256-dimensional MLP, Fourier encoding, training budget, hardware, memory/time requirements, baseline implementations, spectral settings, metric normalization and ground-truth landmark transfer. These details are absent from v1. v2 also supplies a code link, although its supplement retains future-release wording; actual availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: The datasets, representation types and downstream tasks are retained, including cross-representation matching already described in v1. v2 adds evaluation with perturbed landmark locations (Figure 4), extending coverage to noisy landmark inputs.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Diff3F and ULRSSM comparisons, including Diff3F with functional maps in Table 4. It also includes FUSE_DDIM in the main benchmark comparison, beyond the dedicated diffusion comparison retained from v1. KNN-IN-GAUSS becomes FUSE_ANCHOR; that renaming is not an added baseline.

E3.justification: v1's 45-pair embedding comparison is replaced by FAUST/SMAL comparisons with different descriptor dimensions and Euclidean-error/feature-energy reporting. v2 introduces controlled landmark, smoothing, anchor and solver settings. Its supplement also specifies SHREC20 evaluation on remaining common points after selecting six input landmarks, refining v1's stated common-landmark evaluation.

E4.justification: v2 adds landmark perturbation/count studies, controlled embedding-smoothness experiments, smoothing of pretrained features, alternative-anchor tests and solver accuracy/runtime analyses (Figure 4; supplement Figures 14–15 and Tables 9–11). These substantially expand the questions tested beyond v1's embedding and FM-versus-DDIM comparisons.

E5.justification: v2 adds per-pair metric distributions with medians, interquartile ranges and outliers across four benchmarks (Figure 13), supplementing v1's averages. This reports variability across shape pairs; neither PDF establishes repeated-seed uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 replaces embedding results and adds extensive baseline, cross-representation, robustness and computational results. SHREC20 FUSE Euclidean error changes from 0.0846 to 0.0975; the revised evaluation description prevents interpreting this as an established same-setting regression. Newly evaluated ULRSSM leads FAUST/SMAL accuracy in Table 4. Existing SDF and volumetric table values are retained.

M1.justification: The conditional-flow objective, independent per-shape flows, shared-anchor composition and nearest-neighbor retrieval remain unchanged. v2 adds a tested spectral-smoothing preprocessing variant for WKS and pretrained embeddings (supplement Equation 11; Tables 2 and 9), constituting a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: The flow rationale, embedding-selection discussion and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Dataset descriptions are redistributed between the main text and a structured supplement, terminology is standardized, and the narrative is reorganized around prior assumptions, robustness and limitations. These changes extend beyond adding experimental content.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document from two-column to single-column layout, redraws the overview and application diagrams, expands the embedding and benchmark tables, and adds robustness curves, distribution plots and supplementary comparison tables. Several existing figures and tables are retained with relocation or relabeling.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted discussion of template-based methods such as 3D-CODED, FARM and NICP, revises the optimal-transport discussion, and adds references supporting smoothing, implementation and partial-matching directions. It narrows the novelty positioning while retaining the central relationship to flow matching, Geometry Distributions and functional maps.

T1.justification: v2 adds a theorem-based argument about coincident flows for identical embedding distributions and independence from training couplings (Section 4.2). Supplement Section 1.2 adds mathematical reasoning contrasting finite-time FM anchoring with asymptotic DDIM anchoring. The core objective and composition equations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's missing implementation information and limited examination of failure conditions. Stronger comparisons, controlled robustness/smoothness studies and explicit limitations make the work more reproducible and its claims easier to assess. Some bijectivity and exact-anchoring statements remain inconsistent with the added qualifications, but these residual issues do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FUSE research work, with readable text, equations, tables and figures. v1 ends after its references; v2 includes an additional 11-page supplement. All supplied material was included in the comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, robustness experiments, smoothness analyses, runtime measurements and anchor/solver evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original shape-matching experiments, embedding and diffusion comparisons, SDF and volumetric evaluations, and qualitative application results.

results.title: FUSE: A Flow-based Mapping Between Shapes

C1.justification: v1 principally claims high-quality, interactive tabletop scene generation, with manipulation learning presented as an application. v4 makes automated manipulation-data synthesis and zero-shot real-to-sim-to-real policy transfer central contributions in its title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The original scene-quality and alignment contributions remain.

C2.justification: v4 adds focused explanations for Holodeck-table's collision-versus-realism tradeoff, the larger stacking transfer gap through friction/contact/release errors, and TSA's boundary and support priors. The central interpretations of DRO/TSA effectiveness and best-view bias are retained. The limitation concerning more complex support structures also existed in v1.

D1.justification: v4 discloses the retained test set's 74-synthetic/4-real composition and category counts, identifies the motion planner and transfer robot, and illustrates synchronized camera and joint-state data. However, it removes v1's RTX 4090 hardware specification, stage runtimes, and parallelization details. The explicit source-code-release promise is omitted, although the project-page link remains; neither PDF establishes an actual release. Core hyperparameters and prompt templates are retained.

E1.justification: v4 adds policy learning and physical-robot deployment for mango placement, strawberry placement, and block stacking, plus a separate trajectory-replay demonstration. These extend v1's simulated manipulation scenarios into real-world transfer. Real-photo reconstruction already existed in v1, while its dedicated cartoon-input reconstruction example is omitted.

E2.justification: v4 adds evaluated Holodeck-table to the text-driven comparison and SceneGen and FlashSculptor to the image-driven comparisons (Tables 2 and 5). SceneGen and FlashSculptor were cited but not evaluated in v1. The original ACDC, Gen3DSR, MIDI, and MesaTask comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include a 30-prompt text comparison with four GPT-rated criteria, support stability and five-second settling tests with 3 cm/30-degree thresholds, and mean-view scoring over the existing 160-view sweep. Policy evaluation adds domain randomization, 2,000 synthetic trajectories per task, and simulation-versus-reality testing. The original best-view benchmark and user-study protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 adds quantitative support and dynamic-settling analyses, tests sensitivity to best-view versus mean-view aggregation, and expands editing and transfer case studies. The DRO/TSA ablations are retained unchanged. Conversely, v1's efficiency analysis and dedicated cartoon reconstruction case study are removed.

E5.justification: v4 newly reports 50 evaluation trials per task in each domain for its policy-transfer success rates (Section 4.4). This supplies repetition counts for the new experiment, but neither version reports confidence intervals, variability across training seeds, or formal significance tests. User-study aggregation remains unchanged.

E6.justification: The original image-comparison, user-study, and ablation values are unchanged. New results include text-comparison average ratings of 6.27 versus MesaTask's 4.12 and Holodeck-table's 4.08, 100% support stability and 92.13% settling stability, and simulation/real policy success rates of 98/84%, 92/80%, and 90/68%. Mean-view results are also added, while the approximately 32-minute runtime result is removed. These are additional or removed findings, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The instance reconstruction, canonicalization, DRO losses, and TSA anchor selection and scaling remain unchanged. v4 extends the proposed simulation workflow with LLM-based task generation, motion planning, and multimodal trajectory collection (Section 3.3). This is a downstream extension of a framework that already supported simulated manipulation in v1; regrouping four stages into three does not itself change the algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around manipulation-data synthesis. Method subsections are consolidated, Extensions becomes Data Engine Demonstrations, and the appendix is reorganized into qualitative results, video demonstrations, and experimental details. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: v4 changes the predominantly two-column presentation to a single-column layout, redraws the teaser and pipeline, restructures qualitative comparisons, and adds tables and robot/data illustrations. The original scene gallery moves to the appendix, while existing DRO and TSA illustrations are merged into composite figures. Survey screenshots and prompt images are retained despite relocation.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from broad scene synthesis and tabletop datasets toward robotic data collection, digital twins, and real-to-sim-to-real learning. v4 adds discussion and citations including RT-1, Octo, Re3Sim, ROSE, RoboTwin 2.0, and pi0.5, while removing the dedicated tabletop-dataset discussion and references such as TO-Scene and LVDiffusor. This substantially changes the work's research positioning.

T1.justification: The scene parameterization, three DRO loss terms, and RMA scoring mathematics are equivalent across versions. Combining and renumbering equations does not change their substance. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs; the added stability criteria serve as experimental evaluation procedures.

improvement.justification: v1 supported manipulation applicability mainly through scene metrics and qualitative simulated demonstrations. v4 substantially strengthens that evidence with physical-stability tests and policy learning followed by real-robot evaluation (Figure 6 and Table 5). Additional baselines, quantitative text comparisons, and mean-view analysis address meaningful evaluation gaps. Runtime documentation is lost, and transfer evidence remains limited to three tasks in one scene without uncertainty estimates, but the new validation substantially improves support for the paper's practical utility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TabletopGen and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Despite v4's changed title and expanded robotics focus, the core method and retained experiments can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v4 retains original benchmark, ablation, and user-study results and adds text-generation comparisons, physical-stability measurements, viewpoint analyses, and simulated and real-robot policy results.

before.justification: v1 reports original scene-generation comparisons, DRO/TSA ablations, a user study with 126 valid questionnaires, runtime measurements, and qualitative reconstruction and manipulation demonstrations.

results.title: TabletopGen: Tabletop Scene Generation and Interactive Simulation for Robotic Manipulation

C1.justification: v2 claims state-of-the-art performance across FS-PCS benchmarks. v3 narrows this to S3DIS and describes ScanNet performance as competitive, with the results discussion distinguishing unimodal and multimodal comparisons. The central contribution—improving attention-based prototype construction through alignment and restoration—remains.

C2.justification: v3 expands the misalignment explanation from feature scale to mean displacement and anisotropy. It adds substantive discussion of singular covariance, noise amplification, information loss from excessive regularization, dataset-dependent token requirements, and runtime–memory tradeoffs. It also qualifies comparisons with multimodal methods by distinguishing prototype construction from richer pretrained features.

D1.justification: v3 adds a stated public code link, foreground block-eligibility thresholds, eigenvalue regularization and pseudoinverse details, and an SVD implementation intended to avoid precision loss. Parameter counts and resource measurements further document implementation costs. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although v2's explicit statement that the backbone remains frozen is omitted; that omission does not establish changed training.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate indoor few-shot point-cloud semantic segmentation on S3DIS and ScanNet with the same overall way/shot coverage. Added sampling protocols, point-count partitions, and model integrations operate within this retained dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 3–4 add MM-FSS while retaining AttMPTI, QGE, QGPA, COSeg, and FPS + min-dist. New integration comparisons evaluate COSeg and MM-FSS with WARM, and Appendix Table A3 compares VIP-Seg against VIP-Seg + WARM. These expand particular comparison sets without replacing the original baseline suite.

E3.justification: The main benchmark splits, training budgets, and mIoU evaluation remain, but v3 substantially expands the evaluation design. Additions include foreground-oversampling integration tests, controlled capacity and loss configurations, point-count/feature-dimension efficiency sweeps, and whitening tests partitioned by L > D versus L <= D. Diagnostics also gain mean-distance and anisotropy metrics. Newly stated block-eligibility criteria are additional documentation, not evidence of changed preprocessing.

E4.justification: v3 adds loss ablations, parameter-capacity controls, framework-integration tests, efficiency scaling, and eigenvalue-threshold sensitivity studies. It expands normalization diagnostics and token-count analysis across retained settings. The earlier optimization analysis survives in Appendix C.3/Figure A1; Figure 3 instead removes the support-prediction case-study panels.

E5.justification: v2's Table 1 caption specifies 1,000 FPS initializations per episode and aggregation across episodes by performance rank. v3 retains the original summary statistics but omits that repetition count and aggregation explanation, referring only to random seeds. This reduces statistical reporting detail without establishing any change in actual run counts.

E6.justification: The retained benchmark scores are unchanged, including WARM's overall 55.66 on S3DIS and 41.21 on ScanNet. However, v3 adds substantial comparator, loss, capacity, efficiency, regularization, and integration results. Table 2 also revises existing distance values from 284.18/288.81 to 282.61/271.18 and adds mean-distance and anisotropy measurements. These are expanded and revised findings, not improved retained benchmark scores.

M1.justification: The whitening–attention–coloring architecture, losses, and nearest-prototype prediction remain. v3 specifies adaptive eigenvalue regularization and rank-deficient inversion in Section 5.3 and Appendix B, refining v2's plain inverse formulation. It also introduces variants replacing FPS within existing segmentation frameworks. These are localized refinements and adaptations; the PDFs do not establish that retained benchmark experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, motivation, method exposition, and results discussion undergo extensive rewriting and condensation. Experimental settings and results are reorganized, and the optimization discussion moves into the supplementary structure. These narrative changes extend beyond merely inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: The two-column document becomes a single-column layout with extensively resized and rearranged displays. Figure 3 transposes the examples and removes support-prediction panels; the token-sensitivity plot is redrawn and expanded. Several new tables are added, while the original training-stability Figure 5 is retained as supplementary Figure A1.

R1.justification: v3 adds targeted references to MM-FSS, VIP-Seg, language-driven semantic segmentation, and covariance-spectrum bounds. Its positioning more explicitly separates multimodal feature improvements from WARM's prototype-generation contribution and distinguishes sampling protocols. The broader positioning against heuristic FPS remains.

T1.justification: v3 introduces formal mean-distance and instance-wise anisotropy definitions, spectral regularization rules, and treatment of rank-deficient inversion. Appendices A–B add supporting SVD and covariance derivations. These are limited mathematical additions; the compacted attention and loss equations otherwise preserve the earlier mathematics.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the central argument: stronger comparator coverage leads to appropriately narrower performance claims, loss and capacity controls better isolate WARM's contribution, and numerical-stability experiments and implementation details address previously unexplained whitening behavior. These gains improve evidential support and reproducibility despite unchanged benchmark scores. They outweigh the limited reporting losses, particularly the omitted FPS repetition/aggregation explanation and explicit backbone-freezing statement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WARM research, with matching core methods and benchmark experiments. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v2 ends with references; v3 includes readable supplementary Sections A–C.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds loss, capacity, efficiency, numerical-stability, and integration experiments, including supplementary results.

before.justification: v2 reports original S3DIS and ScanNet segmentation results, component ablations, attention analyses, and optimization and token-sensitivity experiments.

results.title: White Aggregation and Restoration for Few-shot 3D Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation

C1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions and conclusion broaden from understanding VGGT to identifying geometric mechanisms across VGGT, DUSt3R and DA3 on synthetic and real-world data. The conclusion also generalizes learned-prior behavior to multiple models, although the input-perturbation experiments remain VGGT-only.

C2.justification: v2 adds architectural explanations for layer timing and directional asymmetry, a semantic-to-geometric transition interpretation, and a proposed DINOv2/iBOT explanation for occlusion inpainting. It removes v1's explicit synthetic-texture bias and unidentified-classical-algorithm caveats. The qualification that knockout effects may involve mechanisms beyond correspondence matching remains.

D1.justification: Appendices A–D add ground-truth sources, real-dataset splits and sampling, triplet construction, feature-matching rules and intervention details. Validation-based early stopping and best-probe selection are newly documented. Conversely, v1's explicit VGGT checkpoint description, 518×518 input size and patch/token specifications are omitted.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates controlled ShapeNet scenes. v2 adds DTU, ETH3D and MipNeRF360 geometric evaluations, SPair71k cross-scene semantic correspondence evaluation, and synthetic three-view configurations. These substantially broaden represented environments and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds DUSt3R and Depth Anything 3 alongside VGGT in the comparative probing, attention and intervention analyses (Figs. 1–3). Appendix B.3 also adds a linear-probe comparator. SIFT and SuperGlue remain the comparators in the retained occlusion and scene-perturbation experiments.

E3.justification: The stated probe-training budget changes from 50 to 30 epochs; this establishes a reported setting change without proving which experiments were rerun. New experiments introduce dataset-specific splits and angular-bin sampling, one-epoch probe controls, DA3 size variants, and feature-matching evaluation with a three-patch tolerance.

E4.justification: v2 adds linear and one-epoch probe controls, triplet consistency, geometric versus semantic feature analyses, DA3 size analysis and block-level knockouts. Image-map and exact-patch interventions already existed in v1 Appendix D and are retained. Some earlier VGGT whole-head intervention combinations are no longer reported.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages, medians and failure rates without repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals or statistical significance tests. Additional result entries in v2 do not change this reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive cross-model, real-world, probe-control and feature-matching results, including DUSt3R's earlier geometric emergence. Retained values also change: the VGGT layer-14/top-four-head knockout increase is 71.7 pixels in v1 Fig. 4 and 70.5 in v2 Fig. 3. Validation/symmetric probing curves and several knockout entries disappear. The occlusion, lighting, repetition and focal-length results are retained.

M1.justification: The core MLP probing, Sampson-loss and attention-knockout framework remains. v2 adapts probe inputs to averaged DUSt3R decoder features and two-/three-token triplet inputs, and adds a neighborhood/block knockout to the existing intervention family.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, model background and discussion are substantially rewritten around the broader study. Detailed scene-perturbation material moves from Section 5.2 to Appendix E, the appendices gain extensive subsection organization, and references move after the appendices.

P2.justification: v2 changes from two-column to single-column layout and reorganizes figures into multi-model, multi-dataset panels. Forward/reverse matching and intervention localities are consolidated into main-text displays, new analyses receive figures, and v1's separate focal-length plots are merged into v2 Fig. 21.

R1.justification: The existing SfM, learned reconstruction and interpretability positioning remains. v2 adds discussion of Han et al.'s VGGT outlier analysis and Maggio et al.'s layer-based retrieval analysis, plus references supporting DA3, the additional datasets, DINOv2 and iBOT.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 retains the projection, essential/fundamental matrix, rank-two SVD projection and Sampson-error equations. Neither version supplies additional theorems or proofs; v2's new mechanistic explanations are empirical interpretations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's single-model, synthetic-only geometric evidence through cross-architecture and real-world validation. Linear and one-epoch probe controls also strengthen the interpretation of decodable geometry. Some useful limitations and implementation disclosures disappear, and the broader learned-prior conclusion exceeds the VGGT-only perturbation evidence. Nevertheless, the expanded validation and controls provide a substantial net improvement in the support and generality of the central geometric findings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same evolving interpretability study, with retained VGGT experiments despite the broader title in v2. Inspection of all pages, including appendices, establishes that the text, equations, figures and references support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original VGGT experiments and reports additional empirical analyses of DUSt3R and Depth Anything 3, real-world datasets, probe designs, feature matching and model sizes.

before.justification: v1 reports original VGGT probing, attention-matching, knockout and input-perturbation experiments, including additional results in Appendices B–E.

results.title: On Geometric Understanding and Learned Priors in Feed-forward 3D Reconstruction Models

C1.justification: The abstract and two principal contributions retain their meaning. The conclusion expands its performance claim from improved shape quality and qualitative scene demonstrations to stronger scene-generation and completion perceptual/layout quality, explicitly qualified by a geometric-diversity trade-off.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies the earlier account of coherent large-scene generation by explaining accumulated degradation, directional asymmetry, and the retry-quality trade-off. It adds interpretations of weaker unconditional geometric diversity, sequential sampling costs, cache-dominated memory, and reconstruction-versus-token-length trade-offs. Existing real-world limitations remain, while the new discussion establishes additional practical boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies 2k mesh-surface points for the retained chair evaluation, explains cache allocation and benchmarking controls, and corrects the printed AdamW epsilon from 1^(-10) to 10^(-10). Most architecture, training, optimizer, and backend-commit disclosures are retained. These documentation additions and corrections do not establish that the underlying retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Both versions use PhotoShape, 3D-FRONT, ASE, and ScanNet++ v2. Shape and scene generation, completion with quarter/half context, and 12 m × 12 m outpainting were already covered. The additions quantify retained scenarios and examine the existing autoencoder rather than introduce new datasets or task coverage.

E2.justification: The chair-generation comparator set remains π-GAN, EG3D, DiffRF, and L3DG. v2 adds L3DG with RePaint to the previously unopposed scene-completion evaluation and conventional vector quantization against LFQ in Table 7. These are focused comparator additions; retraining L3DG on matched chunks primarily changes its evaluation setting.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled scene comparisons using matched chunk training, 256×256 renderings, 16k Gaussian-center points, layout and CLIP metrics, 1,000 generation samples, and 200 held-out contexts with five completions each. Serialization scoring changes from results after 40 epochs to averages over epochs 70–74. New protocols also cover 20-epoch autoencoder comparisons and A100 timing with resampling and backward repainting disabled.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained serialization ablation, v2 tests separate vocabularies and positional encodings (Table 4), autoencoder downsampling and quantization choices (Table 7), and spatial degradation with 0, 5, or 15 retries (Figure 9). It also reports a failed hard-occupancy constraint and analyzes runtime and memory versus available context. These substantially broaden the questions examined.

E5.justification: v1 gives approximate average generation times without dispersion or sample counts. v2 Appendix B and Table 5 report runtime means and standard deviations, plus mean peak memory, across 100 samples. This adds uncertainty reporting for inference measurements, without establishing repeated training runs or uncertainty estimates for generation-quality scores.

E6.justification: v2 adds scene, component-ablation, efficiency, reconstruction, and degradation results. Its new matched scene-generation comparison reports FID 94.85 versus L3DG's 100.98, but lower COV, 0.548 versus 0.692. Serialization train/validation CE changes from 2.346/2.444 to 2.151/2.421 under a different epoch window, so this is not a same-setting gain. The approximate GH200 chunk time changes from 90 to 80 seconds. Chair scores in Table 1 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The sparse LFQ autoencoder, interleaved position/feature tokens, separate prediction heads, 3D RoPE transformer, and sliding-window outpainting remain unchanged. Five-retry resampling already appears in v1 Appendix B; its expanded explanation and the new ablation variants do not establish a change to the proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 trims introductory prose, reorders dataset descriptions, integrates scene completion into Scene Synthesis, expands and renames the ablation section, and revises the conclusion and outpainting discussion. Appendix sections are added around the new analyses. Editing and restructuring are concentrated in these areas; the abstract, related work, and method exposition are largely retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial displays: scene metrics, component ablations, efficiency, and autoencoder tables, plus a three-panel degradation heatmap and two chunked-L3DG galleries. The serialization table is reformatted beside the component ablation. Existing qualitative figures are retained, with relocations and revised captions; v1 Figures 9–11 become v2 Figures 12–14.

R1.justification: All 77 earlier references are retained. Six additions cover RePaint, Neural Discrete Representation Learning, Flash-Decoding, Medusa, and two speculative-decoding papers. They support the new comparisons and efficiency discussion; the main related-work narrative and positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The loss equations and autoregressive formulation are unchanged; Equation 1 is merely repositioned. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and the new empirical analyses do not introduce substantive mathematical reasoning or formal assumptions.

improvement.justification: v1 supports its central scene-generation capabilities mainly through qualitative examples. v2 substantially addresses that evidential gap with matched scene-generation and completion comparisons, while adding ablations that test important design choices. Runtime measurements and degradation analyses also make the computational, geometric-diversity, and long-horizon limitations explicit. Together, these additions substantially strengthen empirical support and the calibration of the paper's conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GaussianGPT with the same authors, core method, and research objectives. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across additions, relocations, and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original generation experiments and adds quantitative scene comparisons, component and autoencoder ablations, inference measurements, and spatial-degradation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original GaussianGPT generation scores on PhotoShape (Table 1), serialization experiments (Table 2), and qualitative scene-generation and completion results, including ScanNet++ results in Appendix A.

results.title: GaussianGPT: Towards Autoregressive 3D Gaussian Scene Generation
