C1.justification: The central diagnosis, training-free attention correction, boundary refinement, and efficient image/video generation claims remain. v2 drops v1's sweeping statements that the method stabilizes all heads and layers uniformly and is compatible with any pretrained DiT, modestly narrowing the claimed applicability.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning modality-dependent learned RoPE biases, LR queries' reliance on coarse context, and high-resolution performance through token counts closer to training conditions. Appendix E replaces v1's discussion of unstable ultra-high-resolution details with concrete texture-transition failures and proposals for better masks and retrained positional encodings. These substantially revise the explanation of applicability and remaining limitations.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents resizer training pairs, Pexels and Aesthetic-Train-V2 data, batch size, and weighted latent/pixel reconstruction and LPIPS losses. Appendix C adds attention-probing sample counts and offset grids, stage schedules, caching thresholds, and baseline configurations. A project-page link is also added. These disclosures materially improve reproducibility without establishing that previously unspecified training procedures changed.

E1.justification: VBench and MSCOCO coverage is retained. Beyond v1's two-resolution experiments, including its existing 480+1920 demonstration, v2 evaluates three and four simultaneous resolution grids, reaching 3840p for video and 2560 for images (Tables 8–9 and 13–14). These substantially expand the spatial-scale combinations required of generation.

E2.justification: v2 adds standalone video comparisons with UniPC, DPM++, ToMe, TeaCache, and MagCache (Table 3). TeaCache and MagCache also become standalone image comparators, whereas v1 evaluated their integration with the proposed method. Image Table 2 adds PI+NTK; RALU, Bottleneck, and ToCa were already evaluated in v1. LR+HR disappears from Table 1, although it remains a comparator in v2 Figure 10.

E3.justification: Image evaluation replaces FID with ImageReward. The main two-stage image comparison changes from 18 steps, 7 LR steps, and 30% HR tokens to 15 steps, 5 LR steps, and 60% HR tokens; the latter setting already appeared in v1's caching appendix. The faster three-stage image setting changes from 9 to 10 steps, and Appendix C specifies DeepGazeI instead of DeepGazeIIE for images. New evaluations also introduce distilled-model and matched-latency protocols.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained boundary and RoPE-only analyses, v2 adds saliency-model robustness (Table 6), HR key/value handling ablations (Table 15), FLUX modality-specific attention curves (Figure 16), failure cases (Figure 17), and prompt-count/timestep sensitivity checks (Figure 24). It also tests generation with and without DyPE. v1's FID-versus-token-ratio plot and four-budget image comparison are absent; v2 introduces a video quality–latency comparison.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2 documents attention-measurement sample counts and checks larger prompt samples, but retains the same averaging estimator and does not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive acceleration, distillation, multiresolution, and ablation results. For example, Table 5 newly reports four-step DMD at 80.15 VBench total and 10.9 seconds, versus DMD plus the proposed method at 80.11 and 5.6 seconds. Image comparison entries are revised under changed settings, and FID results are removed. Many retained video and boundary-ablation scores merely receive percentage formatting or additional precision.

M1.justification: CRPA is renamed PMA, but Section 4 retains query-scale position mapping, HR key/value subsampling for LR queries, bidirectional Boundary Expand-and-Replace, and coarse/mixed/optional-fine denoising. The newly disclosed resizer training losses describe existing learned components; the PDFs do not establish an algorithmic revision.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around generation efficiency and positional scale bias. The title and method terminology change, method explanations are substantially revised, and experiments are reorganized by comparison type. The appendix gains subsections and a figure guide, with results moved before the derivation.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column main layout to a single-column format. Figure 1 becomes a sample montage, Figure 4 is redrawn to contrast both interpolation baselines with PMA, and qualitative comparisons are redesigned with detail crops. Numerous new tables and analysis figures are added, while retained material such as the boundary-ablation table moves into the main text.

R1.justification: The distinction from RoPE extrapolation and positioning relative to RALU remain. v2 adds an explicit claim to be the first work focused on mixed-resolution generation, cites additional mixed-resolution vision precedents, and adds references supporting DyPE, distillation, ImageReward, and training data. Some earlier references, including FID and VideoRoPE, disappear. The principal research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 changes S from native grid spacing in v1 to native resolution scale, explicitly larger for HR, in v2. This corrects the interpretation of alpha = S_q/S_k to agree with the retained stretching examples. The sinusoidal decomposition and its proof are unchanged apart from formatting and relocation from Appendix A to B.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility: new standalone video acceleration comparisons, saliency and key/value ablations, multigrid tests, and concrete failure cases address important gaps in v1. Resizer training and experimental configuration disclosures make the work easier to assess and reproduce. Removing FID analyses reduces continuity, and changed image protocols prevent straightforward historical performance comparisons. Nevertheless, the targeted evidence and documentation gains provide a substantial overall improvement without requiring a new method.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work despite changes to the title and method acronym. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds acceleration comparisons, multiresolution evaluations, robustness studies, and failure analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original attention-response measurements, image and video generation experiments, acceleration comparisons, and boundary-module ablations in the main text and appendix.

results.title: Phase-Aligned RoPE for Mixed-Resolution Diffusion Transformer

C1.justification: The central claims remain that DLA bypasses the decode-encode loop, MESSy transfers auxiliary priors without harmful rigid feature matching, and image-only students exhibit synesthetic alignment without extra inference overhead. The new contribution list and title reorganize claims already present in v1.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations attributing gains primarily to latent representations rather than resampling, and to auxiliary prediction targets rather than predictor architecture alone. It newly argues that handcrafted-feature alignment excludes label co-occurrence and interprets transfer results as evidence against capacity interference. The conclusion also identifies frozen generators as limiting task-specific latent co-adaptation.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies generator variants, four acoustic codebooks, eight-head resamplers, two-layer prediction heads, caption regeneration using class-name synonyms, and the weighted training objective. Section 4.1 adds 50-epoch teacher/student budgets, student training from scratch, AdamW, cosine scheduling, temperature 2.0, and loss weights. These substantially improve documentation without demonstrating that existing settings changed.

E1.justification: V2 retains Imagenette2-320, Caltech101, and ImageNet-100, while adding full ImageNet-1K classification and CIFAR-100 linear-probe transfer from ImageNet-100-trained students. These substantially expand class coverage and introduce evaluation on a different downstream population.

E2.justification: V2 adds the architecture-matched Raw+Perc teacher comparison in Table 1 and the CLS-Pred student comparator in Table 4. Figure 6 also adds LUGPI to the alignment comparison previously containing only the image baseline and MESSy. These substantially strengthen comparisons around the method's central mechanisms; the original KD/LUGPI accuracy comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include freezing ImageNet-100 students for CIFAR-100 linear probing, matching raw and latent teachers' Perceiver resamplers, and controlling prediction targets and teacher representations in Table 4. Existing ViT-B/16, token budgets, dropout, and clustering counts remain; newly disclosed training hyperparameters do not establish changes to existing experiments.

E4.justification: V2 tests whether gains arise from resampler architecture, predictor heads versus auxiliary-modality targets, and latent versus raw teachers. It also adds transfer evidence concerning visual discriminability, LUGPI alignment analysis, and four additional class cases. These extend the original modality ablations and synesthesia analyses substantially.

E5.justification: Both versions state three independent runs. V2 explicitly identifies table entries as means with standard deviations and plots as means, clarifying v1's unspecified ± notation. However, the new ImageNet-1K and approximate raw-teacher results omit uncertainty despite that general statement; no increased run count is established.

E6.justification: Original accuracy entries and baseline/MESSy alignment values are retained. Added outcomes include CLS-Pred's 67.04% on ImageNet-100, CIFAR-100 probe accuracies of 42.4% for LUGPI and 48.1% for MESSy, and ImageNet-1K accuracies of 64.17%, 71.32%, and 69.05% for image-only, teacher, and MESSy respectively. Raw+Perc, raw-teacher students, LUGPI alignment, and additional class results further expand the evidence.

M1.justification: Both versions use undecoded audio/3D latents, Perceiver-based teacher fusion, and multilayer prediction of pooled auxiliary-modality features from student classification tokens. V2 specifies predictor architecture, filtering, and loss weights more fully, without establishing a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites and expands the introduction, related work, method exposition, and experimental narrative. It introduces an explicit contribution list, separates the method into motivation and three stages, and gives setup and scalability their own subsections. This is extensive narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. V2 adds Figures 3–5 redisplaying existing table results, redraws alignment as three dataset panels with LUGPI, expands the class chart from six to ten examples, restructures Tables 1–2, and adds ablation and scalability tables. The original conceptual and pipeline diagrams are retained.

R1.justification: The short prior-work discussion becomes three substantive subsections. V2 discusses BYOL, data2vec, AV-data2vec, JEPA, CRD, and projector-based cross-modal distillation, explicitly identifying AV-data2vec as the closest architectural predecessor. It positions MESSy around synthetic auxiliary-modality targets while acknowledging that predictive heads follow established designs.

T1.justification: V2 retains the original data-processing inequality and adds a chain-rule derivation showing that joint modalities cannot decrease mutual information with the label (Section 3.1, Equations 2–3). This is a limited extension of the mathematical argument, without a new substantial theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's attribution gaps through Raw+Perc and CLS-Pred controls, while transfer and ImageNet-1K experiments broaden validation. Fuller implementation details and explicit acknowledgment of architectural predecessors also improve assessability. Supplementary material remains unavailable, some new results lack uncertainty, and several causal and information-theoretic interpretations overstate the evidence, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support and transparency.

A1.justification: The authors, DLA/MESSy pipeline, and matching original results establish the same research work despite retitling. All supplied pages are readable, but both PDFs end with references and omit the supplementary material cited for generation details, layer ablations, and clustering checks. Those referenced materials cannot be compared.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds controlled comparisons, CIFAR-100 transfer results, and ImageNet-1K evaluation.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original teacher and student classification experiments, modality ablations, latent-alignment measurements, class-level analyses, and generation-efficiency measurements.

results.title: Synesthesia via Direct Latent Augmentation: Bypassing the Decode-Encode Loop for Cross-Modal Distillation

C1.justification: v2 elevates attention-dependent gradient vanishing and its implications for optimization to an explicit main contribution, and adds the claim of superiority over Gershgorin-based softmax bounds. The attention-distribution bound and JaSMin robustness contributions remain, but the paper's central scientific scope now includes weight-gradient dynamics.

C2.justification: v1's brief association of categorical attention with gradient growth is replaced by a weight-specific account of query/key gradient attenuation and distinct value-gradient behavior. v2 also qualifies the connection to attention sinks, explains the accuracy–robustness tradeoff, identifies the causal-masking limitation for k>1, and discusses poor classification under excessive regularization in Appendix H.

D1.justification: v2 adds A100 hardware for observational experiments, reports approximately 8000 total GPU hours instead of 2000, and documents settings for Imagenette and the visual-encoder study. These do not establish increased training budgets for retained experiments. The precise pretrained ViT-L checkpoint link supplied in v1 is removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds Imagenette classification and adversarial evaluation, plus attention-bound analysis using OmniGAIA images. CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet coverage remain. The OmniGAIA experiment evaluates images through a visual encoder; it does not establish coverage of the benchmark's full multimodal tasks.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 1 and Table 1 add empirical comparisons against Gershgorin and classical interlacing softmax-norm bounds; v1's corresponding histogram compares its bound only with exact norms. The unregularized and Specformer robustness baselines, and the prior full-attention bounds, remain.

E3.justification: The full-attention comparison changes from fine-tuned ViT-B/CIFAR-100 in v1 Figure 6, with exact measurements on 100 samples, to ViT-L over 5000 ImageNet samples in v2 Figure 4. New protocols include Imagenette with patch size 16 and batch size 128, normalized gradient correlations, and Qwen3-VL-4B visual-encoder analysis on 100 images with 1500 tokens each. Existing CIFAR training and attack settings largely remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds gradient-versus-bound correlations in Figure 5 and training-gradient analyses in Appendix H, testing vanishing-gradient risks and excessive regularization. Conversely, it removes the mean-versus-max aggregation comparison and the trained attention-map case study from v1 Figure 5. These substantially change the evidence about regularization mechanisms and failure behavior.

E5.justification: Unlike v1's point estimates, v2 Table 2 explicitly reports averages across three seeds with ± values. This reporting is localized to the CIFAR-100 summary; the uncertainty quantity is not defined. Because v1 specifies no seed count, the PDFs do not establish an increase from a particular earlier run count.

E6.justification: v2 adds softmax relative-error results of 0.035 for its bound, 20.19 for interlacing, and 0.85 for Gershgorin. New Imagenette results include AA2 accuracy of 11.95 for JaSMin k=70 versus 6.86 for the baseline, alongside lower clean accuracy. Main CIFAR-100 values become three-seed summaries, such as baseline clean accuracy 91.05 instead of 90.90. Appendix sweeps retain the earlier max-aggregation results while deleting mean-aggregation rows; these are not uniform same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Both logarithmic JaSMin penalties and their maximum aggregation remain unchanged. However, v1 Section 4 also proposes mean aggregation as an alternative; v2 Section 7 withdraws that variant, and its corresponding experimental rows disappear. This narrows the proposed method variants without redesigning the core regularizer.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and theoretical exposition are extensively rewritten. v2 introduces an explicit contribution list and separate related-work section, presents softmax theory before the attention bound, adds a dedicated gradient section, and reorganizes proofs across appendices. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a narrower single-column format with running headers, redraws bound histograms with comparator legends, revises heatmaps, and adds gradient and visual-encoder figures. Tables are restructured for uncertainty reporting and reduced sweeps; the trained attention-map comparison disappears. Some displays, including the whole-model Jacobian histogram, are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around gradient propagation, entropy collapse, attention sinks, and robust vision architectures. It explicitly acknowledges Nair's concurrent 1/2-Lipschitz result and distinguishes its distribution-dependent singular-value bounds from Gershgorin estimates. This changes the novelty comparison beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2 introduces weight-specific Jacobian bounds for query, key, and value matrices in Proposition 2, with proofs in Appendix F, and adds a matrix-calculus derivation in Appendix E. It also establishes comparison with the Gershgorin bound and expands the existing constant-factor comparison proof. The central attention and softmax bounds remain; v2 Proposition 1 already appeared in v1 Appendix C.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the theoretical explanation and validation of the retained contributions. Proposition 2 and the gradient studies replace v1's largely informal gradient discussion with explicit bounds and empirical checks, while direct Gershgorin comparisons test a closer alternative. Three-seed CIFAR-100 reporting and explicit applicability limits further improve evidential support and qualification. The lost mean-aggregation ablations and undefined ± notation are drawbacks, but they do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same attention-distribution bounds and JaSMin regularizer. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Imagenette evaluations, gradient analyses, three-seed CIFAR-100 summaries, and visual-encoder bound measurements on OmniGAIA images.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10/100 training and adversarial evaluations, ImageNet attention analyses, Jacobian measurements, and hyperparameter sweeps.

results.title: Pay Attention to Attention Distribution: A New Local Lipschitz Bound for Transformers

C1.justification: The central contributions and compact, state-of-the-art restoration claim remain. The abstract strengthens the comparative premise by attributing spatial discontinuity, channel redundancy and reconstruction errors to discrete Haar/block-DCT representations, extending v1's narrower discussion of underexploited wavelet approaches.

C2.justification: Section 3.1 adds explanations involving shift variance, secondary aliasing, block-DCT stationarity and channel redundancy. Section 4.1 newly qualifies the efficiency discussion: Freqformer has fewer FLOPs but slower inference than ESDNet-L, tentatively attributed to less optimized attention operations. The central texture/color interpretation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds implementation information for new experiments, including the Haar variant's band-specific modules and 10.921M parameters, and clarifies inference. However, it omits v1's explicit initial learning rate of 0.0002. The abstract changes the code-availability statement from publicly available to a future release; the PDFs do not establish the repository's actual availability.

E1.justification: TIP2018 and LCDMoire move from related-work discussion to actual training and evaluation, alongside retained FHDMi and UHDM experiments. This broadens coverage beyond high-resolution benchmarks to 256×256 natural-scene images and a synthetic, text-focused dataset. Adding adapted RAW/video comparator architectures does not establish evaluation on RAW or video datasets.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds RRID and DTNet on FHDMi/UHDM and STD-Net on FHDMi. The ablations additionally introduce Block DCT and DAT comparisons. Conversely, v1 Table 5's dedicated comparison against ESDNet on separate frequency branches disappears, although ESDNet remains in other experiments.

E3.justification: Existing FHDMi/UHDM splits, metrics, crop/resize sizes and 150-epoch training stages are retained. Added experiments specify TIP2018's 135,000/15,000 training/test split and 256/256 crop/resize sizes, LCDMoire's 10,000/100 training/validation split and 512/512 sizes, and an 8×8 Block-DCT control. These extend the protocol without documenting a redesign of the original benchmark evaluations.

E4.justification: The transform analysis expands from one Haar experiment to quantitative Haar/DCT comparisons and qualitative artifact examples in Table 3 and Figure 7. Table 6 adds full-convolution SCP and DAT architecture controls. The separate branchwise ESDNet analysis is removed, while the resizing and learnable-FCT studies survive as renumbered Tables 4–5.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The expanded results retain the same single-score reporting practice.

E6.justification: New benchmark results include TIP2018/LCDMoire PSNRs of 30.63/45.62, plus added comparator and ablation entries. Freqformer's UHDM PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS change from 22.22/0.8018/0.2434 to 22.24/0.8021/0.2424; FHDMi scores remain unchanged. Haar PSNR changes from 13.32 to 23.01, and Table 6 scores and timings are replaced without establishing identical conditions. Section 3.2's high-frequency resizing PSNR changes from approximately 30 to 25 dB. Section 4.1 adds 0.58 versus 0.25 s/image for Freqformer versus ESDNet-L and revises Freqformer's computation from 2.49 to 2.46 TFLOPs.

M1.justification: The decomposition kernel, dual branches, SA-CA, hierarchical fusion, learnable FCT and two-stage losses remain unchanged. The explicit description of resized low-frequency inference resolves an inconsistent overview in v1; v1 Section 3.2 already specified small inputs during both training and inference.

P1.justification: The section sequence and much of the method exposition remain, with localized rewrites, clearer inference wording and reordered ablation discussion. The title changes 'Efficient' to 'Effective,' asymmetric training terminology becomes more prominent, author/affiliation information changes, and acknowledgements are added.

P2.justification: The document adopts a different template with narrower text, running headers and substantially reorganized displays. New Figures 3 and 7 illustrate transform differences and ablation outputs. Tables 1, 2 and 6 expand; the old branch-comparison table disappears. Ablation tables move from text-wrapped placements to full-width blocks, and qualitative comparisons replace a UHDM example and introduce RRID panels.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 broadens from wavelet-based to frequency-based methods, adding DCT positioning against MBCNN and FHDe2Net and revising the critique of FHDe2Net. STD-Net and generative-restoration references are added. The existing research lineage and principal novelty positioning remain.

T1.justification: The mathematical method and losses are retained. The added equality expressing the high-frequency residual as the original image minus its low-frequency component restates the existing recurrence. No substantive new formal assumptions, theorems or proofs appear.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central design: the expanded Haar/DCT study and new SCP/DAT controls test choices that v1 supported only narrowly. Distinct additional datasets and comparator families strengthen the generality assessment, while measured latency makes the efficiency discussion more candid. These gains outweigh the removed branch comparison, omitted learning rate and less definite code-release statement. Unexplained changes to existing ablation scores and timings remain a reproducibility limitation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Freqformer and are readable through their final references. Text, equations, tables and figures support a reliable comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: Sections 4–4.2 report original results on four datasets, additional comparator evaluations and expanded transform and architecture ablations.

before.justification: Sections 4–4.2 report original FHDMi/UHDM restoration results and experiments testing training strategies, frequency decomposition and architectural components.

results.title: Freqformer: Image-Demoiréing Transformer via Effective Frequency Decomposition

C1.justification: v2 makes OSL an explicit novel contribution and strengthens the claimed outcome from strong global-task performance with limited dense-task benefits to state-of-the-art performance across tasks. In particular, the abstract replaces v1's competitive segmentation claim with a state-of-the-art claim, echoed in the conclusion.

C2.justification: v1 interprets weak segmentation gains as limited compatibility between global alignment and voxel reconstruction. v2 emphasizes MAE initialization and continued MAE training, and discusses remaining limitations relative to CNNs and degradation under longer fine-tuning. It also expands clinical qualifications concerning insufficient accuracy, dataset diversity, and the need for evaluation stratified by findings and patient characteristics.

D1.justification: v2 announces access to COLIPRI weights, inference code, and examples; adds final configuration Tables B.8–B.10, OSL sampling/padding pseudocode, exact split counts, and NIfTI-Zarr preprocessing/storage details. These substantially improve documentation. Some settings remain inconsistent: Table B.8 specifies a COLIPRI-C learning rate of 6e-5, while Section B.1.4 retains 6e-4.

E1.justification: v2 adds the HVS segmentation dataset, covering hepatic vessels and adjacent tumours in 303 cases (Section 4.2). CT-RATE, NLST, RAD-ChestCT, LiTS, Lung, and KiTS23 remain. The broader dataset catalogue in Table A.1 does not establish additional training or evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds MedImageInsight and Curia to classification and report-generation comparisons, adds the pure MAE encoder to classification probing, and adds default nnU-Net and ResEnc-L segmentation references. CT-CLIP also becomes a reported retrieval comparator. BIUD and fVLM already participated in v1's zero-shot comparisons.

E3.justification: Segmentation expands from the first three cross-validation folds to all five. v2 reports 250k-step comparisons alongside 37.5k-step results, although v1 Appendix C.6 already mentioned the longer schedule. Retrieval evaluation specifies deduplication and adds mean/median rank. Zero-shot results distinguish all-class and fVLM-matched evaluations, while thresholded classification metrics are removed.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct ablations testing whether OSL closes the short/native prompt gap (Table 3) and whether MAE initialization enables effective segmentation transfer (Table D.5). Figure D.1 adds abnormality-specific report-generation analysis. Most earlier hyperparameter sweeps are retained in Appendix B; their relocation is not new analytical evidence.

E5.justification: Uncertainty reporting expands to probing and zero-shot classification through 95% confidence intervals based on 100 bootstrap samples (Tables 1–2). Report-generation intervals already existed in v1; v2 newly specifies their 95% level, median estimates, and 500 bootstrap samples. These reporting additions do not establish additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: Results for the revised encoders change substantially. COLIPRI-CRM's CT-RATE probe AUPRC changes from 56.65 to 61.28 (v1 Table 7; v2 Table 1). Its report-generation RadBERT macro F1 changes from 39.7 to 44.9, while RadFact-CT logical F1 (+/-) falls from 69.2 to 66.9 (Table 9 versus D.2). New retrieval, HVS, and long-schedule results appear; segmentation averages also use different fold counts.

M1.justification: v2 introduces the Opposite Sentence Loss, constructing positive/negated sentence pairs and combining their supervision equally with CLIP alignment (Sections 3.2.1 and B.4). It also initializes the MAE-containing encoders with MAE-pretrained weights and includes MAE throughout training, replacing v1's late inclusion. These change the training procedure substantially.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: v1's development framework and extensive method-development experiments move into Appendices A–B, while v2 presents a compact standalone Method section followed by experiments and results. The introduction, related work, discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The original report-processing prompts are largely retained.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn into four objective-specific panels. The PCA comparison moves to the first page and retains only COLIPRI-CRM among the proposed variants. Classification and segmentation tables are restructured, detailed report-generation results move to Appendix D, and new configuration tables, an algorithm display, and an abnormality-wise plot are added.

R1.justification: The central positioning around combining 3D vision-language learning, report generation, and self-supervision remains. v2 updates the supporting literature, adding 2D medical VLE references and new baseline citations while removing some broad natural-image background. Appendix B.4.2 additionally positions OSL against Merlin and fVLM's organ-based approaches.

T1.justification: Appendix B.4 adds formal definitions for OSL sentence sampling, supervision labels, pair probabilities, and the combined alignment objective (Equations 1–7). This is a mathematical formulation of a new training component. Neither version develops theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses two important weaknesses identified in v1—short-prompt brittleness and weak dense-task transfer—with explicit method changes and targeted ablations (Tables 3 and D.5). Expanded baseline comparisons, uncertainty reporting, and implementation documentation substantially strengthen the paper's evidence and reproducibility. The blanket segmentation superiority claim exceeds the CNN comparisons in Table 5, and configuration inconsistencies remain, but these caveats do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the COLIPRI research work. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable, allowing reliable matching across substantial reorganization and scientific revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments for the revised COLIPRI encoders, including classification, report generation, retrieval, segmentation, and component ablations in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original pre-training ablations, classification experiments on CT-RATE and RAD-ChestCT, report-generation results, and segmentation experiments.

results.title: Comprehensive language–image pre-training for 3D medical image understanding

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about RER/VAPR stability, the efficient three-stage LVLM pipeline, and state-of-the-art report quality. The headline improvement claims are unchanged.

C2.justification: The supplement attributes CheXpert-reward instability to high variance and RadGraph reward inversion to entity stuffing, and interprets reward agreement as linguistic–clinical alignment. It also adds explanations of model-size effects, computational constraints, and classifier replacement requirements, substantially extending the interpretation of the retained method.

D1.justification: Appendices C–D supply exact prompts, optimizer and LoRA settings, stage-specific training budgets, policy-update intervals, classifier-label processing, and the 10,000-example MIMIC-CXR RL subset selected after filtering short reports. Hardware and computational details are expanded. These disclosures substantially improve reproducibility without establishing changes to the original experiments.

E1.justification: The work continues to use MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray. Supplementary experiments examine the existing report-generation pipeline and its classifier component. External datasets listed in Table S9 describe prior methods' resources, rather than newly evaluated datasets for REVA-PO.

E2.justification: The external comparator sets in Tables 1–2 are unchanged. Appendix A adds comparisons with alternative reward-based training: Table S5 includes a RadGraph-F1-reward policy, and Appendix A.1 reports collapse when training with CheXpert F1.

E3.justification: The supplement adds several evaluation designs: reward-agreement metrics, classifier AUC evaluation, group sizes 4–6 on A100 GPUs, and 3B-versus-7B comparisons, with 12 versus 9 MIMIC-CXR RL epochs. The main benchmark splits and metrics remain unchanged; newly disclosed settings for existing runs do not establish that those runs changed.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained pipeline and RL-component ablations, v2 supplies reward-choice and reward-inversion analyses, pre/post-RL reward alignment, computational-overhead measurements, group-size sensitivity, model-size comparisons, and classifier diagnostics. These substantially broaden the evidence about stability, design choices, and resource requirements.

E5.justification: Figures S5 and S9 add descriptive variability reporting through within-group reward standard deviations and mean/standard-deviation curves for response-level KL weights. These concern response variability; neither version supplies repeated-training-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–4 and Figures 3–4 retain their results, while the supplement adds substantial numerical and qualitative evidence. For example, Table S5 newly reports CheXpert F1 0.480 and RadGraph F1 0.259 for RadGraph-reward training; Table S7 adds 3B results. Reward agreement, group-size outcomes, classifier AUCs, and computational costs are also newly reported.

M1.justification: The three-stage pipeline, RER weighting, VAPR resets, BLEU-4 reward, and Algorithm 1 are retained. The supplement provides implementation details and evaluates alternative configurations without establishing a revision to the proposed optimization procedure.

P1.justification: The existing abstract and Sections 1–5 remain essentially verbatim and retain their order. v2 adds acknowledgements and an organized A–H supplement, but does not substantially rewrite or reorganize the original narrative.

P2.justification: The original figures and tables retain their displays. v2 adds reward-distribution plots, a reward-inversion example, prompt examples, stability curves, and Tables S5–S9 covering supplementary results and prior-method resources. These substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Appendix H and Table S9 add systematic positioning against prior methods by backbone size, external data, dense annotations, knowledge graphs, and evaluation-data modifications. This introduces a substantial resource-efficiency and comparison-fairness argument, supported by additional references, while retaining the main related-work discussion.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 introduces mathematical definitions of sign-consistency probability and top-1 selection consistency in Equations 11–12. The original method equations and algorithm remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v1 refers readers to reward justification and implementation details absent from its PDF. v2 supplies that evidence and a detailed training recipe, resolving substantial support and reproducibility gaps while preserving the main results. Stage 3 classifier use remains ambiguously described across Figure 1 and Appendix C, but this limitation does not outweigh the substantial gains in completeness and assessability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REVA-PO study, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures. v1 ends after its references; v2 includes Supplementary Material A–H. The retained material and supplementary additions support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and additionally reports reward comparisons, group-size and model-size analyses, computational measurements, and classifier performance.

before.justification: v1 reports original MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray results, training-stage and RL-component ablations, training curves, and generated-report examples in Section 4.

results.title: REVA-PO: Stabilizing Reinforcement Learning for Chest X-ray Report Generation

C1.justification: The central training-free geometric-prior and inverse-problem contributions remain. v2 qualifies superiority claims to the evaluated classical, untrained-neural, and noisy-example-trained methods, and replaces the contribution bullets' broad outperforming statement with strong performance across the three applications.

C2.justification: v2 corrects v1's claims of consistently winning CT metrics: Sections 5.1 and 10.1 acknowledge mixed PSNR rankings and distinguish structural fidelity from PSNR. It also adds a substantive piecewise-planar limitation, explaining curvature-dependent failure conditions and the expressivity/resource tradeoff of using eight regions, supported by the new curved-tube study.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information: ground-truth-anchored voxel grids, 10-voxel padding, nearest-center assignment, jitter, cryo-ET dimensions, hyperparameter guidance, and task-specific runtime/peak-memory measurements. These are disclosures, not demonstrated changes to existing experiments. The abstract adds a repository link and says code is available, although the introduction still promises release upon publication; actual availability remains unresolved from the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same five CT volumes, four cryo-ET datasets, and 28 PointCleanNet shapes. v2 adds a synthetic 64^3 curved-tube denoising scenario to examine curved geometry under different local patch supports (Section 10.5).

E2.justification: v2 adds Neural Attenuation Fields (NAF) to the reported CT comparisons in Tables 1 and 4 and the corresponding figures. The reported cryo-ET and point-cloud comparator sets are retained; the additional mention of 3D TV in point-cloud preprocessing is not accompanied by comparison results.

E3.justification: Section 5.2 introduces a substantial quantitative evaluation protocol for previously qualitative-only cryo-ET results: even/odd projection splitting, independent reconstruction and denoising, and corrected FSC with resolution thresholds of 0.5 and 0.25. The new curved-tube experiment sweeps patch sizes 4–12 and compares M=3 with M=8. Existing CT and point-cloud evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained engine ablations, v2 directly tests curvature preservation versus patch size and region count, measures the associated runtime/memory tradeoff, and plots update norms for approximate proximal reconstruction (Sections 10.5–10.6, Figures 15–16). These add substantive evidence about geometric limitations and optimization behavior.

E5.justification: Section 10.3 newly specifies fixed-seed within-voxel jitter, without giving the seed value or establishing a change in runs. Table 2 retains mean±standard deviation across shapes; neither version adds repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Existing CT, point-cloud, and engine-ablation scores are unchanged, but v2 adds NAF scores, FSC results, resource measurements, and curved-tube/convergence findings. Figure 5 reports 32.14 Å for 3D FoJ versus 39.86 Å for SC-Net at corrected FSC=0.25; at 0.5, SC-Net is better, 55.60 versus 58.24 Å. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 scores.

M1.justification: The junction parameterization, objective, smooth indicators, initialization/refinement procedure, and approximate proximal updates are unchanged. The eight-region configuration used in the new curved-tube study was already defined and evaluated in v1; it is not a new method component.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized rewrites to the introduction, related work, experimental discussion, and limitations; condenses the contribution bullets; and swaps the first two authors' order. It relocates the 2D objective explanation to the appendix and adds analysis subsections while retaining the overall narrative and method organization.

P2.justification: v2 adds the FSC plot/result table, resource Table 8, curved-tube figure, and convergence plot. It expands CT comparison grids with NAF, restructures Table 4 into side-by-side metric panels with best-value bolding, and enlarges/repositions the centriole display. Existing point-cloud and engine-ablation displays are principally retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Harauz–van Heel reference supporting FSC and the NAF paper. It more explicitly positions explicit geometric modeling as complementary to pretrained generative priors and explains the comparison scope excluding paired-clean-data training. The broader related-work framework is retained.

T1.justification: The mathematical model and optimization equations are retained. The 2D objective moves from the main text to appendix Section 7. The added FSC correction is an adopted evaluation formula, and the convergence plot supplies empirical observations rather than a theorem, proof, or new derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses: cryo-ET gains a specified quantitative FSC evaluation instead of relying solely on visual judgments, CT comparisons gain NAF, and curvature limitations receive direct experimental support. It also corrects CT interpretations contradicted by the unchanged tables and discloses consequential preprocessing and resource details. Together these substantially improve evidential support, transparency, and calibration of conclusions. The inconsistent code-release statements and limited scope of the new FSC/convergence tests remain shortcomings but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same 3D Field of Junctions work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including material relocated between sections.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds quantitative cryo-ET evaluation, NAF comparisons, curved-tube experiments, resource measurements, and an empirical convergence analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original CT reconstruction experiments, cryo-ET denoising examples, point-cloud evaluations, and hyperparameter ablations in the main text and appendix.

results.title: 3D Field of Junctions: A Noise-Robust, Training-Free Structural Prior for Volumetric Inverse Problems

C1.justification: v2 adds multi-institutional structured benchmark construction as a central contribution and extends the paper's claims to cross-institution generalization. It redefines the tokenization contribution around foreground-mask guidance and narrows patient-specific attribute extraction to localized lesion measurements. These changes materially extend and reshape v1's three-component, RadGenome-focused contribution statement.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations and limitations absent from v1: institutional reporting style can separate lexical from clinical scores; airway geometry may cause feature dilution; upstream segmentation misses constrain small-nodule detection; and organ-mask errors affect two visual modules, explaining their larger impact. These extend v1's discussion of component synergy and baseline behavior with explicit failure mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 documents encoder layer selection, physical spacing, multi-window processing, DSPy/Llama-based report preparation, anatomical subregions, and revised lesion-extraction pseudocode. It updates context length from 2,048 to 8,192 and LoRA rank from 16 to 128, and supplies a concrete repository address where v1 only states code availability. Conversely, v1's explicit 48-hour/two-A100 baseline comparison cap is no longer documented.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates on RadGenome-Chest CT alone. v2 adds 500 AMC cases sampled from a separate hospital population and evaluates zero-shot cross-institution generalization, substantially expanding evaluation coverage while retaining the six-region chest reporting task.

E2.justification: The main comparison retains RadFM and M3D, removes MedBLIP and CT2Rep, and adds MedM-VL, Med3DVLM, and CT-CHAT (Table 1). The ablation comparison additionally introduces an M3D encoder baseline; the LITA comparator is retained under the LITAenc. label.

E3.justification: Reported training/validation and test counts change from 24,128/1,564 to 23,865/1,551. Inputs change from min-max-normalized 256×256×32 volumes to resampled, cropped, multi-window 448×448×128 inputs, and training increases from three to six epochs per stage. The clinical metric suite changes from CA-F1/GREEN/GPT-4 scoring to GREEN/CRG/GPT-CA. v2 also specifies 30% training subsets for ablations and introduces external zero-shot and 50-case blinded reader protocols.

E4.justification: v2 extends component ablations with encoder comparisons and external generalization tests, and adds analyses of anatomical-region weaknesses, nodule-size sensitivity, and organ-versus-lesion mask corruption (Tables S1, S3, S5). The earlier COVID-19 case is retained with revised outputs in Figure S1, while Figure 3 introduces a different multiregional effusion/consolidation case.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without uncertainty reporting. v2 introduces 95% confidence intervals throughout the main comparison and ablation tables, specifies 10,000 bootstrap replicates, and reports reader-score standard deviations. These additions do not establish repeated training runs or increased seed counts.

E6.justification: The reported results are substantially replaced and expanded. For example, the proposed model's internal GREEN score is 0.278 in v1 and 0.4555 in v2, but changed methods and protocols prevent interpreting this as a controlled gain. New results include AMC GREEN 0.1572 and reader score 6.9792±1.4065. Table S3 also reveals small-nodule detection of 0.1270, below every listed baseline.

M1.justification: Beyond renaming R2 pooling, v2 replaces all-slice averaging and representative-slice selection with organ-bearing slice filtering and mask-guided spatial token selection. It replaces RAD-DINO/SAT with MedSigLIP/TotalSegmentator, removes spatial tokens, and produces one volumetrically pooled mask token per region. Attribute extraction changes from organ volumes and lesion counts/diameters to localized, largest-component lesion measurements (Sections 3.1–3.3; supplementary Algorithm 1).

P1.justification: The title and substantial portions of the abstract, introduction, related work, methods, and results discussion are rewritten. Related work is reorganized into three focused themes, structured reporting moves into a benchmark-construction subsection, component terminology changes, and the supplement is reorganized into dedicated implementation and analysis sections.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. Figure 2 is substantially redrawn with separate tokenizer and attribute-extractor panels; baseline and ablation results become separate tables with confidence-interval rows; and supplementary Tables S1–S5 are added. The COVID-19 illustration is revised and relocated to Figure S1, while the main qualitative figure shows a new case.

R1.justification: The literature coverage is substantially refocused: much of v1's general and 2D medical MLLM survey is removed, while MedM-VL, Med3DVLM, MedGemma, TotalSegmentator, CRG, and DSPy are introduced. The extractor is positioned directly as an Osprey-based volumetric adaptation, replacing v1's explicit inheritance of MAIRA-SEG's extractor settings. These exceed citation renumbering or publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: v1's fixed D+T token-count account gives way to mask-dependent token-set definitions. v2 also specifies normalized volumetric pooling, largest-component mask intersection, and voxel-spacing-aware lesion geometry in Equations 2–7. These are bounded mathematical revisions to the procedure; neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited validation through external-hospital evaluation, blinded human assessment, uncertainty reporting, and explicit failure and robustness analyses. The small-nodule and airway findings make applicability limits more assessable, while expanded implementation details improve reproducibility. Changed protocols prevent attributing score differences solely to the revised method, and the reader study uses only one assessor while mask perturbations remain underdescribed. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in evidential breadth and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MedRegion-CT and its region-focused CT reporting framework, despite substantial revisions and a changed title. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and supplementary materials support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original internal and external benchmark experiments, ablations, lesion-size and segmentation-noise analyses, and a blinded reader study in Tables 1–2 and supplementary Tables S1–S5.

before.justification: v1 reports original RadGenome-Chest CT benchmark results, component ablations, and a qualitative report-generation comparison in Table 1 and Figure 3.

results.title: Region-Aware Multimodal Large Language Model via SlowFast Tokenization and Pseudo-Mask Guidance for 3D CT Report Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about MEMR-Seg, the 177K-dialogue dataset, MediRound, and JCM's mitigation of error propagation. The added evidence does not redefine these main contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix F adds substantial applicability limits: single-entity segmentation per turn, sensitivity to long queries, near-complete loss of general conversational capabilities, and inability to process 3D data or videos. It also attributes the reported weaknesses to sequence-length limitations and task-specific overfitting. These qualifications were absent from v1.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B supply previously missing training losses and JCM quality-target construction, substantially expanding implementation documentation. Appendix D, Table B, and Figure D add reference phrasing, modality names, scenario-level split statistics, and data examples. Appendix E.2 adds a future-release statement for the dataset and model; the existing project URL is retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use MR-MedSeg with the same five interaction scenarios, 168 categories, and nine modalities, plus SA-Med2D-20M evaluation. The appendix describes existing modalities and provides additional examples without establishing expanded task or dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in Tables 1–3 is unchanged, including the human-guided and MLLM-assisted systems, SegLLM variants, and MediRound+READ. Table 4 specifies SAM as SAM (ViT-H), without establishing a newly introduced comparator.

E3.justification: Table A adds a controlled comparison using neither visual reference input, cropped images alone, and crops plus bounding boxes. Existing evaluation metrics, budgets, and splits remain unchanged; Table B's scenario counts sum to the split totals already reported in v1.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds a focused ablation of reference-mask information. Appendix D adds category-frequency analysis, and Figure C adds interactive case studies. The existing backbone and JCM-threshold ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or performance uncertainty estimates. The new dataset-frequency displays provide descriptive counts rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 swaps regular/hard-case entries for Qwen3-VL+IMIS-Net and Gemini-2.5-Pro+MediSee, and selected Dice/gIoU entries for SegLLM. Table 3 changes MedPLIB Dice/gIoU from 39.1/40.6 to 40.6/39.1. Table 4 revises the SAM row from 44.9/27.6/31.9 to 46.7/33.1/37.2, now labeled ViT-H. The appendix adds ablation scores, dataset findings, examples, and qualitative failure observations; MediRound's headline scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The architecture, conversation-history inputs, crop and bounding-box references, teacher forcing, and JCM inference procedure remain unchanged. Appendices A–B disclose training objectives and supervision details; they do not establish a revised method.

P1.justification: The main prose and Sections 1–6 retain their wording and order. V2 appends an overview and organized explanatory Sections A–F, including expanded descriptions of existing interaction scenarios, rather than extensively rewriting the original narrative.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands visual documentation with a JCM training diagram, category-distribution displays, interactive prediction examples, and dataset samples in Figures A–D. Tables A–B add the reference-input ablation and detailed dataset composition. Existing main-text figures and table structures are retained.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion, research positioning, and all 51 bibliography entries are unchanged. The appendix introduces no additional cited works.

T1.justification: Appendices A–B newly specify the mathematical definitions of JCM's IoU-based soft supervision target and composite loss, together with MediRound's text-and-mask training objective. These are limited additions to the formal specification; the original inference equations remain unchanged and no proofs or theoretical guarantees are added.

improvement.justification: V1 refers readers to training and dataset details in an appendix that the supplied PDF lacks. V2 supplies central JCM supervision and training objectives, supporting analyses, and important capability limitations, substantially improving technical transparency and critical assessment. Table A's claim of best performance with both reference inputs overlooks crop-only's higher cIoU, 56.0 versus 55.8, but this limited overstatement does not outweigh the documentation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MediRound work, and their text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. Corresponding main sections match reliably; v2 includes Appendices A–F, which are absent from the supplied v1.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, supplemented by reference-input ablation results, dataset analyses, and additional qualitative examples in the appendix.

before.justification: Tables 1–4 and Figures 6–7 report original segmentation experiments, comparisons, and ablations on MR-MedSeg and SA-Med2D-20M.

results.title: MediRound: Multi-Round Entity-Level Reasoning Segmentation in Medical Images

C1.justification: The central contribution remains confidence-guided augmentation for distillation under unknown covariate shift. However, v1's blanket superiority claim is qualified in v3's abstract and conclusion to best or second-best sample mean accuracy, while the claimed evaluation scope expands to BAR and CelebA-HQ.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning estimation of the theoretical constants and augmentation distribution, applicability to location-sensitive tasks, and failures caused by unnatural generation or stalled optimization. It proposes domain mismatch as an explanation for weaker Hyper-SD results. The earlier two-augmentation optimum is replaced by dataset-dependent scaling conclusions, and the teacher-dependence discussion is revised around the new teacher setup and weaker-teacher experiments.

D1.justification: Appendices B, C and N greatly expand reproducibility information: inversion and denoising settings, separate optimization learning rates, stopping rules, background regularization, Hyper-SD/IP-Adapter configuration, checkpoint references, teacher-logit aggregation and baseline-specific parameters. FLOP measurement assumptions and generation multipliers are documented. Conversely, v1's V100 generation-time measurements are no longer reported.

E1.justification: v3 adds BAR activity classification under place shift and five-shot Oxford Pets evaluation without deliberately imposed covariate shift (Appendix L). It also substitutes CelebA-HQ for CelebA while retaining bird and ImageNet classification. These changes substantially broaden the represented tasks and evaluation scenarios.

E2.justification: Diff-Mix and Diff-II join the evaluated diffusion baselines in v3 Tables 2–3. The TAB combination experiments in v1 are replaced by LfF and uLA comparisons in v3 Table 8; plain Stable Diffusion and CutMixPick evaluations disappear. GIF, DistDiff, DA-Fusion and ActGen remain, with DA-Fusion's spelling change not treated as a new method.

E3.justification: Training changes from 100 epochs with cosine decay and validation-selected checkpoints to 300 epochs with constant learning rates and final-checkpoint evaluation. Main generation budgets become approximately FLOP-matched rather than equal augmentation counts. SpuCo Birds switches from a specially fine-tuned ViT-B teacher to zero-shot CLIP with species aggregation. CelebA-HQ uses reversed official split roles and eight groups rather than sixteen; ImageNet training changes to 100 spurious-feature-selected images per class.

E4.justification: v3 adds component-isolation, weaker-teacher, replacement-probability, target-class and single-step-generator studies, together with explicit failure cases and no-shift evaluation. ConvNeXt experiments replace the TinyViT/ResNet studies, and the ERM-plus-EDRM loss ablation is removed. Existing augmentation-count, stronger-augmentation and synthetic-sample difficulty analyses are revised rather than simply added anew.

E5.justification: Reported group-shift results change from means and standard deviations over three trainings in v1 Table 1 to six in v3 Table 2. Appendix B additionally states that synthetic datasets are generated once and ImageNet training is performed once per method. The uncertainty-reporting framework otherwise remains mean plus standard deviation, without new confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Core results are replaced under revised conditions: ConfiG's ViT-T ImageNet accuracy is 93.3% in v1 Table 2 and 80.02% in v3 Table 3, which is not a same-setting performance decline. Substantial new results include BAR, where ConfiG's mean SMA is 58.66% versus Diff-Mix's 59.28%, and Oxford Pets, where ConfiG trails both evaluated baselines at the smaller augmentation budget.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 changes generation from original-class latent optimization to inter-class prompt-to-prompt initialization followed by optimization toward a different target class. Equation 7 changes from maximizing teacher confidence plus transformed student uncertainty to minimizing student confidence plus transformed teacher uncertainty, jointly optimizing latent, null-text and conditioning. Appendix E also introduces a Hyper-SD variant using IP-Adapter guidance.

P1.justification: The method exposition is reorganized into named discussions of empirical motivation, latent optimization, inter-class mixing and the auxiliary student. Experimental and limitations prose is extensively rewritten, and implementation material is consolidated into Appendix B. The former A.1–A.13 appendix structure is substantially reordered into topical Appendices A–O, with some analyses moved out of the main text.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a different document template and extensively redesigns tables and figures. The large ERM/EDRM comparison table becomes separate comparison and ablation tables; v1's combined Table 2 is separated into ImageNet results and appendix diagnostics. Qualitative panels now emphasize inter-class mixing stages, with new failure-case and generator-variant displays, additional diagnostic plots and revised legends and captions.

R1.justification: The cited literature substantially expands around inter-class augmentation, prompt-to-prompt editing, consistency models, Hyper-SD, IP-Adapter and newer augmentation and robustness research. Diff-Mix becomes explicit motivation for a method component, while additional discussion positions ConfiG relative to fast diffusion and context-guided generation. These are substantive additions beyond citation renumbering or publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix A replaces v1's infinity-norm approximation assumptions with a KL-divergence teacher bound and explicit risk-gap assumptions. Proposition 1 revises the mixing-rate constraint and changes the final bound from min{Ω−Θ, Ω/2} to max{Ω−αΘ, Ω/2}. The lemma and proof are rewritten, and a new derivation connects teacher-label concentration and confidence separation to the required risk gap.

improvement.justification: v3 repairs the unsupported final bound in v1's Proposition 1 and explicitly limits the theory's practical interpretation. It replaces the specially fine-tuned bird teacher, which v1 acknowledged was impractical, with a zero-shot procedure, strengthens component and applicability testing, and documents systematic approximate compute matching. Failure cases and unfavorable Oxford Pets results provide useful boundaries. Although some earlier ablations are lost and changed settings prevent direct performance comparisons, the gains in mathematical soundness, experimental scrutiny and reproducibility substantially improve the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ConfiG research work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, tables and figures, and support reliable comparison despite substantial methodological and experimental revisions.

after.justification: v3 reports original experiments on CelebA-HQ, SpuCo Birds, BAR and ImageNet-100, plus Oxford Pets experiments and extensive appendix analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification and distillation experiments on CelebA, SpuCo Birds and Spurious ImageNet, together with quantitative ablations and qualitative augmentation examples.

results.title: Improving Knowledge Distillation Under Unknown Covariate Shift Through Confidence-Guided Data Augmentation

C1.justification: Beyond the retained sampling- and resolution-generalization claims, v2 adds headline claims of being the first neural-operator CT framework and strong robustness under dataset transfer and noisy measurements. These broaden the claimed novelty and applicability. The abstract's average CNN advantage changes from over 4 dB to over 3.4 dB, while the diffusion speedup claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of rate-specific overfitting, joint-training comparisons, and noise/transfer results as evidence of clinical robustness. Appendix D newly argues for DISCO's locality and efficiency relative to alternative operators and distinguishes matched-configuration costs from full CTO's additional computation. These explanations substantially extend v1's discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, detailed architectures and training settings for the new baselines, per-batch sampling-rate selection, hyperparameter-search procedures, exact parameter/FLOP counts, and inference kernel-caching information. The batch-size disclosure is also revised. These materially expand reproducibility information; actual online code availability was not verified.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained kidney and AAPM datasets, v2 adds LIDC-IDRI lung CT evaluation, clean-training/noisy-testing conditions, kidney-to-AAPM transfer, and super-resolution with increased detector sampling. These substantially broaden the represented data and acquisition conditions. Nine-view evaluation already existed in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds MDPRNet, Learned Primal-Dual, LEARN, and RegFormer to the corresponding AAPM and kidney benchmark comparisons while retaining the original comparators. LEARN and RegFormer also join the super-resolution comparisons, and RegFormer is added to the runtime table.

E3.justification: v2 introduces single-rate versus joint-training controls, 72-view-trained baseline tests at other rates, a matched-parameter/FLOP control, and additional detector-resolution and noisy-input protocols. The reported training batch size changes from 16 in v1 Section 5.2 to 8 in v2 Appendix B.3; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun. Existing kidney/AAPM splits and reconstruction metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original padding and Fourier-axis ablations are retained. v2 adds removal of individual operators and sinogram branches, Bayesian hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, noise and cross-dataset robustness tests, single-rate training controls, and matched-capacity cost-versus-accuracy analysis. These investigate several previously untested explanations for CTO's performance.

E5.justification: Appendix C.4 and Table 6 newly report random-forest feature-importance estimates and Pearson correlations for the hyperparameter sweep. Existing plus/minus reporting is retained. Neither version specifies repeated-training run counts or seeds, and v2 adds no confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The original benchmark table values are retained after relocation, apart from equivalent rounding. v2 adds extensive comparator, control, robustness, and lung CT results: Appendix C.5 reports CTO advantages of 3.06 dB under noise and 9.8 dB under dataset transfer; Table 11 reports 31.11 versus 29.14 dB at matched capacity. The supplementary reconstruction figure also changes CNN/SART annotations from 31.08/26.71 to 31.80/26.75.

M1.justification: The proposed CTO retains its spatial and frequency sinogram branches, averaged outputs, flipped circular padding, image-space DISCO operators, three reconstruction cascades, data consistency, and MSE objective. Expanded explanations and additional ablation configurations do not establish a revision to the proposed method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work discussion, and experimental framing are extensively rewritten. AAPM replaces kidney CT as the main quantitative focus, existing analyses move between the main text and supplement, and the supplementary structure is reorganized. The title changes from Resolution-Independent to Resolution-Agnostic, with accompanying author and affiliation edits.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column to a single-column layout. Figure 1 is redesigned, benchmark tables gain rows and method categories, AAPM and kidney tables exchange main/supplement placement, and Table 2 combines a new training-rate comparison with timing results. Additional analysis tables are introduced, while the existing supplementary figures are reordered and resized.

R1.justification: The accelerated-CT discussion substantially expands, including LEARN, RegFormer, QN-Mixer, MDPRNet, and explicit positioning against Fan et al.'s multi-rate MVMS-RCN. New discussion distinguishes earlier multi-rate approaches from CTO's cross-resolution formulation and asserts first application of neural operators to sparse-view CT. Several earlier classical-reconstruction citations are removed.

T1.justification: The reconstruction equations, Fourier-slice relationship, and Appendix A equivariance derivation remain unchanged. New Appendix D adds a secondary mathematical complexity analysis, specifying operator configurations and asymptotic costs for FNO, DISCO, LocalNO, and DeepONet, plus an argument about pre-discretized DISCO inference cost.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central performance claim. Tables 8 and 11 add training-regime and matched-capacity controls absent from v1's reported comparisons; the matched control retains a 31.11 versus 29.14 dB advantage with equal parameters and FLOPs. Broader baselines, component ablations, and robustness tests address important gaps in comparative evidence. New lung and transfer protocols remain briefly specified, and the batch-size revision is unexplained, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental support and reproducibility disclosure.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CTO research, despite the title and formatting changes. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete supplementary material support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, lung CT evaluation, distribution-shift tests, and additional controlled analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction experiments on kidney and AAPM CT data, super-resolution results, runtime measurements, and padding and Fourier-transform ablations.

results.title: Resolution-Agnostic Neural Operators for Multi-Rate Sparse-View CT

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion redefine the central contribution from Nano-3D's custom multi-module depth network to passive nanophotonic prompting of depth foundation models without architectural additions. V2 adds central claims about reducing the simulation-to-real gap and achieving performance comparable to LiDAR-assisted PromptDA, replacing the earlier emphasis on the compact custom network and commercial-camera comparisons.

C2.justification: V2 explains simulator artifacts and domain-transfer mechanisms, and distinguishes ground-truth-aligned baseline geometry from direct metric prediction. It expands v1's planar-label approximation into explicit cautions about nonplanarity, segmentation error and approximate physical scores. Limitations now emphasize restricted field of view, tube length and absent outdoor validation; v1's shift-extractor texture dependence and four-second runtime discussion disappear.

D1.justification: V2 supplies simulator equations and background-extension pseudocode, spectral/depth sampling details, fine-tuning schedules and real-data mixing instructions. It revises the documented fabrication recipe, including o-xylene to amyl acetate development and CHF3/Ar/O2 to BCl3/Ar etching; this establishes changed documentation, not necessarily newly fabricated hardware. V1's promise to release the implementation upon acceptance is absent.

E1.justification: V2 Appendix A adds evaluation using NYU Depth V2's real indoor imagery and MPI Sintel's animated scenes, broadening the represented domains beyond v1's MIT-CGH-4K simulated evaluation and physical object captures. Hypersim training and the earlier general categories of synthetic and physical depth sensing remain.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained DepthAnything V2 and Depth Pro comparisons, v2 evaluates Lotus, Marigold, Metric3D V2, UniDepth V2, ZoeDepth, LiDAR-assisted PromptDA and fine-tuned DepthAnything controls. V1's Intel RealSense D455 comparison and Shen et al. contour-matching comparison are absent from v2's reported evaluations.

E3.justification: The reported working range narrows from 20–150 cm to 20–120 cm, simulated testing changes from 1024×768 processing to native resolutions, and physical evaluation expands from 28 to 42 scenes. V2 introduces held-out Hypersim testing and three backbone sizes. Its metric suite uses L1, RMSE, AbsRel and delta_0.5 instead of v1's AbsRel, delta_1/2/3 and binary accuracy; new PromptDA simulations use downsampled, noisy ground-truth depth.

E4.justification: V1's shift-extraction and centrosymmetric-matching ablations are replaced by tests of polarization prompting, foundation-model initialization, simulator refinement, individual augmentations and one/three/five real training examples (v2 Table 3). V2 Figure 4 adds analysis of simulator boundary and aliasing artifacts. V1's dedicated low-texture failure examples are no longer presented as a failure analysis.

E5.justification: Mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting continues for simulated results, moving from v1 Table 2 to v2's supplementary comparison tables. However, v2's physical results and ablations report point estimates without the variability accompanying v1's physical depth estimates. Neither version reports training seeds, repeated-training-run counts or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: V1 reports MIT-CGH-4K AbsRel of 0.13 ± 0.07 and physical AbsRel of 0.21 ± 0.07. V2 reports 0.1023 ± 0.0159 and 0.0594, respectively, for Ours-Base (Tables 8 and 2). These are replacement results under changed methods, ranges and protocols, not controlled version-to-version gains. V2 adds extensive benchmark and ablation results while dropping v1's model-size and binary-accuracy results.

M1.justification: V1's explicit PSF-shift extractor and U-Net depth decoder are replaced by fine-tuning DepthAnything V2 on pseudo-RGB inputs containing both polarization channels and their average. V2 also introduces PSF splatting with occlusion/disocclusion handling, polarization-aware augmentation and few-shot real-data adaptation. These substantially change training and inference while retaining the birefringent optical design.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten around foundation-model prompting. Related work becomes background plus related work, and the supplements are reorganized into experiments, software and hardware. Optical derivations and implementation material are redistributed, with v1's duplicated implementation discussion consolidated.

P2.justification: V2 redesigns the overview and computational diagrams, adds simulator-artifact illustrations and replaces most result displays with baseline comparison grids and error-map insets. Tables now distinguish fine-tuning, post-alignment and LiDAR assistance through structured columns and color coding. The PSF validation, meta-unit library and fabrication illustrations are retained or reorganized rather than entirely new.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions the work around physically prompting foundation models, contrasting passive optics with LiDAR-based prompting and conventional computational imaging. It adds substantial depth-foundation, prompting, transformer and splatting literature, including PromptDA, while reducing the dedicated fabrication-literature discussion in v1 Section 2.3.

T1.justification: The rotating-PSF relationship and much of its optical derivation are retained, but v2 Appendix E introduces a substantial mathematical rendering model: normalized Gaussian depth distributions, PSF-derived opacity and continuity-dependent compositing. This changes the modeling assumptions beyond simple point-source superposition. The focusing-phase expression also gains the missing -2π/λ factor (v1 Equation 6; v2 Equation 4).

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence for physical depth cues through matched fine-tuning controls, component ablations and broader domain testing, addressing v1's narrow validation. Simulator analysis and clearer qualifications of physical ground truth also improve scientific accountability. These gains outweigh reduced physical uncertainty reporting and unresolved baseline-score inconsistencies, such as fine-tuned DepthAnything V2's Hypersim L1 of 0.0635 in Table 1 versus 0.0739 in Table 7. The improvement rests on stronger validation and explanation, not direct comparison of errors obtained under changed settings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same underlying metasurface depth-imaging work, sharing the optical design, hardware specifications and PSF measurements despite substantial computational revisions and a new title. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original simulated evaluations across four datasets, experiments on 42 physical scenes and component ablations, alongside retained optical measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original PSF measurements, simulated depth-estimation results, experiments on 28 physical scenes and network ablations in Section 4 and the supplements.

results.title: Physically Grounded Monocular Depth via Nanophotonic Wavefront Encoding

C1.justification: The central contribution remains passive, single-shot metric depth estimation combining a metalens with pretrained depth priors. v3 extends the abstract, introduction and conclusion's performance claim to competing depth-from-defocus methods, broadening the claim beyond v2's monocular-model comparisons without replacing the principal research contribution.

C2.justification: v3 develops explanations separating pretrained-prior benefits from architecture and optical-design effects, and interpreting feature preservation and PSF noise robustness. Section 5 adds specific limitations involving photon throughput, longer exposures, polarization-dependent sampling and noise, and high-frequency imbalance from reflections or polarized illumination. These substantially extend v2's discussion of field of view, depth range, tube length and approximate labels.
