D1.justification: v3 supplies technical details for new comparisons, including two-channel decoder-fusion input, the scaled optics' 1.7 m focus distance, double-helix rotation, and photon/background settings. The original fabrication instructions, sensor specifications, training hyperparameters, A100 hardware and training-time disclosure are retained.

E1.justification: v3 adds FlyingThings3D evaluation at a 1–5 m optical operating range and simulated and physical moving-object sequences testing temporal depth consistency. NYU Depth V2, MPI Sintel, Hypersim and MIT-CGH-4K already appeared in v2; their redistribution between the main text and appendices is not additional coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds Depth Anything v3 and MoGe v2 to the NYU, MIT-CGH-4K and physical comparisons. Table 3 newly benchmarks DeepDfD and Split-Aperture, which v2 cited without evaluating. Appendix I also introduces comparisons against double-helix and conventional-lens PSFs.

E3.justification: The new DfD protocol uses a 5-mm-diameter metalens, 50-mm focal length, 1–5 m range, capacity-matched Small backbone, and log10 and delta1 metrics. New controls vary optics, architecture, pretraining and inclusion of real training data. For retained 100-sample benchmarks, v2 Appendix A.1 specifies validation splits whereas v3 Appendix D.1 specifies test splits; this is a reported setting revision without evidence establishing reruns.

E4.justification: v3 adds controlled optics/architecture/pretraining and input-fusion ablations, CKA feature analysis, backbone transfer, motion consistency, and photon-budget, edge-orientation and PSF-ambiguity analyses. Its sim-to-real ablations test components with and without real training data. Conversely, v2 Table 3's one- and three-real-sample sensitivity results are removed.

E5.justification: v3 newly states that average physical-label uncertainty is below 1 cm; v2 only describes approximate labels and their error sources. The retained benchmark tables use unchanged mean-and-standard-deviation reporting. Neither version specifies a repeated-run, seed or significance-testing protocol.

E6.justification: Substantial new results accompany the DfD comparisons, ablations, backbone transfer and PSF analyses. v3 Table 3 reports MAE 0.022 for Ours-Small versus 0.089 for DeepDfD and 0.086 for Split-Aperture. Physical Ours-Base results change from MAE/L1 0.0344 and RMSE 0.0810 to 0.032 and 0.089 in Table 2. The four retained appendix benchmark tables have identical numerical entries across versions.

M1.justification: The polarization-to-pseudo-RGB mapping, rotating-PSF design, DPT fine-tuning objectives and simulator procedure are retained. v2 Appendix E and v3 Appendix H contain matching soft-slicing, compositing and background-completion equations and Algorithm 1. Renaming 'PSF splatting' and testing additional optical scales or backbones do not establish a changed core method.

P1.justification: The title changes from 'Wavefront Prompting' to 'Wavefront Encoding,' and substantial passages in the abstract, related work, input adaptation and simulator explanation are rewritten. Experiments are reorganized around monocular-model versus DfD comparisons, and the appendix structure expands and reorganizes the original material.

P2.justification: v3 changes the document from two-column to single-column layout and extensively rearranges figures and tables. It adds input-compatibility and disocclusion panels, feature-similarity plots, new comparison and ablation tables, motion sequences, and CRLB/correlation figures. Existing benchmark displays are also relocated and reformatted.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts substantially toward computational optics, DfD, dual-pixel and birefractive imaging. v3 adds discussion and citations including PS2F and defocus-based Marigold, and distinguishes its simulator from earlier alpha-compositing approaches. Stereo-matching and Gaussian-splatting references and their associated motivation are removed.

T1.justification: New Appendix I introduces a Poisson observation model with background, Fisher information and Cramer–Rao bounds for depth and joint depth–edge-orientation estimation, plus inverse-problem conditioning arguments. This substantially expands the formal analysis beyond v2's diffraction and rotating-PSF derivations, which remain in v3 Appendix J.

improvement.justification: Direct DfD comparisons and controlled optics, architecture and pretraining ablations address important gaps in v2's comparative evidence and attribution of gains. Appendix I strengthens the optical rationale, while Section 5 gives substantially clearer practical limitations. These benefits outweigh the removal of one-/three-shot sensitivity results and isolated reporting problems, notably v3 Table 7's real-data RMSE of 0.0096 below its MAE of 0.0348. The improvement primarily concerns evidential support and explanation, rather than a changed core method.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same metalens-based depth-estimation system. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite renaming, reorganization and substantial additions.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds DfD comparisons, controlled ablations, backbone-transfer experiments, moving-object demonstrations and numerical PSF analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original simulated benchmark results, a 42-scene physical evaluation, component and few-shot ablations, and measured metalens responses.

results.title: Physically Grounded Monocular Depth via Nanophotonic Wavefront Encoding

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same novelty claim and three contributions: SKIM, SOMA's coupled deformation model, and propagation to individual muscles. The conclusion is lightly shortened without redefining the claimed contribution.

C2.justification: Section 6 newly acknowledges that force- and co-contraction-driven variation at a fixed joint angle remains unmodeled. Supplementary Section 5 also interprets reduced biceps/brachialis visibility at peak flexion as geometric occlusion while noting continued visibility of lateral bulging and the brachioradialis.

D1.justification: The supplement supplies extensive previously unavailable reproduction details: marker encoding and annotation, dataset organization, mesh specifications, trajectory refinement, network dimensions and activations, Adam training for 20 epochs with batch size 128 and learning rate 0.0001, loss weights, metric definitions, and muscle binding. The project URL and code/data availability claim are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the five-subject SKIM dataset for pose-driven skin and muscle deformation. V2 supplies demographics, acquisition routines, and more examples from that dataset; it does not establish an added dataset, population, or distinct evaluation task.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains LBS and HIT via SMPL as comparators. Tables 3–4 retain the same architecture and regularization variants. Supplementary baseline descriptions clarify these existing comparisons without adding evaluated methods.

E3.justification: Supplementary Section 5 introduces a visibility-evaluation procedure aggregating coverage across frames and subjects, separating motions, and plotting per-frame elbow-flexor visibility during curls. No protocol revision is reported for the retained benchmarks; newly supplied training settings document existing experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds an analysis of marker coverage and pose-dependent occlusion, including elbow-flexor visibility histograms, plus a biceps case study at minimum and maximum flexion. The original architecture and loss ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for its experiments. The new visibility histograms describe variation across observed frames rather than uncertainty in estimated model performance.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 retain their numerical results, including SOMA's 13.43 mm MPME. Supplementary Figure 3 adds coverage results, including 82.1% overall, 94.6% for triceps extensions, and 65.0% for push-ups. Supplementary Figures 4–5 add motion-specific and biceps deformation results.

M1.justification: The pose-driven muscle/skin decomposition, two U-Nets, canonical marker-residual supervision, regularizers, LBS, and barycentric muscle transfer remain unchanged. The supplement documents previously described components without establishing a revised algorithm.

P1.justification: V2 substantially expands explanations through a structured supplement covering dataset construction, marker refinement, experimental setup, volume computation, visibility, qualitative examples, and muscle transfer. The main narrative remains largely intact, with limited conclusion/caption edits and an added acknowledgements section.

P2.justification: The supplement adds subject and annotation illustrations, visibility histograms, extensive deformation panels, and tables documenting demographics, meshes, motions, and dataset size. Existing main figures are retained but resized or reflowed, notably Figures 6–7; Figure 4 and ablation-table captions are refined.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations including Dynamic FAUST, detailed moving-body capture, SFLsh, SoftSMPL, biharmonic weights, muscle incompressibility, and elasticity theory. These broaden supporting references without substantially changing the positioning against surface-only models, inverse anatomy methods, and simulations.

T1.justification: Supplementary Section 4 adds a focused derivation of signed prism volume using FEM shape functions, Jacobian integration, and polynomial-degree arguments establishing exact two-node Gauss–Legendre quadrature. V1 states this computation but does not contain the derivation; the existing regularizer is unchanged.

improvement.justification: V1 defers essential reproduction details to a supplement absent from the supplied PDF. V2 supplies architecture, optimization, preprocessing, and volume-computation details, substantially improving reproducibility and scrutiny. Visibility evidence and the fixed-angle force limitation also improve transparency. Local documentation problems remain, including 2,310 markers versus the stated 1,000 IDs with two instances, but do not outweigh these substantial gains. The main benchmark evidence is unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SOMA, with matching authors, methods, and main experiments. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. The supplied v1 ends after its references; v2 additionally includes the supplement referenced by both versions.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds measured marker-visibility results and additional qualitative deformation examples in supplementary Sections 5–6.

before.justification: V1 reports original SKIM experiments comparing SOMA with LBS and HIT, quantitative architecture and regularization ablations, and qualitative deformation results in Section 5.

results.title: SOMA: From Surface Observations to Muscle Anatomy

C1.justification: The benchmark–metrics–mitigation contribution structure remains. V2 narrows benchmark novelty from the first real-world illusion benchmark to the combination of paired context variation and complex ROI annotation, while broadening the stated target from planar to planar/low-curvature surfaces. These qualify the retained central claims.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly presents DCS/CCS as reference-free structural probes that complement ground-truth metrics and cannot guarantee metric-depth accuracy. It expands the explanation of piecewise-surface grounding, qualifies model-capacity interpretations, and acknowledges that genuine road hazards remain untested. The earlier untested-diffusion limitation becomes a qualified transfer-feasibility finding. These materially sharpen applicability and interpretation.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents the source-image-level 90/10 split, scene and pair counts, three-pixel ring and one-pixel guard construction, and backbone-specific adaptation details. It supplies code and dataset addresses where v1 promised future release. The split is newly disclosed, not demonstrably newly introduced. A reporting inconsistency remains: the main text gives a 1.2% trainable fraction while Appendix J retains 0.7%.

E1.justification: V2 adds actual evaluation on 3D-Visual-Illusion, KITTI15, and Depth-in-the-Wild, substantially extending external illusion and general-depth coverage. Appendix B adds matched non-illusory and Gaussian-perturbed test scenarios. The original 468-scene benchmark and Penn-Fudan/CamVid training data remain; DA-2K evaluation already appeared in v1's appendix.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains its foundation-model comparator roster. V2's new 3DVI comparison includes additional methods such as Metric3D, DUSt3R, VGGT, RAFT-Stereo, Selective-RAFT, and 3DVI. Table 5 adds Simple L1 adaptation and decoder finetuning; encoder finetuning was already evaluated in v1. These substantially broaden the reported comparisons.

E3.justification: The stated crop requirement changes from retaining at least 40% of the ROI diagonal to the ROI occupying at least 40% of crop area. DCS/CCS aggregation is revised, and v2 adds standard depth metrics and globally affine-aligned 3DVI evaluation. Appendix Table A changes the duration study from epochs 1/2/4/6 to 1/2/3/4. These are reported protocol changes; they do not establish which earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a four-scene, sixteen-crop illusion-removal/noise control, loss-weight sensitivity tests, backbone-transfer analyses, simpler adaptation ablations, and a curved-surface case study. The original loss-removal tests remain, but v1's separate epoch trajectories for each removed loss and its extended-training visualization are removed. The questions tested and supporting analyses change substantially.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for its experiments. Additional epochs, model variants, and control conditions do not introduce repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes the proposed method's DCS/CCS from 64.20/2.036e-4 to 58.64/1.907e-4, and ZoeDepth's from 467.7/1.001e-3 to 589.3/1.505e-3. Ablation and duration results are revised, and extensive external-dataset, control, and transfer results are added. Because definitions and settings also change, these updated scores do not establish a same-setting improvement between versions.

M1.justification: The dual-view LoRA pipeline, plane mixture, and HKR/NKP losses remain. Section 4.3 revises the reported objective: the null expert and optional entropy term disappear, negative images receive preservation-only training, and the background mask excludes the entire adjacent ring. Appendix I adds backbone-specific adapter placements for ZoeDepth and Marigold. These refine and extend the retained method.

P1.justification: Beyond changing the title, v2 systematically revises terminology, rewrites the metric and loss explanations, replaces the formal desired-objective presentation with conceptual properties, and condenses the original ablation narrative. The appendix is reorganized around implementation, controls, transfer, and safety. These constitute substantial explanatory and structural editing.

P2.justification: V2 switches from two-column to single-column presentation and redraws the pipeline to show teacher supervision and local-plane fitting in both branches. It adds annotation, curvature, transfer, boundary, and control illustrations; merges the two qualitative loss-ablation figures; and restructures the tables. Most older appendix images are retained and relocated, rather than newly added.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 adds substantive positioning against Yao et al.'s 3D Visual Illusion work and Booster, distinguishing monocular context sensitivity from binocular fusion and reflective-surface challenges. This supports the narrowed novelty claim. Additional stereo, multi-view, and metric-depth references accompany actual comparisons, substantially expanding the relevant research context.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 substantively revises the mathematical definitions. V1 defines per-instance scores using ROI sums and per-pixel averages; v2 defines DCS through the norm of the dataset centroid and average instance norms, and CCS through corresponding off-diagonal projections. The formal carrier assumption also broadens from physically planar to locally low-curvature or piecewise-smooth. These are more than notation changes.

improvement.justification: V1 primarily validates mitigation through its own structural scores and limited preservation checks. V2 adds external ground-truth 3DVI evaluation, broader standard-depth checks, targeted metric controls, and transfer experiments, substantially strengthening validation. Explicit scene-level splitting and boundary implementation details improve reproducibility, while the revised pipeline figure better matches the method description. Some detailed training analyses are lost and reporting inconsistencies remain, but the gains clearly outweigh these limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same 3D-Mirage benchmark and Grounded Self-Distillation research, despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark and adaptation results, external-dataset evaluations, metric controls, and backbone-transfer experiments in Tables 1–5 and the appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, adaptation results, loss ablations, and training-duration experiments in Tables 1–2 and Appendix Tables A–C.

results.title: The 3D Mirage: Probing and Taming 3D Hallucinations

C1.justification: The central claims of training-free initial-noise optimization and superior image-inpainting performance remain. v3 qualifies the novelty framing by explicitly acknowledging earlier noise optimization and identifying its gradient approximation with the straight-through estimator. It sharpens the contribution around Adam-based spectral preconditioning and reduced need for learning-rate tuning.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the mechanism explanation through Adam's per-frequency normalization and globally coupled updates. It discusses learning-rate, blur and divergence tradeoffs, qualifies trajectory linearity near the final denoising steps, and explains applicability to non-flow backbones. These go beyond v1's empirical rationale and broad future-work discussion.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies the spatial-ablation learning rate of 0.05, identifies Claude Sonnet 4.5, and adds implementation settings and exact runtime/memory information. The original implementation recipe and prompt templates largely persist. The explicit code-release promise disappears, but the PDFs do not establish a change in actual code availability.

E1.justification: FFHQ, DIV2K and BrushBench coverage and their mask scenarios are retained. v3 adds full-image inversion of synthetic SD3.5 outputs for convergence testing and describes preliminary Wan video inpainting. The video outputs themselves are only linked externally, limiting assessment of that extension.

E2.justification: The original benchmark comparator sets remain. Appendix H/Table 7 adds InitNo, GoldenNoise and FreeInpaint, including FreeInpaint with BrushNet and BLD-SD3.5; Appendix I/Table 8 adds SD3 ControlNet inpainting. These substantially expand comparisons with relevant noise-optimization and trained methods. FlowOpt and DiNG are discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a randomized, single-blind 2AFC study with 37 raters and 45 scenes, controlled synthetic-image inversion using shared initializations and RMSE, SD1.5/SDXL backbone evaluations, and 10/20/30-iteration budgets. These substantially expand evaluation design; the original main benchmark splits and inpainting settings are retained.

E4.justification: The original component ablations remain, but the single-example convergence analysis becomes a systematic Adam/SGD and learning-rate comparison. Appendices B/C add velocity-linearity diagnostics and latent/noise convergence analyses; Appendix J adds iteration sensitivity. New CLIP-scored qualitative cases examine disagreement between metric scores and visual consistency.

E5.justification: v1 contains no formal uncertainty analysis. v3 Appendix A/Table 5 introduces aggregate and per-baseline 95% confidence intervals for human preference and claims statistically significant advantages. The interval construction and significance test are unspecified, and uncertainty across repeated benchmark runs remains unreported.

E6.justification: v3 adds preference results of 90.0% (1,498/1,665), runtime/memory measurements, baseline scores and analysis results. Tables 1, 2 and 4 also revise existing IR, HPS, CLIP and some AS values: FFHQ SONIC IR changes from 0.114 to 0.280 and CLIP from 20.773 to 24.042, while PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FID remain fixed. The revisions are unexplained, and Table 9 retains older FFHQ values. Revised DIV2K HPS favors BLD, 0.255 versus SONIC's 0.253.

M1.justification: The image-inpainting objective, linearization, spectral Adam optimization, gradient masking and nearest-neighbor filling remain unchanged. Appendix D adds a limited video adaptation: temporal latent masks use the first frame's mask followed by max-pooling over groups of four mask frames.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work and methodological explanations, replaces contribution bullets with themed paragraphs, and standardizes terminology around initial noise samples, spectral preconditioning and spatial constraints. The supplement is reorganized into Sections A–L, with existing prompts and qualitative grids moved to K/L.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation, relocating and resizing figures and tables. Figure 5 is rebuilt as a multi-configuration convergence plot, and new study/analysis figures and Tables 5–9 are added. The original three supplementary qualitative grids are retained as Figures 16–18, rather than new results.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work substantially broaden positioning around earlier GAN inversion, diffusion/flow noise optimization and back-propagation workarounds. Added discussion includes straight-through estimation, D-Flow, DiNG, InitNo and GoldenNoise. The relationship to concurrent FlowOpt is refined from a similar update equation to explicit straight-through equivalence and differentiation through spectral preconditioning.

T1.justification: v1 provides objective and linearization equations without a theoretical treatment of the spectral advantage. v3 Appendix F adds Fourier-domain gradient derivations, SGD-equivalence and Adam-non-equivalence arguments, and short-horizon complexity assertions. These are substantial mathematical additions; the explicit spectral objective in Equation 4 mainly restates the existing method.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens two weaknesses in v1: reliance on proxy preference metrics and limited evidence explaining the spectral advantage. The human study, controlled optimizer comparisons and relevant noise-optimization baselines provide stronger tests of perceptual benefit and mechanism. These gains outweigh reporting defects, including Table 9's unreconciled older scores and the retained DIV2K HPS superiority claim contradicting Table 2. Appendix F's unsupported O(N) propagation assertion also limits the value of the new theory.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SONIC work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and can be matched across substantial restructuring. The video demonstration linked from v3 is not included in the supplied material.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original human-preference results, convergence analyses, baseline comparisons and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative and qualitative inpainting experiments on FFHQ, DIV2K and BrushBench, plus component ablations.

results.title: SONIC: Spectral Optimization of Noise for Inpainting with Consistency

C1.justification: The joint framework, iterative refinement, annotated dataset, and at-least-33% attached-BER reduction claims remain. V2's introduction adds a concrete claim that separate masks improve shadow removal. Its conclusion more specifically emphasizes improved attached detection while maintaining strong cast performance.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of video examples as temporal robustness and the ground-truth-mask light estimator as an approximate performance bound. It expands lighting limitations to extended sources and strong indirect illumination, but removes the explicit limitation about associating cast and attached shadows with individual objects. The central geometry-based explanation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: The new supplement documents the PVT-b5 encoder, input/output adaptations, SBU initialization, 0.05 encoder learning-rate multiplier, TITAN RTX hardware and two-GPU training, normal computation, annotation corrections, and light-direction construction. V2 also adds a project-page address. These substantially expand reproducibility information without demonstrating changes to the underlying implementation.

E1.justification: V2 extends evaluation beyond the curated detection dataset to SRD images, SBU-TimeLapse static-scene videos, and ViSha dynamic-scene videos. It also evaluates downstream shadow removal through human preferences. These introduce substantial coverage of new data environments and task requirements; the original training sources remain.

E2.justification: The seven detection methods and four fine-tuned baselines in main Table 2 are retained. Supplementary Table 1 adds BDRAR†+Normal and SILT†+Normal. New experiments also compare against a standalone light estimator supplied with ground-truth masks and joint-mask ShadowFormer removal. These supplement the existing comparison suite.

E3.justification: New protocols include independent framewise video inference, light-direction MAE evaluation on 42 calibrated WSRD test images, and a randomized preference study with a 40-question pool, 20 questions per participant, and 259 collected votes. V2 also reports shadow/non-shadow error breakdowns. The original training budget and split remain unchanged. CUHK's reported contribution changes from 538 to 528 images, reconciling the stated total without establishing that images were removed.

E4.justification: V2 adds evidence testing whether normal inputs help competing detectors, whether iterative feedback improves light estimation relative to a ground-truth-mask control, and whether predictions generalize to changing shadows in videos. The original geometry, iteration, and loss ablations remain. The earlier multi-object pairing failure example is omitted.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's vote totals and preference percentages are new results, while question randomization is an evaluation-design addition; neither introduces uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Main Tables 2–3 retain their numerical results. Newly reported outcomes include 80.7% preference for separate-mask refinement (209/259 votes), light MAE of 0.061, 0.050, and 0.049 across iterations versus 0.034 with ground-truth masks, normal-augmented baseline scores, additional runtime entries, and cross-dataset predictions. Some duplicated values disagree: BDRAR attached F1 is 53.32 in main Table 2 but 52.32 in supplementary Table 1, leaving the intended value unresolved.

M1.justification: The detection architecture, iterative feedback, and training losses remain unchanged. Section 5.4 adds a downstream procedure using ShadowFormer with joint-mask removal followed by attached-mask refinement within the object region. Supplementary architecture descriptions document the existing detector rather than establish a redesign.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten, with stronger application-led motivation. Problem setup and framework descriptions are consolidated, method subsections are reorganized, and dedicated generalization, application, and supplementary sections reshape the narrative.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout and substantially rearranges existing figures. V1's problem-setup example reappears in supplementary Figure 12. V2 adds removal, video, light-estimation, and dataset-curation displays, groups the ablation table by topic, and introduces expanded supplementary tables.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion of MetaShadow and directional-light video research, plus references supporting ShadowFormer, depth estimation, and the encoder. Several classical shadow/illumination references are removed. The main positioning against methods that merge or overlook attached shadows remains intact.

T1.justification: The single-directional-light assumption, normal–light dot-product rule, and loss mathematics are retained. V2 combines the three light-loss equations into one numbered equation. Additional geometry-preparation details document existing operations rather than introduce substantive theory, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1 by quantitatively evaluating the claimed light-estimation feedback, adding geometry-informed comparison controls, and supplying substantial architecture and dataset-curation details. Cross-dataset examples and the removal study broaden supporting evidence without changing the original benchmark scores. These gains outweigh the dropped instance-pairing caveat and reporting weaknesses, including inconsistent duplicated scores, unclear normal/light coordinate conventions, and incomplete user-study uncertainty reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dataset and iterative shadow–light framework, with matching core equations and experimental tables despite the changed title and format. All pages are readable. V2 includes supplementary material absent from the supplied v1 PDF.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original cross-dataset predictions, light-estimation evaluations, and a shadow-removal user study.

before.justification: V1 reports original shadow-detection comparisons, qualitative predictions, and geometry, iteration, and loss ablations in Section 5.

results.title: Cast and Attached Shadow Detection via Iterative Light and Geometry Reasoning

C1.justification: The central contribution remains reconstruction through local patch diffusion and global optical guidance. v3 explicitly includes experimental validation, narrows the priority claim from the first demonstration to one of the first, and reframes prospective camera benefits as a tradeoff between optical and computational complexity.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limits concerning homogeneous regions, restricted propagation of global context, and suitability for fast capture rather than fast reconstruction. It also explains misregistration tolerance and simulation-to-hardware discrepancies, interprets LoRA's effects, and expands discussion of what chromatic aberration contributes relative to RGB filtering.

D1.justification: v3 supplies fabrication procedures, laser-based PSF characterization, geometric and spectral calibration, and detailed LoRA settings absent from v2. It also discloses gradient checkpointing and high-resolution reconstruction times. Some information is lost: v2's explicit lens-design repository availability statement and several configuration-table details are not retained.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained ARAD1K, ICVL, Harvard, and CAVE coverage, v3 adds real tabletop measurements from a fabricated metalens, CASSI reconstruction on KAIST at benchmark and higher resolutions, and synthetic checkerboards with controlled spatial homogeneity. These introduce substantial new physical and input-condition coverage.

E2.justification: The original eight ARAD1K comparison methods remain. v3 adds UNet-Regress, a full-image MSE regression control using its backbone, and introduces MST-S/MST-L comparators in the new CASSI comparison. The CASSI baseline values are explicitly imported from cited work rather than reported as rerun experiments.

E3.justification: New protocols include six-scene finetuning/eight-scene prototype testing, 640×960×26 reconstruction with 10 guidance iterations, and CASSI evaluation with 28-channel outputs and uncertainty-based pixel exclusion. For retained training, reported EMA decay changes from 0.9999 to 0.99; the written PSNR formula also changes. These disclosures do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds experimental PSF shift-invariance checks, a LoRA ablation, controlled checkerboard failure analysis, backbone-regression comparisons, denoising trajectories, and per-wavelength uncertainty analysis. CASSI pixel-rejection results additionally test whether uncertainty identifies reconstruction errors. Existing patch, lens, and noise analyses are largely retained.

E5.justification: v3 supplementary Figure 7 introduces 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for per-wavelength uncertainty–error correlations. Conversely, v2 explicitly specifies 10 reconstructions with different noise seeds, whereas v3 describes repeated sampling using an unspecified N. An increase in sampling runs is not established.

E6.justification: Most original ARAD1K scores remain unchanged apart from rounding. New results include UNet-Regress at 29.12 dB, prototype averages of 31.20 dB/0.894 SSIM/0.157 SAM, and CASSI averages of 35.46 dB/0.95 SSIM under their respective settings. ICVL mean SSIM changes from 0.95 to 0.94, and v2's five-scene CAVE average is omitted.

M1.justification: The core diffusion, patch rescaling, and guidance algorithm remains. However, v3 adds a substantial physical-system adaptation using calibrated measured PSFs, spatial-offset augmentation, and rank-8 LoRA finetuning. Supplement Section 4.6 also introduces desheared-cube conditioning and CASSI-specific guidance; Section 4.3 adds an optional scheduled-guidance procedure.

P1.justification: The paper is extensively rewritten and reorganized: diffusion background and patch training are merged, cross-dataset evaluation moves earlier, optical comparison and interpretability are combined, and the supplement gains a hierarchical structure and contents list. The title and author list also change.

P2.justification: The layout changes from two columns to one, with extensive figure merging and table restructuring. v2's combined reconstruction table is split between main-text filterless results and supplementary RGB results. Numerous new prototype, calibration, uncertainty, LoRA, CASSI, and failure-analysis displays substantially expand the visual evidence.

R1.justification: v3 acknowledges concurrent filterless imaging by Liu et al. and diffusion-based uncertainty work by Romero et al., while adding references supporting metamerism, LoRA, and computational techniques. Some earlier citations, including PatchScaler, disappear. The broad research positioning remains, but exclusive priority is qualified.

T1.justification: The optical and guidance derivations are substantially retained. Limited mathematical revisions include changing the stated DDIM noise distribution from N(0, sigma_t) to N(0, sigma_t^2 I), and replacing the max(x, xhat) factor in v2's PSNR definition with a unit-peak formulation in v3 supplementary Equation 10.

improvement.justification: v2's hardware-feasibility claim relied on simulation; v3 adds a fabricated system evaluated against reference hyperspectral captures, with calibration and adaptation documented in detail. Controlled failure analyses and explicit applicability limits further strengthen empirical credibility. Reporting gaps remain, including the stated 15-scene total versus six finetuning/eight test scenes and the omitted sampling count, but these do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same optical encoding and guided patch-diffusion work, despite retitling and substantial expansion. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and included appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original simulation results and adds physical prototype measurements, tabletop reconstructions, CASSI evaluations, and controlled failure analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original simulation results, including reconstruction comparisons, model and lens ablations, cross-dataset evaluation, and measurement-noise experiments.

results.title: Filterless Snapshot Hyperspectral Imaging using Guided Patch Diffusion

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction qualify posterior sampling as approximate and uncertainty calibration as empirical, replacing stronger language about sampling the full posterior. They also clarify that the dataset contains 15,000 mock cluster observations. The principal dataset, automation, speed, and reconstruction contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly interprets the lensing losses as practical data-fidelity terms rather than exact likelihood/noise models, and calibration as evidence of marginal coverage. MACS 1206 is framed as a proof of concept, with its selection justified by absence of external convergence or shear. Appendix C newly argues that prior backbone choice is not a significant performance bottleneck.

D1.justification: New Appendix B documents MACS 1206 mosaic alignment, cropping/resampling, flux conversion, and selection of 55 images from 15 sources. Appendix C newly specifies 137 million parameters, approximately 10 hours of training, and an RTX 4090 GPU. A project-page link supplies code/data access information. These substantially improve documentation, although Table 2 drops its previous explicit WL SNR 0.01 label.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same TNG redshift coverage, SIMBA simulations, and MACS 1206 case. The revised cluster counts include redshift snapshots already described in v1; the 15,000 projections and train/test coverage remain unchanged. The new MACS appendix documents an existing experiment.

E2.justification: Kaiser–Squires inversion becomes an evaluated baseline in Table 2 and Figure 5; v1 only discussed it as prior work. Napier et al., UNet, and the MACS 1206 comparison with Caminha et al. are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds held-out deflection and shear RMSE, observed-versus-expected confidence coverage, and MACS 1206 checks using critical curves at source redshift approximately 1.44, image-position RMS, and enclosed mass within 100 kpc. These extend the evaluation protocol; the stated dataset splits, 100-cluster benchmark evaluation, and DAPS inference settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds fractional-error maps in Figure 5 and a brief DDPM++ versus Diffusion Transformer comparison in Appendix C, reporting comparable performance with higher transformer cost. It also revises the calibration analysis and expands the existing MACS 1206 case study. The input-modality ablation and appendix light–mass correlation analysis remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Figure 3 replaces RMSE-versus-predicted-standard-deviation correlation with a reliability diagram assessing observed versus expected confidence levels on held-out data, substantially changing the calibration assessment. Section 6.4 also newly reports uncertainties for enclosed mass and relative mass error across 20 generated samples. Twenty-sample reconstruction summaries already existed; an increase in sampling runs is not established.

E6.justification: Original Table 2 scores are retained, while Kaiser–Squires results and deflection/shear errors substantially expand the results. The new TNG deflection metric favors UNet over the proposed method: 0.411 versus 0.530 RMSE. MACS 1206 newly has image-position RMS of 0.56 arcseconds versus Caminha et al.'s 0.44, and enclosed mass of (7.61 ± 0.04) × 10^13 solar masses versus (7.25 ± 0.02) × 10^13. These are additional comparisons, not demonstrated improvements over v1 performance.

M1.justification: The DAPS updates, EDM objective, and lensing losses are retained. Section 5.1 changes the network input from two to four channels, but v1 Section 6.4 already says three photometry bands were used in training. The PDFs do not establish whether this reflects an architectural change or correction of an inconsistent description.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the prose remain intact. Localized rewrites clarify dataset counting, approximate inference, calibration, and comparisons. A MACS processing appendix is inserted, existing appendices are renumbered, and running author headers and acknowledgements are updated.

P2.justification: Table 2 is transposed and expanded; Figure 3's calibration plot is replaced with different axes and content; Figure 5 gains Kaiser–Squires and fractional-error columns. Figure 6 is substantially rearranged, adds critical-curve comparisons, and changes the convergence display range. These materially revise the presentation of the main evidence.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for diffusion posterior sampling, DDPMs, score-based SDEs, regression calibration, and CLASH observations: Chung, Ho, Song, Kuleshov, and Postman et al. It also corrects MARS's regularizer description from cross-entropy to maximum entropy. The overall novelty positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 removes the explicit identity DLS = DS − DL and instead describes DLS as the lens–source distance. Section 5.2 explicitly states the reduced-shear approximation g = γ/(1 − κ) ≈ γ for κ much smaller than one. These are limited revisions to mathematical definitions and assumptions; no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v1 supported calibration chiefly through error–uncertainty correlation and real-cluster agreement visually. v2 provides a coverage-based calibration check, quantitative MACS 1206 validation, and additional lensing-space comparisons, while qualifying posterior claims and supplying substantial reproduction details. These changes strengthen support for central claims rather than merely increasing reported performance. Real-data evidence remains limited to one proof-of-concept cluster.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DARKCLUSTERS-15K dataset and physics-guided diffusion reconstruction framework. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and can be matched across revisions.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds baseline results, physical reconstruction metrics, revised calibration evidence, and quantitative MACS 1206 comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction experiments, quantitative benchmark results in Table 2, uncertainty and input-ablation analyses, and a MACS 1206 reconstruction.

results.title: Mapping Dark-Matter Clusters via Physics-Guided Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and main conclusion retain the same claims about dense RGB/depth supervision, uncertainty-guided exploration and state-of-the-art NAVSIM performance, including PDMS 93.7 and EPDMS 88.8. The new experiments support these claims without redefining the core contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains weak sensitivity to lower safety thresholds using the finding that approximately 99% of sampled trajectories already exceed PDMS 0.6. It attributes the Waymo shortfall to limited recovery experience under offline/open-loop training. The conclusion replaces the proposed BEV-supervision extension with this concrete limitation and a closed-loop RL direction, while retaining the single-camera limitation.

D1.justification: Section 3.5 now specifies min-max entropy normalization. The abstract replaces a future code-and-demo release promise with a statement that code is available at the same project address; actual availability cannot be verified from the PDFs. Appendix A's backbone, preprocessing, hyperparameters and hardware disclosures are unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix B.3 adds fully reactive HUGSIM evaluation across KITTI-360, Waymo, nuScenes and PandaSet source domains. This substantially extends evaluation beyond the retained non-reactive NAVSIM and open-loop nuScenes settings, including conditions where the policy's actions affect subsequent states.

E2.justification: The new HUGSIM comparison uses a distinct three-comparator lineup: VAD, UniAD and LTF (Table 8). LTF cites the same reference used for TransFuser elsewhere, so it should not automatically be treated as an entirely new algorithm. Comparator membership in the original NAVSIM and nuScenes comparisons is unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 introduces zero-shot reactive rollouts measured by HD-Score, without closed-loop fine-tuning or domain adaptation. It also adds speed-versus-direction perturbations on 1,000 randomly selected straight-driving scenes and a safety-threshold sweep over 0, 0.3, 0.6 and 0.9. Previously documented training budgets, splits and benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 supplements the existing correlation plot and qualitative novelty example with a controlled 1,000-scene diagnostic (Table 3). Section 4.4 adds safety-threshold sensitivity analysis (Table 6), while Appendix B.3 probes transfer to reactive conditions and identifies a Waymo weakness. Existing component ablations and qualitative examples are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Table 3 newly reports ± quantities for L2 error and exploration bonus. Their statistical meaning is not defined, and neither version reports repeated-run counts or seeds. This establishes added spread/uncertainty reporting, but not additional runs or significance testing.

E6.justification: Existing table scores are unchanged. New Table 3 reports speed/direction perturbation L2 values of 5.82±1.74 versus 2.15±0.93 and bonuses of 0.04±0.03 versus 0.29±0.12. Table 6 adds threshold-dependent PDMS results. Table 8 newly reports ExploreVLA HD-Scores of 0.105, 0.360, 0.517 and 0.821: first on KITTI-360, third on Waymo and second on nuScenes and PandaSet among the listed methods. These are additional findings, not improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The backbone, joint trajectory/RGB/depth prediction, safety-gated exploration reward and GRPO training remain unchanged. Specifying the entropy-normalization function adds implementation detail; the PDFs do not establish a changed underlying procedure.

P1.justification: There are localized wording edits in the introduction and related work, expanded experimental discussion, a new Appendix B.3 and revised limitations. Author contact information and an internship footnote are added, and the keyword 'World model' becomes 'World action model.' The main organization and most prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds three compact tables for perturbation statistics, threshold sensitivity and HUGSIM results (Tables 3, 6 and 8). Existing tables are renumbered and redistributed, and Figure 4 is resized. All six figures retain their content, and the overall visual format is preserved.

R1.justification: v2 adds the HUGSIM reference to support the new simulator evaluation and metric. Existing cited works and the substantive positioning in Section 2 are retained; subsequent reference renumbering does not represent additional citation changes.

T1.justification: After Eq. (6), v2 explicitly defines f(H) = (H-Hmin)/(Hmax-Hmin), whereas v1 only states that f bounds the bonus within [0,1]. This adds a mathematical specification of the previously unspecified mapping. The remaining equations are unchanged, with no added theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central exploration mechanism: the earlier qualitative novelty example gains a 1,000-scene controlled test and a safety-threshold study. HUGSIM adds previously absent reactive closed-loop evidence, including a Waymo weakness that motivates a more informative limitation. These address important evidential gaps in v1, although undefined ± statistics and limited closed-loop protocol detail still constrain interpretation and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ExploreVLA and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Existing content can be matched across reflow and renumbering, and the added experiments are identifiable.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds trajectory-perturbation experiments, safety-threshold sensitivity results and closed-loop HUGSIM evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original NAVSIM results, component ablations and qualitative planning/generation outcomes, plus nuScenes results in Appendix B.2.

results.title: ExploreVLA: Dense World Modeling and Exploration for End-to-End Autonomous Driving

C1.justification: The central representation and semantic-distillation contributions remain intact. The abstract and introduction now explicitly claim benefits across UniAD and VAD. The headline safety-score improvement changes from 29.0% to 28.2%, and the introduction's collision-rate reduction changes from 11.3% to 16.1%.

C2.justification: Section 5.4 adds explanations attributing the controls' weaker performance to missing pretrained semantics, weaker CLIP-space supervision, and less direct integration with the LLM. The VQA-ablation interpretation changes from Behavior/Planning dominance to comparable, complementary subsets; the combined subset no longer has the lowest reported impact velocity.

D1.justification: v2 documents the VAD training schedule, parameter matching for the auxiliary control, and answer generation and supervision details for the VLM-AD-style variants. It adds a project website but removes Appendix F's resource URLs and license inventory. Most existing hyperparameters, hardware information, and implementation details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use DriveLM-nuScenes, Ego3D, nuScenes planning evaluation, and NeuroNCAP safety-critical scenarios. VAD and the new supervision controls operate within this retained coverage. The five qualitative driving cases are also retained.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds a randomly initialized auxiliary VQA head and two implemented VLM-AD-style comparators, labeled VLM-AD trans. and VLM-AD CLIP. These substantially expand the planning comparison beyond the undistilled baseline. Section 5.4 distinguishes these implementations from unavailable original VLM-AD resources.

E3.justification: New experimental settings include training VAD decoder heads for 12 epochs with the transferred encoder frozen and matching the auxiliary control's approximately 13M trainable parameters to the projector. VLM-AD-style controls use automatically labeled answers. Existing dataset splits, metrics, and the 20-epoch UniAD training schedule remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 5.4 directly tests whether pretrained LLM semantics provide benefits beyond an auxiliary VQA objective and compares alternative semantic-supervision designs. The VAD experiment additionally tests transfer across driving pipelines. These substantially strengthen the diagnostic evidence; existing downsampling, VQA-subset, and qualitative failure analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 first reports NeuroNCAP scores and collision rates as mean ± standard deviation over 50 random-seed runs, including Tables 4 and 6. v1 provides point estimates without corresponding run-count or uncertainty information. This substantially changes statistical reporting but does not establish that the run count increased.

E6.justification: Table 4 replaces UniAD baseline/1B/8B NeuroNCAP scores of 2.10/2.46/2.71 with 2.38/2.93/3.05, revises collision rates, and adds VAD and alternative-supervision results. Table 6 revises impact velocities and subset rankings. Smaller corrections include Table 2 accuracy from 95.2 to 95.3 and the stated Ego3D L1 reduction from 27.8% to 21.8%. With newly documented 50-seed reporting, the closed-loop revisions should not be interpreted as established same-protocol performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: The BEV tokenization, MLP projector, frozen LLM teacher, VQA supervision, and joint detection regularization remain unchanged. Coordinate conversion moves from Appendix A.4 into Section 4.1. Applying the same distilled encoder to VAD extends evaluation without changing the proposed distillation procedure.

P1.justification: v2 condenses introductory and semantic-manifold explanations, moves coordinate conversion into the main method section, inserts Section 5.4, updates acknowledgments, and removes the resource appendix. These are localized edits and organizational adjustments within a largely retained narrative structure.

P2.justification: Table 4 gains pipeline grouping and additional comparison rows, while Table 6 reorders metrics and accommodates uncertainty reporting. Table highlighting and spacing change. Existing figures are retained and relocated or renumbered, including the velocity plot moving from Figure D.1 to Figure 8; no new qualitative figure content is introduced.

R1.justification: VLM-AD, already cited in v1, receives a substantive methodological comparison in new Section 5.4. References to SpatialVLM and the original Vision Transformer paper are removed. Updates to DrivingGPT and Orion publication metadata do not represent new cited works.

T1.justification: The latent-alignment relation in Equation 1 and the next-token training objective in Appendix A.4 remain unchanged. The semantic-manifold explanation is condensed, without changing formal mathematical reasoning or introducing or removing proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central distillation claim through controls for alternative explanations, transfer to VAD, and explicit simulation uncertainty reporting (Sections 5.1–5.4 and Tables 4–6). These address important weaknesses in v1's planning evidence rather than merely increasing reported performance. VAD still shares the BEV encoder architecture, limiting the generality established. Removing the resource-access appendix is a modest reproducibility loss, outweighed by the stronger experimental evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BEVLM and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary material. Content can be matched across pagination changes and moves between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds alternative-supervision comparisons and evaluation using VAD.

before.justification: v1 reports original representation comparisons, open-loop and closed-loop driving experiments, ablations, and qualitative analyses in the main text and appendices.

results.title: BEVLM: Distilling Semantic Knowledge from LLMs into Bird's-Eye View Representations

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's four contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about RL post-training, randomized branching, multi-view rewards, and DROID rollout quality. The additional experiments strengthen supporting evidence without substantively reformulating these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 explains why text-image HPSv3 rewards cannot directly assess action-conditioned trajectory consistency and why the unavailable teacher motivates an adapted Self-Forcing comparison. It also identifies rollout generation as the dominant training cost. Existing limitations concerning computation and absent explicit physical constraints remain.

D1.justification: Reported training time changes from three to two days on the same eight H200 GPUs. v2 documents settings for the added studies, including SVD adaptation steps, the HPSv3 task prompt, the top-k=2 reward comparison, and policy finetuning details. The core pseudocode, inference settings, and project access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 extends training and evaluation to Bridge with WidowX and RT-1 with Google Robot, beyond the retained DROID setting. It also adds policy improvement on a four-block spatial picking task, distinct from v1's three policy-evaluation tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds two substantive controls: a Self-Forcing-style baseline trained on generated histories to regress ground-truth latents, and an HPSv3 reward replacement in Table 13. These are adapted comparisons, not full reproductions of Self-Forcing or WorldCompass. The original world-model baselines and WorldCompass curriculum comparison remain.

E3.justification: The reported main post-training budget changes from 8,000 to 6,000 steps; this does not establish that the retained results were rerun. New experimental designs include 100,000-step SVD adaptation on Bridge and RT-1, and full pi0 finetuning on 50 rollouts from each world model followed by five real-robot trials per block.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Appendix B ablations, v2 tests whether RL adds value over training on generated histories and compares their learning curves in Figure 13. Table 13 adds an analysis of perceptual rewards versus HPSv3, covering both visual fidelity and training cost.

E5.justification: The paired-comparison significance, policy-correlation p-values, and Appendix D's inter-rater agreement, binomial test, and confidence interval are retained. The added experiments introduce no new uncertainty-estimation or multi-seed reporting practice.

E6.justification: Original DROID table values remain unchanged. Newly reported comparisons include Bridge PSNR of 25.20 versus 26.36 and RT-1 PSNR of 23.81 versus 26.63 for SVD versus PersistWorld, HPSv3 versus perceptual-reward results, and Self-Forcing-style scores and learning curves. The new policy experiment reports progression of 0.350 for the base policy, 0.558 with Ctrl-World, and 0.667 with PersistWorld. Section 4 also corrects the masked-wrist SSIM gain from 5.4% to 4.1%, consistent with unchanged Table 2.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.4 and Algorithm 1 retain the same model, contrastive denoising objective, randomized prefix branching, multi-view rewards, and LoRA/action-encoder updates. The new regression and reward variants are comparison experiments, not revisions to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: Changes comprise targeted additions to Section 4 and Appendix E.2, a main-text summary of the already existing Appendix C policy-evaluation results, and small language, author-formatting, and acknowledgement edits. The overall organization and most existing prose remain stable.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands experimental displays with Tables 13–14 and Figures 12–14, covering reward comparisons, additional embodiments, learning curves, and the policy-improvement setup. Table 2 and Figure 6 are relocated, and the document uses larger page margins. Existing figures and table structures are otherwise retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to RT-1, Bridge, Self-Forcing, Rolling Forcing, and HPSv3. It extends the existing WorldCompass positioning through reward comparisons and discusses the applicability of forcing-based methods, while retaining most related-work discussion.

T1.justification: The mathematical objective and Appendix A's definitions, assumptions, posterior-mixture lemma, optimal-predictor theorem, proofs, and parameterization argument are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps in v1: the Self-Forcing-style control tests RL's added value, Table 14 establishes benefits on two additional robot embodiments, and the new policy experiment supplies direct real-robot improvement evidence beyond policy ranking. Together these substantially strengthen generality and practical relevance. Adapted comparators, limited experimental detail, and only five trials per block without new uncertainty estimates constrain the conclusions, but do not outweigh the substantial gain in supporting evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PersistWorld and contain readable main texts, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–E. Corresponding content can be matched despite layout changes and added experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original DROID rollout evaluations, ablations, a human preference study, and comparisons between simulated and real-robot policy performance.

results.title: Persistent Robot World Models: Stabilizing Multi-Step Rollouts via Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims about probabilistic camera-conditioned radar generation, BEV conditioning, evaluation metrics, and perception/editing applications. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining them.

Appendix C.4 adds a detector-training compatibility analysis. Existing conditioning, bandwidth, recovery, seed, and nighttime analyses remain.

This clarifies statistical reporting; the PDFs do not report additional repeated training runs, changed seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds nuScenes results, including RadarGen versus RGB2Point CD Loc. of 3.50 versus 3.85 and foreground hit rate of 0.49 versus 0.18. It also reports mixed-training NDS of 0.48 and range-image reconstruction CD increases from 0.31 to 3.72 m with SANA and 0.28 to 4.91 m with the LiDAR autoencoder. All three v1 tables retain identical numerical values in their matched v2 tables.

M1.justification: The BEV radar representation, foundation-model conditioning, SANA denoiser, and IRL1/FISTA point recovery remain unchanged. The added timestamp explanation and experiments do not establish a revised RadarGen procedure.

P1.justification: v2 makes limited grammatical corrections, clarifies introductory motivation and notation, updates acknowledgments, and adds appendix subsections C.5 and C.6. Most prose and the main section sequence are retained rather than extensively rewritten.

Existing appendix Figures 7–12 are retained as supplementary Figures 1–6.

R1.justification: The bibliography retains the same works, but Appendix C.6 develops the comparison with previously cited LiDAR Diffusion, explaining why radar adaptation requires a different autoencoder and RCS/Doppler outputs. The gains concern evidential support: mixed training only matches real-only NDS, and nuScenes split details remain underspecified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RadarGen and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Corresponding material can be matched despite extensive reformatting and changed figure/table numbering.

results.title: RadarGen: Automotive Radar Point Cloud Generation from Cameras

No run count or variability estimates are supplied, and the disclosure does not establish increased repetitions.

Runtime and seed-dependent outcomes are added; earlier binwise ablation entries are removed.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.4 retain the same SDF representation, Structure-VAE, multimodal flow model, physical losses, inference guidance, and refinement pipeline. The additional SDF-generation and SAM3D-integration descriptions disclose details without establishing a changed procedure.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized grammar and author-name corrections, rewrites Section 4.4, reorganizes Appendix A/B, and adds a supplementary title and acknowledgements. Most of the abstract, introduction, method exposition, and conclusion remain closely matched.

Existing illustrations are retained, with local resizing, caption edits, and layout changes.

DexYCB broadens transfer evidence, while implementation and seed disclosures improve transparency. Although binwise ablation detail is lost and DexYCB quality comparisons are limited by unequal successful-sample subsets, the new evidence resolves important gaps in support for the unchanged method.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same reconstruction method. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, references, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds component and robustness ablations, DexYCB evaluation, timing results, and a seed-sensitivity example.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated reconstruction and pose-estimation results, real-robot experiments, and sensing and tactile-noise ablations in Tables 1–3 and Appendix B.

results.title: Physically Grounded 3D Generative Reconstruction under Hand Occlusion using Proprioception and Multi-Contact Touch

New Tables 6 and 10 compare fusion strategies and symmetric versus asymmetric LoRA allocations. Sections 7.1-7.2 additionally examine localization-threshold sensitivity and MLLM resolution/modality sensitivity, substantially extending the earlier diagnostic evidence.

It integrates the framework into the evaluation protocol, moves component ablation into the main text, reorganizes the supplement into numbered sections, and extensively rewrites appendix lists as connected prose.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the two-column layout with a single-column format, merges v1 Tables 4-5 into Table 4, adds several experimental tables, and places fine-grained tables alongside their discussion. Figure 4 adds TPF and Figure 1 updates the model comparison. Existing qualitative image panels are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation through equal-budget rank controls, alternative fusion comparisons, stricter localization evaluation, MLLM sensitivity tests, and quantified annotation-quality checks. These address important evidential gaps in v1, while concrete resource information improves reproducibility. Some new summaries disagree with their tables, notably Section 7.1's accuracy-drop calculations, but these reporting defects do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RGB-Thermal grounding benchmark and RGBT-VGNet baseline, renamed RGBT-GroundBench in v2. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

P1.justification: V2 revises the abstract and introduction, adds an explicit contributions list and acknowledgements, and polishes or condenses several results paragraphs. results.title: OpenEarthAgent: A Unified Framework for Tool-Augmented Geospatial Agents

C1.justification: The central contributions—unified understanding, planning, and generation with two decoding alternatives—remain intact. The abstract strengthens its claimed L2/collision reductions from 5.9%/9.2% to 7.3%/10.4%, while the introduction extends its stated planning-performance claim to nuScenes as well as Bench2Drive.

C2.justification: v2 attributes AR's better planning results to more explicit token-space supervision. v4 instead explains AR+Diffusion's revised advantage through continuous geometric detail and reduced exposure bias, while positioning AR for reactive control and AR+Diffusion for slower, high-fidelity or offline use. It additionally interprets the ordering ablation through the action-to-observation causal direction and the new real-world results as evidence of generalization.

D1.justification: v4 Appendices C–D substantially expand implementation disclosure: Hungarian matching and focal/L1 perception-pretraining losses, Gaussian MLP parameterization and reparameterization, a recurrent BEV waypoint decoder, and how planning losses use detected boxes and lane boundaries. These clarify previously underspecified components rather than establish new ones. v4 also supplies A100 inference speeds of 2 fps for AR and 0.4 fps for AR+Diffusion; the project-page access information is equivalent.

E1.justification: v2 evaluates on Bench2Drive and its Chat-B2D annotations; mentioning nuScenes detection metrics does not establish nuScenes evaluation. v4 adds actual nuScenes training/evaluation for planning and future-image generation, plus DriveLM GVQA evaluation. This substantially extends coverage from simulated driving to real-world data and another understanding benchmark.

E2.justification: v4 adds a nuScenes planning comparison involving Drive-VLM, Doe-1, OmniDrive, and FSDrive alongside retained planning baselines. Its new GVQA comparison includes the DriveLM baseline, Cube-LLM, TrackingMeetsLMM, SimpleLLM4AD, OmniDrive, and FSDrive. The corresponding Bench2Drive baseline sets and image-generation comparator set remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the stated AR+Diffusion output resolution from 256×256 to 512×1024, materially changing its experimental setting. v4 also introduces the official nuScenes train/validation split, DriveLM GVQA metrics, an ordering-control experiment, and A100 inference-speed measurements. The Bench2Drive 950/50 split and 220-route protocol remain unchanged; collision values converted to percentages do not constitute a new metric.

E4.justification: v4 Table 7 adds a focused ablation testing whether planning should precede image generation, comparing both orders on trajectory error, collisions, and FID. Section 4.5 also quantifies the architectures' speed trade-off. The earlier module-removal and Chat-B2D image-generation ablations are retained, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Gaussian latent variables and v2's qualitative discussion of diffusion variance are not statistical uncertainty reporting for experimental results.

E6.justification: v4 adds nuScenes and GVQA results and revises existing scores. Bench2Drive FID changes from 6.4 to 7.2 for AR and from 7.1 to 6.6 for AR+Diffusion (v2 Table 3; v4 Table 4). AR+Diffusion's 3-second L2 changes from 1.092 to 1.066, with its stated resolution also changing. Chat-B2D CIDEr/BLEU/ROUGE-L change from 66.3/52.9/78.3 to 66.7/53.5/78.6. v4 newly reports nuScenes average L2 of 0.30/0.29 for the two branches and a GVQA final score of 0.59. Percentage conversions in retained collision results are equivalent representations.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the QT-Former/VLM backbone, Gaussian latent trajectory planner without KL regularization, planning-conditioned generation, AR and AR+Diffusion alternatives, and the same joint objectives. v4's expanded perception and planner appendices disclose implementation details without establishing a changed default algorithm.

P1.justification: v4 substantially reorganizes the experimental narrative: planning, generation, and VQA results are consolidated; the scattered AR/diffusion discussion becomes a dedicated comparison section; metric definitions move to Appendix A; and the Chat-B2D ablation moves into the main text. The perception appendix is rewritten and subdivided, and planner explanations are expanded. Much of the introduction, core method, and conclusion remains recognizable.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column formatting, with extensively rescaled and relocated displays. Figure 1 is recomposed, generation figures incorporate or replace examples with nuScenes imagery, and new qualitative Figures 7–8 appear. New benchmark and ordering-ablation tables are added, while the old standalone architecture-comparison table is redistributed across other comparisons. Some tables and the retained VQA figure become visibly smaller.

R1.justification: v4 updates the literature discussion with works such as DriveVLA-W0, DriveVA, VLGA, G2DP, OccSim, and navigation world models, and adds references supporting the new benchmarks and baselines. The three related-work categories and the central positioning around jointly modeling trajectories and visual futures remain unchanged, making this a contextual expansion rather than a fundamental repositioning.

T1.justification: Equation (4) changes the memory bank's first time index from t−n to t−n+1, correcting its consistency with the stated n-frame bank. The principal probabilistic formulations and losses remain equivalent, and neither version introduces theoretical guarantees or proofs. The expanded cosine-similarity expression is mathematically unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses an important weakness of v2's predominantly simulation-based validation by adding real-world nuScenes planning/generation results and DriveLM GVQA comparisons. The ordering ablation directly tests a central design choice, and Appendices C–D materially improve implementation transparency. These gains substantially strengthen the paper's evidence and inspectability. Changed decoder resolution and continued absence of run statistics limit architectural comparisons, and some displays lose legibility, but these limitations do not outweigh the broader validation and clearer documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UniDrive-WM, with matching core methods and identifiable corresponding experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: v4 retains original Bench2Drive experiments and reports additional nuScenes results, DriveLM GVQA evaluations, and a planning/generation-order ablation.

before.justification: v2 reports original Bench2Drive planning, perception, image-generation, and VQA results, including closed-loop evaluations and appendix ablations.

results.title: UniDrive-WM: Unified Understanding, Planning and Generation World Model For Autonomous Driving

C1.justification: The principal claims remain the DOMINO dynamic-manipulation benchmark, PUMA's combination of historical motion and future prediction, its approximately 6.3-point success-rate advantage, and transfer benefits from dynamic data. The added experiments broaden support without redefining the abstract and introduction's central contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.4 replaces the assertion that dynamic manipulation subsumes static skills with a qualification about overlapping manipulation primitives. New discussions interpret history length, excessive prediction horizons, and cross-level transfer. Appendix F adds substantive failure modes and limitations concerning stop-on-contact dynamics, bimanual coordination, control delays, and sim-to-real errors.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies Qwen3-VL-4B initialization, hidden dimension, the 14-dimensional action head, absence of additional proprioceptive input, DINOv2-B/14 supervision, and distributed-training details. It also documents trajectory construction and rejection rules, physical motion generation using strings, and real-robot adaptation. A project-page link is added while the code URL is retained.

E1.justification: v3 extends the simulation evaluation to five physical AgileX Piper manipulation tasks, including Lift Bottle as an adaptation of Shake Bottle. It also evaluates unseen speed conditions: alpha=0.05 and randomized alpha in [0.5, 1.5]. These substantially expand deployment-domain and environmental coverage beyond v1.

E2.justification: ContextVLA, previously only cited, is newly evaluated against PUMA on the 10-task subset in v3 Table 10. The comparator membership of the main Table 3 remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 introduces real-robot protocols with 50 demonstrations and 20 trials per task, 10-task transfer experiments comparing direct training with Level-1 initialization and LoRA, doubled-data experiments, and a controlled latency benchmark. The retained training description changes per-device batch size from 16 to 8; Table 3 also revises InternVLA-M1's stated backbone from InternVL to Qwen2.5-VL. These disclosures do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's retained component ablations and ACT complexity analysis, v3 adds task-type breakdowns, a history-aware comparator, history-length and N=6 prediction-horizon tests, cross-level transfer, speed-shift robustness, and doubled-data analysis. Appendix C also adds simulation and physical-policy rollout examples. These address substantially more questions about PUMA's behavior.

E5.justification: Section 4.6 newly specifies latency averaging over 500 inference queries after 50 warm-ups, adding repeated-measurement reporting absent from v1. Neither version reports multi-seed training variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. No increased repetition of the retained success-rate experiments is established.

E6.justification: The headline Table 3 result remains 17.20% SR and 34.97 MS. Substantial new results include physical-robot SR of 42% for PUMA versus 24% for pi0.5, and 10-task SR of 20.9% versus ContextVLA's 7.8%. The extended horizon ablation reports 13.62% at N=6 versus 17.20% at N=4, adding evidence that longer prediction is not uniformly beneficial.

M1.justification: PUMA retains its historical optical flow, action/world queries, object-centric future supervision, action loss, and auxiliary cosine loss. The three-stage data-collection description makes the previously described dynamic execution stage explicit. Additional implementation disclosures and LoRA transfer experiments do not establish a redesign of the core method.

P1.justification: Most original prose and section ordering are retained. v3 makes local wording and cross-reference corrections, shortens the conclusion, adds experimental subsections, and reorganizes the expanded appendix with author contributions and discussion sections. This is a limited editorial revision alongside substantial new scientific content.

P2.justification: v3 adds a physical-robot setup/results figure, simulation and real-world rollout panels, a data-generation schematic, and tables for task categories, transfer, latency, and extended analyses. Existing figures and result tables are largely retained and renumbered, while the new displays substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds references and brief positioning concerning autonomous-driving VLAs, parallel task execution, 3D understanding, and scene-level world models, plus an AdamW citation. The original related-work framework and central distinction from prior manipulation methods remain. Numerous venue updates refer to the same previously cited works.

T1.justification: Appendix D.3 adds explicit mathematical specifications for trajectory generation, including back-calculation equations, clipped half-normal speed sampling, and segment-mixture probabilities. The POMDP, metric definitions, and learning objectives remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof. The new speed distribution conflicts with the uniform specification retained in Section 2.3.
