improvement.justification: v1's PUMA evidence was concentrated in Level-1 simulation. v3 substantially strengthens validation through physical-robot experiments, cross-difficulty and speed-shift tests, and targeted history/prediction controls. Fuller implementation disclosures and explicit limitations also improve reproducibility and interpretation. The physical study remains small, uncertainty intervals are absent, and the sampling descriptions are inconsistent, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DOMINO benchmark and PUMA model. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching the retained embedded animation frames across versions.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original real-robot results, inference measurements, and further ablation and generalization experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation experiments, including baseline comparisons, PUMA ablations, and static/dynamic transfer evaluations in Section 4 and Appendix D.

results.title: Towards Generalizable Robotic Manipulation in Dynamic Environments

C1.justification: The central claims remain the first fully quantized intermediate-fusion system, near-full-precision accuracy, 3.2-fold latency reduction, a +9.5 mAP30 gain, and improved scaling under memory constraints. New experiments support these existing claims; the revised conclusion emphasizes the deployment focus already present in v1.

C2.justification: Appendix D.5 adds a focused explanation of rounding-bias accumulation and complementary AdaRound/alignment roles, including stronger language about reaching a globally optimized state. Appendix E.2 acknowledges that intertwined online error sources limit attribution. Existing V2X-ViT and 2-bit limitations remain discussed, although the dedicated main-text limitations paragraph is removed.

D1.justification: v2 explains how codebook weights are generated through Gumbel-Softmax, explicitly specifies nL=128 and nR=1, and documents Gaussian positional/heading perturbations for the retained robustness experiment. It also describes ROS-bag packaging for online evaluation. These improve documentation; the established hardware, training budgets, and promised code release remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds online perception evaluation through ROS-bag streaming on V2X-ReaLO across V2V, I2I, and V2I modes (Appendix E.2, Table 12). This substantially extends evaluation beyond static and simulated-latency accuracy settings. v1 already discussed the deployment platform and measured latency, but did not report this online accuracy evaluation.

E2.justification: The external baseline suites, including Where2comm, CodeFilling, PD-Quant, and LiDAR-PTQ, remain. v2 adds an explicit model-quantization-only control to the system comparison in Figure 6 and additional naive-rounding configurations in Table 11, providing limited extensions of the evaluated comparator configurations.

E3.justification: New protocols include INT2/8 evaluation, AP70 assessment by distance, four system configurations across three fusion architectures, and offline-versus-online evaluation on V2X-ReaLO. Existing training/calibration budgets and the simulated communication-delay protocol remain unchanged. These additions substantially expand evaluation design without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained calibration, alignment, codebook, and pose-error studies, v2 adds computation-versus-communication decomposition (Figure 6), a 2-bit failure test (Table 5), and analyses of AdaRound/alignment complementarity using strict localization metrics and naive-rounding controls (Tables 10-11). These directly test previously underexamined component roles and operating limits.

E5.justification: Both versions specify averaging latency over 10 runs, in v1 Appendix D.1 and v2 Appendix E.1. v2 adds no seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or other uncertainty-estimation practices.

E6.justification: Most matched results remain unchanged, including Tables 1-3 and power measurements. v2 adds online QuantV2X mAP30/50 results of 50.1/40.1, 58.0/45.7, and 45.9/36.6 for V2V, I2I, and V2I, plus decomposition and alignment results and INT2/8 AP30/50 of 40.8/37.0. One retained codebook-ablation value changes: system mAP50 for 128 codes and one selection rises from 41.9 to 42.2 (v1 Table 10; v2 Table 14), matching the main table.

M1.justification: The three-stage pipeline, codebook objectives, calibration algorithm, and heterogeneity/spatial alignment losses remain unchanged. Section 2.3 newly explains Gumbel-Softmax training weights and hard inference selections, but does not establish a change to the previously described procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. v2 moves related work into the appendix, places references before the appendices, reorders model-level appendix material, and makes localized explanatory and terminology edits. It also updates author/contact information and adds acknowledgements.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a substantially different document template with changed typography, margins, headers, and float placement. It redraws the overview, adds the two-panel decomposition Figure 6 and Tables 5 and 10-12, and rearranges retained displays. The scaling plot's axis notation changes from mAP0.3 to equivalent mAP30 without changing its results.

R1.justification: v2 adds STAMP to the cooperative-perception discussion and bibliography. The broader positioning against communication-only optimization remains unchanged. Moving related work to Appendix A and updating citation styles or publication metadata do not introduce additional substantive positioning changes.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and Equations (1)-(10) are retained, with only equivalent notation changes. The new computation-latency grouping restates the existing latency decomposition. No theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is added.

improvement.justification: v1 supported deployment claims mainly through measured timing and simulated-latency accuracy. v2 adds online streaming evaluation across three collaboration modes and controls testing model/communication contributions and alignment at stricter precision thresholds. This substantially strengthens the central deployment argument and exposes operating limits. The new global-optimization language exceeds the formal evidence, and online attribution remains confounded, but these limitations do not outweigh the improved experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe QuantV2X and contain readable methods, equations, experiments, figures, tables, and appendices. Content can be matched reliably despite substantial reformatting, renumbering, and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds online V2X-ReaLO evaluation, system-component comparisons, and further quantization and alignment ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original perception experiments on DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, and OPV2V, together with quantization ablations, latency measurements, and power measurements.

results.title: QuantV2X: A Fully Quantized Multi-Agent System for Cooperative Perception

C1.justification: The central claim of interactive, single-frame-initialized autoregressive LiDAR generation and the SDE/NM contributions remain. v2 drops the nuScenes evaluation protocol as a headline contribution and explicitly promotes the conditional feature encoder in the contribution list.

C2.justification: v2 explains current bounding boxes as simulator feedback and interprets the benefit of updated scene information over historical-input forecasting. It adds sensor-type and crowded-scene matching limitations, background-transformation reasoning, and an accuracy/latency tradeoff discussion. Its positive SDE interpretation also replaces v1's warning about additional errors at very long horizons.

D1.justification: v2 adds training epochs/steps, batch size, learning rate, scheduler, GPU hardware/time, pretrained VAE initialization, circular convolutions, sampling settings, metric preprocessing, SDE pseudocode and a code-access URL. These substantially expand reproducibility information. However, v1's explicit construction of 176 valid sequences containing 20 frames is omitted.

E1.justification: The nuScenes-only evaluation expands to KITTI-360, introducing 64-beam scans alongside nuScenes' 32-beam scans. v2 also evaluates downstream 3D object detection and generation under perturbed or missing bounding-box conditions, substantially broadening task and input-scenario coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds UniScene, OpenDWM, DriveLiDAR4D and LiDARCrafter to the nuScenes generation comparison, retaining LiDARGen, LiDM and RangeLDM. Temporal comparisons additionally include OpenDWM-DiT. The existing 4D-Occ and ViDAR forecasting comparators remain.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce TTCE/CTC, KITTI-360 FRD/FPD, detection mAP/NDS and object-level CD/EMD. Additional protocols sweep 10-200 denoising steps and specify bounding-box perturbation and dropping probabilities. Newly disclosed training settings do not establish that existing experiments changed their training budgets.

E4.justification: v2 extends the SDE/NM ablations with temporal-consistency measurements and revised horizon selections. It adds a box-free control, denoising-step accuracy/latency analysis, and systematic bounding-box shifting/dropping tests in Tables 6-9 and Appendix H. The original interactive-editing demonstration is retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or error bars. The additional experiments retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Numerous results are added, and LaGen's reported nuScenes MMD/JSD changes from 0.35/3.97 in v1 Table 2 to 0.11/2.77 in v2 Table 1 under unchanged table scaling. Protocol continuity is insufficient to establish a controlled performance gain. New Table 5 favors LaGen on CTC but LiDARCrafter on TTCE. Some duplicated results conflict: two-frame 4D-Occ's 9.5-second CD is 55.47 in v2 main Table 6 and 65.92 in supplementary Table 5.

M1.justification: The LDM, SDE, NM and autoregressive loop remain. Equation (6) changes the specified attention query from bounding-box features to intermediate U-Net features, and Section 4.4 introduces a box-free forecasting variant. Expanded encoder and convolution descriptions primarily disclose implementation details.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the experimental narrative into generation, temporal consistency and downstream forecasting, replacing the dedicated benchmark subsection. It consolidates the standalone inference subsection, revises introductory positioning and contribution wording, and adds extensive organized technical explanations throughout the supplement.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, with retained figures resized and repositioned and several captions shortened. Forecasting tables are consolidated, generation comparisons gain conditional/unconditional grouping, and new tables, SDE visualizations, metric curves and full-sequence comparison grids substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to contemporary generators including Genesis, DriveLiDAR4D, UniScene, OpenDWM, LiDARCrafter and La La LiDAR. v2 acknowledges LiDARCrafter's autoregressive generation and distinguishes LaGen through interactive per-step control, materially refining its novelty positioning.

T1.justification: New Appendices E-F introduce an autoregressive error recursion, Taylor-expansion/Jacobian-regularization argument, claimed contraction guarantee, and motion assumptions supporting SDE. v1 contains algorithm equations and intuitive motivation but lacks these theoretical derivations. The contraction guarantee is asserted without establishing the required spectral-radius bound.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical support through relevant conditional-generation comparators, a box-free forecasting control, temporal-consistency measurements, and robustness/latency evaluations. Detailed implementation disclosures and explicit applicability limits also materially strengthen reproducibility and interpretation. These gains outweigh reporting regressions: the benchmark-construction recipe disappears, duplicated baseline scores conflict, and Appendix E does not establish its claimed contraction guarantee. The improvement rests on stronger evaluation and documentation, not simply additional pages or better reported scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LaGen framework. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable throughout, including v2's Appendices A-J. The supplied v1 ends with references and contains no appendix.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices H-J report original generation, detection, temporal-consistency, forecasting, ablation and robustness results, including additional KITTI-360 experiments.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original nuScenes generation, forecasting, module-ablation and interactive-editing results in Tables 1-5 and Figures 6-7.

results.title: LaGen: Towards Autoregressive LiDAR Scene Generation

C1.justification: v2 qualifies v1's claim that policy improvements yield only marginal gains: the abstract now says perception and test-time strategies often yield larger gains, while the introduction and conclusion emphasize reliable policy comparisons under unified configurations. The conclusion drops the 'first' empirical-study claim. The central decomposition, performance and human-gap contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning cross-dataset transfer, frontier information-gain/travel-cost trade-offs, restrictive PPO updates, and why height information may require more training data. It also proposes that structured maps explain similar CNN/Transformer performance. Some interpretations overreach: A.4 asserts a shared detector ordering that is not consistent across the metrics in Tables 1 and 5.

D1.justification: v2 supplies project and repository links, explicitly identifies PPO, and expands human-study documentation with the interface, observation restrictions and prohibition on repeated episodes. These clarify existing work without establishing that the human experiment changed. Hardware and training-budget disclosures are retained; release wording remains inconsistent between the introduction and A.2.

E1.justification: v2 extends the Gibson navigation evaluation to HM3D, using five test scenes for perception comparisons and the full 20-scene HM3D v1 validation split for component evaluation (A.4). This materially broadens environmental coverage. MP3D and AI2-THOR evaluations remain proposed future work.

E2.justification: Table 1 substantially expands perception comparisons by adding RF-DETR-Seg, RF-DETR+SAM2 and YOLO11-XL under both corner and frontier policies. The new HM3D comparison also evaluates YOLO11-N. Table 4 retains the same ten named prior navigation baselines and the human baseline.

E3.justification: New experiments specify five-scene detector testing, 20-scene zero-shot testing without retraining, FPS reporting, and PPO clipping settings of 0.2 and 0.001. These extend the established evaluation procedures. The original 500-step limit, dynamic-step calculation, success criterion, navigation metrics and two-million-frame training budget remain unchanged; expanded human-study controls are newly disclosed details.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of frontier-goal selection, PPO update constraints and height information (Tables 7–9), plus cross-dataset component ablations on HM3D (Table 6). New Figures 7–9 illustrate untrapping, dynamic-goal and remapping behavior. The original failure analysis and perception visualizations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, variability estimates or significance tests. The added experiments continue reporting point estimates; the expanded human-study description introduces no new statistical estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Retained Gibson results are unchanged, including the continuous policy's 84.4% SR/48.2% SPL and humans' 98.0% SR/53.3% SPL. Substantial new results appear in the expanded Table 1 and Tables 5–9: RF-DETR-Seg obtains 52.4% SR/24.2% SPL on five HM3D scenes, and the height-map ablation reports 75.1% SR versus 78.3% with the obstacle map. These are added comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: v2 introduces tested procedure variants using detector-plus-SAM2 segmentation, nearest/farthest frontier selection, and a height-map channel replacing the binary obstacle channel. These extend the framework; its principal architecture, reward functions and test-time algorithms remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, conclusion and most recommendation passages are rewritten, and policy-learning and human-study explanations are expanded. Numbered experimental subsubsections become paragraph headings, the appendix is reorganized, and references move after the appendix. These constitute extensive narrative and structural revisions beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–9 and Figures 7–10, expands Table 1, and redraws Figure 2 with failure-mode annotations. Table 4 becomes a full-width summary containing one own-policy row instead of four; the other policies' results remain elsewhere. Typography, margins, headers and recommendation boxes change throughout, while original perception Figures 7–9 reappear as Figures 11–13.

R1.justification: v2 adds connections to MOPA for random/frontier goal selection, PPO and broader robotics learning, contemporary detectors, and 3D-LLM/ForesightNav for spatial representations. These broaden supporting context and attribution while retaining the central positioning as an empirical study of modular ObjectNav components.

T1.justification: The reward definitions, map and action formulations, and dynamic-step equation remain unchanged. The new PPO and height-map discussions provide empirical analysis and intuitive explanations, without new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's broad design recommendations rested on Gibson evaluations. v2 substantially strengthens their empirical basis through HM3D testing, including 20-scene zero-shot component ablations, and targeted tests of additional policy-design assumptions. Clearer human-study documentation also improves assessability. The overgeneralized detector-ranking claim and continued absence of uncertainty estimates limit interpretation, but the new validation materially improves support for the paper's central conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same modular ObjectNav study. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds HM3D evaluations, frontier-selection, PPO-clipping and height-map experiments, and qualitative navigation cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gibson experiments and component ablations, a five-person human baseline, and analysis of 1,000 navigation episodes.

results.title: What Matters in RL-Based Methods for Object-Goal Navigation? An Empirical Study and A Unified Framework

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion newly claim scalability to high-dimensional humanoid control. The central contributions—unified planning and imagination, interleaved training, and hierarchical memory—remain intact, as do the original navigation and zero-shot generalization claims.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets goal conditioning as helping unseen-environment generalization and discusses the accuracy-versus-imagination-cost tradeoff, including potential quantization benefits. The domain-shift and fixed-token-budget limitations remain; the explanation of disappearing ego-robot regions is slightly qualified from absent to rare training examples.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents baseline retraining on the shared datasets and Aether's checkpoint-only exception, and expands the abstract's availability statement from code to code and models. Most implementation details and appendix prompts are retained, but the explicit per-GPU batch size of 1 and gradient accumulation of 2 are omitted. These documentation changes do not establish altered original training settings.

E1.justification: v2 adds training and evaluation on the navigation subset of the 1X Humanoid Dataset, extending coverage to humanoid embodiment and high-dimensional joint-angle control. The original four navigation datasets and held-out TartanDrive coverage are retained.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Aether to the visualization comparison, which previously contained Diamond and NWM. v2 specifies checkpoint-based evaluation because Aether lacks released training code and uses an incompatible camera-pose action space. The navigation comparator set is unchanged, including when extended to humanoid evaluation.

E3.justification: v2 adds a separately trained humanoid setting with 6599/733 training/evaluation trajectories, a joint-versus-separate training control using identical data and schedules, a retrained goal-image removal control, and per-trajectory latency evaluation. Existing dataset splits, preprocessing, navigation/visualization metrics, and the 20-epoch LoRA setup remain unchanged. Newly stated baseline-retraining information does not establish a change to the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct tests of joint versus separate planner/world-model training (Table 4) and whether goal conditioning affects unseen-environment generalization (Section 4.3). Appendix B.2 adds an inference-cost analysis, and Figure 4 adds a moving-pedestrian qualitative case. The original loss, context, memory, layer-selection, and interleaving ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new estimated 4-bit latency is a point projection, not statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Matched original tables and Figure 5 retain their values. v2 adds Aether scores, humanoid results, ablation outcomes, latency results, and qualitative findings. For example, Table 8 reports humanoid SR 0.81 for full UniWM versus 0.51 for NWM; Table 4 reports SR 0.71 for unified versus 0.65 for separate training. Table A1 reports 82 seconds per UniWM trajectory and explicitly labels the 16-second quantized figure as estimated.

M1.justification: v2 reports a limited action-interface extension: a separate UniWM instance uses 25-DoF humanoid joint-angle actions instead of the original translation/yaw commands (Sections 4.1 and 4.5). The backbone, losses, hierarchical memory, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. The humanoid adaptation is not described in implementation-level detail.

P1.justification: v2 extensively edits the introduction and experimental narrative, changes the title and author/affiliation information, moves related work from Appendix A into main Section 2, introduces an explicit experimental-settings subsection, and places references after the appendices. Existing appendix methods and metrics are reorganized rather than removed.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the title block, typography, colors, table styling, and framework diagrams in Figures 1–3. It adds Tables 4, 8, and A1, a humanoid Figure 7, and an additional Figure 4 case. Original appendix figures are retained as Figures A1–A5 with revised placement and formatting.

R1.justification: v2 adds contemporary world-model, driving, humanoid, and quantization references, plus targeted distinctions from MVoT's narrow 2D reasoning and WorldVLA's single-step action-sequence prediction without trajectory memory. These refine the novelty discussion while retaining the original positioning around unified prediction/control and structured memory.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, losses, memory-fusion equations, attention equation, and appendix metric definitions are retained. v1 Equation 12 becomes v2 Equation A1 without substantive revision. Neither version adds theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked a matched test isolating joint from separate planner/world-model training; v2 Table 4 addresses this central attribution gap. Together with the goal-conditioning control, humanoid evaluation, baseline-training disclosures, and inference-cost analysis, this substantially strengthens the paper's empirical support and assessability. The gains are qualified by sparse humanoid-adaptation and timing details, omitted batch-scheduling details, and the explicitly estimated rather than measured 4-bit latency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UniWM, despite the revised title and presentation. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained and added content.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds humanoid navigation results, further controlled ablations, an Aether comparison, and inference-time results.

before.justification: v1 reports original navigation and visualization experiments on four training/evaluation datasets, zero-shot TartanDrive results, ablations, and qualitative examples.

results.title: Towards Unified World Models for Visual Navigation via Memory-Augmented Planning and Foresight

C1.justification: The central attention-based risk assessment and safety/utility claims remain, but v3 adds low calibration-data requirements and low pre-deployment cost as headline contributions. Its abstract and introduction reposition the advantage around robustness across attacks and efficiency relative to steering defenses, including a claimed 126.6-fold reduction in pre-deployment overhead.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of steering baselines' distribution-shift failures, calibration-source/size robustness, and safety versus over-refusal tradeoffs. Supplementary Section 8 replaces v1 Appendix G's attack-versus-defense explanation of refusal-vector performance with a query-specific geometric explanation. The original visual-attention mechanism remains central.

D1.justification: v3 adds executable-style pseudocode, discloses the H200 GPU and Xeon CPU used for cost measurements, details preparation procedures and timings, and specifies baseline layer, strength and threshold configurations. Calibration parameters are updated. Conversely, v1's promise to release code upon publication is removed without replacement access information.

E1.justification: v3 retains the original safety and utility benchmarks while adding JOOD attacks using out-of-distribution image combinations, gradient-based visual adversarial attacks, XSTest and OR-Bench over-refusal tasks, and suffix-injected MM-Safety queries. These substantially broaden the evaluated input conditions and safety requirements.

E2.justification: v3 adds AutoSteer and ASTRA to the retained FigStep, CoCA, ECSO and ETA comparisons, including safety, utility and throughput evaluations. This introduces direct comparisons with contemporary multimodal steering defenses, beyond v1's prompting and response-refinement baselines.

E3.justification: Default risk calibration changes from 100 unsafe SPA-VL examples to 100 held-out examples from AutoSteer's calibration dataset, with revised parameters. v3 also adds LLaVA-OneVision-7B, calibration wall-clock measurements, and a visual-adversarial protocol averaging four perturbation settings over 200 prompts. New baseline tuning experiments use GPT-4o for MM-Vet scoring; the main benchmark evaluation retains GPT-4-0613.

E4.justification: v3 adds calibration-source/size sensitivity, alternative-object FDR analysis, fixed-strength steering comparisons, suffix robustness, baseline hyperparameter sweeps and overhead breakdowns. Prototype-source and refusal-vector studies are revised and expanded in some respects, although the prototype-source study narrows to one backbone. v1's binary-steering and image-removal ASR ablations disappear; related image-removal FDR analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Added calibration sample-size comparisons and benchmark averages do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive results for new attacks, comparators, a backbone and computational costs, and replaces several retained-model scores. For LLaVA-1.5-7B, reported MM-Safety/SPA-VL/FigStep ASRs change from 4.1/8.3/2.2 to 2.6/7.6/2.8 under revised calibration, rather than establishing a controlled performance gain. Rankings are no longer uniformly favorable: v3 Table 1 reports VAA ASR of 12.1 for ETA versus 14.3 for MoRAS on this backbone.

M1.justification: The core EWRE and adaptive-steering equations remain unchanged. A limited input change is documented: v1 Appendix A.1 includes the original question when generating visual context, whereas v3 Supplementary Section 1.1 and Algorithm 1 use the image and context-generation prompt alone. Renaming RAS to MoRAS is not itself a method change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten, and RAS is renamed MoRAS. The method exposition separates the attention diagnosis from query reformulation. Lettered appendices become numbered supplementary sections with a contents guide, and implementation and sensitivity discussions are reorganized.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the overview diagram, restyles and reorders attention illustrations, and substantially restructures the main comparison table. LLaVA-1.5-13B results move to a supplementary table. Figure 7 gains a calibration-cost panel, while new tables and sensitivity heatmaps materially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from a substantial training-alignment discussion toward direct positioning against AutoSteer and ASTRA, emphasizing calibration costs and attack generalization. New attack, over-refusal and dataset references support this expanded positioning, while several training-alignment references and discussions are removed.

T1.justification: The attention aggregation, FDR, prototype averaging, weighted cosine similarity, sigmoid risk mapping and refusal-vector equations retain equivalent mathematical content. The attention definition moves to supplementary material; no new theorem, proof or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation through direct steering-defense comparisons, broader adversarial conditions, explicit over-refusal tests, and calibration sensitivity and cost breakdowns. These address important gaps in v1's evidence for robustness and practical efficiency. The gains outweigh the removed component ablations and code-release pledge. Some superiority wording exceeds Table 1's mixed rankings, and neither version quantifies run-to-run uncertainty.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same three-stage steering work, renamed from RAS to MoRAS. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds attack, calibration, over-refusal and computational-cost results in Section 4 and the supplementary material.

before.justification: v1 reports original safety, utility, throughput, ablation and qualitative results in Section 4 and Appendices C-H.

results.title: Attention Misses Visual Risk: Risk-Adaptive Steering for Multimodal Safety Alignment

C1.justification: v1 claims the first TTA framework for VLODs. v2 removes that priority claim, acknowledges TTAOD-F, and emphasizes an efficient alternative without a teacher. Its abstract and conclusion newly claim superiority over the prior specialized state-of-the-art method, while retaining the IWE and IPS contributions.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's small-object explanation, v2 identifies rider/person ambiguity and explains how IWE can reinforce incorrect classifications. It connects resolution and label-merging experiments to this failure mechanism. It also adds learning-rate sensitivity as a rationale for adapters and interprets pseudo-labeling results as evidence that IoU weighting generalizes beyond entropy minimization.

D1.justification: v2 specifies ChatGPT-5 and the prompt-generation instruction, adapter and batch-normalization learning rates, and RTX3090 hardware for the new comparison. It omits v1's explicit implementation-source and offline-versus-online text-embedding disclosures. The code link and principal adapter configuration remain unchanged; these disclosures do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: v2 adds the specialized Aquarium underwater domain and a Cityscapes task merging rider into person. Previous dataset coverage is retained. COCO-C already appeared in v1 Appendix A; evaluating Grounding DINO there does not itself add dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v2 introduces direct comparison with the specialized prior method TTAOD-F in Tables 5 and 16, alongside batch-normalization and standard pseudo-labeling comparators in new studies. The FFT reference row disappears from the corresponding YOLO-World efficiency comparison. The original TPT, VPT, DPE, and Adapter baselines remain.

E3.justification: New controlled evaluations test eight versus seven Cityscapes classes, 640 versus 1024 input resolution, and batch-normalization versus adapter updates. The Grounding DINO comparison adds memory and latency measurements and explicitly uses batch size 4 for TTAOD-F versus 1 for VLOD-TTA. The original principal single-image, single-step protocol is retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct IWE/IPS component ablations, parameter-subset and warm-start studies, transfer of IoU weighting to pseudo-labeling, and Cityscapes label-confusion and resolution analyses. These address component contributions and failure mechanisms previously untested. Earlier prompt, hyperparameter, augmentation, backbone, and fine-tuning analyses remain, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Averaging over datasets and corruption conditions already occurs in both versions.

E6.justification: Matched existing benchmark tables have identical numerical entries. Substantial new results include component ablations, Cityscapes class-wise failures, and Aquarium mAP of 11.9 for zero-shot versus 14.5 for VLOD-TTA. New Grounding DINO comparisons report average mAP of 26.0 for TTAOD-F, 26.2 for VLOD-TTA, and 27.3 for its warm-start variant under the stated differing settings.

M1.justification: The core IWE objective, IPS scoring, and episodic adapter updates remain unchanged. Section 4.3 adds secondary procedural variants: warm-start initialization for VLOD-TTA*, adaptation through batch normalization, and IoU-weighted mean-teacher pseudo-labeling. These extend rather than replace the principal method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. Prompt-averaging and efficiency discussions move into the main text, hyperparameter sensitivity moves into the supplement, and fourteen appendix subsections become five thematic supplementary sections. This constitutes substantial narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template and table presentation, redraws Figure 3, combines earlier prompt and adapter plots into Figure 4, and consolidates sensitivity plots into Figure 6. It adds Cityscapes Figures 8–9 and multiple experimental tables, while restructuring the efficiency table to include AP50.

R1.justification: The positioning changes from an absence of prior VLOD TTA to detailed differentiation from TTAOD-F's mean-teacher architecture and computational costs. v2 also distinguishes online TTA from offline source-free adaptation with additional references. This substantially changes the research relationship, beyond bibliographic and citation-style updates.

T1.justification: The core mathematical definitions, entropy objectives, adapter parameter-count formulas, and cosine–Euclidean equivalence proposition and proof are retained. Moving the proof from Appendix A.1 to Section 6.1 and rendering the fusion equation inline do not alter the mathematics.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens comparative and explanatory support through the specialized TTAOD-F comparison, direct component ablations, and experiments exposing Cityscapes failure mechanisms. These address important gaps in v1's evidence and clarify applicability. Reporting weaknesses remain: the efficiency comparison uses unequal batch sizes, and the warm-start weather average is 38.6 in Table 5 but 39.0 from Table 16's entries. These limited weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support and interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VLOD-TTA by the same authors. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete supplementary material are readable and support reliable matching across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, component ablations, Cityscapes diagnostic experiments, and Aquarium evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original detection experiments, ablations, efficiency measurements, and corruption evaluations in Section 4 and Appendix A.

results.title: VLOD-TTA: Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Object Detectors

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: replacing fused global memory with local memories, coverage-driven retrieval, multi-anchor control, and improved consistency and visual quality. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: New Appendices H–I substantially qualify applicability through accumulated synthesis errors, pose drift, view-dependent reflections, unreliable geometry in unfamiliar scenes, and backbone-limited inference speed. v2 also explains the runtime-quality trade-off and distinguishes static spatial memory from dynamic object-state tracking.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents 16×–32× point-cloud downsampling, camera-control primitives, scene-dependent step magnitudes, four-frame stationary phases for memory updates, and runtime hardware/resolution. These expand implementation disclosure; the PDFs do not establish changes to the retained generation procedure.

E1.justification: RealEstate10K, DL3DV, and the existing open-domain static and gaming scenarios are retained. v2 adds an explicit reflective-surface failure case in H.4/Figure 13, broadening the tested scene conditions. Longer sequences and additional initial images primarily change evaluation design.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark, camera-control, and free-form comparisons retain their comparator membership and baseline descriptions. New efficiency and stress tests reuse SPMem. LiveWorld is discussed as a complementary approach, not evaluated as an additional baseline.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark protocols remain unchanged. New protocols include 20 initial images with repeated 80-frame exploration and 80-frame return phases through 2400 frames, revisit PSNR against the initial image, controlled history-fusion rendering tests, and runtime/memory evaluation on an RTX PRO 6000 with Wan2.2-5B at 81×480×832.

E4.justification: v2 adds history-dependent runtime analysis, a controlled diagnostic of rendering degradation under global fusion, repeated-revisit stress testing, and a reflective-surface failure study in Appendices G–H. These substantially extend the original memory, fusion, attention, and retrieval-count ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. The new 20-image sample and repeated camera cycles describe evaluation design rather than stochastic replication or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the camera-control table retain identical values. New results include 275 seconds/39 GB for K=4 in Table 4, long-horizon PSNR decay and SPMem rendering failure around frame 1120 in Figure 10, and rendering degradation from 44.83 to 16.15 dB in Figure 9. H.1 inconsistently prints 44.93 for that initial value.

M1.justification: Local memories, coverage-driven retrieval, Algorithm 1, multi-anchor attention, pose-guided fusion, and training objectives remain unchanged. Initial-anchor selection and character masking already appear in v1 Appendices B and F. The monitor extension in v2 H.3 is presented prospectively, without establishing a change to the implemented method.

P1.justification: Existing prose is selectively condensed and clarified, with an added process-visualization subsection, revised appendix headings, numeric citations, and affiliation/acknowledgment updates. Most original paragraphs and the main narrative sequence remain recognizable; the scientific additions do not constitute wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: The two-column main paper becomes single-column, substantially resizing and relocating figures and tables. v2 adds the efficiency table and Figures 8–13. Its main-text Figure 6 redisplays and annotates part of v1's appendix visualization; all original figure imagery is retained. Figure 2's caption also clarifies the visibility coloring.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially broadens cited literature across camera control, dynamic view synthesis, and memory/caching approaches, including PostCam, See4D, AnyView, Flow Caching, and WorldCompass. H.3 additionally positions AnchorWeave as complementary to LiveWorld's dynamic memory. The closest-work distinction from SPMem, Spatia, and MagicWorld remains.

T1.justification: The diffusion objective, mathematical setup, and greedy retrieval algorithm are retained. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations appear; the added scaling and robustness explanations are empirical.

improvement.justification: v1's long-horizon evidence chiefly comprised qualitative examples up to 241 frames. v2 adds a 20-image, 2400-frame quantitative stress test, computational scaling measurements, and concrete failure analyses, substantially strengthening assessment of the paper's central long-horizon claims and practical limits. Uncertainty estimates remain absent, and Table 4 does not clearly reconcile its Wan2.2 runtime setting with quality values matching the CogVideoX ablation, but these reporting limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AnchorWeave. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and matchable despite extensive reformatting and added supplementary analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains these results and adds runtime measurements, rendering diagnostics, and quantitative long-horizon stress tests.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, component ablations, camera-control measurements, and qualitative generation experiments.

results.title: AnchorWeave: World-Consistent Video Generation with Retrieved Local Spatial Memories

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: interactive environmental dynamics from one image, geometry-aware alignment, a hash-based global motion field, bidirectional propagation, and approximately 12-second updates. Localized object-motion integration and the broader future-work scope are also retained.

C2.justification: V2 interprets visual quality more selectively, acknowledging video models' frame-quality advantage while emphasizing temporal quality. It adds explanations of PerpetualWonder's difficulty with diffuse dynamics and nonlinear opacity schedules' loop discontinuities, and acknowledges residual holes and increased interaction complexity. The existing rigid-motion limitation remains.

D1.justification: V2 identifies Pexels and Unsplash as image sources and supplies interface controls and questionnaire details in Appendix D.6–D.7 and Figs. 10–12. Appendix B's architecture, normalization, optimizers, learning rates, and iteration counts are retained, as are the GPU and runtime details.

E1.justification: V2 adds hands-on evaluation of camera navigation, region selection, and motion guidance with participants from design or software-development backgrounds (Appendix D.7). Environmental-scene and object-motion coverage otherwise remains similar. Increasing the main benchmark from 10 to 60 scenes within retained environmental categories is principally a sample-size change.

E2.justification: PerpetualWonder joins the main quantitative comparison. Both PerpetualWonder and 4DGS-Cinemagraphy join Fig. 4 and the human preference comparison, which previously included only video-generation baselines. The new interactivity study also evaluates a WonderWorld-style baseline interface. Comparator coverage therefore expands across several distinct evaluations.

E3.justification: The main benchmark changes from 10 scenes to 60, balanced across four categories. GPT-4o PhysReal/PhotoReal evaluation is replaced by four VBench metrics and GPT-5.5 PhysReal. The preference study changes from 170 participants evaluating 10 scenes each on two criteria to 95 participants evaluating multiple scenes on four criteria. V2 also introduces distant-pair consistency metrics, hole-rate measurement, and a seven-point interactivity evaluation.

E4.justification: V2 supplements the retained alignment and motion-field ablations with direct global-consistency evaluation over distant points. Appendix D.4 compares linear, exponential, and sigmoid opacity schedules; D.5 quantifies boundary holes, reporting 9.8% for forward-only propagation versus 0.9% for bidirectional propagation. These add direct tests of previously less-supported coherence and rendering-stability properties.

E5.justification: V1's human preference table reports percentages without uncertainty. V2 Table 2 adds explicitly identified 95% confidence intervals, and Table 7 supplies additional ± values whose statistical meaning is unspecified. This introduces uncertainty reporting, but neither version documents repeated training runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Main comparison results are replaced under changed conditions: LivingWorld's PhysReal is 0.87 in v1 and 0.655 in v2, which does not establish a same-setting decline. V2 adds VBench results, global cosine scores of 0.91 versus 0.54/0.66 for the alignment alternatives, revised human preferences, and hole-rate and usability results. Existing MCA/FMV values, the supplemental in-the-wild table, and the module-runtime breakdown are retained.

M1.justification: The Eulerian flow predictor, Kabsch alignment with refinement, hash-based motion field, regression objective, and bidirectional propagation with linear opacity blending remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 is retained. The revised overview and named opacity scheduler clarify existing components rather than establish a changed procedure.

P1.justification: Section 3 consolidates alignment and field learning under Motion Field Generation, revises several explanations, and standardizes global-motion-field terminology. Experimental prose and appendix navigation are updated, and acknowledgements are added. The introduction, related-work structure, conclusion, and existing implementation appendix remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Figs. 2–3 are substantially redrawn, Fig. 4 expands and rearranges the comparator display, and Fig. 7 is revised. Main comparison, alignment, and preference tables are restructured, with the preference results moved into the main text. New benchmark, schedule, questionnaire, interface, hole-rate, and usability displays substantially expand the visual presentation. V1 Figs. 8–10 survive as v2 Figs. 13–15.

R1.justification: V2 adds VBench and two image-source references and elaborates PerpetualWonder's role as a complementary physics-based comparator. PerpetualWonder was already cited in v1. The broader related-work narrative and novelty positioning remain stable; reference reordering and publication-metadata updates do not introduce additional works.

T1.justification: Appendix C.3–C.4 adds mathematical definitions of global cosine similarity and magnitude ratio averaged over distant point pairs, including the ratio's stated range. Existing method equations and local-consistency definitions remain substantively unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method: it complements v1's small GPT-based automatic benchmark with VBench and broader comparisons, directly tests global coherence and boundary coverage, and evaluates actual interface use. Confidence intervals and clearer method diagrams improve assessability. The preference-study population decreases, and Appendix D.2 inconsistently claims to follow the revised main protocol while retaining GPT-4o/PhotoReal results. Despite these limitations, the new evidence addresses important gaps in support for the paper's central claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LivingWorld and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Inspection of all 28 pages of v1 and 36 pages of v2 supports reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark comparisons, expanded motion analyses, a revised 95-participant preference study, and a new 20-participant interactivity study.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark comparisons, motion-component ablations, runtime measurements, additional in-the-wild results, and a 170-participant human preference study.

results.title: LivingWorld: Interactive 4D World Generation with Environmental Dynamics

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion newly emphasize that multimodal training from scratch can compete with pretraining given sufficient labels, and that geographic batching particularly benefits rare samples. These substantially broaden the paper's principal conclusions beyond v1's benchmark and aggregate adaptation findings.

C2.justification: v2 expands interpretation of multimodal inputs versus pretraining, proposes gradient alignment and reduced dilution as explanations for long-tail gains, and interprets the ablation as evidence against dependence on one modality. Table A.15 also explicitly qualifies TTT's benefits by discussing deterioration for Galileo and ConvNeXtV2A-MM on the random split.

D1.justification: v2 documents Galileo's configuration and ConvNeXtV2A-MM's categorical encoding, spatial broadcasting and 926 input channels. Table A.16 newly reports selected TTT iteration averages, and Explorer split filtering changes from planned to reported as implemented. Table A.9 restates existing hyperparameters rather than changing them.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same biomass, soil nitrogen, soil organic carbon, soil pH and species datasets, with the same 12 modalities and geographic coverage. The new analyses examine the existing data rather than introduce another task or test environment.

E2.justification: v2 adds Galileo and randomly initialized ConvNeXtV2A-MM to finetuning, linear-probing and JT/TTT comparisons. Galileo S2 also enters the input-modality comparisons. These additions substantially strengthen the comparator set, particularly through the multimodal model trained from scratch; v1's randomly initialized baseline accepted only RGB.

E3.justification: Added diagnostic protocols stratify residuals and species average precision by frequency, omit individual reconstruction modalities, and evaluate reconstruction using R² or categorical accuracy. The original splits, training subsets, 100-epoch budget, batch size and validation-based selection remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds long-tail analysis (Figure 8), a DINOv3 Sat leave-one-modality-out ablation (Figure A.16), an analysis of selected best models (Table A.17), and quantitative reconstruction diagnostics (Tables A.18–A.27). These substantially extend v1's linear-probing comparisons, relative-improvement analysis and qualitative reconstruction visualization.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports using one seed for the new long-tail analysis and modality ablation. The original benchmark retains seeds 41–43, standard-error reporting and one-sided Wilcoxon tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction; no increase in its repeated-run count is reported.

E6.justification: The original raw finetuning, linear-probing and JT/TTT scores are retained, but substantial results are added. ConvNeXtV2A-MM ranks first overall on the random split and fourth geographically with full training data (Table A.10). Table A.15 adds negative random-split TTT relative improvements for some new-model configurations. New diagnostic findings are reported, and the expanded Figure 7 comparison reports p < 0.05 rather than v1's p < 0.01.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains joint training, normalized per-modality gradient updates, frozen reconstruction decoders, encoder resets and geographic batching. The additional model variants serve as experimental comparators; the proposed TTT-MMR procedure is unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 edits the abstract, introduction and results, consolidates v1 Sections 5.2–5.5 under one Results subsection, and moves the existing hyperparameter discussion into the appendix. Most related-work, dataset, method and data-construction prose remains closely matched.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to one, rearranges Figure 1 and Table 3, and expands model legends and table columns. New analysis figures and diagnostic tables substantially change the visual presentation. The enlarged duplicate figures from v1's Section S.6 are removed while their underlying plots remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds Hong et al.'s foundation-model survey and expands positioning relative to weak-label and auxiliary-task TTA. Galileo was already cited in v1 but receives fuller discussion in v2. The broader related-work framework remains stable.

T1.justification: The reconstruction-loss and normalized-gradient update mathematics remain equivalent despite revised notation and equation formatting. Metric definitions and geographic encodings are retained; neither version adds substantive theoretical results or proofs.

improvement.justification: The multimodal baseline trained from scratch addresses an important missing control in v1's assessment of pretraining. The modality ablation and quantitative reconstruction diagnostics also substantially strengthen scrutiny of TTT. Some conclusions remain limited by single-seed evidence, and Table A.17 names MPMAE as the best geographic-biomass model although Table A.10 ranks ConvNeXtV2A-MM first. These weaknesses temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial improvement in the paper's empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MMEarth-Bench and TTT-MMR. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds evaluated models, a modality ablation, long-tail analysis and quantitative reconstruction results.

before.justification: v1 reports original finetuning, linear-probing and test-time-training results across five environmental tasks and two test splits in Section 5 and the supplementary material.

results.title: MMEarth-Bench: Global Model Adaptation via Multimodal Test-Time Training

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds a novel Diagnosis Fairness criterion and Approximate Diagnosis Fairness metric for medical diagnosis. V2 replaces that novelty claim with scalable enforcement of existing path-specific counterfactual fairness through conditional independence and a connection to standard equalized odds, broadening the claimed scope to high-dimensional modalities.

C2.justification: V2 adds an explanation of baseline over-correction and under-correction, acknowledges omitted exogenous influences, and explains that its sufficient independence constraint can suppress information that PSCF would permit. These materially qualify the causal mechanism and applicability, alongside new interpretations of synthetic and demographic experiments.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a repository address and reports code availability, whereas v1 only promises release; Appendix C.3 still retains the future-release wording. It also adds component FLOP costs, synthetic-generation parameters and statements about shared training and tuning controls. Existing hardware, software and principal hyperparameter disclosures are largely unchanged.

E1.justification: The three medical datasets, diagnosis tasks and eight downstream MIMIC-CXR tasks are retained. V2 adds focused coverage through a synthetic SCM, age-based fairness evaluation across the three datasets, and joint gender-by-age evaluation on MIMIC-CXR (Table 3; Appendices D.2 and D.4).

E2.justification: V2 adds SUBG and Group-DRO to the main comparison on all three datasets, retaining Vanilla, AD and FAAP. This substantially broadens the central comparison to include data balancing and worst-group robust training alongside the original adversarial approaches.

E3.justification: The main 90/10 split and stated hyperparameters are retained. Supplementary protocols add an 80/10/10 train/validation/test split with validation-based tuning, an age threshold of 60, and synthetic interventional DE/IE evaluation. Renaming EO to EOp and ADF to EOd preserves their formulas and does not change the retained metrics.

E4.justification: V2 adds tests of direct-effect suppression versus indirect-effect preservation, validation-based hyperparameter selection, age and joint-attribute robustness, demographic composition, and computational overhead. These substantially extend the retained architecture and hyperparameter ablations, downstream transfer evaluation and GradCAM analysis.

E5.justification: V1 presents point estimates without run counts or uncertainty. V2 introduces mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting throughout Table 1, discloses five repetitions in Appendix C.1, and reports five-seed averaging for the synthetic experiment. This establishes a substantial reporting change without establishing whether the retained experiments were rerun.

E6.justification: V2 adds results for new baselines, demographic settings and appendix studies, including synthetic SPARC direct and indirect effects of 0.027 and 0.171. Shared Table 1 point estimates remain unchanged, but ablation values change: Table 2 MIMIC ResNet50 accuracy changes from 84.67% to 84.26%, and the CheXpert CMI values at noise strengths 0.2 and 0.3 are interchanged.

M1.justification: The central JSD-MI pretraining, additive masking, conditioned discriminator, losses and alternating optimization remain unchanged. Appendix D.4 adds limited proposed adaptations: matching the discriminator head to multivalued sensitive attributes and conditioning on fair-path parents for richer causal graphs.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statements and conclusion are extensively rewritten around SPARC. Theory now precedes the method instantiation, proofs move to Appendix A, and the appendices are reorganized into theory, settings, implementation and additional experiments. This exceeds terminology or numbering changes.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document from two columns to one, redraws the causal diagram, expands Table 1 with uncertainty and ranking annotations, and adds demographic plots and supplementary tables. Figures 2–4 retain their underlying content while being resized or relocated; the overall visual organization changes substantially.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands causal-fairness positioning, including Kusner's counterfactual fairness, Chiappa and Gillam's PSCF, and information-theoretic equalized-odds literature. It replaces v1's assertion that prior fairness metrics are causal-model agnostic with a contribution explicitly framed around making established PSCF tractable.

T1.justification: Appendix A substantially rewrites Theorem 1's proof, restoring summation over X and explicitly invoking ignorability and consistency. V2 removes v1's reversed sufficiency statement following Theorem 2 and introduces an epsilon-relaxed PSCF definition. These are mathematical revisions beyond relocating proofs or changing notation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves the paper's theoretical grounding and empirical support: it repairs v1's reversed implication and proof derivation, acknowledges existing PSCF/equalized-odds concepts, and adds direct causal-effect validation, broader baselines and repeated-run uncertainty. These address important weaknesses in the original justification. Table 9's caption and protocol description remain inconsistent, and output fairness still cannot certify the stronger input-independence condition, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same underlying causal fairness framework and retain corresponding methods, datasets and experiments despite substantial renaming and reframing. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original medical-image experiments and adds baseline comparisons, demographic evaluations, synthetic causal-effect validation and supplementary experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original medical-image classification experiments on MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert and TCGA-LUAD, together with transfer evaluations, ablations and GradCAM analyses.

results.title: SPARC: Scalable Path-Specific Counterfactual Fairness via Causal Conditional Independence

C1.justification: The central claim of training-free, distribution-preserving continuous speculative decoding remains. v2 broadens the headline empirical claim from MAR acceleration up to 2.33× to over 2× across three model families and two resolutions. It also elevates alignment's avoidance of repeated diffusion inference into an explicit contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive discussion of applicability to explicit continuous PDFs, GMMs, alternative diffusion samplers, and untested audio/video domains. It expands explanations of alignment, rejection-sampling cost, and masking's speed/quality tradeoff. Its limitations discussion adds a batch-size explanation but drops v1's short-generation limitation; interpretations accompanying the removed visual ablations also disappear.

D1.justification: v2 reports code as available rather than forthcoming and documents additional model-specific details, including xAR's k=1 configuration and Harmon's separate text embeddings and memory-limited batches. The A100 hardware, official checkpoints, and 50,000-image MAR evaluation remain documented. v1's explicit statement that temperature and CFG follow MAR defaults is omitted, without establishing an actual setting change.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from ImageNet 256 × 256 unconditional/class-conditioned generation to Harmon text-to-image generation at both 256 × 256 and 512 × 512 resolutions. xAR adds another model on the retained ImageNet task. GMM, audio, and video applications are discussed but not experimentally evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 Appendix G.5 and Table 8 add MAR-H masked generation as an alternative acceleration comparator, evaluated across six masking configurations. The original vanilla-model and pure-draft comparisons remain. xAR and Harmon are additional host models, not competing decoding methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds xAR-B/H and Harmon-0.5B/1.5B configurations, uses xAR's tokenwise k=1 setting, and evaluates Harmon with smaller batches because of memory limits. New protocols include 100-step DDIM at batch size 256, rejection-sampling timing at batch size 1, and masked-generation sweeps. Alignment evaluation adds token distance, while speedup and ablation tables narrow the retained MAR model-pair sweep.

E4.justification: v2 adds alignment-distance measurements, DDIM testing, a rejection-sampling runtime breakdown, and masked-generation speed/quality analysis. It removes the visual alignment and pre-filling ablations in v1 Figures 10 and 12 and reduces their model-pair sweeps. Existing CFG, temperature, rejection-count, and acceptance-heatmap analyses are retained through relocation or consolidation.

E5.justification: v2 Section 4.2 explicitly identifies the reported uncertainty as standard deviation; v1 presents the same ± values without identifying their type. Both appendices already specify ten evaluation runs, and the shared uncertainty values are unchanged. There is no documented increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Shared MAR-H/MAR-B speedups and MAR FID/IS entries remain unchanged. v2 newly reports up to 2.72× for xAR, 2.54× for Harmon at 512 resolution, and 2.30× for MAR with DDIM, alongside token-distance, runtime, and masking results. These are additional experimental settings, not same-setting MAR improvements. Speedup and ablation rows involving MAR-L are removed.

M1.justification: The acceptance rule, shared-noise trajectory alignment, token pre-filling, rejection sampling, and Algorithm 1 remain equivalent. v2 emphasizes avoiding repeated diffusion inference, but its rejection threshold and Gaussian sampling procedure already appear in v1 Equation 11 and Algorithm 1. Additional host models and sampler configurations do not establish a changed decoding algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and methodology are extensively rewritten. The method narrative changes from question-based subsections to continuous formulation, inconsistency mitigation, and resampling. The supplement is reorganized into separate algorithm, limitations, implementation, applicability, disclosure, and experiment sections, with some main-text analysis moved into it.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, redraws Figure 2, restructures speedup and ablation tables, and adds several experimental tables. Existing analyses are consolidated into v2 Figure 10, while two visual ablations are removed. The final qualitative galleries are retained with identical image content despite renumbering and resizing.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion involving xAR, Harmon, DiCoDe, DDIM, and LANTERN++, while trimming works such as FLUID, DART, RAR, Medusa, and BiLD. The central positioning against discrete speculative decoding remains intact. Publication updates for retained references do not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 introduces Theorem 1 and a substantial Appendix A.1 proof quantifying the expected squared-distance reduction from shared Gaussian noise. This mathematical result is absent from v1. The distribution-preservation proof is retained, while Corollary 1 largely formalizes the rejection-threshold derivation already present in v1.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially broadens v1's single-model validation through xAR, Harmon, higher-resolution, and DDIM experiments. The alignment theorem and distance measurements, direct rejection-sampling timings, and masked-generation comparison strengthen the explanation and evidence for practical efficiency. These gains outweigh the narrower MAR ablation coverage, although image-quality validation remains limited to MAR and does not establish preservation on the newly evaluated models.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same continuous speculative decoding work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the extensive reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original MAR results and adds xAR and Harmon speed measurements, DDIM experiments, runtime measurements, and masked-generation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original MAR speedup, acceptance-rate, FID/IS, ablation, and qualitative results, including additional experiments in its supplement.

results.title: Continuous Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Image Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: order marginalization improves AR classification, surpasses diffusion classifiers with up to 25-fold faster inference, and competes with DINOv2. The additions provide supporting evidence without changing these headline claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning generalization beyond RandAR and practical differences between equivalent-in-expectation scoring objectives. Appendix H hypothesizes that perceptual fidelity increasingly dominates FID at low values, while Appendix I distinguishes fast generation from fast classification. Existing error explanations and computational limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies sources for the MaskGIT-B checkpoint and COCO-to-ImageNet mapping, documents disabling RAR order annealing, and makes the WILDS tokenizer description consistent with Appendix A. The original core training schedules, hardware disclosure and code/model access information are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix G adds ObjectNet and COCO evaluation while retaining the earlier ImageNet and WILDS coverage. These introduce non-image-centric object views and multi-object recognition, with COCO requiring recovery of multiple ImageNet-mapped objects rather than one class.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds comparisons involving adapted RAR-B, MaskGIT-B and RandAR scored as masked diffusion. The WILDS comparison adds raster-order RandAR at both model sizes. Appendix I additionally evaluates three MeanFlow classifier variants against DiT, substantially expanding the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include B-scale AR/MD comparisons with evaluation-budget sweeps through K=60, COCO-to-ImageNet mapping with K-recall@K, and three MeanFlow scoring strategies. The WILDS tokenizer statement changes from MaskGIT to LlamaGen with noise, matching the existing Appendix A; this correction does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds architecture generalization through RAR, AR-versus-MD scoring sensitivity to computation, an XL no-noise ablation, raster-order controls on WILDS, and generation-quality versus classification analysis. Appendix I also tests whether few-step generation translates into efficient classification. These substantially extend v1's retained analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three-seed averaging for the WILDS discriminative baselines. v2 introduces no additional repeated-run disclosures, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty-reporting practices. The new evaluation-budget sweeps concern scoring procedures rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises the relabelled A-VARC+ rows: ImageNet-Val scores change from 0.683 to 0.717 for L and 0.661 to 0.719 for XL; RandAR's main scores remain unchanged. Substantial new results cover RAR/MD, XL augmentation, WILDS raster controls, ObjectNet/COCO, generation FID and MeanFlow. Table 12 places RandAR above DiT but below DINOv2 on both added datasets.

M1.justification: The central RandAR classifier and Equation (5) remain unchanged. Section 6.6 adds an adaptation of RAR trained without order annealing, and Section 6.7 introduces alternative masked-prefix scoring of RandAR. These extend the procedures without replacing the core method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the narrative sequence are retained. v2 inserts Sections 6.6–6.7 and several appendix sections, introduces AO-AR terminology, adds the HSE affiliation and corrects names such as ResNet-151 to ResNet-152. These are localized additions and edits rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds the paired B-scale/MD tables, ObjectNet/COCO and FID tables, and a MeanFlow runtime plot. Table 4 gains model-size groups and the WILDS table gains raster rows. These substantially expand the visual evidence; the earlier qualitative Figure 9 is retained as Figure 10. Page margins also increase throughout.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly connects its objective to masked-diffusion research and extends the efficiency discussion to contemporary few-step diffusion methods. These relationships, supported by new any-order/diffusion and MeanFlow/distillation citations, substantially broaden the research positioning beyond v1's discussion. Existing cited works are retained.

T1.justification: Unlike v1, Appendix D derives a claimed equivalence between the order-averaged AR objective and a masked-diffusion ELBO using expectations over masked subsets. This is a substantive theoretical addition. As written, Equation (6) introduces a 1/N normalization inconsistent with the earlier full-sequence likelihood definition.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in support for generality and efficiency through another AR architecture, WILDS raster controls, multi-object/non-image-centric evaluation and MeanFlow comparisons. These strengthen the central argument while documenting DINOv2's remaining advantages, and the WILDS tokenizer correction improves consistency. Equation (6)'s normalization problem weakens the theoretical addition, but the broader empirical validation provides a substantial overall benefit.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same order-marginalized generative classification study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds RAR, masked-diffusion, ObjectNet/COCO and MeanFlow evaluations, among other analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original classifier training, ImageNet and WILDS evaluations, token-order experiments, tokenizer ablations and runtime measurements.

results.title: Revisiting Autoregressive Models for Generative Image Classification

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on text-to-image acceleration demonstrated with SANA and FLUX. v3 broadens the central applicability claim to image generation, text-to-video, image-to-video, and image editing, and explicitly claims the first effective post-training solution for deeply compressed latent adaptation. The earlier abstract's 138× NVIDIA 5090 claim is removed.

C2.justification: v3 distinguishes failure modes across models, including blurred FLUX outputs, ineffective Qwen edits that copy inputs, and Wan training collapse. Appendix B assigns different roles to patch alignment and output alignment: capability recovery versus faster convergence. Appendix H adds substantive explanations of reconstruction-versus-long-video-generalization tradeoffs and the chunk-size choice, extending v1's more general representation-gap explanation.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands reproducibility information with model-specific hyperparameters, resolution-lifting schedules, data sources and counts, LoRA settings, stage-wise training costs, decoding-cost breakdowns, and DC-AE-V architecture and padding pseudocode (Appendices E–H). These include newly documented details rather than necessarily changed procedures. Conversely, v1's DiT/SANA settings and explicit project-code link are omitted.

E1.justification: v3 removes ImageNet class-to-image coverage and adds text-to-video and image-to-video evaluation on VBench/VBench-I2V, bilingual image editing on GEdit, and video reconstruction on Panda70m/UCF101. It adds Aesthetic-4K evaluation and reports training with Pexels/Unsplash images, FusionX-generated videos, and Pico-Banana editing pairs. These substantially change the represented data and task requirements.

E2.justification: The MJHQ comparison removes SANA-1.6B/4.8B and adds Z-Image-Turbo while retaining the other image baselines. New comparisons include Diffusion-4K, video generators, FLUX.1-Kontext, Step1X-Edit, and video autoencoders. Appendices B and G additionally evaluate layer-wise learning-rate decay, gradual LoRA, autoencoder latent alignment, TaylorSeer, and AnyFlow; SVDQuant was already evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: v1 benchmarks latency and throughput with torch.compile; v3 specifies TensorRT and transformer-backbone latency. The reported FLUX output-alignment and end-to-end batch sizes change from 256 to 512 (v1 Table 5; v3 Table 12). New evaluation designs include matched-data fine-tuned controls, fixed-resolution video comparisons, Qwen2.5-based editing assessment, and multi-rater human studies. These are reported protocol changes, not evidence that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's combined alignment, LoRA, and guidance-objective ablations, v3 separates patch-embedder and output-layer alignment, tests alternative stabilization and latent-alignment strategies, and extends convergence analyses to video and editing. Appendix H adds chunk-size sensitivity, long-video reconstruction checks, and controlled autoencoder substitutions. Appendix G expands acceleration-combination analyses. The earlier DiT/SANA ablations are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v3's human studies disclose sample and rater counts and preference percentages, but introduce no uncertainty estimates; those additions concern evaluation design and results.

E6.justification: Retained DC-Gen-FLUX entries change: 1K CLIP Score is 27.94 in v1 Table 2 versus 28.02 in v3 Table 1, while GenEval changes from 0.72 to 0.71. Training and timing settings also change, preventing a controlled performance-gain interpretation. v3 adds substantial video, editing, human-preference, reconstruction, and acceleration results, while removing ImageNet, SANA, and NVIDIA 5090 result sets. Several retained ablation values also change.

M1.justification: The core embedding-alignment and LoRA pipeline is retained, but v3 introduces DC-AE-V with chunk-causal temporal modeling and a video encoder, decoder, and discriminator (Section 3.5; Appendix H). It also adapts image-to-video conditioning by repeating the input image four times before encoding. Separately naming patch and output alignment does not itself introduce a new stage: both operations existed in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, and conclusion are extensively rewritten.
