Experiments are reorganized by task; the guidance-correction derivation moves into Appendix A; and the former compact appendix becomes separate sections for ablations, visualization, human evaluation, settings, costs, acceleration combinations, and the video autoencoder. The narrative changes substantially alongside the scientific expansion.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the opening image-only showcase with a multi-task figure and redraws the pipeline to display patch alignment, output alignment, and fine-tuning separately. It adds training curves, human-study tables and interfaces, video/editing comparisons, and autoencoder diagrams. Existing cost and ablation displays are relocated or reorganized, and the main image table replaces throughput with latency.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning around video diffusion, editing, video autoencoders, sparsity, and acceleration. Section 3.4 explicitly contrasts DC-Gen with OpenSora-2.0's latent adaptation, while Appendix H distinguishes chunk-causal modeling from IV-VAE, LTX Video VAE, and Video DC-AE. This goes beyond citation renumbering or bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Appendix H adds a formal chunk-causal convolution construction and defines total video compression as 3f²t/c (Equation 11), extending the earlier spatial formulation. The main alignment loss and guidance-correction derivation remain substantively equivalent, with expanded algebra in Appendix A. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the central alignment and quality-preservation claims. Unlike v1's bundled alignment ablation, Appendix B isolates the two alignment components and tests credible alternatives; matched-data controls and human studies improve assessment of retained capabilities. Expanded implementation and cost documentation also improves auditability. These gains outweigh the lost ImageNet/SANA coverage and code-link disclosure. Reporting weaknesses remain: Figure 22 gives a 14.8× video speedup at 2160p, whereas Table 16 implies about 9.2×, and statistical uncertainty remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DC-Gen and provide readable methods, equations, figures, tables, and appendices sufficient for reliable comparison. v3 substantially extends the same research work.

after.justification: v3 reports original image generation, video generation, image editing, human evaluation, and video-autoencoder experiments, including extensive appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet class-to-image experiments, SANA and FLUX evaluations, component ablations, and inference benchmarks.

results.title: DC-Gen: Post-Training Diffusion Acceleration with Deeply Compressed Latent Space

C1.justification: The central architecture-agnostic, interpretable rubric-reward contribution remains. The introduction refines the control contribution from a general user-controllable interface to developer-controlled rubric categories adjusted through system-prompt edits. The abstract now explicitly describes validation on both AR and diffusion models.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for binary feedback benefiting discrete correctness, excessive rubrics introducing redundancy, and aesthetic gains arising from decomposed supervision. Appendix D discusses API cost, accessibility, and difficulties distilling general-purpose graders. These substantially extend v1's retained counting-failure and sampling/grader tradeoff discussions.

D1.justification: v2 supplies all three prompting templates, including rubric-selection priorities, diffusion hyperparameters and EMA details, human-study instructions/interfaces, rubric caching, and runtime/API-cost information. It also newly specifies AR CFG scale 7.5 and DPG prompt rewriting; these disclosures do not establish changes to the earlier AR experiments.

E1.justification: Training retains JourneyDB and Synthetic-1M, and generation evaluation retains GenEval and DPG-Bench. Additional backbones, aesthetic scoring, and human judging do not establish new generation-task or prompt-domain coverage; no distinct new dataset or input scenario is identified.

E2.justification: Appendix B.1 adds continuous-score rubric supervision as an evaluated alternative to the proposed binary supervision. The external reward comparator set remains CLIPScore, HPSv2, Unified Reward, LLaVA-Reward-Phi, AR-GRPO, and X-Omni; the earlier sampling and grader comparison sets are retained.

E3.justification: New diffusion experiments introduce Qwen-Image and FLUX configurations, LoRA training, and diffusion-specific sampling settings. v2 also adds CLIP+MLP aesthetic evaluation and human protocols covering preference, rubric validity, and grader agreement, including 1,000 prompt–rubric pairs and ten annotators. Previously specified AR training settings are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test binary versus continuous feedback, rubric counts of 4/8/10/12, aesthetic quality alongside compositional accuracy, and human agreement with rubrics and graders. Appendix D adds cost and convergence analysis. Earlier sampling, normalization, Best-of-N, counting-failure, grader, and rollout-budget analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 newly displays error bars for human preference and judge agreement in Figure 5 and discusses lower variance. Their definition and estimation procedure are unspecified. Neither version reports training seeds or repeated-training-run counts, so additional training repetitions cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: All 32 original main benchmark rows retain their values. New diffusion results include RubricRL GenEval scores of 0.9091 for Qwen-Image and 0.8969 for FLUX (Table 3). New human results report 98.1% rubric consistency and 94.8% grader agreement; additional ablation, aesthetic, and cost results substantially expand the evidence.

M1.justification: v2 adds an implemented diffusion branch using DiffusionNFT, including velocity-space optimization and an EMA sampling policy (Section 3 and Appendix A.4). v1 implements only AR training with GRPO. The shared binary rubric reward and original AR sampling procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Local rewrites clarify AR/diffusion branches and developer control, related work gains numbered subsections, normalization variants are renamed, and supplementary material is organized into Sections A–E. This is not a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, redraws Figures 2–3, and restructures benchmark tables. New displays include diffusion and ablation tables, a human-study plot, prompt-template panels, and annotation screenshots. Earlier qualitative grids are largely retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to FLUX, DiffusionNFT, and the CLIP+MLP aesthetic predictor, while removing T2I-R1. DiffusionNFT enters the discussion of diffusion RL. The broader positioning against composite and unified rewards, and the rubric-reward novelty claim, remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 adds mathematical specifications for DiffusionNFT's bounded optimality probability, positive/negative velocity mixtures, regression objective, and EMA update. This formalizes the added optimizer; the original rubric, GRPO, and sampling mathematics is retained, with no new theorem, proof, or theoretical guarantee.

improvement.justification: v1 claimed architecture independence while testing only AR models and lacked direct rubric-reliability validation. v2 substantially addresses these gaps through diffusion comparisons, human studies, and targeted design ablations, while full prompts and optimizer details improve reproducibility. Undefined human-study error bars and appendix editing inconsistencies limit reporting quality, but do not outweigh the stronger support for the central contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RubricRL and contain readable main texts, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary material. Original experiments and visual examples can be matched despite extensive reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original diffusion-model evaluations, human studies, aesthetic measurements, and further ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original text-to-image RL experiments on GenEval and DPG-Bench, including sampling, normalization, grader, and rollout-budget ablations.

results.title: RubricRL: Simple Generalizable Rewards for Text-to-Image Generation

C1.justification: The framework, small-data GRPO, and IV-Edit contributions remain central. v2 strengthens the conclusion with an explicit claim of improvements across MMDiT backbones without compromising efficiency, and Appendix D adds a first-of-its-kind claim for coherent parallel editing across numerous regions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting dense masks to attention-kernel overhead and latency growth to longer text sequences. Appendix H interprets external results as task-domain generalization and expands discussion of CLIP metric misalignment. Appendix D adds arguments about alternative editing approaches' locality and coherence limitations.

D1.justification: v2 specifies FlexAttention, fused visibility testing, bitset storage, and the attention implementations used for timing. Earlier training-data construction details and the project-page address remain. Hardware and detailed training hyperparameters are still not supplied.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix H adds evaluation on MagicBrush and SmartEdit, extending coverage beyond IV-Edit to their more constrained, locality-focused editing scenarios. The existing IV-Edit composition and training-data sources remain unchanged.

E2.justification: v2 adds Flux.2-Klein-9B to Table 1. Tables 6–7 introduce HIVE variants, MagicBrush-tuned InstructPix2Pix, MagicBrush, InstructDiffusion, and SmartEdit-7B comparisons. Table 3 additionally compares accelerated RePlan with unaccelerated RePlan and multi-turn Kontext. Earlier comparison methods are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include a blinded study of 100 randomly sampled pairs with 12 experts, randomized output ordering, and majority voting; latency comparisons across one to five regions and different attention implementations; and external-benchmark evaluations using their respective metrics and annotation-derived region-guidance controls. Existing IV-Edit scoring and training settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds acceleration ablations and region-count scaling measurements in Table 3, contrasts full RePlan with annotation-guided attention injection in Tables 6–7, and adds many-region editing case studies in Figures 7, 10, and 11. Earlier planner, reasoning, training-stage, attention-rule, overlap, and perturbation analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new human-study voting protocol and preference percentages do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: New results include the Klein comparison, with Overall scores of 3.45 without RePlan and 3.92 with it; human preferences of 35% RePlan, 15% Kontext, and 50% ties; and five-region latencies of 54.1 seconds accelerated versus 113.8 unaccelerated and 221.0 multi-turn. Tables 6–7 add external-benchmark scores. Matched earlier numerical results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 5.3 adds a rule-group attention acceleration variant using per-token bitsets and fused, on-the-fly visibility computation instead of storing a dense mask. This changes attention execution while preserving the planner, five visibility rules, and two-stage GRPO objectives.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites and expands the benchmark rationale, introduces numbered benchmark and ablation subsections, and adds appendix contents, keywords, and acknowledgements. It removes the short LLM-polishing disclosure. Most existing methodological and analytical prose is retained.

P2.justification: The document adopts substantially different typography, margins, running headers, and float placement. Earlier Tables 2–3 are merged; Table 1 gains shaded RePlan rows; new latency and benchmark tables and three multi-region figures are added. Existing qualitative panels are retained despite relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Gemini 2.5, GPT-4o, FlashAttention, FlashAttention-2, FlexAttention, DiT, and latent diffusion. Appendix D adds novelty positioning against cut-and-paste, layer-based, inpainting, and ControlNet approaches. The main related-work account otherwise remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 5.3 introduces mathematical definitions for group-membership and visibility bitsets, their bitwise visibility condition, and a memory-complexity argument reducing explicit-mask storage from O(n²) to O(n ceil(k/W)) machine words. Existing method equations and reward definitions are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's reliance on IV-Edit and automatic judging: two external benchmarks, a blinded human study, and controlled latency comparisons directly support generalization, instruction following, and efficiency. The gains are not uniform: MagicBrush CLIP-T decreases from 0.2913 for Kontext to 0.2866 for RePlan, qualifying the broad improvement language. Missing timing hardware and uncertainty estimates limit interpretation, but the added complementary evidence provides a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RePlan work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, tables, and figures. Renumbered and relocated material can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds a human preference study, latency measurements, another backbone evaluation, and MagicBrush and SmartEdit results.

before.justification: v1 reports original IV-Edit evaluations, planner and training ablations, global-rephrasing comparisons, attention analyses, and bounding-box perturbation results.

results.title: RePlan: Reasoning-Guided Region Planning for Complex Instruction-Based Image Editing

C1.justification: v2 removes v1's claim to be the first layout-conditioned AR text-to-image framework. Its abstract and introduction add claims of transfer to standard next-token models and exposure-bias mitigation, while the contributions emphasize validation across multiple benchmarks. These materially revise novelty and applicability claims beyond the retained structured-masking and quality/layout-control contributions.

C2.justification: The main interpretation of masking and the quality/layout tradeoff remains. v2 adds explanations for exposure-bias mitigation, global-prompt disambiguation of overlaps, and complementary reward weaknesses: VQA can overlook inaccurate boundaries and false positives, while detection can neglect detailed semantics. It removes v1's speculation that a stronger AR backbone could close the image-quality gap.

D1.justification: v2 discloses SFT runtime of three days on eight MI300X GPUs, GRPO runtime of four hours on eight MI250 GPUs, reward coefficients, and which baseline results were imported or reproduced. Conversely, v1's approximately one-million-sample SFT disclosure and Qwen3-14B redundancy-filter identification disappear. Their omission reduces documentation and does not establish a change to the SFT sample count.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained LayoutSAM training data and LayoutSAM-Eval evaluation, v2 adds OverLayBench-Complex for densely overlapping layouts and T2I-CompBench for compositional generation, including numeracy and spatial reasoning. These broaden the evaluated input conditions and task requirements. Simple/Regular OverLayBench results are referenced but not supplied.

E2.justification: In the corresponding LayoutSAM-Eval comparison, v2 removes Ranni and Be Yourself and adds PlanGen, InstanceAssemble and SiamLayout-FLUX. The original SiamLayout comparator is retained as SiamLay-SD3. Additional reported comparisons include EliGen on OverLayBench and SDXL, PixArt-alpha, DALL-E 3 and Show-o on T2I-CompBench. PlanGen adds a direct autoregressive competitor absent from v1.

E3.justification: v2 adds Grounding DINO filtering requiring training-sample mIoU and precision above 0.9, increases the within-box layout-advantage weight from 1.1 to 1.2, and evaluates detection metrics on 895 selected LayoutSAM-Eval samples. It removes IS reporting and introduces OverLayBench-specific metrics and GPT-5.2-generated layouts for T2I-CompBench. The principal SFT and GRPO iteration counts, batch sizes and learning rates remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's HPS-versus-CLIP-layout ablation is replaced by an expanded analysis separating HPS, VQA and detection rewards. v2 Table 5 and Figure 6 test whether semantic rewards miss localization/false-positive errors and whether detection rewards sacrifice attribute fidelity. The retained masking ablation gains detection metrics and qualitative failure examples in Figure 5. Referenced supplementary tokenizer and weight studies cannot be inspected.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports evaluation seeds, repeated-run counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. Both present point estimates. The unchanged GRPO group size of four describes training rollouts, not repeated experimental trials.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces SMARLI's spatial/IR values of 95.33/69.08 with 95.55/74.81 under revised reward and training settings; FID remains 18.16. These are not controlled same-setting gains. New benchmark tables and revised reward ablations add substantial results, while the original masking-ablation values are retained. The expanded comparison also changes rankings: SiamLay-FLUX leads spatial accuracy and PlanGen leads FID in v2.

M1.justification: The layout reward changes substantially: v1 averages cropped-region CLIP similarities, whereas v2 combines VLM-based binary VQA scores with Grounding DINO mIoU and precision scores. This introduces new reward components targeting semantic consistency, localization and false positives. The tokenizer, structured masking and stepwise GRPO trajectory replay remain substantially the same; their expanded explanations do not establish additional algorithm changes.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work and method explanations are extensively rewritten. Preliminary material moves inside Method, masking is organized around named principles, and experiments are divided into separate layout-to-image and text-to-image evaluations. Front matter also changes, including an additional author and affiliation, keywords and acknowledgments.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column to a single-column layout. Figure 1 moves before the abstract with refreshed examples; Figure 2 changes its reward diagram; and Figure 3 revises the comparison grid. New overlap and ablation figures are added. Tables gain parameter counts and detection metrics, and the reward table separates VQA and detection components. The original ablation tables are matched despite renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions SMARLI relative to PlanGen, explicitly acknowledging an existing AR layout-generation approach and motivating improvements to interference and image quality. It adds discussion of InstanceAssemble and literature supporting the new rewards and benchmarks. The earlier TwFA/LayoutEnc discussion and citations disappear. This changes the novelty argument, not merely bibliography formatting.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 4 defines a new weighted VQA/mIoU/precision reward, replacing v1's prose definition of average regional CLIP similarity. This is a limited mathematical-definition change. The GRPO objective, tokenizer equations and overall advantage combination are otherwise retained, with no new theorem, proof or formal guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence beyond v1's single-benchmark, diffusion-only comparison: it adds a direct AR competitor, challenging overlapping-layout evaluation, and spatial metrics and reward-component controls that examine concrete failure modes. Its novelty positioning is also more qualified. These gains materially improve support for the central layout-control claims, rather than merely raising reported scores. Missing supplementary evidence, removed IS reporting and reduced training-data disclosure remain limitations, but do not outweigh the stronger main-paper validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of SMARLI, with identifiable corresponding methods, equations, figures and tables. Neither contains an appendix or embedded supplement. However, v2 refers to unavailable supplementary Janus-Pro results, OverLayBench Simple/Regular results, and tokenizer/weight ablations, limiting verification of those additions.

after.justification: v2 reports original SMARLI evaluations on LayoutSAM-Eval, OverLayBench-Complex and T2I-CompBench, together with masking and reward ablations in Tables 1–5.

before.justification: v1 reports original SMARLI results on LayoutSAM-Eval, masking and reward ablations in Tables 1–3, and generated-image examples.

results.title: Layout-Conditioned Autoregressive Text-to-Image Generation via Structured Masking

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: broader reasoning coverage, dual-reference evaluation, a synthetic CoT-annotated training dataset, and improved editing through Bagel fine-tuning. The additional experiments support these existing contributions without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v3 newly interprets game-data inclusion as positive transfer to real-world editing. Appendix K also characterizes previously displayed gem deletion and box duplication as 'Logical Hallucination,' connecting them to object permanence, conservation, and state consistency. These extend the existing interpretation of reasoning failures without changing the paper's overall account.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands reproducibility documentation through Appendix L's operational rules for all nine game categories, including coordinates, movement, projections, scoring, puzzle variants, and move-selection priorities. It also specifies loss weights of 2 and 1 and adds the human-evaluation interface. These are newly documented details; the PDFs do not establish corresponding changes to the underlying implementation.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 2,700-example benchmark, 100,421-example training dataset, eight primary dimensions, eighteen categories, and RISEBench/KRISBench evaluations. The additional studies use retained coverage; the expanded game-rule descriptions do not establish newly introduced tasks.

E2.justification: v3 substantially expands the UniREditBench comparison by adding Bagel, Lumina-DiMOO, DreamOmni2, and UniWorld-V2 to Tables 2 and 7. Bagel already appeared in v1's RISEBench comparison, but its participation in the in-domain comparison is new. The existing comparators are retained.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a six-expert study of 200 randomly selected samples across four models, MAE-based evaluator validation, alternative reference settings, Qwen3VL-32B-Instruct evaluation, Gemini-3-Pro binary CoT assessment, and training-data ablation/scaling settings. The KRISBench evaluator designation also changes from GPT-4.1 in v1 Table 4 to GPT-4o in v3 Table 6, although identical numbers do not establish that this experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v1 lacks the systematic validation and ablations introduced in v3 Section 5.4 and Appendices B and F–I. These examine human–VLM agreement, omission of either reference modality, scoring weights, evaluator dependence, game-to-real transfer, CoT causality/alignment, and performance as training data increases from 20K to 100K.

E5.justification: v3 Appendix B/Table 5 adds estimated Pearson correlations between human judgments and GPT-4.1 scores under six weighting schemes, providing a limited addition of correlation statistics. Neither version reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the new analyses remain point estimates.

E6.justification: The retained GPT-4.1 UniREditBench tables revise many scores: UniREdit-Bagel's overall score changes from 78.87 to 78.15 and GPT-4o's from 71.64 to 73.39. v3 also adds baseline rows and substantial validation/analysis results, including real-world averages of 73.81 without game data versus 75.74 with it, and CoT scores of 0.99 and 0.84. RISEBench and KRISBench numerical results are retained. The PDFs do not explain the cause of the revised in-domain scores.

M1.justification: The synthesis pipeline, Bagel fine-tuning procedure, reasoning-text and flow-matching objectives, and dual-reference scoring formula remain unchanged. Newly specified loss coefficients and empirical support for the existing scoring weights do not establish a changed method.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main section sequence are retained, with grammatical refinements, updated authorship/affiliation text, and modest explanatory edits. v3 adds Section 5.4 and reorganizes the appendix around the new analyses, but does not extensively rewrite the existing narrative.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column to a single-column layout, with extensive resizing and relocation of existing displays. Table 1 gains comparison columns, benchmark tables gain rows and revised styling, and v3 adds validation/ablation tables, reference and scaling plots, and a human-evaluation interface figure. Existing qualitative comparisons are largely retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations including FreeInpaint, ControlThinker, CompBench, ImagDressing-v1, ImagPose, and ComplexBench-Edit, while removing the sentence-embedding and Game-RL bibliography entries. Expanded Table 1 and Appendix A distinguish reference modalities, explicit rules, action control, and intra-game tasks. The central positioning relative to earlier editing benchmarks remains intact.

T1.justification: The scoring equations and training-loss formulations are mathematically unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs. The added game rules and empirical correlation analysis provide task documentation and evaluation evidence rather than new theoretical derivations.

improvement.justification: v1's central evaluation-reliability claim relied chiefly on qualitative illustration. v3 adds direct human validation and reference ablations in Section 5.4, addressing an important evidential gap, while transfer, scaling, evaluator comparisons, and explicit game rules strengthen validation and reproducibility. Reporting remains imperfect: Section 5.3 retains the old +17.08 game-world margin although revised Table 2 implies 18.41, and uncertainty estimates remain absent. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UniREditBench, UniREdit-Data-100K, and UniREdit-Bagel. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting and added analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original model evaluations and adds human evaluation, reference ablations, transfer experiments, CoT assessments, and training-data scaling results.

before.justification: v1 reports original UniREdit-Bagel training and evaluation results on UniREditBench, RISEBench, and KRISBench, including quantitative tables and qualitative comparisons.

results.title: UniREditBench: A Unified Reasoning-based Image Editing Benchmark

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list expand the central contribution to feedback-driven refinement of both behavior and video, including appearance preservation through the new Video Reviewer Agent. The introduction also adds comparable latency as a contribution. The supported editing operations and nearly twofold instruction-alignment claim remain.

C2.justification: v2 develops the realism-versus-appearance tradeoff and explains how video review addresses it, interprets the coarse comparison as evidence for the agentic architecture, and acknowledges mild geometric/lane degradation from diffusion. Runtime interpretation changes from fastest to comparable. Conversely, the explicit pedestrian-editing limitation and the rare-vehicle training-bias explanation are removed; the median-barrier failure remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds the Video Reviewer prompt, masked-frame inputs, bounded averaging rules for parameter updates, a five-iteration cap, and detailed latent-guidance equations. It also identifies TwinLiteNet for lane evaluation and expands runtime accounting. Existing agent prompts and training settings are largely retained, but v1's specification of Cosmos-Predict2.5 Base rather than Auto is omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds downstream 3D object detection with BEVFormer trained using real and edited Waymo images (Section 6.5), extending evaluation from editing quality to the utility of generated training data. The original 30 editing scenes, object-grounding coverage, and editing operations are retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds ChronoEdit followed by Wan 2.2 as an evaluated composite baseline (Section 6.4, Table 10) and explicitly compares coarse outputs against ChatSim (Table 9). The original Cosmos/ChatSim editing comparisons and Grounding SAM/4DLangSplat grounding comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The new video ablation uses insertion/replacement instructions, three configurations, and appearance alignment alongside FID/FVD. New protocols introduce 3D Consistency, NTL-IoU, and detection AP at three IoU thresholds using 8,000 real frames with or without 8,000 edited frames. The counterfactual ablation also changes its stated instruction source from v1 Table 2 to v2 Table 1; identical results leave a rerun versus a cross-reference error unresolved.

E4.justification: v2 adds a controlled comparison separating coarse rendering, diffusion alone, and diffusion with video review; an explicit coarse-output comparison against ChatSim; and geometric/lane hallucination analysis with qualitative lane visualizations. Existing behavior and grounding analyses remain. The specific green-convertible appearance-failure case in v1 Figure 11 is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Random image selection for the grounding experiment remains unchanged.

E6.justification: Retained Table 1 quality/user-study scores and grounding/behavior results are unchanged. New results include video-reviewer appearance alignment of 85.28% versus 65.47% without review, coarse-to-refined 3D Consistency of 74.07 to 72.64 and NTL-IoU of 52.11 to 50.96, additional comparator scores, and detection AP@0.5 of 0.0533 versus 0.0635 with edited training data. Runtime values and accounting also change. The new video-ablation results do not establish a same-setting performance change from v1.

M1.justification: v2 adds a Video Reviewer Agent to the existing rendering and diffusion pipeline. It evaluates realism and appearance preservation, then iteratively adjusts denoising strength and masked latent-space L2 guidance (Sections 3.7 and 8.3). This changes inference substantially; the existing grounding, counterfactual behavior generation, and trajectory-review procedures remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten around three shortcomings of prior methods and two motivating insights. Runtime discussion moves into the main experiments, and supplementary experiments are reorganized into numbered subsections. Much of the existing method exposition and original agent prompts remains unchanged.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column to a single-column format with extensive resizing and rearrangement. Figure 2 gains a video-review feedback loop; new reviewer, comparator, and lane-preservation figures and experimental tables are added. Runtime tables are restructured, the editing-capabilities figure is rearranged and loses its removal panel, and the convertible-failure figure is removed.

R1.justification: The related-work families and capability comparison remain, with stronger emphasis on multimodal reasoning and feedback, including an updated contrast with SimSplat. New citations support the added components and evaluations, including SDEdit, ChronoEdit, Wan, WorldScore, DriveDreamer4D, and BEVFormer. Citations to earlier collaborative-agent inspirations and pedestrian-animation work are removed.

T1.justification: v2 Section 8.3 adds mathematical definitions for video refinement, particularly the masked residual, L2 loss, and scaled noise-prediction update in Equations 7–9. This is a localized extension of the formulation. The scene-graph definition, counterfactual Cartesian product, and compatibility constraints are retained; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens its treatment of v1's documented appearance-drift problem. The new controlled ablation raises appearance alignment from 65.47% to 85.28% with review while retaining similar FID, and the added coarse comparison and hallucination measurements clarify both contributions and tradeoffs. Detailed reviewer documentation further supports reproducibility. Removing the explicit pedestrian limitation, rare-vehicle failure discussion, and Cosmos variant disclosure weakens transparency, but the methodological and evidential gains outweigh these losses. The original headline benchmark scores remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LangDriveCTRL with the same authors, core pipeline, and retained experiments. Their main text, supplementary sections, equations, tables, figures, and agent prompts are readable and can be matched despite extensive reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds video-reviewer experiments, hallucination measurements, another editing baseline, and downstream object-detection results.

before.justification: v1 reports original Waymo editing experiments, a 26-participant user study, object-grounding comparisons, and behavior and video refinement ablations.

results.title: LangDriveCTRL: Natural Language Controllable Driving Scene Editing with Multi-modal Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden the contribution from a practical label-free approach to a framework with supervised DD-CPP and label-free TF-CPP. They also recenter the principal claim on backward-transition policy supervision versus forward-process targets. Claims about avoiding preference labels now apply specifically to TF-CPP.

C2.justification: V1's limitation that final-output preferences cannot directly support its practical method is replaced by discussion of policy-pair quality and construction cost. V2 adds explanations distinguishing pairwise optimization from fixed-target regression and relating degradation strength to downstream performance. It also explicitly acknowledges that D-KTO and SPO outperform DDSPO on some aesthetic metrics.

D1.justification: V2 adds an implementation-access link and substantial configuration details for DD-CPP and the new backbones. Appendix D specifies policy-training LoRA rank, learning rate, checkpoint selection and beta, plus timing hardware, precision and measurement procedures. The earlier approximate overhead statement is supplemented by measured costs; existing SDXL generation and training resource estimates remain.

E1.justification: DDSPO training expands to actual Pick-a-Pic preference image pairs through DD-CPP. V1 used Pick-a-Pic through supervised comparators and qualitative prompts, while training DDSPO on generated pairs. The alignment and aesthetic tasks and existing evaluation datasets remain; the additional backbones principally change experimental settings.

E2.justification: V2 Appendix C adds directly evaluated SoftREPA and a CFG-style target-regression baseline. It also evaluates SPO for text-image alignment, whereas v1's reported SPO comparison concerned aesthetics. These additions substantially broaden comparison with competing annotation-free and stepwise approaches. SoftREPA was already cited in v1 but was not evaluated there.

E3.justification: V2 adds SD3-Medium and SD3.5-Large configurations, supervised policy-pair training, and a blinded human-evaluation protocol with 15 annotators judging 30 prompt-matched pairs. New analyses introduce a 1,000-prompt CLIP/LAION evaluation and controlled hardware timing. Existing TF-CPP training settings are largely retained; these are predominantly new experimental protocols.

E4.justification: V2 adds tests of whether fixed CFG-style target regression explains TF-CPP, quantifies training/evaluation distribution mismatch using FID, measures effective prompt-degradation strength, and benchmarks computational overhead. It also examines SPO's alignment failures. Existing dataset-size, beta, prompt-strategy, negative-image and joint-objective analyses are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates without repeated-evaluation uncertainty. V2 Table D adds means and standard deviations over five generation seeds for aesthetic comparisons on two backbones, keeping checkpoints fixed. Timing measurements are averaged over 30 microbatches after five warmups. This is a limited extension of uncertainty reporting, not evidence of repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Original Table 1 and prompt-based DDSPO scores are largely retained. V2 Table 3 adds Pick-a-Pic-trained DDSPO results: HPSv2/PickScore of 27.60/21.50 on SD-1.5 and 29.09/22.71 on SDXL. Additional backbone, comparator, degradation and timing results substantially expand the evidence. Figure C newly reports overall human preferences of 42.9% for DDSPO, 36.0% for Diffusion-DPO and 21.1% ties.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 adds DD-CPP: separately training winning and losing diffusion models on preferred and dispreferred images, then using their predictions as DDSPO targets. This introduces a substantial training procedure beyond v1's prompt-conditioned reference model. The original objective and prompt-based implementation, renamed TF-CPP, remain.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, contribution narrative, practical-method exposition, conclusion and limitations around DD-CPP and TF-CPP. It consolidates v1's separate joint-objective and dataset-size appendix sections into extended results and introduces a dedicated alternative-comparison section. These changes materially reorganize the narrative beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: V2 changes the main text from two columns to one, merges v1 Tables 2/3 and 5/6, and splits the aesthetic table by backbone. It reorganizes qualitative displays, including moving earlier appendix examples into Figure 2. New displays include the human-preference chart, additional comparison tables and a DD-CPP image gallery; many existing plots and images are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Christiano et al., Ouyang et al. and the SD3 rectified-flow work. It expands discussion of the already cited SoftREPA and refines distinctions from Diffusion-DPO and SPO. The broader literature coverage and related-work organization remain largely intact.

T1.justification: Appendix A corrects losing-branch distribution arguments in Equations (19) and (28), replacing incorrectly used winning variables with losing variables and restoring a losing-policy superscript. The core mathematical objectives and derivation structure remain; no substantial new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's explicit restriction concerning final-output preference data by implementing and evaluating DD-CPP. Pick-a-Pic-trained comparisons, blinded human judgments, generation-seed uncertainty and targeted mechanism analyses substantially strengthen validation beyond v1's automatic scores. Added implementation and cost details improve reproducibility. The new SD3-M CompBench comparison has an aggregation inconsistency between Table 2b and its stated protocol, limiting that comparison, but this does not outweigh the substantial gains in applicability and supporting evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DDSPO research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds supervised DDSPO evaluations, human judgments, generation-seed analyses, alternative-method comparisons and computational measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original two-dimensional simulations, image-generation evaluations, ablations and qualitative comparisons in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: Direct Diffusion Score Preference Optimization via Stepwise Contrastive Policy-Pair Supervision

C1.justification: The benchmark, hybrid editing agent, claimed performance advantage, and remaining long-horizon difficulty remain the central contributions. v3 revises the advertised scale from 800+ to 1,300+ edits and explicitly strengthens the benchmark contribution to include validation against human experts. The introduction also adds a statistical-power claim based on comparisons with other agent benchmarks.

C2.justification: v3 explains ChatGPT Agent's relative advantage on Structure tasks through native GUI handling, contrasting this with PPTPilot's tendency to over-edit master XML. It also adds a plateau-based rationale for the three-pass refinement cap. The detailed failure examples and limitations concerning ambiguous instructions, cross-application workflows, and specialized domains are retained.

D1.justification: New Appendix I and Table D document baseline interfaces, backbones, context limits, retry budgets, timeouts, latencies, and an approximately $700 evaluation cost. Appendix J changes the release statement from planned to released and specifies screenshots, structural diffs, judge prompts, and raw outputs. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although availability itself cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate PPTArena's 100 decks and 2,125 slides across the same editing taxonomy, plus T2US and PPTC-R. Revised edit totals and sourcing-pool sizes do not establish additional task or domain coverage. The human and batching studies assess existing editing tasks.

E2.justification: v3 adds Kimi-K2.6 to the matched subset comparison and reports Gemini CLI and ChatGPT alongside the subset baselines in Table 4. The other principal comparators remain. The earlier Poster2Agent label corresponds to Paper2Poster, which remains reported in v3's text and Appendix Table A.

E3.justification: Reported configurations change from GPT-5/Gemini 2.5 Pro to GPT-5.2/Gemini 3.1 Pro, and the T2US backbone changes from Gemini 2.5 Flash to 3.0 Flash. The hard-subset selection description shifts from poor model performance to structural difficulty plus breadth. v3 also reports 1,340 edits rather than 800+, introduces a blind 25-expert evaluation on a stratified 10% subset, and adds a 105-slide-pair page-wise control. These are documented setting changes and new protocols, without establishing which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantial validation of the evaluation pipeline: human–judge alignment, repeated-call consistency, and batched versus page-wise visual scoring. It also reports the router's 66% programmatic versus 34% XML usage. The executor ablations, alternative-judge comparison, and illustrated failure cases already existed in v1 and are largely retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides no corresponding repeated-judge uncertainty analysis. v3 Table 8 first reports five judge runs per example, majority agreement of 78%/95% for IF/VQ, and standard deviations reported as 15.4%/9%. It also introduces Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall human–judge correlations. This adds statistical validation and variability reporting, rather than establishing an increase over a previously specified run count.

E6.justification: PPTPilot's full-benchmark IF/VQ changes from 2.36/2.69 to 2.57/2.69, and its subset scores from 1.71/1.54 to 1.87/1.91 (v1 Table 3; v3 Tables 4–5). v3 adds Kimi scores, human ratings, latency measurements, and judge-validation outcomes; reported average operations change from 5.1 to 13.4. The ablation and T2US scores remain unchanged. Revised models and settings prevent interpreting the changed scores as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The semantic planning, routing between programmatic and XML editing, validation, and reflection procedures are retained. SSIM screening and the detailed two-stage editing paths already appeared in v1's appendix. Updated backbone versions are experimental configuration changes; no new algorithmic component or procedure is established.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: detailed ablations move from main Section 5.2 to Appendix E.3, difficulty analysis moves into the main benchmark section, and separate sections present judge reliability and human comparisons. The abstract, conclusion, and dataset explanation are rewritten or expanded, and the title, author list, and bibliographic text are revised.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. v1 Figures 2–3 are merged into v3 Figure 2, the pipeline diagrams are redrawn, and the main results are separated into subset and full-benchmark tables. New latency, human-validation, and configuration tables accompany extensive resizing and restyling of appendix figures and code listings.

R1.justification: v3 adds an explicit comparison with the concurrent, independent PPTArena benchmark, contrasting its GUI tasks over 12 source files with this work's scope. It also adds SWE-bench Multimodal scale positioning and a Kimi reference. Much of the extensive bibliography revision supplies author, title, and publication metadata for already cited works rather than changing research positioning.

T1.justification: Neither version presents new theoretical propositions or proofs. The existing scoring rubrics and diff-computation logic are retained; the added correlation and consistency measurements are empirical statistics, not new mathematical results.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens a central weakness of v1: automated evaluation lacked measured human alignment and judge repeatability. The expert study, repeated-judge analysis, and batching control directly support the benchmark's credibility, while matched comparisons and baseline budgets improve interpretability and reproducibility. Reporting problems temper these gains: revised counts and configurations are not fully reconciled, and Figure G retains older PPTPilot scores despite Tables 4–5. These limit precise performance interpretation but do not outweigh the substantial new validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PPTArena and PPTPilot. Their complete main texts and appendices, including tables, diagrams, examples, and prompt listings, support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark experiments and adds human evaluations, judge-consistency measurements, and a page-wise scoring control in Sections 5.2–5.3 and Appendix E.2.

before.justification: v1 reports original agent evaluations and ablations in Tables 3–4, plus cross-judge and T2US experiments in Appendix B.

results.title: PPTArena: A Benchmark for PowerPoint Editing

C1.justification: Both versions claim a jointly learned LoRA basis and input-dependent router, state-of-the-art visual-analogy performance, and improved generalization to unseen transformations. v2's single-inference-pass wording makes the existing inference-time specialization more explicit without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: v1 mainly notes difficulty with transformations far from training data. v2 substantially develops applicability boundaries: obtaining clean reference pairs is difficult, changing reference identity can damage preservation, conflicting inputs can produce combined edits, and subtle or multi-component transformations can fail. It also proposes CLIP downsampling as a possible explanation for missed small details.

D1.justification: v2 adds Einsum implementation details, disclosure that mixing is recomputed each timestep, a possible caching optimization, timing hardware, baseline adaptation settings and the exact prompt-reduction instruction. Existing optimizer, checkpoints and training hyperparameters remain. The same project link is retained, but v2 mentions code without v1's explicit data-availability statement; actual availability cannot be established locally.

E1.justification: Relation252k training and the original 100-task, 840-triplet evaluation remain. v2 adds qualitative TEdBench examples using Imagic-edited references and tests reduced-detail prompts, conflicting text/image instructions and non-identical reference pairs. These extend input-condition coverage within the existing visual-analogy task.

E2.justification: v2 Appendix B.1 and Table S2 add evaluated comparisons with Diffusion Image Analogies, the authors' DIA-Kontext adaptation, and PairEdit. PairEdit was cited but not evaluated in v1. The original single-LoRA, RelationAdapter, VisualCloze and EditTransfer comparisons remain, substantially broadening comparison to methods requiring per-example optimization.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled prompt-reduction and input-perturbation evaluations, a 100-image A100 timing experiment, DIA configuration selection across 20 options on 540 test images, and PairEdit strength comparisons. These substantially extend the evaluation design. Existing training settings, main metrics, task-wise aggregation and user-study protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained capacity, activation, encoder and reference-pair ablations, v2 tests reduced prompt information, reference-pair misalignment, conflicting text/image inputs and sensitivity to reference-image generation sources. Appendix A.2 adds efficiency analysis, while Appendix B.7 documents failures involving unfamiliar styles, multi-component edits and subtle changes.

E5.justification: Appendix A.2 newly reports timings of 33.4 ± 0.4 and 32.4 ± 0.3 seconds averaged over 100 images, without defining the ± statistic. This adds statistical reporting without documenting repeated-seed experiments. The existing 68% Wilson intervals and human/VLM agreement statistics are unchanged.

E6.justification: The original numerical results remain unchanged, including Table 1 and v1 Table S2, now v2 Table S3. New Table S2 reports LoRWeB pairwise preference rates of 86.5% against DIA, 68.6% against DIA-Kontext, and 75.6%/86.3% against PairEdit at strengths 0.6/0.8. Reduced-prompt results, timing measurements and additional qualitative findings substantially expand the reported outcomes.

M1.justification: v1 Section 3.2 explicitly applies Eq. (2), mixing A and B factors separately. v2 instead specifies Eq. (5), summing weighted products B_i A_i. These operators are not equivalent: cross terms and achievable rank differ. This substantially revises the stated method specification, although the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed or the earlier description was corrected.

P1.justification: v2 edits the abstract and selected introductory, related-work and discussion passages, expands explanations, and adds appendix subsections and acknowledgments. The main section sequence and much of the original prose remain, so the language and narrative changes are targeted rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation, extensively resizing and relocating existing displays. v2 expands Figure 3, adds Figure 8 and several supplementary comparison, robustness and failure figures, plus a new baseline table. The earlier supplementary table and figure material is largely retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citations for DIA, LoraHub, NeRF analogies, earlier stylization and color-transfer approaches, and work supporting the new experiments. It more explicitly distinguishes learned routing from test-time optimization while retaining the original weight-space motivation and generalization positioning.

T1.justification: v2 revises the mathematical composition rule in Eq. (5) and adds a short argument that constant routing can recover a single LoRA with rank up to Nr. These are localized mathematical revisions; the flow-matching objective and analogy definition remain unchanged, with no extensive new theoretical development.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and practical understanding through optimization-based comparisons, prompt-dependence controls, measured inference overhead and concrete applicability limits. These address important gaps in v1's support for generalization and usability while retaining its original results. The unexplained mixing-rule revision and qualitative nature of several robustness tests remain limitations, but the added controls and explicit failure analysis provide a substantial net improvement in paper quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LoRWeB. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting and appendix expansion.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds baseline comparisons, timing measurements, robustness experiments and failure analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original visual-analogy experiments, quantitative comparisons, ablations and a 33-participant user study.

results.title: Spanning the Visual Analogy Space with a Weight Basis of LoRAs

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a single universal perturbation, two semantic losses and a data-free variant. V2 extends its principal comparative claims to optimization-free methods and explicitly claims a favorable performance–latency–memory trade-off against these alternatives.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations of prompt-independent semantic injection, attribute-level target transfer and category-independent suppression using the retained ImageNet-Excluded results. It qualifies semantic transfer to DiT models, discusses EditShield's instruction-editing advantage, and expands discussion of mask sensitivity and purification robustness.

D1.justification: V2 documents FastProtect calibration, GPT-4 prompt elaboration and the existing ImageNet-Excluded experiment's 136-class exclusion and 10,000-image sampling. It adds a project-page URL but removes v1's explicit code/data/seeds release statement and inpainting perturbation-budget disclosure. Actual external resource availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

E1.justification: V2 adds ImageNet-Edit, MagicBrush instruction-edit pairs and DiffusionGuard's real-image inpainting benchmark, extending v1's synthetic evaluation and COCO/DomainNet coverage. Noun-free and null-prompt evaluations introduce distinct text-conditioning scenarios. Inpainting and diffusion-transformer evaluation themselves already existed in v1.

E2.justification: FastProtect joins retained editing comparisons, and DiffVax joins the original inpainting comparison. Complex-prompt and purification comparisons gain image-specific and optimization-free comparators. EditShield disappears from the original white-box and training-size comparisons, while its SD1.4/2.0 transfer results are retained elsewhere and a MagicBrush comparison is added.

E3.justification: Core training and diffusion settings remain stable. V2 removes DINO similarity, replaces AHIQ with LPIPS for imperceptibility, and introduces FastProtect budget calibration at 22/255 and CPU timing. The retained SD1.5 inpainting evaluation is described as black-box for Ours rather than white-box; unchanged scores do not establish that it was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds null-prompt mechanism controls, noun-free prompt tests and qualitative budget tests at 2/255–6/255, while expanding complex-prompt and purification analyses. GrIDPure replaces AdverseCleaner. Conversely, v1's checkerboard-target study and 16/255 black-box comparison disappear. Training-size, loss-component, ImageNet-Excluded and convergence analyses already existed in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions state averaging over 10 random seeds and retain the same plus/minus reporting and across-target mean/standard-deviation practice. New result rows do not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation procedure, repeated-run count or significance test.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive benchmark and comparator results while removing DINO and several ablation entries. Retained universal scores are mostly unchanged, but Table 4's Ours CLIP similarity changes from 0.670 to 0.673. Table 3's JPEG LPIPS changes from 0.419 to 0.511 without an explained cause, so this is not an established same-setting gain. New MagicBrush results favor EditShield over Ours on LPIPS, 0.588 versus 0.568.

M1.justification: The target semantic injection and source semantic suppression losses, universal perturbation optimization, data-free variant and additive inference procedure remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 move to the appendix; expanded explanations and new evaluations do not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: The introduction and related-work narrative are substantially rewritten. Theory and pseudocode move to the appendix, empirical discussion is reordered, and previously isolated appendix tables receive dedicated explanatory subsections. These changes substantially reorganize the document beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: V2 redesigns Figure 1 with three defense categories and a latency/performance/memory plot, separates the framework illustration, adds mechanism and real-image figures, and restructures numerous tables. Typography and page layout change throughout. Appendix figure/table numbering now overlaps some main-text numbering.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions the work relative to optimization-free defenses, especially FastProtect and DiffVax, rather than principally per-image optimization. Related work also expands to purification-resistant methods such as BlurGuard, DCT-Shield and AntiPure, alongside additional editing defenses.

T1.justification: The objectives, cross-attention equations, residual update and attention-map invariance argument are mathematically retained. V1 Section 4.4 becomes v2 Appendix A.5 with revised explanation, without a new proof, derivation or formal assumption.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important evidentiary gaps: FastProtect/DiffVax comparisons directly test the central efficiency claim, new real-image benchmarks extend the existing COCO/DomainNet validation, and null-prompt controls provide stronger evidence for semantic injection. These gains substantially improve the paper despite narrower retained metric/ablation coverage, unexplained JPEG-score revisions and some numbering ambiguity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same universal image-immunization work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark evaluations, comparator results and controlled qualitative experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original immunization experiments, transferability and robustness evaluations, ablations, and a 20-participant user study.

results.title: Universal Image Immunization against Diffusion-based Image Editing via Semantic Injection

C1.justification: V3 adds a central contribution that prompt-level debiasing can reduce inter-group disparity while producing a homogenization effect within groups, prominently stated in the abstract, contribution list, and conclusion. It removes v1's separate contribution claim to formally define object bias and softens the 'first systematic framework' novelty language. The core object-stereotyping and implicit-default claims remain.

C2.justification: V3 distinguishes demographic differences from harmful amplification and adds substantial interpretation of mitigation tradeoffs, including Flux's contrasting behavior and the nonsignificant aggregate VAC effect. It extends the prompt-adherence explanation to Imagen, adds limitations concerning discrete demographic categories and intersectionality, and discusses extractor dependence and framework extensibility. These substantially revise v1's shorter discussion of diversity, commercial risks, and limited coverage.

D1.justification: V3 adds generation parameters for the new models, explicitly documents unlabeled discovery inputs, expands the attribute taxonomies, and specifies attention checks and the dominance threshold used to select value shifts. The repository reference remains, but its availability statement now mentions code and prompts without v1's explicit inclusion of generated images; this does not establish that files were actually removed.

E1.justification: V3 expands object coverage from cars, laptops, backpacks, cups, and teddy bears to include sofas, toasters, and clocks. It also adds Latinx ethnicity prompts while retaining the existing age and gender groups (Table 1). These additions broaden represented object domains and demographic populations.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically compares SODA against competing auditing frameworks: T2IAT, TIBET, and OpenBias remain related work. The additional generators are audit subjects, and alternative VLM extractors are robustness variants, rather than competing audit baselines.

E3.justification: V3 adds FLUX.2 Pro and Qwen-Image to the main evaluation, separate Nano-Banana-2 runs, and selected-subset prompt and cross-VLM protocols. Discovery samples increase from 18 to 20 images per model-object combination. Human validation changes from discovery checks across 15 combinations and classification checks on 270 images to 1,040 assignments across six combinations, with revised annotation categories and attention checks. Imagen generation is now reported through Replicate with specified resolution, steps, and guidance, replacing the Google API/default-quality setting (Appendix A).

E4.justification: V3 adds prompt-wording sensitivity and mitigation experiments (Section 5.5), cross-VLM robustness checks (Appendix E), CLIP/UMAP distribution analyses, and an unseen-model generalization test (Appendix K). Qualitative analysis adds Qwen face insertion and Imagen/Flux object-category shifts, while v1's detailed Imagen door and backpack-configuration cases are dropped.

E5.justification: Reported BDS permutation counts increase from 1,000 in v1 to 10,000 in v3 Appendix F. V3 also introduces paired t-tests for mitigation effects and significance tests for cross-VLM Pearson correlations, and explicitly reports that aggregate VAC changes are not statistically significant. These extend statistical assessment beyond the original BDS tests.

E6.justification: BDS, CDS, VAC, validation, and qualitative results are extensively revised or added. For example, v1 Table 4 ranks Imagen highest in average VAC at 0.662; v3 Table 4 ranks Qwen highest at 0.633 and Imagen lowest at 0.343. These summarize different coverage and settings, not same-setting performance changes. New results include a reported 30.9% average CDS reduction under stereotype-discouraging prompts and pooled cross-VLM correlations of 0.855–0.895.

M1.justification: The four-stage SODA pipeline, two-phase attribute discovery and assignment, four fixed plus four discovered attributes, and default GPT-4o extraction remain. Alternative extractors and mitigation prompts are experimental variants; the PDFs do not establish a redesign of the proposed audit procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, results narrative, discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten, and related work is condensed. Numbered sections and lettered appendices reorganize the document, including relocation of generation settings and detailed results. This exceeds wording changes associated solely with added experiments.

P2.justification: V3 changes the document from two-column to single-column layout, redraws example and framework figures, and adds UMAP and unseen-model figures. The main BDS table becomes a model-level summary with rank shading, while full object-level results move to Appendix G and significance counts receive a separate table. Existing concentration examples, taxonomies, and interface displays are expanded or relocated, alongside new mitigation and cross-VLM tables.

R1.justification: V3 adds references on geographic representation, representational harms, directional bias amplification, pluralistic alignment, and newly evaluated models. It sharpens the distinction from T2IAT, TIBET, and OpenBias through controlled baseline comparisons, while retaining the central positioning around demographic-conditioned object bias.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions of BDS, CDS, and VAC remain equivalent in Equations 1–3. Neither version provides theoretical proofs, and v3 adds no substantive formal assumptions, derivations, or mathematical guarantees.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the audit's empirical credibility by directly testing dependence on the extraction VLM and prompt wording, and by examining whether mitigation improves both disparity and diversity. These address important untested dependencies in v1, while broader object and demographic coverage supports applicability. The gains outweigh narrower human-validation coverage and the abstract's overgeneralized homogenization claim, which the main text qualifies as model-dependent with nonsignificant aggregate VAC changes.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SODA study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, despite substantial expansion of the experiments.

after.justification: V3 reports an 8,000-image main evaluation across five models and eight object categories, plus original prompt experiments, cross-VLM validation, and a Nano-Banana-2 evaluation in the appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original analyses of 2,700 generated images across three models and five object categories, including quantitative bias measurements, qualitative findings, and human validation.

results.title: When Cars Have Stereotypes: Auditing Demographic Bias in Objects from Text-to-Image Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: structured spanning-tree orders preserve generation performance, enable flexible inpainting, and require minimal architectural changes. The additional experiments support these claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations involving convergence speed, locality, center-bias dependence, and inpainting behavior across model families. Appendix A explicitly discusses realistic violations of masking assumptions, distinguishes single-pass limitations from successive completion, and identifies unexplored traversal and tie-breaking choices.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly identifies the cloud instance and reports 65, 80, 160, and 385 A100 GPU-days across STAR configurations; existing hyperparameters and code access remain unchanged. The rewritten masking pseudocode moves initialization outside the retry loop, leaving resampling after rejection unspecified.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-100 representation learning and linear-probe classification, extending coverage beyond ImageNet generation and inpainting. Appendix A also demonstrates an inpainting scenario with all corners masked and disconnected partial observations.

E2.justification: The inpainting comparison expands from RAR to include DiT-XL/2 and RandAR-L/XL in v2 Table 2 and Figure 6. This adds diffusion and flexible-order AR comparators to the central downstream evaluation, although these methods already appeared in the unchanged generation comparison.

E3.justification: New protocols include center-bias quartiles evaluated using 50k generated images, and iGPT-S configurations trained on CIFAR-100 for 100k steps with intermediate-feature linear probes and checkpoint perplexity. DiT inpainting uses latent blending. The printed mask sampler additionally excludes masks covering all corners; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of performance across center-bias strengths, extends spatial entropy analysis to STAR, reports sampling overhead, and analyzes representation-learning convergence and overfitting. Appendix A adds a case study outside the single-pass masking assumptions. The earlier order/traversal ablations and appendix sequence-entropy analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Section 3.2 changes the reported entropy-estimation budget from 100 sampled permutations per validation image to 30 sampled orders per image for each analyzed model. This changes the estimator's sampling budget, without establishing additional independent training runs. Neither version reports training-seed counts or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results: Table 2 reports average inpainting FID of 2.07 for STAR-XL, 2.58 for RandAR-XL, 3.40 for RAR-XL, and 4.58 for DiT-XL/2. Figures 8a and 9 add center-bias and representation-learning findings. Table 1 and the retained order/traversal ablation scores are unchanged; the additions are not demonstrated improvements over v1 STAR scores.

M1.justification: The core architecture and spanning-tree training procedure remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 extends completion to separate trees for disconnected mask components and revises root selection across their boundaries. Appendix A additionally demonstrates successive postfix completions for masks violating the single-pass assumptions.

P1.justification: Method motivation and experimental interpretation receive extensive rewriting and reorganization. v2 introduces a Discussion section, reorganizes analyses around locality, center bias, entropy, and overhead, moves the earlier appendix entropy discussion into the main text, and restructures the supplement.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. Entropy figures are combined and expanded, the traversal table is transposed, the inpainting comparison panel is rebuilt, and new algorithm, center-bias, representation-learning, and successive-completion illustrations appear. The appendix sample grids are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Blended Latent Diffusion, DetailFlow, FlowAR, CART, and work connecting permutation AR with masked-model objectives. These additions broaden supporting context while retaining STAR's positioning as a simple structured-order alternative within autoregressive visual generation.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 generalizes the boundary-depth argument to multiple disconnected mask components and changes the stated necessary depth inequality from strict greater-than in v1 Equation 3 to greater-than-or-equal in v2 Equation 5. v2 also adds entropy-chain reasoning about ideal order invariance and finite-budget convergence.

improvement.justification: The added RandAR and DiT inpainting comparisons address an important evidential gap in v1's central editing claim. Center-bias tests directly examine the design premise, while explicit masking limitations clarify applicability. These gains substantially strengthen the paper despite unchanged headline generation scores and the localized retry-pseudocode omission in Appendix B.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same STAR research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and rendered figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original STAR experiments and adds inpainting comparisons, center-bias analyses, and CIFAR-100 representation-learning results.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet generation and inpainting results, order and traversal ablations, and token-entropy analyses.

results.title: Spanning Tree Autoregressive Visual Generation

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the claimed applicability from text-conditioned image generation to image and video generation. The introduction explicitly claims the best diversity-quality trade-off in both domains. The central training-free condition-annealing and scale-travel contribution remains.

C2.justification: V2 explains why prompt rewriting offers less variation for highly constrained prompts and distinguishes changing the prompt from increasing diversity under a fixed condition. It also interprets repeated refinement as trading computation for quality. The existing limitations of additional inference cost and approximately 6% residual artifacts remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds video and class-conditioning hyperparameters, a detailed training/data-processing recipe for the Kaleido adaptation, model-size/resolution specifications, and a project-page URL. Original image settings and hardware/runtime disclosures remain. However, the relocated sampling-control tables lose v1's explicit statement identifying their evaluation prompt set.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates text-conditioned image generation. V2 additionally evaluates text-to-video generation using VBench-2.0 prompts and class-conditioned generation on ImageNet. Appendix I also introduces LAION training data for the adapted Kaleido comparator. MS-COCO, MJHQ-30K, and existing text-alignment evaluations remain.

E2.justification: Appendix I adds actual comparisons against CSD-VAR and an adapted Kaleido method; CSD-VAR was only cited in v1. The prompt-rewriting comparison also changes membership: v1's Switti comparison disappears, while v2 directly compares Infinity with and without prompt rewriting and DiverseVAR.

E3.justification: New protocols include InfinityStar-8B generation at 480p with 81 frames, VBench diversity and quality metrics, and class-conditioned evaluation using ten images per ImageNet class with FID, precision, and recall. Additional tests vary model size, output resolution, and refinement count. The retained main image experiments keep their original settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of repeated scale-travel, sensitivity to model size and resolution, and a detailed-prompt case study comparing prompt rewriting and its combination with DiverseVAR. Existing scheduler and scale-parameter ablations remain. The CFG sweep is moved into the main text but loses its zero-guidance condition.

E5.justification: V2 explicitly identifies three seed-indexed generations in its video comparisons, whereas v1 only discusses varying random seeds generally. This is limited additional seed reporting: neither version provides confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-evaluation uncertainty estimates, and existing runtime averaging remains unchanged.

E6.justification: Table 1's image scores are unchanged. New results include video diversity/quality scores of 0.487/0.804 for DiverseVAR versus 0.270/0.806 for InfinityStar, and class-conditioned FID of 5.560 versus 10.578 for VAR. V2 also adds repeated-refinement, scalability, fine-tuning-baseline, and combined prompt-rewriting results. Zero-CFG results, Switti prompt-rewriting results, and several qualitative examples are removed.

M1.justification: The core condition-annealing and scale-travel algorithm remains unchanged. Limited inference extensions apply it to InfinityStar's keyframe stage and to class-label embeddings, while Appendix F.4 introduces repeated scale-travel execution rather than the original single refinement.

P1.justification: V2 selectively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and refinement explanation, expands the prompt-rewriting discussion, and promotes sampling-control discussions from the appendix into Section 5.4. The supplement gains a contents page and reorganized subsections, while the overall six-section narrative and much existing prose remain.

P2.justification: The paper changes from two-column to single-column formatting with extensively rearranged displays. Figure 1 is redesigned to include video, new video and prompt-rewriting figures are added, and sampling-control tables move into the main text. Appendix image galleries are substantially reduced, while new experimental tables expand the presentation.

R1.justification: The existing VAR and diffusion-diversity positioning is retained. V2 extends the discussion to autoregressive video work, including VideoPoet, Emu3, and InfinityStar, and positions its training-free approach against fine-tuning alternatives. Kaleido and supporting evaluation/tool references are added; CSD-VAR was already cited.

T1.justification: The VAR factorization, noise-injection schedules, multi-scale encoding, and scale-travel mathematics are retained. V2 removes the illustrative diffusion time-travel equations while shortening that background analogy; this changes exposition rather than the work's formal assumptions, reasoning, or guarantees. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's two text-to-image backbones through video and class-conditioned experiments and comparisons with trained diversity methods. Repeated-refinement tests and quantified combinations with prompt rewriting also clarify practical trade-offs. Some controls and examples disappear, and the scalability discussion understates the 8B ImageReward drop from 1.29 to 0.81. Nevertheless, the broader, directly relevant comparative evidence materially improves support for the method's applicability and usefulness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DiverseVAR by the same authors. Their complete main texts, references, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds video generation, class-conditioned generation, scalability analyses, and evaluated fine-tuning baselines.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-generation experiments on Infinity and Switti, including quantitative comparisons, ablations, runtime measurements, and qualitative results.

results.title: DiverseVAR: Balancing Diversity and Quality of Next-Scale Visual Autoregressive Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: single-model self-adversarial distillation, reduced training-memory requirements, DTC/TAR, and flexible one-to-many-step restoration.
