New efficiency and supplementary evidence supports these existing claims rather than redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of smaller-backbone applicability, stable early adversarial learning, and TAR's weighting as arising from distribution matching. It also clarifies the distinction between flexible standard-diffusion sampling and useful low-step restoration. The main limitations concerning model capacity and independent fidelity–realism control remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The supplement adds training pseudocode, the combined loss and timestep-dependent loss weights, sampling distributions, bfloat16 precision, checkpointing, and the precise 47,496-iteration count. The abstract adds a code-repository link. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's shorter optimizer, LoRA and hardware description; the link alone does not verify resource availability.

E1.justification: Training still uses LSDIR and FFHQ, while evaluation retains RealSR, DRealSR and DIV2K-Val for super-resolution. The Z-Image experiments change backbone configuration, and additional visual examples do not establish a new dataset, domain or task.

E2.justification: The original Table 1 comparator set is retained. New efficiency comparisons include DMD, ADD and SFT on Z-Image (main Figure 5), and PiSA-SR in supplementary Table 1. Supplementary Figure 2 also adds a DiT4SR curve and OSEDiff reference point to the sampling-budget comparison, substantially broadening evaluated comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 adds common-backbone Z-Image-6B/A100 memory and iteration-time benchmarking, inference latency measurements, and training-memory tests specifying 512×512 inputs, batch size 1 and checkpointing. Original accuracy protocols remain unchanged. Supplementary Algorithm 2 specifies rectification timesteps U(0.05,0.95), differing from U(0,1) in both versions' main text; this reporting discrepancy does not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained DTC/TAR ablations, v2 adds an intermediate TAR schedule, comparative sampling-budget analysis, loss curves, and early-training visualizations of one-step estimates and fake trajectories. It also examines applicability to a smaller backbone. These provide substantial new evidence about schedule sensitivity, training stability and low-step behavior.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random-seed studies, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added loss curves describe training dynamics rather than uncertainty across independent runs.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in the original benchmark, sampling and ablation tables are unchanged. Substantial new results include Z-Image training memory of 31.8 GB for TEASR versus 65.6 GB for ADD, with iteration times of 3.8 versus 2.1 seconds; inference costs; and additional TAR, sampling and training-stability outcomes. These are added measurements, not improvements to the original accuracy scores.

M1.justification: The SAD framework, dual-branch DTC architecture, TAR weighting, reconstruction objectives and any-step inference procedure are retained. The new supplementary training algorithm and loss-weight details document implementation without establishing a redesign of the proposed method.

P1.justification: The existing narrative and section organization are largely retained, with localized introduction and TAR rewrites, terminology clarifications, corrected author/running headers, and acknowledgments. An efficiency subsection and organized supplement are added, but the original paper is not extensively rewritten or reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adds efficiency charts and tables, a hyperparameter table, training pseudocode, loss plots, a comparative sampling plot, training-progression images and extensive qualitative grids. Original displays are retained, with several relocated or renumbered. The new visual presentation is substantial beyond pagination changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations covering PiSA-SR, controllable and time-aware one-step SR, and adjacent restoration/generation work. It newly contrasts TAR with multi-forward averaging and fixed-timestep approaches. The central positioning relative to TwinFlow, FACM and distribution matching remains intact; duplicate consolidation and publication updates do not constitute new cited work.

T1.justification: v1 motivates TAR's existing weight (1-s)^2/s through noise-dependent guidance reliability. Supplementary Section 4 in v2 adds a mathematical derivation connecting KL divergence, score differences, flow velocities and the stop-gradient rectification objective. This substantially expands the theoretical treatment without introducing a different TAR weight.

improvement.justification: v1 supports its central training-efficiency claim largely through model counts. v2 adds measured costs, including a common-backbone comparison, concrete 20B-model memory requirements, detailed training documentation, and targeted sensitivity and stability evidence. These substantially strengthen validation and reproducibility while retaining the original results. The measurements reveal a memory–iteration-time tradeoff, and the main-text/algorithm timestep discrepancy remains a reproducibility issue, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TEASR, with matching authors, method and original experiments. Text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. The supplied v1 ends after references; v2 includes an additional readable supplementary section.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original efficiency measurements, TAR sensitivity results, training curves and qualitative training-stability analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original super-resolution results on RealSR, DRealSR and DIV2K-Val, along with sampling-step comparisons and DTC/TAR ablations in Tables 1–3.

results.title: TEASR: Training-Efficient Any-Step Diffusion Transformer for Real-World Image Super-Resolution

C1.justification: Both versions claim that direct motion guidance struggles on distilled generators and that training-free teacher-guided endpoint interpolation with adaptive supervision improves motion quality while preserving speed. The trajectory-restoration framing and expanded supporting experiments retain the central claims and contributions.

C2.justification: v1's limitations paragraph focuses on missing inference-time quality checking. v2 adds substantive limitations concerning underrepresented object-motion combinations, source-target structural mismatch, and fine-grained latent attention, linked to the human-to-monkey climbing failure (Appendix D). It also adds interpretations of runtime/memory tradeoffs and discusses unpaired teachers with unshared latent spaces.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly specifies DDIM inversion steps, extraction timestep and attention blocks, guidance schedules, resolutions/frame counts, and VB LoRA, scheduler, and optimization details. Some earlier baseline-initialization and AnimateDiff threshold details disappear. Reproducibility remains limited by Nmax being described as a per-sample event cap while Algorithm 1 caps inner denoising steps. The project link and promised code release remain unchanged.

E1.justification: TurboBench and AnimateBench remain. v2 adds LOVEU-TGVE's broader appearance and motion editing scenarios, comprising 76 videos and 304 edit pairs, and easy/medium/hard prompt conditions on DavisBench (Section 4.1, Appendix B.4). This expands the tested editing conditions; DAVIS source data itself was already represented in v1.

E2.justification: The original TurboBench and AnimateBench comparator sets remain. v2 newly evaluates MOFT and DiTFlow on DiT systems, including direct distilled-model controls, and adds Tune-a-Video and PointMotion to the LOVEU-TGVE comparison (Tables 2, 7–8, 10–11). Tune-a-Video and the work called PointMotion were previously cited but not evaluated as these comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds DiT model configurations and Flow-sim, Appearance Diversity, and Pick Score evaluations. Reported TurboV2 settings also change: activation thresholds move from 380–420 to 480–500, truncation becomes motion-dependent, and noise blending changes from k=0.01 to 0.05 or 0.3. The motion-strength sweep changes from 500–2000 to 0.05–0.2. These are reported setting revisions; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 expands guidance-strength sweeps and adds activation/truncation sensitivity tests, motion-type and optical-flow analyses, direct VB-only controls, memory/time analysis, and a climbing-motion failure case (Tables 4–5, 9–10, 12; Figure 8). Conversely, v1's separate inverted-noise component ablation and both noise-blend-factor sweeps are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The 50-participant, 36-pair user study retains the same reporting practice and percentages.

E6.justification: TurboBench scores, AnimateBench scores, and user-study percentages are retained. v2 adds extensive DiT, LOVEU-TGVE, subgroup, sensitivity, and resource results. For example, its new Table 10 reports VB+DiTFlow at MF 0.540 and 34 seconds versus MotionEcho at 0.733 and 54 seconds. These are newly reported comparisons, not v1-to-v2 performance gains. Noise-initialization ablation results are removed.

M1.justification: v2 adds DiT/flow-model adaptations using MOFT, DMT, and DiTFlow objectives, reference key/value injection, and iterative latent optimization (Section 3.5, Appendix A.1). Algorithm 1 also changes teacher re-noising from the student's motion-unguided prediction to its motion-guided prediction. Appendix C still uses the unguided estimate, leaving that particular procedural change internally ambiguous.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and method explanation, incorporates Preliminaries within Methods, and reorganizes the appendices around implementation, results, derivation, limitations, and ethics. AnimateDiff discussion moves to the appendix. The narrative restructuring extends beyond simply inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the pipeline and diagnostic figures, adds runtime bars and DiT/failure panels, restructures tables with backbone and component columns, merges guidance-strength tables, and relocates the AnimateBench table. It also changes typography and page layout and resizes or relocates many retained qualitative figures.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands from the earlier emphasis on UNet diffusion and motion customization to DiT generators, trajectory distribution distillation, and additional guidance approaches. Newly discussed works include Wan, CogVideoX, Video-Blade, DiTFlow, MOFT, OPAD, and FlexiMMT, broadening the research context beyond citation renumbering.

T1.justification: The endpoint interpolation already appears in v1 Equation 5. v2 corrects the squared-loss gradient step factor from lambda to lambda/2 and adds derivations of its proximal formulation and equivalent noise-prediction correction (Appendix C). These provide a limited formal extension of the existing update.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the framework's broad applicability through DiT adaptations and comparisons, broader editing tests, teacher controls, sensitivity/resource analyses, and explicit failure boundaries. Detailed implementation recipes address much of v1's sparse reproducibility documentation. These gains outweigh the loss of noise-initialization ablations and remaining inconsistencies between endpoint formulas, pseudocode, and teacher-budget descriptions, although those inconsistencies still impede exact reproduction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MotionEcho, with matching authors, core framework, and retained experiments despite the changed title. All 33 pages of v1 and 48 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds DiT-based evaluations, LOVEU-TGVE results, sensitivity tests, motion-type analyses, memory measurements, and a failure case.

before.justification: v1 reports original TurboBench and AnimateBench experiments, component and hyperparameter ablations, qualitative results, and a 50-participant user study.

results.title: When Distillation Breaks Motion Control: Restoring Generative Trajectories for Fast Video Generators

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the benchmark framing from realistic capture conditions to controlled exposure-duration variation. The central claims about parallel temporal modeling, exposure-conditioned restoration, benchmark performance, efficiency and real-world generalization remain. Reordering and consolidating the contribution list does not establish a new method contribution.

C2.justification: v2 acknowledges that capacity explains much of the fixed-exposure PSNR gain, while exposure conditioning retains benefits under changing exposure. It distinguishes fixed-input guidance tolerance from failures under temporal guidance corruption and softens the interpretation of interpolation to unseen exposures. Camera-model exclusions become more explicit, but v1's separate discussion of 2D-flow failures under rotation and non-rigid motion is removed.

D1.justification: v2 specifies synthesis indexing, the 80-frame interval at 1920 fps, exact exposure duty cycles and random-walk pseudocode. These clarify the existing generation pipeline rather than establish changed data generation. Core hardware and hyperparameters are retained. Some details disappear, including v1's explicit GoPro bicubic-preprocessing statement and expanded refinement/attention equations.

E1.justification: Restoration coverage remains REDS-ME, REDS-RE, GoPro and the same real-world examples, with unchanged exposure ranges and upscaling task. v2 adds an auxiliary exposure-level classification evaluation of existing ETE embeddings in Section S4.1; it introduces no new restoration dataset or domain.

E2.justification: v2 substantially expands comparisons testing the exposure-conditioning contribution: Table 4 adds a capacity-matched no-ETE model, Table 5 compares three alternative conditioning designs, and Table S2 adds FGDF without ETM alongside CDF. VRT is newly evaluated in Tables 1–2. Conversely, the FGDF-based upsampling comparator from v1 Table 5 is removed.

E3.justification: Existing restoration splits, metrics and training settings remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial controlled evaluation designs: capacity matching, interventions on guidance while holding video inputs fixed, separate transition-frame reporting, and cosine-similarity k-NN evaluation with k=5. It also specifies a 10-frame, 180×320 memory comparison. These are added protocols, not evidence that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds capacity-controlled and alternative-conditioning ablations, temporally corrupted guidance tests, quantitative embedding separability, and an unconditioned-FGDF control. The kernel-response visualization becomes bidirectional, testing both short- and long-exposure inputs. The existing fixed-input sensitivity analysis is retained and relocated, while the FGDF upsampling ablation is removed.

E5.justification: Section S4.1 newly reports five-fold cross-validation for estimating exposure-classification accuracy. This does not establish repeated restoration-training runs. Neither version reports restoration seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Headline restoration scores remain unchanged, but substantial diagnostic results are added. The capacity-matched no-ETE model scores 29.88 dB on REDS-RE versus 30.13 for the full model; random wrong-level guidance yields 29.47 dB. ETE classification reaches 92.0%, and the new memory comparison reports 20.5 GB for VRT versus 6.2 GB for FMA-Net++. New comparator rows are added, while the 29.29 dB FGDF-upsampling result is removed.

M1.justification: The proposed architecture, exposure conditioning, degradation/restoration networks, filtering, losses and three-stage training remain substantively unchanged. HRBP is renamed HRBA. Newly evaluated conditioning alternatives are experimental comparators, not replacements for the proposed method.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial explanatory passages are rewritten, HRBP terminology becomes HRBA throughout, and method exposition is reorganized. Physical-model and loss material move into the main text; the standalone FGDF section is merged into network descriptions. The supplement is extensively restructured into Sections S1–S6.

P2.justification: The document switches from two-column to single-column presentation, with extensively resized and relocated figures and reformatted metric columns. Exposure examples and analyses move into the main text; kernel visualizations are redesigned and combined with t-SNE. New tables, a confusion matrix and algorithm display are added, while the training-stage schematic is removed. Most qualitative restoration images are retained.

R1.justification: VRT was already cited, but v2 explicitly acknowledges its sequence-level parallelism and distinguishes FMA-Net++ through computational and memory efficiency. Swin Transformer and Digital Image Warping are added, while several low-light and blur-synthesis references are removed. VRT's preprint-to-publication update is bibliographic rather than a newly cited work.

T1.justification: v2 adds precise mathematical definitions of indexed high-frame-rate averaging and exposure duty cycles in Equations S2–S3. The continuous motion/exposure model and training losses already appear in v1's supplement and are largely relocated or restated. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens attribution of the central exposure-conditioning contribution. Unlike v1's unequal-capacity and CDF-only comparisons, the matched-capacity and unconditioned-FGDF controls, conditioning alternatives and guidance interventions test competing explanations directly. The revised interpretation acknowledges the capacity confound and defines the benchmark scope more accurately. Removing the upsampling ablation and flow-limitations discussion reduces completeness, but these losses are outweighed by the stronger controlled evidence and more qualified conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FMA-Net++ research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete supplementary material support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds controlled exposure-conditioning comparisons, guidance-corruption experiments and quantitative evaluation of exposure embeddings.

before.justification: v1 reports original restoration experiments, benchmark comparisons, component ablations and qualitative results on synthetic and real-world videos.

results.title: FMA-Net++: Motion- and Exposure-Aware Joint Video Super-Resolution and Deblurring

C1.justification: The central claims about training-free, controllable hard negatives and adaptive layer selection remain. The abstract and introduction revise the claimed HPS advantage over CFG from +0.46 to +0.54, and the contribution list explicitly adds hardness quantification. The introduction also qualifies APG/CADS complementarity as holding across most experimental settings.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of beta and EMA half-life, model-capacity trends, and Pareto trade-offs. It explicitly states that hardness alone does not determine quality, identifies standard EMAG's substantial computational overhead, and discusses PAG's difficulties with joint attention. Appendix G explains EMAG-Q's efficiency–quality trade-off. The original modality and ethical limitations remain, relocated to Appendix H.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access URL, A100 hardware and timing details, batch size, warmup and measurement counts, and peak-memory reporting. It documents query-EMA implementation and fused-attention compatibility, clarifies maintenance of EMA buffers across candidate layers, and expands the SD3 PAG adaptation details. v1 already supplied basic hyperparameters, sampler choices, and HPS subsampling information.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate COCO 2014 text-conditioned and unconditional generation with SD3, and ImageNet class-conditioned and unconditional generation with DiT at 256 and 512 resolution. The additions vary guidance procedures, parameters, and computational budgets within this retained coverage; they introduce no new dataset, domain, or task.

E2.justification: PAG, previously evaluated only for unconditional DiT, is added to SD3 conditional and unconditional comparisons and associated sweeps. Table S6 also expands the existing ERG comparison to include SAG and SEG. Most comparator membership remains unchanged; PLADIS is discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: The reported SD3 sampling budget changes from 26 to 28 steps, and the default conditional EMAG scale changes from 1.75 to 1.5. v2 introduces joint CFG/method-scale sweeps and Pareto-based selection, supplementing the retained fixed-CFG DiT experiments. New protocols measure embedding-based hardness, standalone guidance, reduced budgets down to four steps, and controlled runtime. The changed stated settings do not establish that every retained result was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's scale and middle-layer ablations, v2 quantifies negative hardness, tests fixed layers 1–18, sweeps guidance windows and EMA decay, and examines reduced-step and standalone guidance. It also evaluates EMAG-Q approximation quality and efficiency, analyzes PAG failures, and visualizes timestep-dependent layer selection. These additions substantially expand mechanism, sensitivity, and practical-performance analysis.

E5.justification: v1 reports fixed-seed results without uncertainty estimates. v2 adds between-seed standard deviations across seeds 8, 56, and 64, using 1,000 samples per seed for the methods in Table S22, and displays HPS uncertainty in Table 2. Appendix A distinguishes these smaller variance-estimation runs from the single-seed 40,000-sample main evaluation. Timing standard deviations are also introduced.

E6.justification: The main SD3 EMAG result changes from FID/HPS 22.980/29.68 to 22.890/29.76; SAG changes from 18.743/28.40 to 23.039/29.28. Table S7 revises PRDC values, while DiT Tables S8–S10 retain their numbers. Numerous new results cover EMAG-Q, hardness, efficiency, sweeps, and robustness. Because reported SD3 settings also change, the revised scores are not isolated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The original attention-map EMA, adaptive layer selection, and guidance updates are retained. However, v2 introduces EMAG-Q, which accumulates and blends query embeddings instead of post-softmax attention maps, enabling fused attention computation without storing the full attention-map EMA. This is a substantive new inference variant, detailed in Section 3.4 and Appendix G.

P1.justification: Existing material is substantially reorganized: Hopfield motivation, sampler details, unconditional pseudocode, and limitations move from the main text into dedicated appendix sections. The hardness discussion is expanded and restructured, method subsection organization changes, and the conclusion is shortened. These are substantial structural edits beyond simply appending experiments.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column template with differently arranged floats. Existing figures and tables are relocated and resized, including moving the main guidance-scale plot into the appendix. New hardness charts, Pareto plots, layer-selection heatmaps, efficiency tables, and multipage sweep tables substantially alter the visual presentation; some qualitative galleries are also replaced.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to PLADIS, DINOv2, Token Perturbation Guidance, and Where and How to Perturb. Appendix B contrasts PLADIS's spatial enhancement of positive conditioning with EMAG's temporal construction of negative predictions, while newer perturbation papers support the PAG discussion. The broader positioning and previous bibliography are retained.

T1.justification: Appendix G adds a multi-step Taylor/Jacobian argument for approximate first-order equivalence between query-space and attention-map EMA, including small-logit-variation assumptions and approximation-error terms in Equations 28–35. This theoretical development is absent from v1. The earlier Hopfield mathematics is largely retained and relocated, rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves empirical scrutiny and practical assessability through broader controlled sweeps, quantitative hardness tests, seed variability, and explicit computational-cost measurement. EMAG-Q addresses the newly documented efficiency bottleneck: Tables 4 and S16 report reduced time and memory with a small matched-setting quality trade-off. These additions address important validation and usability gaps in v1. Conflicting HPS values under nominally matching settings in Tables S20/S21 and inconsistent hardness terminology weaken parts of the new analysis, but do not outweigh the substantial overall gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EMAG research, with matching authors, central method, datasets, and retained experiments. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, support reliable comparison despite extensive additions and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical experiments and adds original hardness measurements, efficiency comparisons, parameter sweeps, and cross-seed evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original SD3 and DiT image-generation experiments on COCO and ImageNet, including quantitative comparisons, ablations, and generated examples.

results.title: EMAG: Self-Rectifying Diffusion Sampling with Exponential Moving Average Guidance

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain the sink-trap diagnosis, geometric-versus-linguistic expressivity mismatch, and native 3D editing driven solely by a target prompt. The expanded experiments support these existing claims without redefining their scope or novelty.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 adds a mechanism explanation in which out-of-distribution conditional guidance destabilizes the velocity difference used by CFG. The conclusion adds an argument for continued relevance under limited 3D data availability. Existing limitations involving rare poses, large semantic shifts, and unstable editing remain.

D1.justification: Appendix G documents the LLaVA evaluator, scoring rubric, and averaging procedure. Section 5.3 specifies three generative sampling passes, and the acknowledgements add Jean Zay H100 resource information. These disclosures do not establish changes to the retained TRELLIS implementation or hyperparameters.

E1.justification: DT4D editing, synthetic 3D prompt-diversity and inversion tasks, and COCO/DiffusionDB image inversion remain covered. The additional generators extend existing evaluations across models, without introducing a distinct reported data population or task scenario.

E2.justification: Section 5.3 and Table 3 add Vox-E and Instant3DiT to the editing comparison alongside TRELLIS and VoxHammer, substantially broadening comparison to methods using image priors. Figure 16 supplies corresponding visual comparisons. Vox-E was previously cited but was not an evaluated editing baseline.

E3.justification: Editing evaluation expands from SigLIP alone to SigLIP, CLIP, and LLaVA-1.5-7B ratings using a five-level rubric documented in Appendix G. Prompt-diversity and inversion evaluations also add two generator configurations. The existing 30-view editing protocol and TRELLIS sampling settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Tables 1–2 extend diversity and prompt-sensitivity analyses from TRELLIS to LN3Diff and GaussianAnything, directly testing whether the central findings generalize across 3D generators. Section 4.1 also reports unsuccessful trials of earlier generators, without detailed scores. The DT4D Euler/NTI ablation and supplementary image-inversion analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The existing mean-plus-or-minus reporting practice is retained, including for added inversion-result rows. v2 introduces no new repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 add generator results; for example, LN3Diff reports mean L1 values of 1.75, 1.82, and 0.05 for true, approximate, and empty prompts. Table 3 adds baseline results and CLIP/VLM scores, including 0.2829/3.98 for the proposed method, and Figure 16 adds qualitative comparisons. Previously tabulated values remain unchanged. Section 5.3 removes the 197-second VoxHammer timing and explicit 20-fold speedup, adds an over-one-hour Vox-E timing statement, and retains the method's nine-second timing.

M1.justification: The method remains unconditional Euler inversion of TRELLIS structure latents, optional null-text optimization, and resampling with the target edit prompt. Appendix A and Algorithm 1 retain the same procedure; additional generator evaluations do not introduce a method component.

P1.justification: Localized edits correct grammar, consolidate the preliminary explanations, rewrite comparison paragraphs, and shorten future-work discussion. Appendix G is added, and affiliation and acknowledgement text are updated. The overall narrative and main section order are retained.

P2.justification: Tables 1–3 gain model columns, result rows, or metric columns, and Figure 16 is added. The reconstruction and editing figures exchange order and numbering, while table captions and several page placements change. Existing figure imagery and the overall visual design are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Instant3DiT, LN3Diff++, GaussianAnything, LLaVA, Shap-E, XCube, and GaussianCube, supporting the expanded evaluations. The related-work organization and central positioning of native 3D editing relative to methods using image priors remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and algorithmic equations retain their substance. Section 3.2 removes a duplicate Euler equation and displays a CFG expression already present equivalently in v1 Appendix A; this is a restatement rather than new theory or a derivation.

improvement.justification: v1's broad findings depended primarily on TRELLIS, while editing comparisons used two baselines and SigLIP alone. v2 substantially strengthens this evidence through additional generator checks, comparisons with two methods using image priors, and complementary CLIP and documented VLM evaluation. These additions address important weaknesses in generality and comparative validation. Settings for the added generator experiments remain sparsely documented, but the empirical gains clearly outweigh this remaining limitation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their full main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated figures and retained supplementary experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds generator evaluations, editing baselines, and additional editing-quality measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original prompt-diversity, inversion, reconstruction, and editing experiments, including DT4D results and supplementary COCO/DiffusionDB image-inversion results.

results.title: Beyond Prompts: Unconditional 3D Inversion for Out-of-Distribution Shapes

C1.justification: The abstract and three introductory contributions retain the same claims about training-free aesthetic-aware acceleration and improved speed-quality trade-offs across three backbones, including 2.11× speedup and +11.9% ImageReward on Lumina. The revised conclusion incorporates new supporting evidence without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new evidence as showing human-perceived benefits, robustness without aesthetic adjectives, and applicability beyond centered subjects. It adds region jitter as an explanation for dynamic-mask degradation and frozen unmasked details as a failure mechanism. Appendix F also reinterprets anchor-hit statistics as vocabulary coverage rather than inference activation. These substantially expand applicability and mechanism discussion.

D1.justification: v2 clarifies the skip-ratio/percentile mapping and explicitly describes SD3's AesMask-guided spatial path with uniform CFG. The FLUX.1-dev reference gains a checkpoint URL. Hardware, precision, core cache schedules, and the project URL remain unchanged, while the statement that competing baselines use official/default cache intervals is removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds controlled descriptor-free versus descriptor-added prompts and targeted difficult-scene and non-centric scenarios, including crowds, clutter, and abstract art (Tables 14-15 and 18). These extend tested input conditions within the retained text-to-image task; the original Pick-a-Pic evaluation remains.

E2.justification: The original per-backbone comparator sets are retained. New comparisons include dense generation, FORA, and a variant without Spatial CFG in the human study, plus dense generation and TaylorSeer in the FLUX.1-schnell test. These are limited comparison extensions without a new external acceleration method.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a randomized blind study with 15 annotators, 60 pairs, four questions, and tie-excluding win rates; a 200-base-prompt wording experiment; static, five-step, and per-step mask-refresh controls; and a four-step FLUX.1-schnell evaluation. These substantially expand evaluation design. The original 10,000-prompt protocol and 30/28-step backbone settings remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component, token-weighting, sparsity, and mask-timing ablations, v2 adds descriptor and complex-scene robustness, a human comparison without Spatial CFG, static-versus-dynamic masks, explicit masking/guidance overhead diagnostics, and mined failure cases with mitigation experiments (Section 4.3 and Appendix E). These investigate several previously untested vulnerabilities.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports binomial tests of non-tie human votes against a 50% null, stating p < 0.001 for the main comparisons except alignment against dense generation. It also specifies two seeds for the new hard-scene tests. The retained main experiments still use three fixed seeds, with no added confidence intervals for their scores.

E6.justification: v2 adds human overall win rates of 67% against dense generation, 89% against FORA, and 66% against the no-Spatial-CFG variant, alongside new robustness, distilled-model, and mask-refresh results. Existing values also change: Lumina Aesthetic score becomes 6.0414 rather than 6.1414 in Table 1, and spatial-only latency becomes 8.65 rather than 8.72 seconds in the runtime decomposition. The headline 2.11× speedup and 0.8410 ImageReward remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core algorithm and Equations (1)-(13) remain unchanged. However, v1 Appendix E.3 specifies uniform-token fallback below anchor similarity 0.60, while v2 Appendix F.3 explicitly retains top-r selection without that fallback, resolving a conflict with the existing main-text description. v2 also introduces delayed-mask and entropy-based corrective variants for failures, although their precise rules remain underspecified.

P1.justification: v2 adds a human/robustness subsection and appendix, revises the conclusion and anchor-coverage explanation, fixes cross-references, and moves references before the appendices. Keywords and a corresponding-author marker are added. Most existing narrative and method prose remains intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds a substantial table suite for human judgments, robustness, overhead, distilled-model compatibility, and mask refresh (Table 3 and Tables 13-18); Table 13 repeats the main human-study results. Retained tables gain colored highlighting and some revised labels. All twelve figures are retained, with Figures 4 and 5 brought onto the same page.

R1.justification: v2 adds Mao et al.'s Ctrl-Z Sampling and expands Section 2.1 to mention trajectory changes through controlled exploration. The other cited works are retained; the expanded FLUX reference identifies the same existing backbone.

T1.justification: The mathematical method definitions and Equations (1)-(13) are retained, with no new theorem, proof, or derivation. The added p = 100q relationship explains equivalent percentile and implementation notation.

improvement.justification: v1's perceptual-quality claims relied on automatic proxies and qualitative examples. v2 substantially strengthens their support through direct human judgments and targeted tests of descriptor dependence, difficult scenes, mask stability, and overhead. It also resolves the Table 1/Table 2 aesthetic-score inconsistency and conflicting anchor-selection documentation. These address important validation and clarity gaps, although some new experimental protocols and failure-mitigation parameters remain underspecified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AccelAes and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across the added sections, renumbered tables, and relocated references.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds human preference judgments, prompt and scene robustness experiments, distilled-model evaluation, and mask-refresh and failure analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation-quality and runtime measurements on three DiT backbones, component ablations, sensitivity experiments, and anchor-coverage analysis.

results.title: AccelAes: Accelerating Diffusion Transformers for Training-Free Aesthetic-Enhanced Image Generation

C1.justification: v1's abstract claims 98% of CLIP performance at half cost; v2 strengthens this to matching or beating full-cost frozen CLIP. The introduction also extends the efficiency claim across multiple architectures. The central NoisyCLIP, benchmark, and early-stopping contributions remain.

C2.justification: v1 treats NoisySigLIP's weaker retrieval performance as limited transfer across backbones. v2 attributes it to sigmoid-versus-softmax discrimination and emphasizes robust transfer for visual selection (Section 5.4). It also interprets the new DiT results as architectural transfer and revises failure-case explanations in Appendix F.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page address where v1 only promised future code and data, and documents DiT VAE decoding and shorter generation schedules. Core training hyperparameters and hardware remain unchanged. The PDFs alone do not establish whether the linked resources are actually available.

E1.justification: v2 extends evaluation from SDXL-generated representations to zero-shot transfer on SD3.5 and FLUX.1 [dev] trajectories, testing substantially different latent input distributions (Section 5.4). The two caption benchmarks remain, and renaming factual consistency as latent-to-text retrieval does not introduce another task.

E2.justification: LatentCLIP-8 and LatentCLIP-4-plus become evaluated comparators in the main Best-of-N experiments and Appendix C tables. LatentCLIP also enters qualitative comparisons. v1 cited LatentCLIP but evaluated primarily frozen CLIP and SigLIP, so this materially strengthens comparator coverage.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a blind preference protocol using 100 randomly sampled GenAI-Bench Basic image pairs, comparing selections at latent step 20 and excluding strict ties (Appendix C.3). New DiT experiments use zero-shot evaluation, VAE decoding, and shorter generation schedules, including 28 steps. Existing SDXL training and benchmark settings are retained.

E4.justification: Section 5.4 adds tests of robustness to changing the generating architecture, and Appendix C.3 independently checks automatic evaluation through human preferences. Appendix F expands and revises failure examples with LatentCLIP. Training-range, encoder-training, and model-size ablations already existed in v1 and are retained.

E5.justification: The new human study reports inter-rater agreement, κ = 0.724, adding a statistical reliability assessment absent from v1. Neither version reports confidence intervals or repeated-training-run variability; the revision does not establish increased replication.

E6.justification: v2 adds LatentCLIP scores, DiT alignment-versus-cost curves, and 61.3% human preference for NoisyCLIP among non-tied trials. Existing Table 1 and encoder-ablation scores remain unchanged. It also replaces some qualitative selections and removes the dedicated latent-30 Best-of-N panel and Appendix C average-gap columns.

M1.justification: The contrastive objective, frozen text encoder, and training interval 20–29 remain unchanged. v2 adds an inference adaptation for DiT inputs: model-specific VAE decoding replaces the linear latent-to-RGB conversion used for SDXL (Section 4.5).

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, the abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around three challenges, and the results narrative is reorganized. Factual consistency becomes latent-to-text retrieval within alignment analysis, while training-range analysis moves ahead of Best-of-N and backbone discussion becomes generalization analysis.

P2.justification: v2 changes from two-column to single-column layout, extends Figure 1 with an early-stopping schematic, redesigns alignment plots, adds DiT plots and LatentCLIP rows, and expands qualitative grids. The combined appendix benchmark table becomes separate Basic and Advanced tables, and the latent-30 Best-of-N panel is removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to FLUX.1 Kontext, SANA 1.5, and b-CLIP. It sharpens positioning against the already-cited LatentCLIP by emphasizing early noisy-latent ranking rather than final-stage superiority. The related-work survey is otherwise largely retained.

T1.justification: The definition accompanying Equation 3 relaxes Φ from a linear transformation to a general transformation, consistent with the added VAE decoding. Equations 1–3 otherwise retain their mathematical form, and no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical validation by addressing v1's missing latent-specialized comparison and SDXL-only, automatic evaluation through LatentCLIP tests, cross-architecture transfer, and human preferences. These additions make the central efficiency argument more credible. The stronger abstract overstates the retained SDXL results, which still report a small drop against full-cost CLIP, and the human study lacks annotator counts and uncertainty estimates. These shortcomings limit, but do not outweigh, the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NoisyCLIP research despite the changed title and format. Their methods, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds LatentCLIP comparisons, cross-architecture evaluations, and a human preference study.

before.justification: v1 reports original alignment, Best-of-N, factual-consistency, ablation, and qualitative results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Early Estimation of Language to Latent Alignment in Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The central contribution remains improving tail-class diversity and fidelity through unconditional contrastive regularization and conditional–unconditional alignment. v3's introduction additionally claims that implicit conditional diversification is theoretically and empirically better than directly diversifying conditional latents. This strengthens the claimed justification without changing the principal research objective.

C2.justification: v3 introduces a substantive shortcut explanation for conditional contrastive learning and interprets alignment as distilling diversified unconditional representations. Appendix A.4 newly discusses the feature-depth tradeoff between overall FID and recall/sFID. The main ImageNet interpretation shifts from improved recall at similar precision to FID, IS, and tail-FID gains. Appendix A.2 also refines the training-cost limitation through an explicit speed–memory tradeoff.

D1.justification: v3 adds batching pseudocode, throughput and memory measurements, explicit latent normalization, and selected loss weights α = γ = 0.05. Most existing training details remain. However, it drops v2's explicit 50-step ODE sampling specification for ImageNet and 100-step DDIM specification for the main TinyImageNet/Places comparisons, creating some reproducibility losses alongside the added detail.

E1.justification: Both versions cover ImageNet-LT, TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, CIFAR10-LT, and CIFAR100-LT, including conditional generation and CIFAR unconditional generation. The added ImageNet imbalance factor of 0.001 changes sample allocation within retained coverage, rather than adding a dataset, population, or task.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 compares CCUA with SiT and Dispersive Loss. v3 adds CBDM and REPA to that ImageNet-LT comparison and evaluates DiffROP in Table 11. CBDM was previously evaluated only in the U-Net comparisons, while REPA and DiffROP were discussed but not evaluated. This substantially broadens the relevant transformer comparator set.

E3.justification: v3 adds ImageNet evaluation at imbalance factor 0.001, adds FIDtail to the main transformer comparison, and introduces an approximately equal-training-time comparison of 700k CCUA steps against 900k SiT steps. It also evaluates controlled variations in feature depth, loss weights, and alignment schedules. Training checkpoints are now reported as 250k–900k steps instead of 40–160 epochs; matching retained results do not establish longer training or reruns.

E4.justification: v3 adds extensive ImageNet loss-weight and component ablations, four feature-depth choices, alignment-scheduler comparisons, extreme-imbalance testing, and expanded batch-resampling analyses (Tables 4–6 and 12–14). The isolated TinyImageNet UCL-only and AL-only results from v2 Table 4 disappear, as does the rose/table sample case study in v2 Figure 9. Other qualitative analyses are retained and relocated.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix A.2 and Table 10 report CIFAR100-LT FID for seeds 0, 42, and 2025, with approximate deviations for DDPM and CCUA. v3 removes this limited seed-robustness analysis without replacement uncertainty reporting. This establishes a reporting loss, not that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: v2 Table 1's CCUA results survive unchanged as the N-layer rows of v3 Table 13. The newly emphasized N/4 configuration reports FID 15.08 and recall 17.27 at 900k steps, versus 16.41 and 21.34 for the retained N configuration; this is a configuration tradeoff, not a same-setting improvement. v3 adds substantial baseline, tail-FID, ablation, extreme-imbalance, and efficiency results. Most U-Net/CIFAR scores remain, while seed results and some qualitative evidence are removed.

M1.justification: The two-loss CCUA framework remains. However, v3 selects features from the N/4-th SiT block for its main results instead of the final block used in v2, retaining the final-block variant in Appendix A.4. Appendix A.1 also extends the stated t/T weighting of UCL from TinyImageNet-LT and Places-LT to all datasets. These are limited procedural revisions.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and method narrative are extensively revised around the interaction of the two losses. v3 adds a dedicated motivation subsection, reorganizes the alignment discussion, expands the framework explanation, and restructures the appendices into implementation, acceleration, quantitative, ablation, and qualitative sections. It also updates the author/affiliation block and removes the LLM-use appendix.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a substantially different page template, typography, text area, and running-header layout. It adds the conceptual contrastive-learning diagram in Figure 2, expands Table 1 with comparators and FIDtail, and introduces several analysis tables. Retained figures are resized or relocated, while v2's rose/table sample panel is removed. These changes exceed simple renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: v3 adds references on contrastive predictive coding and resampling by Oord et al., Shi et al., and Zhang et al. It removes v2's explicit statement that UCL generalizes DiffROP and develops positioning around avoiding shortcuts in conditional contrastive learning. The broader relationships to GAN alignment, REPA, and Dispersive Loss remain.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.2 adds a mutual-information decomposition, I(h;x,c) = I(h;c) + I(h;x|c), and reasoning about class-only shortcuts when regularizing conditional latents. The existing Gaussian KL-to-MSE derivation remains substantially unchanged. The addition is a limited mathematical rationale, without a formal proof of comparative superiority.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens previously limited transformer validation through direct CBDM, REPA, and DiffROP comparisons, tail-specific evaluation, and controlled studies of consequential design choices. The encoder analysis exposes fidelity–diversity tradeoffs, while Appendix A.2 makes computational costs concrete. Removing the three-seed analysis and some sampling details weakens transparency, and the revised main configuration is not uniformly better. Nevertheless, the broader comparative evidence and substantially better characterization of method behavior provide a clear net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CCUA for long-tailed diffusion models. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and included appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original generation experiments and adds baseline comparisons, sensitivity studies, extreme-imbalance results, and implementation throughput and memory measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original image-generation experiments, baseline comparisons, loss ablations, qualitative analyses, and a three-seed evaluation across the main text and appendices.

results.title: Contrastive Conditional–Unconditional Alignment for Long-tailed Diffusion Model

C1.justification: v1's central validation concerns manifold-aware interpolation. v2 broadens the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to claim complementary validation of global geometry through interpolation and local geometry through guidance correction. It additionally claims improved generation quality without reduced text alignment and transfer of that benefit to distilled models without extra student inference cost.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about interpolation metrics failing to reflect visual quality at low noise levels and explicitly frames video interpolation as a geometry proxy. It explains guidance-weight robustness and deterioration from accumulated approximation errors over additional solver iterations. It also identifies evaluation on newer architectures as unfinished work and expands the interpretation of the FIM-based comparator's limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds complete MorphBench prompt tables, FID sample counts, guidance implementation settings, and detailed LCM/LoRA training parameters. Hardware reporting changes from all experiments using an A100 to separate A6000, A100, and H200 assignments. Conversely, v1's statement that source code is attached as supplementary material disappears; the PDFs do not establish whether actual code availability changed.

E1.justification: v2 evaluates MorphBench metamorphosis, explicitly excluded in v1 because of its global shape changes. It also adds text-conditioned generation evaluated on MS-COCO 2014 validation prompts and distillation training on Conceptual 12M. The earlier synthetic, face-image, and video interpolation coverage remains.

E2.justification: The previously cited but unevaluated FIM-based metric of Azeglio and Bernardo becomes a comparator in image interpolation, video interpolation, and the prompt-adjustment ablation. New generation experiments evaluate CFG and CFG++, while distillation compares corrected and ordinary CFG teachers. The original five interpolation baselines remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include 30,000-image generation evaluated with FID and CLIP Score, four-step distilled-model evaluation, and interpolation using Stable Diffusion v2.0-base. Spectral analysis expands from one endpoint to all sampled CelebA-HQ images. Synthetic-step reporting also changes inconsistently: v2 Section 4.1 says training uses 50 steps, whereas Appendix D.1 specifies 1,000 training and 50 generation steps; an actual training change is therefore unresolved.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's prompt-adjustment ablation and qualitative noise-level study, v2 adds checkpoint-robustness experiments, quantitative noise-level sweeps for image and video interpolation, and guidance-weight and conjugate-gradient-iteration ablations. It also extends the prompt-adjustment comparison to the FIM-based metric and replaces the single-image spectral example with dataset-level analysis.

E5.justification: v1 reports no significance tests or repeated-run uncertainty analysis. v2 introduces one-sided exact binomial tests for interpolation comparisons, five matched-seed distillation runs with a reported significance result, and median, interquartile, and minimum–maximum spectral bands. These are newly reported practices; they do not establish additional runs of the retained interpolation experiments.

E6.justification: Previously reported interpolation numbers are retained, including the method's MB(A) FID of 27.44 and DAVIS MSE of 8.777 × 10^-3. v2 adds metamorphosis results, FIM-based comparator scores, different-checkpoint results, guidance and distillation outcomes, and sensitivity results. For example, new Table 5 reports distilled-model FID of 16.98 versus 17.91 for CFG; this is a new comparison, not a v1-to-v2 performance gain.

M1.justification: The metric G = J^T J and interpolation optimization are retained. Section 3.2 adds a distinct guidance-correction procedure: regularizing the guidance perturbation using the metric, approximately solving the resulting linear system with one conjugate-gradient step and finite-difference products, and applying correction to the distillation teacher.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method exposition, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around global and local geometric validation. The main-text preliminaries move into Appendix A, the method gains separate metric and algorithm subsections, and the appendices are reorganized. These changes substantially alter the narrative beyond accommodating new experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds geometric illustrations, algorithm boxes, guidance examples, prompt tables, and quantitative ablation plots. Table 2 is restructured into two metric blocks. Earlier video examples from v1 Figures 4 and 6 are consolidated into v2 Figure 7, while the spectral display is redesigned with distribution bands. Other interpolation examples are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around guidance, contrasting its geometric correction with CFG++ and TCFG and adding guidance and distillation literature. It develops the distinction between its full Jacobian spectrum and the previously cited FIM-based metric's rank-one score direction. Related work is also reorganized into an explicit taxonomy of interpolation approaches.

T1.justification: The original metric and spectral argument underlying Proposition 1 remain. v2 adds the guidance-correction variational formulation and its approximate linear-system derivation in Equations 4–5, with assumptions about neighboring-time geometry and Jacobian symmetry. It also develops the rank-one limitation of the FIM-based metric and explains why using the score Jacobian directly can yield an indefinite metric.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central geometric argument by testing previously excluded metamorphosis cases, evaluating the FIM-based competitor, expanding spectral evidence beyond one image, and adding statistical and sensitivity analyses. The guidance experiments provide evidence beyond interpolation, while the new ablations expose metric and solver limitations. These gains outweigh the removed code-attachment statement and the conflicting synthetic-data training-step descriptions, which remain documentation weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same score-Jacobian Riemannian metric research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including material relocated in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original interpolation experiments and adds guidance-correction, distillation, checkpoint-robustness, and sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data, image-interpolation, and video-frame-interpolation experiments, plus prompt-adjustment ablations and spectral analyses.

results.title: Be Tangential to Manifold: Discovering Riemannian Metric for Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The central claims of model-agnostic, reward-guided escape from local optima and improved conditional generation remain. v2 makes the efficiency advantage of fewer, deeper searches an explicit experimental contribution and revises the abstract's stated NFE increase from approximately 7.6× to 6.72×.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations and limitations concerning high-reward plateaus, fixed-threshold instability, late-stage reward overfitting and diminishing returns. It discusses the Hunyuan-DiT numeracy exception and hypothesizes mechanisms behind spatial-relation results. The supplement explicitly limits conclusions about large-scale inference because of resource constraints, extending v1's more general quality–efficiency discussion.

D1.justification: v1 already documents core hyperparameters and an RTX 3090. v2 adds image resolutions, CPU specifications, a second RTX 4090 setup, Ubuntu and CUDA versions, and PyTorch 2.4.0/Diffusers 0.32.2. It also documents revised configurations and expands baseline descriptions. These refine reproducibility information; no code or data release instructions are added.

E1.justification: Pick-a-Pic and DrawBench are retained. v2 adds systematic compositional evaluation on T2I-CompBench, reporting color, shape, texture, spatial-relation and numeracy results in Tables 2 and 4. This substantially extends the evaluated prompt population and explicit compositional requirements.

E2.justification: The main comparator set remains DDIM, Resampling, Z-Sampling and SOP; Resample is renamed Resampling. Within the reward-model comparison, v2 Table 3 adds a CLIPScore-guided variant to the HPSv2, AES, PickScore and ImageReward variants evaluated in v1 Table 2.

E3.justification: Reported main settings change from λ=15, N=20, unrestricted depth and δ=0.01 to λ=40, N=4, maximum depth 3 and δ=0; SOP candidates change from 5 to 4. v2 adds Hunyuan-DiT evaluation, compositional category scores and approximately compute-matched controls. These changes prevent treating revised scores as same-setting gains. Figure 4's exact threshold sweep is ambiguous because its caption and legend disagree.

E4.justification: v2 adds depth-versus-width analysis in Figure 2, approximately compute-matched Always-explore comparisons in Table 5, exploration-probability sweeps in Table 6 and exploration-window sensitivity in Table 7. It expands reward-model testing and qualitative cases. The existing threshold/depth analysis is retained in revised supplementary Figure 4, rather than removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Increased search candidates and additional result rows do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced or added under revised settings. For example, Ctrl-Z's SD2.1 ImageReward scores change from 0.776 to 1.138 on Pick-a-Pic and from 0.685 to 1.025 on DrawBench. SOP now exceeds Ctrl-Z on SD2.1 PickScore in both benchmarks, reversing v1's ordering. Hunyuan-DiT, CompBench and additional ablation results substantially expand the evidence. HPS rescaling and equivalent rounding are excluded from this judgment.

M1.justification: The core reward-guided inversion sampler remains. Algorithm 1 changes the exploration condition from t ≤ T−λ to t ≥ T−λ, aligning it with the early-exploration prose already present in v1. It also moves the stopping test outside the N-candidate loop. These are localized revisions to the reported procedure.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites and consolidates related work, revises method explanations, compresses the main experimental-settings section and moves expanded settings into the supplement. The ablation narrative is reorganized around depth versus width, with threshold analysis moved to supplementary material and new interpretation and limitations sections added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn using layered two-dimensional landscapes. Tables gain model groupings, NFE columns and revised highlighting, alongside new benchmark and ablation tables. The threshold plot is relocated and redrawn, and qualitative displays gain changed examples, colored borders and an additional image grid.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for T2I-CompBench, Hunyuan-DiT and Choi et al.'s Fair Sampling through Switching Mechanism. The overall positioning against fixed-depth exploration and other inference-time techniques remains. Bibliographic formatting changes do not represent additional research-positioning changes.

T1.justification: The substantive DDIM, clean-image estimation, inversion and reward-threshold mathematics in Equations 1–6 is retained. Noise-schedule and index notation is cleaned up, but no new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs appear.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence that was limited to one architecture and two benchmarks: Hunyuan-DiT and compositional evaluations test generality, while depth-versus-width and approximately compute-matched ablations directly examine the claimed exploration advantage. Added implementation details and substantive failure conditions improve assessability. Figure 4's conflicting labels and Algorithm 1's unclear stopping check remain weaknesses, but the broader, more diagnostic validation provides a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Ctrl-Z Sampling work. Text, equations, algorithms, tables and figures are readable throughout. v1 has no separate appendix; v2 includes readable supplementary material on PDF pages 11–16.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments with Stable Diffusion 2.1 and Hunyuan-DiT, adds T2I-CompBench results, and includes additional quantitative ablations and qualitative examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original Stable Diffusion 2.1 experiments on Pick-a-Pic and DrawBench, including baseline comparisons, ablations and generated-image examples.

results.title: Ctrl-Z Sampling: Scaling Diffusion Sampling with Controlled Random Zigzag Explorations

C1.justification: The benchmark novelty, three-stage framework, and generalization claims remain substantively unchanged. The abstract corrects the claimed advantage from 3.5% accuracy and 11.0 IoU to 3.1 and 10.1 points, matching unchanged Table 1 values for ForeSea versus VideoRAG. This is a limited quantitative correction.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations concerning backbone-independent grounding gains, complementary person/global context, caption quality, and scale robustness. Appendix B.2 shifts from justifying VISTA over CLIP to identifying retrieval limitations relative to newer encoders. Some new interpretations overreach: Appendix B.1 claims Hybrid has the highest average scores, although Table 6 gives it 64.6% multimodal accuracy versus ForeSea's 65.4%.

D1.justification: Section 3.2 newly documents two-stage verification, removal of 50% of initial generations, Qwen3-VL-32B-assisted checking, and manual corrections. V2 also specifies global/hybrid retrieval budgets, encoder checkpoints, and 320×240 video resolution. These improve documentation, but do not establish that the existing benchmark was regenerated or its preprocessing changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 1,041-question ForeSeaQA benchmark with six subtasks and text-only/image-text queries, plus VideoMME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench. LongVideoBench already appears in v1 Appendix B.3. The new caption controls and size/scene analyses use retained benchmark coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds predicted-caption and oracle-UCA-caption baselines and evaluates VideoRAG with VideoLLaMA3 in Table 3. Appendix B.2 expands the CLIP-versus-VISTA/GCL retrieval comparison to include SigLIP, SigLIP2, and EVA-CLIP. These substantially broaden the actual comparison methods, while Table 1's original comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: V2 adds shared-backbone comparisons, caption-only controls, and encoder substitutions. Table 3 specifies a 64-frame LLaVA-Video comparison and hybrid retrieval budgets of two person tracks plus 24 global frames, or one plus 12 for LLaVA-Video. Appendix C.3 introduces size and scene stratification. These extend evaluation design substantially; existing benchmark metrics and default settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's spatial-grounding, retrieval-budget, and person-versus-global ablations, v2 adds hybrid retrieval tests, encoder sensitivity, backbone swaps, and predicted-versus-oracle caption controls. Appendix C.3 adds query-image-size and scene-type analyses. These address component dependence, visual-grounding requirements, and surveillance robustness.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for model performance. V2 continues reporting point estimates; its additional subgroup results do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Existing main, latency, and open-domain scores are retained, but substantial new results appear. V2 Table 3 reports ForeSea-Hybrid at 66.9% accuracy/18.4 IoU and oracle captions at 83.2%/31.1. Newly evaluated VideoRAG with VideoLLaMA3 reaches 68.1%/9.9, versus ForeSea's 66.0%/13.6, revealing an accuracy–localization tradeoff. Encoder and subgroup results are also added. These are additional configurations, not same-setting improvements to the original ForeSea results.

M1.justification: V2 introduces ForeSea-Hybrid, combining person-centric retrieval with global-frame retrieval, whereas v1 evaluates these separately. This is a limited procedural extension; the default tracker, multimodal encoder, and VideoLMM pipeline remain unchanged. Appendix B.2's VISTA-to-GCL terminology does not establish a backbone replacement, since v1 already specifies GCL-trained VISTA.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are rewritten and tightened, Appendix B.1–B.2 discussions are revised, and new experimental subsections are inserted. The overall narrative structure, core method exposition, conclusion, and dataset-generation prompt templates are retained, making this localized editing and expansion rather than a wholesale restructuring.

P2.justification: V2 adds Table 3 and expands the ablation, subtask, and retrieval tables. The latency and open-domain tables are reduced and placed side by side. All six figures retain their graphics, with changes mainly involving placement, table formatting, and page reflow.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Qwen3-VL, EVA-CLIP, SigLIP, and SigLIP2 supporting the verification description and encoder experiments. The main related-work organization and positioning of ForeSeaQA and ForeSea remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The benchmark definitions, embedding equations (1)–(2), and temporal-IoU definitions and conventions remain unchanged. The evaluation-metrics appendix moves from C.3 to C.4 without mathematical revision; no new proofs or theoretical results appear.

improvement.justification: V1's main RAG comparisons used different generator backbones. V2 Table 3 adds shared-backbone controls that separate grounding benefits from generator strength, addressing an important weakness in the empirical argument. Caption controls and surveillance subgroup analyses further strengthen validation. These gains are substantial despite retained best-accuracy claims and new Hybrid-ranking language that conflict with Tables 3 and 6.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ForeSea framework and ForeSeaQA benchmark. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices A–C are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains the original empirical evaluations and adds hybrid retrieval, encoder and backbone comparisons, caption-only baselines, and surveillance subgroup analyses.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original ForeSea evaluations, ablations, retrieval results, latency measurements, and open-domain benchmark results.

results.title: ForeSea: AI Forensic Search with Multi-modal Queries for Video Surveillance

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: a unified B-rep-based MLLM, code alignment and two-stage training supporting four CAD tasks. Additional experimental support does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations involving segmentation-pretraining bias and AAGNet's coarser UV sampling, and interprets the Llama experiment as backbone robustness. Supplementary Section B.1 further interprets alternative command sequences as evidence against memorization. These extend the existing mechanism discussion without substantially changing its overall scope or adding a substantive limitations analysis.

D1.justification: v1 provides little implementation information beyond the backbone and decoder depth. New Appendix A documents four H100 GPUs, tokenization, contrastive temperature, AdamW learning rates, scheduling, dropout, epochs, batch sizes, DeepSpeed configurations, projector dimensions and validation-based checkpoint selection. Appendix B also identifies OpenCASCADE for visualization. These are substantial reproducibility disclosures.

E1.justification: Both versions use DeepCAD for reverse engineering, completion and error correction, and SGP-Bench for CAD-QA. The appendix supplies further examples within this coverage, without adding datasets, task requirements or distinct test environments.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds retrained, B-rep-conditioned DeepCAD and Brep2Seq comparators for both completion and error correction, substantially strengthening comparisons with matching inputs. Completion removes GPT-4, GPT-3.5, LLaMA3 and Mistral while retaining CAD-Llama. Table 1 removes MultiCAD and View2CAD; the CAD-QA comparator set is unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 adds GPT-5 visual assessment of isometric renders against ground truth on a 0–5 scale, alongside settings for new baseline controls and encoder/backbone ablations. Existing splits, masking and corruption ranges, and 8,096-point Chamfer-distance evaluation remain unchanged. Appendix A's training budgets are newly disclosed, rather than established revisions to earlier settings.

E4.justification: Table 3(a) adds tests of omitting Phase 1 alignment, segmentation-pretrained encoder initialization, replacing UV-Net with AAGNet, and using Llama-3.2 1B. These examine previously untested dependencies of the approach. Supplementary Section B.1 also adds command-count and command-order ambiguity cases with accompanying accuracy and distance values.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, variability estimates or significance tests. The added experiments do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The headline reverse-engineering ACCcmd/ACCparam/CD changes from 89.39/81.93/0.499 to 89.34/82.01/0.464. The earlier tuple reappears under Pre-trained Encoder, so this is not an established same-setting gain. v3 adds substantial baseline, ablation, VLM-score and qualitative results, plus completion CD/IR entries. Table 3(b)'s error-correction invalid-ratio ranking reverses; CAD-QA accuracies remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed UV-Net/CoCa alignment, losses, frozen encoder, three-layer projector and two-stage LLM training remain unchanged. Added encoder and backbone variants are ablations. v3 explicitly specifies scratch initialization, but v1 does not specify initialization sufficiently to establish a changed core procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose are retained. v3 tightens method and downstream-task explanations, explicitly labels the two phases in subsection headings, standardizes terminology, fixes the running title, updates contact details and adds acknowledgements and organized supplementary sections.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains a VLM column and moves; Table 2 merges completion and error correction into a larger shared display; Table 3 expands its ablation rows. Eight supplementary figures substantially extend the visual presentation with ambiguity analyses and task examples, including some reused reverse-engineering examples. The main framework figures are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds the AAGNet reference and removes Mistral 7B, Ouyang et al.'s instruction-following paper and the original LLaMA reference. The related-work narrative and positioning against task-specific CAD models and BrepLLM remain substantially unchanged. Most other bibliography edits add metadata or DOI links.

T1.justification: Equations 1–9 retain the same feature mappings, losses and accuracy definitions, apart from punctuation and formatting. No new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs appear.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses two weaknesses of v1: downstream comparisons confounded by input modality and sparse training documentation. B-rep-conditioned baselines in Table 2, stronger component controls in Table 3 and Appendix A's training recipe make the central contribution more assessable and reproducible. Removed comparators narrow comparison breadth, and uncertainty reporting remains absent; the 92.69 versus 92.96 completion-accuracy discrepancy also persists. Nevertheless, the improved controls and documentation provide a clear substantial net gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BrepCoder research. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v3 additionally contains readable supplementary Sections A–B.

after.justification: v3 retains original task evaluations and adds comparison results, ablations, visual-quality scores and supplementary qualitative results.

before.justification: Sections 4.2–4.4 and Tables 1–3 report original BrepCoder experiments on reverse engineering, completion, error correction and CAD-QA, including ablations.

results.title: BrepCoder: A Unified Multimodal Large Language Model for Multi-task B-rep Reasoning

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes broad cross-benchmark generalization, robustness and 3D grounding. v2 narrows the abstract and conclusion toward fine-grained/spatial improvements and ordinal-depth/RoI evaluation, while adding claims of transfer across backbones. This materially changes the claimed scope, although the dataset and core resource contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the earlier cropping-based explanation of Doc/Text degradation with evidence supporting inference-format mismatch. It newly discusses source-dependent gains, mixed backbone transfer, weaker document rationales, noisy nonmetric depth, inference latency and cascading localization failures without backtracking. These substantially qualify applicability and explain failure mechanisms.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page URL, identifies GPT-4o-mini as the evaluator, specifies score-field parsing and malformed-output handling, and adds dropout/DDP details. Training-setting documentation is revised. Most hardware, LoRA, image/token budgets and generation prompts were already supplied in v1; the PDFs do not establish availability of the linked resources.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the 489K/165K resources, the same eleven source datasets across four domains, and MME/V* evaluation. The new audits, prompt comparisons and source-removal ablation operate within this existing coverage.

E2.justification: The main Visual-CoT and grounding comparator sets remain unchanged. However, v1 Table 5's external-benchmark comparison is replaced by v2 Table 7, which adds Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL-based trained variants while removing MiniGPTv2, VisCoT-7B and LLaVA-NeXT from that comparison.

E3.justification: v2 adds matched direct-QA tests of fixed checkpoints, one-epoch InternVL training, source-removal experiments and a stratified 2,200-example audit. It revises the appendix learning rate from 1e-5 to 2e-5 and changes the main-text ViT setting to frozen, matching v1's appendix. Table 2 newly specifies sample-weighted averages, although Appendix C still says macro-averaging. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained dataset/zoom ablations and user study, v2 adds substantial analyses of output-format sensitivity, backbone transfer, dependence on training sources, annotation quality and automatic-judge validity (Tables 3, 6, 7 and 12-16). These test important questions that v1 did not empirically address.

E5.justification: v1 mainly reports point estimates. v2 newly reports five judge evaluations per example, Wilson 95% confidence intervals for the annotation audit, and confidence intervals for evaluator scores, correlations, weighted kappa and agreement. The five-pass disclosure does not establish an increase over a known v1 run count; additional training seeds are not reported.

E6.justification: Table 2 retains per-dataset scores but revises several averages, including VisReason-Pro from 0.807 to 0.802 and VisCoT-7B from 0.580 to 0.614; ablation values also change. Substantial new results cover direct-QA inference, InternVL transfer, source removal, annotation quality and judge calibration. For example, newly reported VisReason-Pro direct-QA scores are 0.856 on MME and 0.791 on V*, under a different inference protocol from the retained multi-round results.
