M1.justification: The dataset-generation algorithms, autoregressive LoRA fine-tuning objective and adaptive zoom-and-verify procedure remain unchanged. The additional backbone and inference-format experiments do not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the abstract, contribution statements, related-work discussion, experimental interpretation and conclusion. It introduces dedicated error-analysis, transfer and limitations discussions and reorganizes the appendix into lettered sections with a substantial additional-results section.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout with running headers. Table 2 becomes stacked panels, the external comparison is redesigned, and new format-analysis, transfer, audit and calibration tables are inserted. Figure 6 gains a bird comparison; most existing pipeline, prompt and appendix-example figures are retained and resized or relocated.

R1.justification: Related work adds discussions and citations for VGR, Zebra-CoT, CodePlot-CoT and other works, while removing the LLaVA-Plus citation. Positioning becomes more qualified around scale, multi-round RoI supervision and ordinal-depth coverage, but retains the existing model-oriented/dataset-oriented framework. Bibliographic updates and duplicate consolidation are presentation changes.

T1.justification: The probabilistic formulation, training loss, coordinate operations and grounding-metric definitions are retained. Neither version introduces new theorems, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations relative to the other.

improvement.justification: The 2,200-example annotation audit and human calibration of the evaluator address important validation gaps in v1's automatically generated dataset and scoring pipeline. Matched inference-format tests and transfer/source-removal analyses also support substantially better-bounded claims and clearer limitations. These gains improve the paper's evidential credibility rather than merely increasing reported performance. Residual problems, especially the conflicting weighted-versus-macro averaging descriptions, limit reproducibility but do not outweigh the added validation and more careful interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VisReason and VisReason-Pro work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds inference-format comparisons, second-backbone experiments, source-removal results, an annotation audit and evaluator calibration.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training experiments, benchmark and grounding results, dataset/zoom ablations, and a blinded human evaluation in Section 5.

results.title: VisReason: A Large-Scale Dataset for Visual Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion redefine the claimed selection contribution as max-sum diversification rather than greedy k-center selection. The central claims of complementary diversity/relevance pruning, a training-free two-stage framework, and approximately 2.6-fold acceleration remain. The introduction now states validation across four LVLM configurations.

C2.justification: The layer-selection interpretation reverses: v1 Appendix C.2 argues that single-layer checks are insufficient and favors interleaved checks; v2 Supplementary Section 3.3 favors 7L/8 and attributes early-pruning failures to interrupted cross-modal alignment. V2 also interprets random-pivot results as enabling encoders without [CLS] tokens and removes v1's explicit limitation concerning pruning-related computational overhead.

D1.justification: V2 Algorithm 1 explicitly documents feature normalization and masking selected indices, clarifying implementation of cosine similarity and candidate exclusion. The supplement specifies the added Qwen and InternVL checkpoints, and pruning defaults are revised. Hardware disclosures and benchmark-processing information remain largely unchanged; no implementation-code access information is added.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same eight image and four video benchmarks and retain the Video Detail Caption qualitative example. MMBench becoming MMBench-EN is a labeling clarification. The additional backbones do not introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds DivPrune to the main image comparisons at both LLaVA-NeXT sizes, the video comparisons, and the efficiency comparison. V1 cites DivPrune but does not evaluate it in these comparisons. Adding this directly relevant diversity-based competitor substantially strengthens the comparator set; the previous methods and their stated exclusions remain.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluation configurations using Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and InternVL2-8B, beyond LLaVA-NeXT-7B/13B. The reported default threshold changes from 0.03 to 0.10, and candidate pruning layers change from L/2, 5L/8, 6L/8, and 7L/8 to 7L/8 alone. Benchmark splits, sample counts, and metrics remain substantially unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 Supplementary Section 3.1 adds a focused ablation comparing [CLS], random, center, and farthest pivot selection at two retention ratios. The threshold sweep replaces 0.01 with 0.15, and the layer sweep removes the five-candidate configuration including L. Existing stage ablations, decoding-attention analyses, and qualitative cases remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability estimates. Both average decoding-attention plots over 100 samples per benchmark. The new random-pivot experiment adds no uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced, and DivPrune and additional-backbone results are added. Table 1 reports LLaVA-NeXT-7B averages changing from 97.3% to 98.2% at 25% retention and 95.1% to 95.0% at 10%; these accompany revised methods/settings, rather than establishing controlled improvements. Table 2 changes ToDRE's video averages from 105.0%/103.3% to 103.1%/100.9%. FasterVLM's 25%-retention VideoMME entry also changes from 36.9 to 33.8.

M1.justification: Section 4.1 and Algorithm 1 replace greedy k-center selection, which minimizes maximum similarity, with max-sum diversification, which minimizes cumulative similarity. V2 also introduces random pivot selection for encoders without a [CLS] token and changes Stage 2 from four candidate pruning layers to a single check at 7L/8. These alter the actual pruning procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, selection-method exposition, and layer-selection discussion undergo substantial rewriting. The title, author/affiliation block, and section terminology change. Lettered appendices preceding the references become a separately numbered supplementary document following the references.

P2.justification: The document changes from predominantly single-column to two-column layout. V1 Figures 1 and 3 are combined into v2 Figure 1, the framework diagram is redrawn, and backbone and pivot-ablation tables are added. Existing supplementary visualizations are enlarged and relocated. A long supplementary proof equation also extends into the neighboring table area.

R1.justification: V2 replaces the Gonzalez k-center citation with Ji et al.'s 'Efficient interactive fuzzy keyword search' citation for max-sum diversification, adds the InternVL 2.0 reference, and explicitly characterizes DivPrune's min-max strategy in the supplement. Most related-work discussion and cited works remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 4 substantively changes the mathematical selection objective from maximum similarity to summed similarity; v2 adds a cumulative-update equation and its distance interpretation. The appendix's orthogonality assumptions, independence lemma, redundancy definitions, and covariance proof are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's empirical support: it directly compares against the closely related DivPrune and tests portability beyond the LLaVA family through Qwen and InternVL evaluations. The pivot ablation further supports the adaptation to different encoders. These substantially strengthen the competitiveness and generality claims. Removing the overhead limitation and introducing unexplained discrepancies between nominally matching 10% results in Tables 1 and 5, such as MME 1464.4 versus 1469.3, weaken reporting but do not outweigh the stronger validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ToDRE. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial revisions and restructuring.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark and efficiency results, including additional backbone evaluations and a new pivot-selection ablation.

before.justification: V1 reports original image/video benchmark evaluations, inference-efficiency measurements, ablations, attention analyses, and qualitative examples.

results.title: ToDRE: Effective Visual Token Pruning via Token Diversity and Task Relevance

C1.justification: The core claims about coordinate-free intrinsic-attention grounding, anchor aggregation and data-efficient fine-tuning remain. v3 adds an explicit claim of scalability through additional desktop-domain training data and extends its headline performance claims to five benchmarks.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the mechanism interpretation: visual-sink tokens are described as functional cross-modal proxies that need not be semantically informative, and anchor-weight similarity supports that explanation. Section 4.5 interprets layer/head contributions and pruning outcomes. The results discussion adds data-scaling interpretations and explicitly qualifies UI-Vision results as in-domain, while the soft-variant tradeoff discussion disappears.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents FlashAttention combined with eager extraction of selected attention rows, a 28×28 patch setting, measured GPU-hours and inference times, and the sources of UI-Vision/MMBench comparator scores. The existing hardware, batch size, learning rate, anchor-token formatting and project access link are retained.

E1.justification: v3 adds desktop-focused GroundCUA training data while retaining the original training mixture for GUI-AIMA-lite. Evaluation expands beyond ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2 and OSWorld-G to UI-Vision's basic, functional and spatial desktop tasks, MMBench-GUI-L2's basic and advanced grounding, and supplementary ScreenSpot-v1 evaluation.

E2.justification: Retained benchmark comparisons gain Qwen3-VL, GroundNext, GTA1, InfiGUI-G1 and GUI-Actor-with-verifier variants. InfiGUI-R1 additionally enters the ScreenSpot-v2 comparison, although it already appeared elsewhere in v1. Standalone GPT-4o is removed from ScreenSpot-Pro, and the new benchmark tables include additional comparators such as Holo2 and Aguvis.

E3.justification: v3 introduces the 509k-instruction training regime and larger-data ablation, verifier, timing and top/bottom-30% head-pruning protocols. The stated second-pass crop changes from 448 to 616 pixels, retaining 2× zoom. Exact counts are inconsistent: 250k versus 200k additional GroundCUA instructions, and 259k versus 254k larger-ablation examples. The unexplained OSWorld-G-Refine table label does not establish a changed test split.

E4.justification: v3 adds controls testing gradient flow through head weights, weighted labels for GUI-Actor, verifier compatibility and head importance through pruning. It also adds runtime analysis and token-frequency evidence, and replaces v1's embedding-versus-attention correlation examples with anchor-versus-query head-weight similarity analysis. Most original 45k ablations and zoom-error counts remain; the soft-weighting ablation is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added experiments continue to report point estimates without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: ScreenSpot-Pro base/zoom scores change from 45.2/58.6 in v1 to 49.8/57.0 for v3-lite and 53.8/61.5 for the expanded model. These are updated results under revised settings, not controlled before-and-after gains. v3 adds UI-Vision 60.0, MMBench-GUI-L2 79.1, and extensive pruning, verifier and timing results. Existing comparator entries also change, including GUI-Actor-3B's ScreenSpot-v2 average from 90.4 to 91.0.

M1.justification: The anchor token, visual-sink selection, head aggregation, patch-label loss and two-step grounding procedure remain. v3 removes the alternative soft KL-based head-weighting variant from v1 Section 3.4 and evaluates an optional GUI-Actor verifier composition in Appendix B. The new efficient-attention discussion documents implementation without establishing that the main algorithm changed.

P1.justification: The introduction and methodological exposition are extensively rewritten. v1's five method subsections become three reorganized subsections, combining preliminaries with anchor aggregation and grouping labeling with training/inference design. Experimental organization, the abstract, conclusion and appendix structure are also revised substantially.

P2.justification: Benchmark tables are expanded and regrouped, with denser layouts and inline citations. v3 adds Tables 3 and 7–10, token-frequency and head-weight figures, and a new similarity visualization replacing v1 Figure 5. The zoom-analysis table replaces accuracy with net-improvement counts and relabels Relax@2 as Relax@3. Pipeline graphics, convergence curves and qualitative grounding examples are retained or relocated.

R1.justification: The central positioning against TAG and GUI-Actor remains largely unchanged. Citations expand to support newer comparators, datasets and implementation, including Qwen3-VL, GroundCUA/GroundNext, FlashAttention, UI-Vision and MMBench-GUI. Samaran et al. replaces the Nguyen et al. attention-supervision citation, and the GUI-ARP reference is removed.

T1.justification: The principal aggregation, similarity, patch-label and loss equations are mathematically retained despite reorganization. v3 removes the alternative distribution-matching definition in v1 Equation 11 and adds a complexity argument reducing attention extraction from O((|V|+|Q|+1)^2) to O((|Q|+1)|V|). No theorem or proof development is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central design and efficiency claims. Larger-data controls give GUI-Actor the same weighted labels, addressing a comparison confound, while stopped-gradient tests, head pruning and measured training/inference costs address questions left largely unresolved by v1's small-data ablations and convergence plots. Broader comparisons and clearer exposition add value. Inconsistent training counts, unexplained score revisions and overbroad state-of-the-art wording remain weaknesses—for example, UI-Vision's 60.0 trails GroundNext-3B's 62.1—but the added validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GUI-AIMA with the same authors and core framework. All pages, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison, despite some internal reporting inconsistencies.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds benchmark results, head-pruning tests, larger-data ablations, verifier experiments and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original GUI-grounding results, component ablations, convergence measurements and zoom-in error analyses in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: GUI-AIMA: Aligning Intrinsic Multimodal Attention with a Context Anchor for GUI Grounding

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution summary, and main conclusion retain the same central contributions: RoboTracer's metric-aware training, the 30M-QA TraceSpatial dataset, and TraceSpatial-Bench. The headline 79.1% aggregate success and 36-percentage-point advantage over Gemini-2.5-Pro are retained. The softened title and additional supporting experiments do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v3 newly emphasizes process RFT over dependence on high-quality geometric inputs, interpreting the revised encoder ablation and noise test accordingly. It adds interpretations concerning annotation scalability, benchmark alignment, lifting alternatives, data-generation utility, and potential navigation use. The conclusion newly acknowledges difficulty with rotation-critical manipulation requiring 6D poses, while retaining the earlier appendix limitations.

D1.justification: v3 explicitly describes 6–12 sparse waypoints, trace correction, motion-planning constraints and smoothness costs, and Code-as-Monitor integration. Appendix A supplies limited setup details for the added controls and fine-tuning experiments. Most existing architecture specifications, hyperparameters, hardware descriptions, processing instructions, and access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds SpatialRGPT-Bench and SAT VQA evaluations, three real-robot tasks involving metric offsets, release height, and obstacle avoidance, and a noisy-depth test scenario. These extend the existing spatial-reasoning and tabletop-manipulation coverage without introducing a substantially different domain. The larger TraceSpatial-Bench sample count is a protocol expansion.

E2.justification: v3 adds Magma and fine-tuned RoboRefer-2B/LEO-7B to TraceSpatial-Bench, learned and oracle lifting baselines in Appendix A, and specialized SpatialRGPT/SAT comparisons. The real-robot comparison replaces OpenVLA with MolmoAct and adds fine-tuned MolmoAct. Additional comparators also appear in the retained 2D referring and tracing experiments.

E3.justification: Appendix A adds independently relabeled 100-sample and expanded 800-sample evaluations alongside the original benchmark. It also reports 8B RFT, lifting controls matched for data/backbone/training schedule, and MolmoAct fine-tuning using 50 successful rollouts. The original benchmark's spatial and collision thresholds remain unchanged; these are additional protocols, not evidence that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds depth-noise robustness, training with annotations regenerated through the 2D pipeline, outdoor-data removal, same-backbone dataset-benefit comparisons, native-versus-lifted 3D controls, and independent-relabeling checks for benchmark alignment. These substantially broaden the questions tested beyond v1's data-recipe, encoder, scale-supervision, and coordinate ablations.

E5.justification: Appendix A newly specifies 20 trials per additional real-robot task, providing explicit repeated-evaluation counts. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or variation across training seeds. This disclosure does not establish an increase in repetitions for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include 8B-RFT success of 54% on the original benchmark and 57.125% on the 800-sample relabeled benchmark, plus three new robot-task scores of 55%, 50%, and 35%. Existing entries also change: Qwen3-VL-4B/8B overall success changes from 6/8% to 4/6%, RGB-intrinsics-depth SFT from 39% to 38%, and no-encoder RFT from 22% to 36% (v1 Tables 4/8; v3 Tables 5/9). The principal RGB-RFT result remains 39%.

M1.justification: The RoboTracer architecture, coordinate representation, SFT loss, and process-reward RFT remain unchanged. Section 4.5 adds a downstream adaptation: fine-tuning MolmoAct using successful RoboTracer-guided episodes and generated traces as auxiliary supervision. Expanded descriptions of sparse waypoints and planning do not establish a redesign of RoboTracer.

P1.justification: v3 retitles the paper, updates author information, expands the representation-advantages and experimental discussions, inserts supplementary Section A, simplifies appendix heading levels, and moves references after the appendices. Most original prose and the main narrative sequence remain intact; the much larger page count primarily reflects formatting.

P2.justification: The document changes comprehensively from two-column to single-column layout, resizing and relocating figures and tables throughout. v1 Table 1 is split into v3 Tables 1–2, comparison tables gain rows or columns, and new supplementary Tables 10–12 display added evidence. The existing figure sequence and appendix demonstrations are largely retained rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: Related work adds references including Magma, Think3D, and RoboBrain 2.5, while dropping works including G2 VLM and SpatialReasoner. New discussion distinguishes RoboTracer from RoboRefer by task, metric features, and temporal modeling, and explains its relationship to dense-action VLAs. The underlying positioning around metric-grounded 3D tracing remains stable.

T1.justification: The mathematical coordinate representation, scale-regression objective, reward definitions, planning cost, and evaluation definitions are retained. The added representation advantages and applicability discussion are conceptual or empirical; no new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation appears.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's small in-house benchmark and limited controlled alternatives. Independent relabeling, the 800-sample evaluation, matched lifting/data controls, and fine-tuned 3D baselines address important weaknesses in assessing generalization and attributing benefits. Additional robot tasks and the rotation-critical limitation improve applicability assessment. Unexplained score revisions and retained prose saying RFT is limited to 2B despite new 8B results leave consistency and reproducibility gaps, but do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RoboTracer, TraceSpatial, and TraceSpatial-Bench. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite the changed title and layout.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark relabeling and expansion, model-scaling experiments, controlled comparisons, and additional robot evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, ablations, simulation results, and UR5/G1 robot experiments, including supplementary results.

results.title: Towards Spatial Trace with Reasoning in Vision-Language Models for Robotics

C1.justification: The contribution shifts from a comprehensive MCQ benchmark to a rationale-sensitive, open-ended benchmark. v3's abstract adds the claim that thinking models induce more bias in reasoning chains, while its conclusion adds claims about synthetic-image distribution shifts and advantages over multiple-choice evaluation. These materially expand and redefine the central claims.

C2.justification: v1 treats agreement between MCQ answers and reasoning as evidence of benchmark robustness. v3 instead argues that constrained choices can inflate scores, interprets ambiguity handling as a principal failure mechanism, and attributes additional failures to reasoning chains and synthetic visual cues. Appendix A newly identifies missing intersectional evaluation and explicitly excludes bias mitigation; the earlier warning about internet-image bias remains.

D1.justification: v1 provides model architectures and prompt templates but relatively limited execution settings. v3 adds detailed scoring rubrics, filtering prompts and thresholds, hardware/software information, and inference settings including temperature 0, 1,024 maximum tokens, resolution 512, batch size 256, and bfloat16. Synthetic-generation settings are also documented. Newly disclosed settings do not, by themselves, establish changes to earlier experiments.

E1.justification: The nine broad domains remain, but represented subgroups change from 60 to 50. Disability coverage, for example, contracts from eight groups including autism and mental illness to physical disability and blindness (v1 Figure A.2; v3 Figure A.1). v3 also evaluates disambiguated contexts and synthetic-image counterparts, adding materially different evidence conditions and visual environments.

E2.justification: The main comparison expands from nine to 19 models. Additions include InternVL3, Gemma-3, Aya-Vision, Qwen2.5 variants, Phi-4, and three thinking models; Gemini-1.5-Flash is replaced by Gemini-2.0-Flash and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite. Scaling comparisons also switch to InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL and omit the earlier LLaVA scaling comparison.

E3.justification: v1 primarily evaluates 7,500 MCQs using answer correctness and bias rates. v3 reports 14,144 question–image pairs over 4,497 real images, primarily using open-ended rationales and answers scored by GPT-4.1-mini on five ordinal criteria, with harmonic-mean summaries. New disambiguated controls use spatial references and accuracy/grounding criteria; synthetic experiments compare matched real-image subsets. These are substantial replacements and additions to evaluation design.

E4.justification: Blind-versus-vision, base-LLM, and scaling analyses already exist in v1 and are revised in v3. v3 adds disambiguated controls, real-versus-synthetic sensitivity tests, criterion-level error analyses, thinking-model case studies, and human/alternative-judge validation. Conversely, v1's option/image-shuffling tests and MCQ–reasoning correlation analysis are not retained as corresponding analyses.

E5.justification: Statistical validation shifts from v1's shuffle standard deviations and MCQ–reasoning correlation to human–judge agreement statistics in v3. Appendix V and Table A.5 introduce observed agreement and Cohen's kappa, including quadratic weighting, for 1,000 sampled responses; overall agreement is 0.9100 and weighted kappa 0.8128. This does not establish any increase in repeated or seeded benchmark runs.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and expanded. In v1 Table 3, GPT-4o leads with 10.79% bias, and InternVL2-8B is the best listed open model at 62.00%. In v3 Table 3, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite leads at 80.89%, and Phi-4-MM leads the listed open models at 74.30%. These use different data and scoring, so they are not direct performance gains. Disambiguated, synthetic-image, and judge-validation results are newly reported.

M1.justification: The benchmark-construction procedure changes substantially. v1 uses Qwen-2.5 querying/anonymization, CLIP filtering, and a dual-query stitching procedure. v3 describes GPT-4o-mini querying/anonymization, OCR filtering, agreement among three semantic-alignment models, synthetic/leakage screening, and face blurring (Section 3.1; Appendices L–O). These are procedural changes, beyond renaming or additional documentation.

P1.justification: Beyond the benchmark/title rename, the abstract, introduction, construction description, evaluation narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v3 introduces a dedicated discussion subsection and reorganizes the appendix around controls, scoring criteria, filtering, computation, and validation. Ethical limitations and social impact move from the main text into the supplement.

P2.justification: v3 moves the taxonomy graphic to the opening page, redraws the construction pipeline, and removes the separate paired-image pipeline figure. Comparison tables are expanded, example panels are redesigned, and new radar plots, a synthetic–real heatmap, agreement tables, and structured prompt boxes substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The comparative positioning changes substantively: v1 promotes MCQs as easier to evaluate than open-ended benchmarks, whereas v3 emphasizes open-ended reasoning and real multi-actor scenes over MCQ and synthetic alternatives. v3 adds VLBiasBench to the benchmark comparison and cites newer reasoning models and synthetic–authentic domain-gap research. Much of the underlying related-work survey remains.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations. v3's ordinal scoring rubrics, harmonic-mean reporting, and agreement statistics change empirical evaluation rather than introduce a theoretical contribution.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens measurement validation and reproducibility: disambiguated controls address whether failures reflect missing evidence, human and alternative-judge comparisons assess evaluator reliability, and detailed rubrics/settings make the procedure more inspectable (Appendices E, Q, and V). These address important weaknesses of v1's primarily MCQ-based validation. Disability coverage narrows, and some interpretations remain overstated, particularly causal claims about thinking from unmatched model comparisons. Nevertheless, the added controls and documented validation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BBQ-derived visual stereotype benchmark, renamed from SB-Bench to BBQ-V. Their main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison. The redesigned dataset and scoring protocol prevent direct comparison of many performance values, but do not limit document comparability.

after.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of 19 LMMs, disambiguated and synthetic-image experiments, human–judge agreement, and comparisons between automated judges.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of nine LMMs, model-scaling experiments, modality comparisons, and option/image-shuffling analyses in the main text and appendices.

results.title: BBQ-V: Benchmarking Visual Stereotype Bias in Large Multimodal Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same lightweight construction, modality-preserving fusion, and graph-retrieval contributions. The four-task state-of-the-art claim and average 43.3× speedup and 23.9× cost reduction are unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of component complementarity, parameter robustness, scalability, and coarse-context support when grounding is imperfect. Appendix B also introduces an explicit failure mechanism: ambiguous visual references weaken entity grounding and propagation, allowing plausible but factually incorrect evidence to dominate. This substantially expands the earlier success-focused discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds a public source-code availability statement and repository address in the abstract, plus parameter ranges and hardware conditions for the new analyses. Existing implementation descriptions, preprocessing instructions, prompts, and default hyperparameters remain unchanged; repository availability itself is not verified by the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate E-VQA, InfoSeek, ScienceQA, and CrisisMMD across the same four tasks. The added analyses vary corpus sizes and configurations within existing coverage; the failure examples remain within the existing VQA scope.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in all corresponding benchmark tables, the efficiency figure, and retained case studies. The new failure cases use the existing VaLiK, MMGraphRAG, and Qwen3.5-27B comparators; added citations do not introduce evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends the evaluation design with component-removal controls, E-VQA (5k) retrieval-parameter sweeps, and construction-time measurements from 1k to 100k documents with a doubled-GPU condition (Tables 1, 6, and 8–11). These are additional protocols; the original splits, metrics, backbone configurations, prompts, and default hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: v1 has successful case studies but no component ablations or parameter sensitivity tests. v2 adds ablations of hierarchy, node fusion, and propagation across multiple tasks, four sensitivity analyses, construction scalability tests, and two failure cases examining ambiguous visual references.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new analyses continue to report point estimates.

E6.justification: v1 Tables 1–4 exactly match v2 Tables 2–5 in reported scores. Substantial new results include E-VQA (5k) R@1 of 57.8 versus 25.5 without propagation, sensitivity measurements, failure outcomes, and 100k construction times of 63.4 hours versus 32.8 with doubled GPUs. These are added results, not improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The textual parsing, entity-driven visual grounding, multimodal node fusion, hierarchical graph, and PageRank retrieval procedures remain unchanged. Section 3 and Appendix A.1 retain the same algorithm and extraction rules; the new ablations evaluate existing components.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites introduction, related-work, and case-study passages, adds an ablation subsection and acknowledgements, and expands appendix discussion. The overall narrative order is retained, with the method and conclusion largely unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds six tables covering scalability, ablations, and sensitivity, plus Figure 8 showing two failures. Existing displays are retained with renumbering, relocation, scaling, and limited caption edits. The document also changes from compact pages to letter-size pages with substantially wider margins.

R1.justification: Eight cited works are added, including Simple is Effective, Think-on-Graph 2.0, and Subgraph Retrieval Enhanced Model. Section 2 expands discussion of lightweight triple scoring and decoupled subgraph retrieval while retaining the same overall positioning. Publication and bibliographic updates to existing references are not new works.

T1.justification: The graph definitions, incidence matrices, aggregation and fusion equations, PageRank update, and appendix relation-extraction formulations are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's important lack of direct validation of its three central components through Table 6, while sensitivity tests and explicit failure cases strengthen robustness assessment and clarify applicability limits. These additions substantially improve empirical support without changing the retained benchmark results. Uncertainty reporting remains absent, and Table 1's 5k construction time of 2.9 hours is not reconciled with Figure 3's 4.4 hours, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the stronger diagnostic evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MG2-RAG research. All 32 pages of v1 and 34 pages of v2, including equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–B, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds scalability measurements, component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity results, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval, VQA, reasoning, classification, and graph-construction efficiency results, with qualitative examples in the main text and appendix.

results.title: MG2-RAG: Multi-Granularity Graph for Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation

C1.justification: The central claims of efficient compression, progressive training, and strong retrieval performance remain. The abstract and conclusion replace memory-footprint emphasis with training-time reduction, and the conclusion drops v1's stronger assertion that performance is limited by training quality rather than capacity.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations explaining pooling's loss of fine detail and convolution's adaptation failure, motivates 64 tokens through an explicit accuracy/computation tradeoff, and argues robustness to judge choice. These extend the retained compression-and-training explanation without fundamentally changing it.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the PyTorch interpolation function, pixel-unshuffle factor 2, and intermediate token-grid sizes. It newly discloses the stage-1 public/in-house split of 26.2M/5.8M and the LoRA ablation's global batch size. Most hardware, hyperparameters, and prompt templates were already documented and are relocated.

E1.justification: v2 adds MME evaluation of 14 multimodal-understanding subtasks and concurrent-request serving scenarios in Appendices B.2 and B.5. The training corpora and principal natural-image, visual-document, and cross-modal retrieval benchmarks are retained.

E2.justification: v2 Table S1 newly compares bilinear interpolation against Conv2d and AdaptiveAvgPool2d, while Table 6 adds InternVL3-8B as an alternative judge. Comparator membership in the principal retrieval benchmark tables remains unchanged.

E3.justification: The training-efficiency comparison changes from unequal global batches in v1 Table 9—6,144 for vanilla and 3,456 for compressed—to 3,456 for both in v2. New protocols include token-budget sweeps, MME accuracy evaluation, and vLLM latency/throughput testing at 5, 10, and 20 concurrent requests. The reported judge size also changes from Qwen3-VL-7B to 8B; this alone does not establish rerunning.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands tests of design choices: stage-omission controls, judge-model robustness, alternative compression operators, and token-budget effects on retrieval and multimodal understanding. It also revises the training-efficiency control. The LoRA analysis is retained as Table S3, and v1's hard-negative analysis is redisplayed in Figure 4 rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new judge-agreement percentage is an evaluation result, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Reported 8B MMEB embedder/E+R totals change from 71.8/72.8 to 71.9/72.9, and VisDoc totals from 75.0/75.8 to 74.9/75.5; several cross-modal scores also change. v2 adds extensive compression, MME, token-budget, judge-agreement, and serving results. Revised training-duration results use changed batch controls and should not be interpreted as same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The proposed bilinear compression, three-stage training, judge-based curation, and jointly trained reranker remain unchanged. Pixel unshuffle, described explicitly in v2, already appears in v1 Figure 2. Added compression alternatives are experimental comparisons, not replacements for the proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 extensively reorganizes existing material: methodology and implementation prose are condensed, related work gains thematic subdivisions, and templates, training-data descriptions, implementation settings, and LoRA analysis move into organized appendices. Numerous passages are edited, and author/header information changes.

P2.justification: The document adopts substantially different typography and page geometry. v2 adds token-sensitivity and compression-workflow figures, converts the hard-negative table into a plot, restructures the stage-ablation table, relocates existing displays, and splits the instruction tables across three parts.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated visual-token-compression discussion covering feature transformation, merging, pruning, and learned queries, citing works including DivPrune, LLaVA-PruMerge, and VisionZip. It explicitly positions the contribution against compression research focused on generation, substantially expanding v1's embedding-centered positioning.

T1.justification: v2 introduces the explicit attention-computation reduction definition r = 1 - (v/256)^2 in Section 5.4 and Appendix B.4; v1 only states the general quadratic-cost argument. Existing embedding normalization and training losses remain equivalent, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central design choices. Matching batch sizes addresses a confound in v1's training-efficiency comparison, while token-budget, compression-operator, restoration, and judge tests address previously untested assumptions. Concurrent vLLM measurements also strengthen deployment relevance. Although small score revisions remain unexplained and uncertainty reporting is still absent, the improved controls and targeted validation provide a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Magic-MM-Embedding and retain the same central framework and retrieval experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original retrieval experiments and reports additional compression, token-budget, judge, multimodal-understanding, and concurrent-serving results.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval scores, inference measurements, and training, hard-negative, and LoRA ablations in Tables 3–10.

results.title: Magic-MM-Embedding: Towards Visual-Token-Efficient Universal Multimodal Embedding with MLLMs

C1.justification: The central noise-reduction and object-level RAG contributions remain. V2 expands the headline claims from improved Replica captioning to state-of-the-art real-world object and relationship prediction, resilience to geometric corruption and readiness for robotic deployment. Its conclusion additionally claims hallucination-free graphs, substantially strengthening the claimed reliability.

C2.justification: V2 attributes relationship gains to reduced propagation of node-caption errors and explains noise tolerance through aggregated geometry, intact crop images and reliable contextual anchors. It discusses ghosting under poor localization and explicitly characterizes the system as offline, proposing future integration as a low-frequency semantic backend. These extend v1's interpretations of component effectiveness and mapping efficiency.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies 64 candidate viewpoints, robot sensors and computing hardware, the odometry/data-collection workflow and approximately $0.50 GPT-4o cost per FunGraph3D scene. Conversely, the supplied v2 omits v1's mapping pseudocode, voxel examples, exact CLIP pretraining checkpoint and code/evaluation-script release statement. Further prompts and profiling are deferred to unavailable supplementary material.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates Replica. V2 retains Replica evaluation and adds SceneFun3D, FunGraph3D, physical indoor robot observations and pose-corrupted reconstruction scenarios. This substantially broadens the represented environments and sensor conditions.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds evaluated comparisons against Open3DSG, including its fused-node variant, and OpenFunGraph alongside ConceptGraphs and ConceptGraphs-Detector. V1's separate segmentation comparison disappears, removing its comparisons with MaskCLIP, Mask2former plus Global CLIP features, ConceptFusion variants, OpenMask3D and Clio-batch.

E3.justification: V2 introduces evaluation on 20 SceneFun3D and 24 FunGraph3D scenes, object and predicate Recall@K, ground-truth filtering and BERT-based predicate matching. It adds Gaussian pose perturbations with translation standard deviation 0.02 m and rotation standard deviation 1 degree. V1 specifies GPT-4-0613/GPT-4o-mini for its main experiments; v2 evaluates GPT-4o and LLaVA-v1.5-7b variants. The unchanged Replica scores do not establish that those experiments were rerun under the newer configurations.

E4.justification: V2 adds pose-noise stress tests and deployment analysis addressing localization drift, reconstruction ghosting and robustness. The four original component ablations remain, with appendix heatmaps incorporated into Figure 3. V1's detailed LLaVA crop-versus-re-shot case study is absent from the supplied v2.

E5.justification: V2 newly reports an inter-annotator reliability check: three annotators, 100 randomly sampled units and Fleiss' kappa of 0.76, with majority voting for disagreements. V1 provides no corresponding agreement statistic. Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or seed-based variability.

E6.justification: V2 adds real-world benchmark and noisy-pose scores in Table 1 and qualitative deployment findings; these concern new settings. V1 Table 1's Replica human-evaluation values remain unchanged in v2 Table 2, while v1's segmentation Table 2 is absent. Overall ablation scores are unchanged, but office0 frequency-weighted IoU is swapped between the full pipeline and w/o Concat: 48.08/30.10 in v1 Figure 5 becomes 30.10/48.08 in v2 Figure 3(f).

M1.justification: The dynamic mapping, re-shot verification, caption clustering, nearest-object RAG and eight-relation pipeline remain. However, v1 Equation 3 explicitly shifts and scales semantic similarity as (cosine + 1)/2, whereas v2 Section 3.1 describes it simply as cosine similarity. The compressed specification does not establish whether the fusion rule changed or its explanation was shortened.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten around a diagnose-then-rectify and active-photographer framing. Mapping subsections are condensed, experiments are reorganized, and some appendix material moves into the main text. V1's separate ethics, reproducibility and appendix sections are absent from the supplied v2.

P2.justification: V2 substantially redraws Figure 1, introduces a detailed viewpoint-scoring diagram and a robot-deployment figure, and merges v1 Figures 3 and 5 into a six-panel ablation figure. The Replica table gains grouped colored headers, and a new real-world comparison table replaces the separate segmentation display. The document format and figure arrangement also change throughout.

R1.justification: V2 replaces the dedicated runtime-related-work discussion with viewpoint-aware semantic reasoning. It positions RAG-3DSG against passive frame selection in BBQ, MomaGraph and DAAAM, and connects its active verification framing to Think3D and Chain-of-View. Added functional and dynamic scene-graph literature substantially updates the research positioning.

T1.justification: V2 retains equivalent voxel-size and view-scoring formulas, including renamed scoring weights. It omits v1's explicit dynamic matching-threshold formula, cluster-score averaging definition and final graph formalization from Sections 3.1.3, 3.2.2 and 3.4. This reduces formal specification; neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's Replica-only evidence through real-world benchmark comparisons, controlled pose perturbations and physical deployment. The annotator-agreement check also improves support for the retained human evaluation. Reduced mathematical and implementation detail, unavailable supplementary material and hallucination-free wording unsupported by the retained 0.82 node and 0.91 edge precision are drawbacks. Nevertheless, the added evidence materially addresses the earlier version's limited support for real-world applicability and robustness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RAG-3DSG and have readable text, equations, tables and figures. V1 includes Appendix A; v2 ends with references and defers parameter analyses, prompts and runtime profiling to Supplementary Material absent from the supplied PDF. The available content supports comparison, but those deferred materials cannot be assessed.

after.justification: V2 retains original Replica results and reports SceneFun3D/FunGraph3D comparisons, pose-noise experiments, annotator agreement and a physical robot deployment.

before.justification: V1 reports original Replica human evaluations, semantic-segmentation and runtime results, component ablations, and an appendix case study.

results.title: RAG-3DSG: Enhancing 3D Scene Graphs with Re-Shot Guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation

C1.justification: The introduction changes 'nearly eliminating' duplicate predictions and hallucinations to 'substantially suppressing' them, and the conclusion replaces 'hallucination-free' with 'less hallucinated'. These meaningfully qualify reliability claims while preserving the central contributions, novelty positioning and state-of-the-art claims.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands explanations of failure conditions and design tradeoffs: misleading bright/transparent re-shots, isolated-render degradation, contextual dilution from additional retrieval, overcorrection without uncertainty guidance, and sparsity-versus-efficiency effects. Section 3.3 also explains the ambiguity-reduction rationale for the retained eight-category relationship taxonomy.

D1.justification: v3 supplies material deferred but absent from the supplied v2: fusion pseudocode, representative prompt templates, factory calibration, 50 ms synchronization, pose interpolation and offline server processing details. It specifies KMeans with K=3 and consensus-score averaging, and reports approximately 0.78 s/iteration for reasoning and 0.26 s/object for rendering. Some few-shot demonstrations remain omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions use SceneFun3D, FunGraph3D, eight Replica scenes and the indoor robotic deployment. v3 adds analyses and quantitative scoring within this retained coverage. Point-density manipulations change preprocessing and testing procedures without establishing a new dataset, population or task.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Passive VLM with GPT-4o and GPT-5.2, Re-shot VLM with GPT-4o, and Ours Node + CG Edge as evaluated comparators. Appendix A.4 additionally compares against ConceptGraphs in the existing robot deployment. These substantially expand comparative controls while retaining the original benchmark baselines.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce segmentation-and-merging-only CLIP evaluation, voxel-size and merging-threshold sweeps, single-factor viewpoint scoring, retrieval counts of 1/3/5, unguided refinement and point-density perturbations. Appendix A.4 applies randomized three-expert scoring to robot data. The original benchmark splits, metrics, default hyperparameters and injected pose-noise levels remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Figure 3 ablations, v3 tests passive model scaling, isolated re-shots and node-versus-edge contributions in Table 1. Appendices A.2–A.5 add hyperparameter sensitivity, retrieval and uncertainty-guidance ablations, density robustness and concrete failure/recovery cases, substantially broadening diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report three annotators, Fleiss' kappa of 0.76 on 100 sampled units and majority-vote resolution. v3 adds no repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance-testing procedures; the additional robot evaluation reuses the existing annotation practice.

E6.justification: Existing scores in Tables 1–2 and Figure 3 are retained, but substantial results are added. Examples include isolated Re-shot VLM reaching 59.4% SceneFun3D object R@3, Table 3 reporting mF1 of 28.26/27.66 for top-3/top-5 retrieval versus 30.78 for top-1, and robot node precision of 83.8% versus ConceptGraphs' 65.6%. Further additions include parameter sweeps, density effects and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: The overall pipeline is retained, but new Algorithm 1 scales the embedding dot product by 1/2 and adds 1/2, whereas Section 3.1 in both versions describes semantic similarity as cosine similarity. Because the pseudocode is presented as documenting the existing mapper, the PDFs do not resolve whether this represents a procedure change or a documentation inconsistency. Newly specified clustering and prompts alone do not establish a method change.

P1.justification: v3 substantially expands the explanatory structure through a seven-part appendix containing worked examples, protocol-analysis-conclusion discussions, deployment explanations and annotated prompt templates. The main section order remains stable, with localized rewrites of consensus generation, relationship generation and robustness discussion, plus a new mechanism-analysis paragraph and acknowledgements.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains an Analysis block with four comparator rows. v3 adds Figures 5–11, Tables 3–4, Algorithm 1 and multiple boxed prompt templates, substantially expanding visual presentation. Existing principal displays are retained with relocation, running-header changes and small label corrections.

R1.justification: v3 adds PSG-Nav to the introductory navigation citations. The broader related-work discussion and passive-versus-active positioning remain stable. Consolidating the duplicated CLIP reference does not remove a distinct cited work.

T1.justification: The mathematical framework and main Equations 1–3 are retained, and Appendix Equation 4 repeats the voxel-scaling rule. No new theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs or derivations appear; the added pseudocode principally documents implementation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v2's missing supplementary documentation and limited diagnostic support. Explicit implementation information, targeted controls, failure analyses and quantitative robot comparison make the method more reproducible and its evidence more assessable; qualifying the hallucination claims also improves accuracy. Statistical uncertainty remains unreported, some prompt examples are omitted, and the new fusion pseudocode contains a score-normalization ambiguity, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in documentation and validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same RAG-3DSG work, with matching methods and experiments. The supplied v2 ends after its references; v3 includes Appendix A.1–A.7. Text, equations, tables and rendered figures support comparison without unresolved reading gaps.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds mechanism comparisons, hyperparameter and density experiments, failure cases and quantitative robot evaluation.

before.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, human evaluations, component ablations, pose-noise experiments and robotic deployment outcomes in Section 4.

results.title: RAG-3DSG: Enhancing 3D Scene Graphs with Re-Shot Guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation

C1.justification: V1 presents identifying centroid prediction as a key counting component and constructing an improved baseline as central contributions. V2 drops that emphasis and foregrounds C-REX as a plug-in applicable to any REC architecture, demonstrated on three architectures. Its headline improvement claims change from over 22% MAE and 10% RMSE to up to 28% and 24.5% under the revised comparisons.

C2.justification: V2 introduces discussion of negative-token scarcity in extremely dense scenes and potential scaling with larger backbones. It interprets the joint-loss and Molmo experiments as support for specialized visual supervision, explicitly qualifies paraphrase robustness for CAD-GD, and illustrates accurate-looking counts that still select incorrect instances in Figure 8. V1's top-N label-noise justification and centroid-centered explanations are removed.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents 20/30-epoch training schedules, learning-rate decay, checkpoint/retraining provenance, and CAD-GD density-map construction. It omits v1's explicit AdamW optimizer, weight decay of 1e-4, and loss weights of 1, 5, and 0.005. The direct code-repository link becomes a project-page link. These are documentation and access-instruction changes; the PDFs do not establish changes to omitted parameters or actual resource availability.

E1.justification: REC-8K and FSC-147 remain, but v2 removes the CARPK drone/parking-lot evaluation, eliminating v1's separate cross-dataset transfer test. V2 adds evaluation on paraphrased REC-8K expressions, introducing a linguistic-variation scenario.

E2.justification: V2 adds CAD-GD comparisons, including its density-guided inference variant, and Molmo2-4B. The FSC-147 comparison removes exemplar-based methods including FamNet, BMNet+, CounTR, and CACViT. Earlier REC comparators such as ZSC, TFOC, CounTX, and CountGD remain in supplementary Tables 6–7; their relocation is not removal.

E3.justification: Reported detection thresholds change from 0.30/0.36 to 0.25/0.35 for CLS/other tokens. V2 adds Swin-B configurations alongside Swin-T, reports precision and recall separately, evaluates density-guided CAD-GD inference, and specifies zero-shot and two-shot Molmo protocols. The count-range analysis also merges the three lowest bins into 0–20. These are substantive protocol changes, beyond newly disclosed training details.

E4.justification: V2 adds image-text versus image-only versus joint-loss ablations and paraphrase robustness testing. Its selection ablation adds bipartite matching and removes the N + 2log2(N) alternative. Count-range and qualitative analyses expand to paired comparisons across three architectures, while v1's attribute-wise MAE analysis and centroid-baseline component ablation disappear. The positive-anchor loss ablation is retained in Table 4b.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The sample counts accompanying count-range plots describe evaluation examples, not repeated runs.

E6.justification: V1's REC MAE/RMSE of 5.06/17.53 survives as the top-N ablation in v2 Table 4a. New matching-based GroundingDINO+C-REX results are 4.38/17.93 with Swin-T and 4.20/16.76 with Swin-B. V2 adds extensive architecture, paraphrase, and Molmo results while removing CARPK and attribute-level scores. Findings include CAD-GD paraphrase MAE worsening from 6.85 to 8.02 with C-REX. Changed methods and protocols preclude treating cross-version scores as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: V1 selects positive tokens by cosine similarity to the class-masked referring expression, taking the top N tokens. V2 instead uses bipartite matching between predicted locations and ground-truth points, changing the contrastive labeling procedure and supervision. It also integrates C-REX into GroundingREC and CAD-GD by replacing their image-text losses while retaining their other objectives. The positive-anchor contrastive loss itself remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around embedding-space choice and architectural portability. The baseline-centered method subsection disappears, remaining method explanations are reordered and expanded, and the supplementary narrative is reorganized. This is substantial editorial restructuring beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. The original pipeline figure is replaced by two conceptual comparisons, tables are rebuilt around paired baseline/C-REX configurations and backbones, and qualitative grids are extensively revised. The earlier REC comparison is split and moved to supplementary tables; the count-range plot is regrouped and the attribute-wise chart removed.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands research positioning: CAD-GD becomes an important REC predecessor, counting VQA is distinguished from localized REC, intra-image contrastive learning is related to person re-identification, and VLM/tool-based counting is discussed. These additions introduce substantive comparisons and citations beyond v1's focus on GroundingREC and detection-versus-density counting.

T1.justification: The positive-set definition changes from the cosine-similarity arg-top-N construction in v1 Equations 2–3 to location-based bipartite matching in v2 Section 3. The supervised and modified contrastive-loss formulas otherwise remain algebraically unchanged. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central embedding-space and portability claims through three-architecture comparisons and direct image-text/image-only/joint-loss ablations, addressing important gaps in v1. Paraphrase and expanded failure analyses also clarify applicability. These gains outweigh the removed CARPK and attribute analyses and reduced hyperparameter disclosure. Some conclusions still overgeneralize: Table 4a shows worse test RMSE for matching than top-N selection, and Table 2 shows GroundingREC test MAE worsening from 10.12 to 12.46 with C-REX.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe C-REX for referring expression counting, despite the changed title and substantial revision. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary materials are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments across three architectures on REC-8K and FSC-147, plus contrastive-loss ablations, paraphrase robustness tests, and Molmo evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original C-REX and baseline experiments on REC-8K, FSC-147, and CARPK, including quantitative results, ablations, and qualitative examples.

results.title: What is the Right Embedding Space for Contrastive Learning in Referring Expression Counting?

C1.justification: Despite the broader title and shortened abstract, the main claims remain prompt-space conditioning without external prompts, asymmetric background suppression, strong COD performance with 21.26M trainable parameters and transfer to medical segmentation. The SOD evaluation supplies additional evidence for the existing generalization claim.

C2.justification: Appendices E–H substantially expand interpretation of conditioning pathways, logit formats and computational overhead. The brief existing over-suppression limitation becomes a detailed account of truncation, topological fracture and missing instances. The appendix also limits the evidence to foreground-background segmentation and identifies broader semantic and complex multi-instance segmentation as future work.

D1.justification: v2 adds reproducibility details for the appendix controls, including the approximately 34K-parameter bypass projection, zero dense embeddings, binarization threshold and logit multipliers. It also documents wall-clock versus CUDA-event timing procedures. The main architecture specifications, training hyperparameters, hardware and LoRA settings are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix A adds standard RGB salient object detection, training on DUTS-TR and evaluating on DUTS-TE, DUT-OMRON, HKU-IS, ECSSD and PASCAL-S. This extends coverage beyond the retained COD and medical polyp tasks.

E2.justification: Table 5 introduces a substantial SOD comparator set, including F3Net, GateNet-X, Samba, VSCode-S, SAM2-UNet and SAM2-LPNet, alongside retained SAM adaptations. Available competitor scores are quoted from their papers. Tables 1 and 4 retain their comparator membership; Figure 6 additionally includes MedSAM in the polyp qualitative comparison.

E3.justification: The added SOD evaluation uses maximum F-measure and maximum E-measure and includes published competitor results. Appendix E introduces controls sharing decoder architecture, initialization and training recipe, with specified prompt-input transformations. Appendix F adds synchronized CUDA-event profiling. The existing COD and polyp training protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component and design ablations, Table 6 reports controlled null-prompt and encoder-bypass comparisons and explicit sigmoid, binarization and logit-scaling analyses. Tables 7 and Figures 5–8 add runtime decomposition, qualitative case studies and internal visualizations of failure cases.

E5.justification: Table 7(b) newly reports timing variability and averaging over 200 runs after 50 warm-up iterations. Both versions already report three-seed averaging and COD10K MAE of 0.017 ± 0.001; no increase in accuracy-evaluation run counts is documented.

E6.justification: Table 3 changes CAMO MAE for Minimal-SPG direct output from 0.028 to 0.058 and Minimal-SPG + PromptSpace from 0.019 to 0.049, without explaining the revisions. Tables 1, 2 and 4 retain their numerical results. Tables 5–7 add SOD scores, conditioning/logit results and component timings, while Figures 5–8 add qualitative outcomes.

M1.justification: The SPG, frozen prompt encoder, PSG, residual anchoring, propagated mask tokens, decoder, LoRA adaptation and training losses remain unchanged. Appendix A explicitly uses the same architecture for SOD; the new ablation variants do not revise the proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title, condenses the abstract, adds keywords, replaces placeholder running headers and clarifies Table 3 terminology. It appends a claim-and-evidence roadmap and sections A–H, while retaining nearly all main-text prose and section ordering.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–7 and Figures 5–8, providing new benchmark, ablation, runtime and qualitative displays. Figures 1–4 are retained. Table 3 moves below its discussion and receives revised labels and notes; the document also gains a boxed abstract and wider page margins.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially broadens the comparison literature to SOD specialists and additional SAM adaptations. Nineteen works are added, covering the new methods and benchmark sources, increasing the bibliography from 38 to 57 entries. Section 2's original positioning relative to feature adaptation and automatic prompting remains intact.

T1.justification: The method equations, mathematical definitions and loss formulation are retained. The appendix adds empirical analyses and interpretive discussion, without new theorems, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: The fixed-decoder controls and quantified logit-format analyses in Table 6 substantially strengthen evidence attributing gains to prompt conditioning. The SOD evaluation and explicit failure visualizations also better substantiate generalization and define its limits beyond v1's brief limitations discussion. Quoted SOD baselines limit comparison fairness, and the retained speed claim requires caution given the higher synchronized timings in Table 7, but the added controlled evidence and failure analysis provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IP-SAM research. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 has no appendix; v2 adds readable Appendices A–H.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds IP-SAM results on salient object detection, conditioning ablations, runtime measurements and qualitative failure analysis. Quoted competitor scores in Table 5 are distinguished from the authors' results.

before.justification: v1 reports original COD experiments, component and design ablations, and medical polyp segmentation results in Tables 1–4.

results.title: IP-SAM: Rethinking Prompt-Conditioned Segmentation for Prompt-Absent Deployment

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about unified scene graphs, OP3DSG, UniGraph3D, performance, and robotic applicability. The supplement adds supporting evidence without redefining those core contributions.

C2.justification: The supplement substantially extends interpretation through arguments about generalization beyond the unified benchmark, dependence on dataset merging, and specific occlusion/reflection/misclassification failure mechanisms. It also qualifies memory measurements as detection-stage only. Section A.3 overstates uniform superiority: Table 9 gives SceneFun3D spatial R@3 of 61.5 for OP3DSG versus 62.1 for OpenFunGraph++.

They also document the 11 canonical relation labels and nine affordance categories. These are disclosures about existing work, rather than demonstrated setting changes.

The source-dataset breakdowns reuse data already represented in UniGraph3D.

E2.justification: The retained UniGraph3D comparisons contain the same ConceptGraph, FunGraph, OpenFunGraph, and KeySG variants. The added supplementary comparisons use subsets of existing ConceptGraph/OpenFunGraph variants; no new comparison method or replacement in a corresponding retained experiment is established.

E3.justification: Section A.1 adds an efficiency evaluation using detection-stage peak GPU memory and graph-construction VLM/LLM call counts. Existing retrieval, localization, and ablation protocols remain unchanged, and Section A.3 explicitly preserves detector and LLM settings for the source-dataset evaluations.

E4.justification: The original ablations and localization sensitivity study remain unchanged. v2 substantially expands diagnostic evidence through efficiency analysis, source-dataset breakdowns examining dependence on benchmark merging, and multi-scene case studies documenting occlusion, reflection, and thin-object recognition failures (Sections A.1, A.3-A.4).

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. The added tables continue reporting point estimates; the dataset-frequency plots do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1-5 retain their numerical values, while Tables 6-9 add substantial results. Table 6 reports detection-stage peak memory of 8.08 GB for OP3DSG, 11.43 GB for ConceptGraph, and 11.90 GB for OpenFunGraph; Table 7 adds ReplicaSSG scores, including OP3DSG object R@3 of 59.7. Source-dataset scores, qualitative failures, and label-frequency plots are also newly reported.

M1.justification: The detection, part-aware fusion, prior-graph construction, and LLM reasoning procedures in Section 4 are unchanged. Supplementary Section B supplies implementation details, including SAM and robot execution components, without establishing a change to the underlying procedures.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain essentially unchanged. v2 appends an organized supplement with a contents list and Sections A-C, alongside a small corresponding-author footnote edit; there is no extensive rewriting of the existing paper.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 6-10, a six-panel scene visualization in Figure 6, and two label-frequency charts in Figure 7. These substantially expand the presentation of evidence and dataset documentation. Existing main-paper figures and table structures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 retains all 64 original references and adds four works supporting supplementary details: A*, Segment Anything, LLaVA, and HomeRobot. The related-work discussion and central positioning remain unchanged; other citation changes are renumbering.

T1.justification: The graph formulation in Section 3 and mathematical definitions and equations in Section 4 are unchanged. The supplement adds experimental analysis and documentation without introducing new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical revisions.

improvement.justification: v2 fills important gaps in v1, which referred readers to supplementary implementation and dataset details that were absent from the supplied PDF. Explicit fusion settings and annotation categories improve reproducibility, while ReplicaSSG evaluation, source-dataset breakdowns, and failure cases substantially strengthen empirical assessment. The detection-only memory scope and overbroad superiority statement in Section A.3 temper, but do not outweigh, these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OP3DSG and UniGraph3D work, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures. v1 ends with references; v2 retains the main paper and adds Supplementary Sections A-C. The supplied material supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds efficiency measurements, ReplicaSSG evaluation, source-dataset breakdowns, and qualitative failure cases in Supplementary Section A.

before.justification: v1 reports original node, edge, and affordance evaluations, localization sensitivity tests, component ablations, and robot demonstrations in Sections 5-6.

results.title: OP3DSG: Open-vocabulary Part-aware 3D Scene Graph Generation for Real-world Environments

C1.justification: v4 drops the abstract's claim that MOCHA performs on par with larger multimodal models. The central object-level multimodal-distillation contribution, personalized-detection application, and +10.1 average improvement claim remain. Its conclusion emphasizes tested student architectures, supporting the existing architecture-agnostic framing.

C2.justification: v4 explains the oracle-versus-detection retrieval gap using single versus multiple candidate boxes, interprets smaller gains on larger or different students through capacity and architectural mismatch, and attributes training efficiency to embedding caching. It also interprets classifier ablations as evidence of representation robustness. The existing detection-only, training-cost, and prototype-scaling limitations remain.

D1.justification: v4 provides a project-repository URL and requirements.txt pointer, documents deterministic augmentation and teacher-embedding caching, adds parameter counts and linear-probing settings, and clarifies retrieval evaluation. E1.justification: Both versions use COCO and OpenImages for pretraining/distillation and PerSeg, POD, CORe50, and iCubWorld for personalization. The added architecture, classifier, and efficiency experiments do not introduce different datasets, task requirements, or input environments.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain the same teacher and comparison-method sets, including AuXFT, ViLD, KL divergence, KL plus MSE, and OFA. The new ablations vary student architectures and downstream classifiers while retaining undistilled, AuXFT, and MOCHA supervision comparisons.

Existing task metrics, few-shot regimes, and 50/20-epoch distillation budgets remain. The expanded retrieval-protocol explanation documents existing experiments rather than establishing a changed protocol.

These test architectural generality, representation robustness, and efficiency beyond v1's component studies. The earlier PCA, loss, translator, initialization, learning-rate, toy, and qualitative analyses are retained.

No new seed counts, repetition counts, confidence intervals, or statistical-testing procedures are documented. Additional result rows and timing variability extend the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark, component-ablation, PCA, and Wilcoxon table values are unchanged. v4 adds substantial architecture, classifier, and efficiency results; for example, Table 3 reports RT-DETR-l PerSeg scores of 43.5 without distillation, 45.2 with AuXFT, and 47.0 with MOCHA. Appendix A.4 revises reported 50/20-epoch training times from 48/20 hours to 28/11 hours. These are added results and revised timing reports, not improved scores in the retained comparisons.

M1.justification: The overall pipeline, translator, PCA targets, and combined objective remain. Section 3.4 revises the specified relational-loss formulation: Eq. (7) replaces temperature-scaled Euclidean distances with normalized distances, explicitly excludes diagonal entries before softmax, and removes the explicit temperature. This establishes a limited formulation revision, not that retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: v4 rewrites the abstract and conclusion, revises introductory and results explanations, and substantially reorganizes the appendix into performance evaluation, additional ablations, implementation, qualitative results, and limitations. References move after the appendix, citations become numeric, and several unresolved cross-references are repaired.

P2.justification: v4 adds architecture, computational-cost, and classifier tables, while some rows repeat existing comparisons. It extensively restyles tables, captions, headings, and pseudocode, including smaller gray uncertainty values and colored algorithm comments. Existing figures are retained with resizing, relabeling, and relocation; the PCA and qualitative appendix displays change order.

R1.justification: v4 adds references for YOLO11, RT-DETRv2, and SimpleShot and removes the Deeply-Supervised Nets and Going Deeper with Convolutions references. Related work newly identifies AuXFT as the only prior work with a similar setup and sharpens distinctions from prompt-driven recognition. The broader research positioning remains.

T1.justification: Eq. (7) revises the mathematical definition of relational affinities through distance normalization, explicit diagonal exclusion, and removal of temperature. v4 Table 6 also introduces asymptotic distillation-cost expressions. The remaining loss equations and PCA fitting formulation are retained; no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v1's architectural-generality and deployment-efficiency claims had limited direct validation. v4 substantially strengthens them through additional detector families, classifier ablations, and explicit latency, memory, and training-cost comparisons, while improving reproducibility and explaining the otherwise puzzling retrieval-score differences. Some new interpretation overreaches: Table 7 reports YOLOv11l CORe50 5-shot accuracy of 61.0 for MOCHA versus 63.5 for AuXFT despite claiming superiority across all settings. This qualification does not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MOCHA and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across restructuring and renumbering, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and adds student-architecture experiments, few-shot-classifier ablations, and computational-cost measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original personalized-detection experiments on four datasets, component ablations, PCA studies, qualitative results, and Wilcoxon tests.

results.title: MOCHA: Multi-modal Objects-aware Cross-arcHitecture Alignment

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims about AU-guided alignment and subject-specific test-time adaptation. The added efficiency sentence makes the existing Figure 1 comparison explicit without redefining the contributions.

C2.justification: v3 newly interprets AU tuning as the larger component contributor, argues that gains persist beyond window-selection advantages, and attributes better phrase-level performance to cleaner localized semantic anchors. It also discusses generalization to common FER and possible alignment confounds from alternative video encoders. Existing BAH limitations remain.

D1.justification: v1's statement that code will be made public is replaced by an explicit repository link, and v3 adds a project-page link.
