P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column formatting. Figure 3 is transposed and expanded; the original detection table is reorganized into zero-shot and appendix few-shot comparisons. Existing ablation figures are rearranged, with threshold panels added. New spatial-control/PCA displays, VisA and threshold tables, and extensive paired-image galleries substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to AnoStyler, FLUX, AnomalyGPT, MRAD and the VisA source paper. Section 2.2 now positions DeltaDeno against AnoStyler alongside AnomalyAny. The broader diffusion-editing background and few-shot versus zero-shot positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definition of the combined prompt loss in Section 3.3 changes by assigning an implicit unit coefficient to L_ctx instead of the explicit balancing coefficient. The remaining diffusion, attribution and attention formulations are retained, and neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: Relative to the supplied v1, v2 resolves important verification gaps: it quantifies dependence on SAM and threshold choices, discloses key implementation values, and supplies broader benchmark, backbone and comparator evidence. Appendix D also makes evaluation limitations more explicit. These additions substantially strengthen reproducibility and empirical scrutiny. The unclear history of the newly specified test subset, missing uncertainty estimates and unspecified GPU limit the gains but do not outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeltaDeno work, and their supplied text, equations, tables and figures are readable. However, v1 refers to additional dataset results and implementation details in supplementary material that is absent from its 10-page PDF. V2 includes Appendices A–E, leaving some uncertainty about the earlier supplementary coverage.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and reports additional VisA, FLUX, threshold-sensitivity, SAM-dependence and computational-efficiency results.

before.justification: V1 reports original anomaly-generation results, downstream MVTec AD detection experiments and component ablations in Tables 1–3 and Figures 3–5.

results.title: DeltaDeno: Zero-Shot Anomaly Generation via Delta-Denoising Attribution

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add attention imbalance as a central diagnostic contribution and a leading-performance claim on BFT. The introduction and conclusion also advocate internal prior generation as a default design principle for unified tracking. This substantially broadens v1's contribution framing around MOTR's hidden detector, prior-injection strategies, and competitive DanceTrack performance.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations linking attention polarization to impaired discovery and linking dataset-dependent attention to target deformation. Appendix A explains that shorter MOT17 clips improve detection while slightly harming association and do not close the competitive gap. Conversely, v1's explicit limitation that integration into CO-MOT or MOTRv3 remains untested is omitted.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page link, animal-dataset training settings, and explicit attribution of the existing query-denoising strategy. It omits v1's MOT17-specific 180-epoch training budget and learning-rate decay every 80 epochs. Most optimizer, preprocessing, initialization, and runtime-hardware details are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual training and evaluation on BFT and AnimalTrack, extending human tracking to birds and other animals with deformation, occlusion, and different motion conditions. DanceTrack, MOT17, and the existing COCO/CrowdHuman training resources remain represented; MOT17 moves to Appendix A.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 introduces reported comparisons with JDE, FairMOT, CenterTrack, SORT, QDTrack, TransCenter, and TransTrack, beyond the comparator set evaluated in v1. Conversely, the MOT17 comparison drops SUSHI, CoNo-Link, ByteTrack, GHOST, and OC-SORT. DanceTrack comparator membership remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds 20-epoch BFT and AnimalTrack training protocols, learning-rate decay at epoch 16, and respective re-identification windows of 15 and 10. Appendix A adds a three-frame MOT17 training condition alongside the original five-frame condition. Section 4.4 and Appendix B introduce layer-wise and token-level attention evaluation. The existing DanceTrack training schedule and tracking metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses examine whether detect queries disproportionately attend to existing tracks, comparing attention mass and entropy across decoder layers and between MOTR and SelfMOTR. Appendix B extends these diagnostics across three datasets, and Appendix A tests MOT17 clip length. Earlier component, proposal-source, threshold, data-scaling, and decoder-depth ablations are retained, sometimes relocated or consolidated.

E5.justification: v2 newly presents KDE estimates of token-level attention distributions in Figures 5b and 7, plus shaded bands around layer-wise averages in Figure 5a. The bands' statistical meaning is unspecified. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, defined confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds BFT and AnimalTrack results, including SelfMOTR HOTA of 71.1 and 45.5, and new attention-distribution findings. MOT17's original 57.5 HOTA is retained alongside 58.4 under the new three-frame condition, rather than a same-setting improvement. DanceTrack SelfMOTR remains at 69.2 HOTA, while MeMOTR's reported HOTA changes from 63.4 to 68.5. SPAM's MOT17 MOTA changes from 89.2 to 80.7.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same shared-parameter detection and tracking passes, confidence-conditioned proposal queries, ten additional learned anchors, and proposal-loss weight of 0.5. The added distillation equation explains an existing strategy, and the attention diagnostics do not alter the tracking algorithm. Denoising was already present in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work narrative, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Related work gains thematic subheadings, the explicit contribution list and standalone Discussion section disappear, and MOT17 plus selected ablations move into new appendices. These changes substantially reorganize the paper's narrative.

P2.justification: v2 changes from a two-column to a single-column layout, redraws the SelfMOTR architecture diagram, adds attention plots and the animal-benchmark table, and consolidates several ablation tables. It also corrects Figure 2's reversed track-query legend labels. Figures and tables are extensively resized and relocated; generic running-header placeholders remain in v2.

R1.justification: v2 adds attention-sink studies as conceptual inspiration, together with references for new datasets, comparators, and denoising. The MOTChallenge reference is removed. The central positioning against external-detector MOTRv2/MOTRv3 and CO-MOT's additional query management remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4.4 introduces a mathematical definition of cardinality-corrected Track-Attention Mass and defines normalized attention entropy for the new diagnostic analysis. This is a limited formal addition; the SelfMOTR equations remain equivalent, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the unchanged method: Table 3 tests applicability in two non-human domains absent from v1, while Section 4.4 and Appendix B provide measurements directly relevant to query interference. Figure 2 also resolves contradictory condition labels. These gains outweigh the omitted MOT17 training-budget details, although the attention evidence remains correlational and the target-trained animal experiments do not establish the claimed transfer beyond the training regime.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SelfMOTR work. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and v2 Appendices A–C are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds BFT and AnimalTrack results, decoder-attention measurements, and a shorter-clip MOT17 experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original SelfMOTR experiments on DanceTrack and MOT17, detection-prior ablations, detection–association analyses, and runtime measurements.

results.title: SelfMOTR: Revisiting MOTR with Self-Generating Detection Priors

C1.justification: The instance-first thesis remains, but v2 broadens the central contribution to attribute binding and both text-to-image and layout-to-image control. Its abstract, introduction and conclusion foreground three-benchmark validation, superiority over count-supervised approaches and IntraCompBench as a named contribution. v1 principally emphasized improved class/instance generation and the reported 52%/83% accuracies.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of CountGen's mask proposals, failures of exclusive box masking, image-quality tradeoffs and seed stability. It also identifies ambiguous parsed counts and missing 3D understanding as applicability limits. The runtime limitation remains, while v1's argument that normalization prevents transferring several baselines and its proposed SDXL-Turbo extension are removed.

D1.justification: v2 documents GPT-OSS-20B prompt parsing through instructions, examples and approximate cost, specifies normalized coordinates and bilinear attention upsampling, and identifies the reused layout annotations. This substantially expands implementation information beyond v1's assumed class/count inputs. However, v1's blanket single-A100-80GB experimental hardware statement is no longer provided. Both versions still promise code upon publication.

E1.justification: v2 adds HRS-Bench evaluations, color/texture/complex-composition tasks from T2I-CompBench, and layout-conditioned generation with overlapping boxes. These extend v1's counting-focused coverage substantially. IntraCompBench retains the earlier COCO-derived benchmark's classes and prompt construction; its new name does not establish new coverage. T2I-CompBench Numeracy also already appeared in v1 as T2I-CompBench++ Numeracy.

E2.justification: v2 adds Self-Cross to SD1.5 and SD3.5-M comparisons and evaluates A&E, SynGen, InitNO and TEBOpt against ISAC on SD3.5-M, where v1 lacked those comparisons. CountGen is newly evaluated on SDXL, while GLIGEN and CAR&SAR support the new layout comparison. Bounded Attention receives qualitative comparisons. Counting Guidance and the TokenCompose/IterComp comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include reuse of released HRS-Bench box layouts, best-of-10 selection on Flux.1-dev and Qwen-Image, and FID/CMMD measurements against native SDXL outputs. Original COCO sampling and detector-ensemble procedures remain. However, v2 Section 4.1 describes exact-count/all-class success while Appendix A.2 retains fractional detection accuracy, leaving any actual change to that scoring procedure unresolved.

E4.justification: v2 adds a semantic-overlap heatmap, CountGen-combination analysis, distributional image-quality evaluation, attention-layer ablation and a transparent-object failure case (Figure 2, Tables 10/13/14 and Figure 15). Earlier schedule, MPO and clustering ablations remain. Conversely, v1's separate propagation/normalization diagnostics and SDXL-Turbo dynamics analysis are removed, rather than merely relocated.

E5.justification: v1 reports multiple images and qualitative seed examples but provides no uncertainty estimates for its Numeracy table. v2 Appendix C.4 and Table 16 newly report 30 seeds and means with standard deviations for SD1.5/SDXL Numeracy results. This reporting improvement is confined to that evaluation; v1's unspecified Numeracy run count prevents inferring an explicit increase in runs.

E6.justification: Many original COCO scores and ablation values persist, but v2 adds substantial compositional, layout, comparator and latent-selection results. For example, its new layout experiment reports GLIGEN counting F1 of 66.58 without ISAC and 71.28 with ISAC. Numeracy values change from 54.3% to 55.0% for SD1.5+ISAC, 50.7% to 51.1% for SDXL, and 63.4% to 64.0% for SDXL+ISAC, now with 30-seed reporting; these are not established same-setting gains. Changed SD1.5 efficiency values in v2 Table 2 remain unreconciled with the older values retained in Table 15.

M1.justification: v1 combines instance separation with a class-overlap penalty. v2 Section 3.3 extends this to explicit token-pair repulsion and attribute binding, introducing a binding loss absent from v1. Appendix C.1 also adds an alternative inference procedure that selects candidates using accumulated ISAC losses without backpropagation. The underlying clustering, MPO and attention-propagation components remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Separate preliminaries are condensed into method background, the method is organized into named phases and a scheduling subsection, and experiments and appendices are substantially reorganized. Terminology changes from class disambiguation to semantic separation accompany this broader narrative revision.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the opening comparison, redraws the method overview, restructures the main results table and adds heatmaps, parser examples, layout comparisons, failure illustrations and analysis tables. Several earlier standalone figures disappear. Retained displays are distinguishable from additions: for example, v1 Figure 2 becomes v2 Figure 3, and v1 Figure 15 becomes v2 Figure 22.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially reframed around training-free guidance, count supervision, layout control and benchmark limitations. New discussions include Self-Cross, GLIGEN, Attention Refocusing, HRS-Bench, OverLayBench and TIFA. CountGen, already cited in v1 as Make It Count, receives substantive comparative and complementarity analysis. The earlier MCR/TweedieMix discussion and several segmentation/distillation references disappear.

T1.justification: v2 formally defines repulsion/binding token-pair sets and the binding objective based on 1 minus MPO in Section 3.3, extending v1's class-only objective. The central MPO, foreground-mask, clustering and attention-propagation definitions remain mathematically equivalent. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's largely counting-focused evidence: Tables 2–4 add broader compositional tasks, comparisons on SD3.5-M and layout evaluation using shared box inputs. Parser documentation, quantified seed variability and concrete failure analyses address important reproducibility and applicability gaps. Conflicting exact-versus-fractional accuracy definitions and unreconciled efficiency figures weaken reporting, and the quality metrics measure deviation from SDXL rather than directly proving aesthetic preservation. Nevertheless, the expanded comparative evidence and methodological documentation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ISAC research, with matching authors, core framework and retained experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds compositional benchmarks, layout-conditioned generation, latent-selection results, quality analyses and seed-variability measurements in Section 4 and the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-generation experiments, baseline comparisons, ablations and qualitative analyses in Section 5 and the appendices, including Tables 1–4 and 8–11.

results.title: ISAC: Training-Free Instance-to-Semantic Attention Control for Multi-Instance Generation

C1.justification: The original source-free, unsupervised ranking and two-pass efficiency claims remain. v2 broadens the main contribution from zero-shot microscopy ranking to multiclass biomedical challenge models and post-UDA selection. Its introduction also makes the failure of most classification-derived ranking methods on biomedical segmentation a prominent scientific claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds decision-boundary and feature-geometry explanations, including why LEEP behaves differently from embedding-based baselines. It revises v1's preference for hard consistency and feature perturbations toward broadly comparable performance. New limitations address collapsed predictions, consistently wrong structures after adaptation, cell/nucleus task confusion, residual connections and poor alignment with boundary-sensitive metrics (Sections 3.2, 5–6 and supplementary Sections 10 and 12.4).

D1.justification: Compared with v1's brief setup, v2 supplies dataset-specific split counts and volume identifiers, resampling and patch-processing instructions, perturbation ranges, instance postprocessing, GPU specifications and CUDA/PyTorch versions. It explains nnU-Net planning and public models' instantiation procedures. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation. Code release is newly promised on acceptance, but availability is not established.

E1.justification: v2 adds 42-class 3D ToothFairy2 CBCT segmentation, Covid-IF cell segmentation and mitochondria patch classification. Within retained nuclei coverage, SBIAD634 is removed from semantic target evaluation and DSB2018 from instance target evaluation; both datasets remain elsewhere. These changes are supported by v1 Figure 2 and v2 Sections 4.1 and 8.

E2.justification: v1 quantitatively compares CTE only with CCFV. v2 Table 1 retains CCFV and adds NLEEP, GBC, Hscore, LEEP, LogME, NCTI, Regularised-Hscore and Transfer Score. Transfer Score also provides a post-UDA comparator in Table 3. Both versions report no alternative ranking baseline for instance segmentation.

E3.justification: The evaluation moves beyond predominantly U-Net model banks to diverse architectures and models trained with and without augmentation. Reported mitochondria candidate counts increase from 3 to 15 and cell counts from 5 to 8. Cell evaluation changes from 256-by-256 tiles to full z-slices. Added experiments introduce classification, multiclass CBCT, Mean Teacher/AdaBN adaptation and supervised fine-tuning protocols. The three correlation metrics are retained.

E4.justification: v1 already tests input versus feature perturbations, hard versus soft consistency and dropout strength. v2 substantially extends sensitivity analyses across perturbation types, strengths and placements. It adds classification-versus-segmentation diagnostics, checks baseline rankings against final supervised fine-tuning, and investigates stable-but-incorrect predictions and cell/nucleus confusion (Figure 2, Table 25, supplementary Sections 11–12 and Figures 5–6).

E5.justification: v2 adds correlation p-values and significance indicators at 0.05 and 0.01 in Tables 2–3 and supplementary tables. Across-dataset means and standard deviations were already reported in v1. Both retain a single perturbed pass plus an unperturbed pass; no new seed-based replication or confidence-interval procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Microscopy summaries are replaced under revised settings: for example, Table 1 reports mitochondria CTE-NHD feature Kendall correlation of 1.00 with 3 candidates in v1 and 0.69 with 15 in v2. These are not comparable fixed-protocol performance estimates. New findings include ToothFairy2 overall Kendall and Spearman correlations of 1.00 for gamma-based CTE-NHD, post-UDA results, public-model rankings and extensive perturbation results. v2 also reports strong supervised LEEP performance absent from v1's comparisons.

M1.justification: The perturb-and-compare estimator, median aggregation and core consistency measures remain. v2 adds weighted per-class aggregation for multiclass segmentation and dropout across all layers or bottleneck-plus-skip connections, extending v1's bottleneck perturbation (Sections 3.3–3.4; supplementary Section 10). CTE-VRand becomes CTE-ARS with the same formula.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and the paper gains dedicated Related Work, Motivation, Experimental Setting and Limitations sections plus a structured supplement. The methods narrative is reordered and expanded. The title, author list and Rand-score terminology also change.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the overview, replaces the original correlation panels with classification comparisons and illustrated model-ranking case studies, and presents expanded sensitivity evidence in supplementary tables. Summary tables are substantially restructured, with new dental and UDA tables, supplementary Tables 5–33 and failure-example Figures 5–6.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands research positioning through a dedicated Related Work section covering supervised transfer metrics, unsupervised adaptation validation, generalisation and uncertainty estimation. Added literature includes Transfer Score, LogME, NCTI, adaptation methods and generalist biomedical segmenters. It explicitly challenges the proposed extension of classification ranking methods to segmentation, beyond v1's brief introductory positioning.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.3 extends the consistency-score definition from foreground-restricted calculation to weighted per-class aggregation for multiclass masks. Otherwise, the core EI, NHD, Rand-score and perturbation mathematics remain equivalent, and the same-task transfer assumption persists. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs; v2's expanded margin discussion is conceptual motivation.

improvement.justification: v1's broad claims relied on small, mostly U-Net banks and one supervised comparator. v2 substantially strengthens validation through diverse architectures, supervised and unsupervised baselines, and experiments testing classification-versus-segmentation and fine-tuning explanations. Detailed reproducibility information and explicit stable-but-wrong failure cases make applicability much easier to assess. Some reporting inconsistencies remain, including nuclei model counts in Tables 1 and 20, and code is only promised, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and interpretability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CTE research despite the changed title and expanded scope. Text, equations, figures and tables support comparison throughout. v1 ends after its references; v2 includes supplementary Sections 8–12, which were also inspected.

after.justification: v2 reports original microscopy, classification, ToothFairy2, post-adaptation and public-model ranking results, with additional experiments and failure examples in the supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original microscopy segmentation-ranking experiments, quantitative correlations in Tables 1–2, and perturbation analyses in Figures 2–3.

results.title: Unsupervised Source-Free Ranking of Biomedical Segmentation Models Under Distribution Shift

C1.justification: The central claim that sequence-conditioned, training-free feature transformation improves MOT remains. v2 extends the stated contributions to successful integration into hybrid trackers and associated state-of-the-art claims, beyond v1's emphasis on appearance-only trackers and zero-shot transfer. The underlying research objective is unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 interprets limited MOT17 gains through already-separable appearances, supplements the MASA discussion with dependence on initial feature quality, and uses supervised FLD to argue for sequence-specific adaptation. Expanded limitations discuss motion-dominated hybrid pipelines, inability to directly modify end-to-end trackers, density-related computational costs, and omitted recent comparators.

D1.justification: v2 documents oracle confidence scores, explicit per-table ablation settings, and visualization sampling details, including 15-frame examples and 10 sequences with 40 frames each. It clarifies the timing boundary and reports baseline speed. The code link changes from HELLORPG to MCG-NJU; actual repository availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

E1.justification: The four original benchmarks remain. v2 adds MOT20 validation experiments for crowded pedestrian tracking in Appendix B.2 and Table 11, extending coverage within the existing pedestrian-tracking domain rather than introducing a different task.

E2.justification: v2 adds ByteTrack-ReID, OC-SORT-ReID, Hybrid-SORT-ReID, several end-to-end comparators, and training-set-supervised FLD. Comparator membership also contracts: Deep OC-SORT disappears from DanceTrack comparisons, although evaluated on MOT20, and StrongSORT disappears from MOT17. DiffusionTrack's DanceTrack comparison is retained in appendix Table 12.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include the worst-1000 similarity-margin diagnostic, a training-set-fitted FLD control, with/without-HAT hybrid-tracker comparisons, and shared-FastReID-weight MOT20 validation. Table 12 expands DanceTrack evaluation with localization and identity precision, recall, and error-count metrics. These additions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds discriminability-versus-association analyses, cross-dataset separability comparisons, and supervised-versus-history-aware FLD ablation in Table 9. It extends the fusion sweep to alpha = 0.4 and reports unsuccessful confidence-weighting and hard-trajectory-weighting attempts in Appendix D. The original component sweeps and qualitative separation evidence are largely retained.

E5.justification: Unlike v1, v2 reports regression statistics and shaded fit bands: Figure 2a gives R-squared = 0.630 and p = 2.17e-6; Figure 6a gives 0.296 and 0.000111. The bands' confidence level and construction are unspecified. Neither version reports repeated-run or seed uncertainty for benchmark tracking scores.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial hybrid, MOT20, supervised-FLD, diagnostic, and detailed-metric results. For example, HAT-OC-SORT-ReID achieves 81.2 HOTA on SportsMOT, and HAT-FastReID-MOT achieves 61.2 on MOT20 validation. The retained tuned, non-joint-training SportsMOT row changes from 79.3/72.1 to 78.9/71.3 HOTA/AssA. Many original scores remain, while some metric entries are removed.

M1.justification: The core procedure remains history-supervised FLD over recent features, temporally weighted trajectory centroids, and fusion of original and transformed similarities. The centroid component is renamed and historical labeling explained more explicitly. Hybrid experiments reuse this transformation without specifying a new HAT component or altered projection procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v2 separates Preliminary from Method, introduces an explicit contribution list, reorganizes comparisons by tracker family, incorporates the former zero-shot section into broader comparisons, and substantially restructures the appendices with a new Discussions section.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column formatting, with extensively reorganized tables and figures. v2 adds correlation and distribution plots, fitting-strategy and MOT20 tables, compact and detailed MOT17 presentations, and a rotated extended-metrics table. Existing pipeline and feature visualizations are reused or rearranged, and several tables have reduced metric columns.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially around appearance customization, discussing adaptive affinity, trajectory long-tail handling, TOPIC, CATrack, and appearance purification. v2 explicitly distinguishes these approaches from sequence-specific feature-space adaptation and claims the first systematic explanation and practical solution. This goes beyond v1's broader tracking-paradigm survey.

T1.justification: v2 formally defines the positive-versus-hardest-negative similarity margin and its worst-1000 aggregation. It corrects the class-mean denominator from N in v1 Equation 6 to Nc in v2 Equation 5. However, the explicit multivariate trace criterion and eigenvector characterization are replaced by a less precise matrix quotient. Neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 demonstrated gains but lacked a direct control testing history conditioning against globally fitted FLD and offered no hybrid-integration evidence. v2's Table 9, separability analyses, hybrid experiments, and MOT20 evaluation substantially strengthen explanatory support and demonstrated applicability. Added implementation details and limitations improve scrutiny. These gains outweigh local defects: the less precise Fisher objective and Section 5.3's claim to surpass SambaMOTR despite Table 1 reporting 66.9 versus 67.2 HOTA.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HATReID-MOT work, with matching authors, core method, and substantial overlapping experiments. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive restructuring.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds hybrid-tracker evaluations, MOT20 validation results, supervised-FLD comparisons, and quantitative feature-discriminability analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original tracking experiments on DanceTrack, SportsMOT, MOT17, and TAO, including component ablations, feature visualizations, and inference speed.

results.title: History-Aware Transformation of ReID Features for Multiple Object Tracking

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the expert-grounded CoE benchmark, two-stage REVEAL framework, and claims of better detection, generalization, and explanation fidelity. Although v2 moderates wording in its abstract and conclusion, its introduction retains the state-of-the-art claim and Table 1 retains the first-reasoning-dataset claim. Added evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning expert aggregation, annotation reliability, complementary Pixel Noise cues, and limited gains from stronger annotation models attributed to saturation. Appendix C qualifies model-size scaling under limited data, and Appendix H acknowledges failure on a convincing synthetic cat. The multi-view reward discussion also drops v1's assertion of self-supervised discovery of novel transformation-invariant artifacts.

D1.justification: V2 supplies expert-to-input mappings, clarifies that experts operate offline without additional training, and identifies Qwen3-VL-8B as the reward assessor. It documents loss/reward weights and training details including 58K samples, 10 SFT epochs, one RL epoch, AdamW at 1e-5, and eight A800 GPUs. These are newly available disclosures, not demonstrated changes to prior settings. V2 promises future code and data release but supplies no release location.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on REVEAL-Bench++, covering FLUX, FLUX2, Z-Image, Qwen-Image, and SD3.5 as generators stated to be absent from training. This substantially extends the evaluated generator population beyond v1's REVEAL-Bench and GenImage coverage; merely citing some generators in v1 did not establish their evaluation.

E2.justification: V2's main comparisons include AIGI-Holmes alongside retained detectors, and Table 6 adds the best individual expert, majority voting, and decision trees. AIDE and VIB-Net disappear from the full-data in-domain comparison but remain in the GenImage comparison. V2 also supplies large-model comparisons in Appendix D; v1 references such an appendix without providing its contents, so those comparisons cannot all be called newly conducted.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a balanced 10,000-image recent-generator test and an anonymized explanation study using 100 images and three annotators with majority voting. New controls test answer-first supervision and alternative annotation configurations. Section 3 also revises the reported curation sequence: v1 selects 60K images before expert annotation, whereas v2 describes selecting 60K from approximately 6M annotated samples. Newly supplied training settings do not establish changes to earlier training budgets.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained backbone, CoE/GRPO, and perturbation analyses, v2 adds an answer-first ablation, expert-guided versus direct-LLM annotation analysis, Pixel Noise expert removal, and stronger-annotator experiments. Appendices provide explanation preferences, agent-versus-embedding examples, and detailed success and failure cases. These substantially expand tests of reasoning, annotation quality, and applicability.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new three-annotator majority-vote procedure defines the human evaluation protocol; it does not introduce uncertainty estimation or inter-rater agreement statistics.

E6.justification: V2 adds recent-generator scores, answer-first accuracy of 82.39%, human preference of 63% versus 37% for AIGI-Holmes, and annotation-ablation results. Matched GenImage per-generator scores remain unchanged; the REVEAL mean changing from 95.00 to 94.96 reflects exclusion of the in-domain column. Figure 5 also revises REVEAL's robustness results under the same stated perturbations: JPEG quality 60 rises from approximately 58% to 72%, without an explanation of the revision.

M1.justification: The stated reinforcement-learning objective changes substantially: v1 Equations 7 and 16 use advantage-weighted log probabilities with KL(old policy || current policy), whereas v2 Equations 7 and 13 use clipped probability-ratio objectives with KL(current policy || reference policy). This revises the specified optimization procedure, although implementation changes or reruns are not established. The two-stage framework and three reward components remain.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and experimental narrative, expands expert and optimization explanations, incorporates backbone comparisons into the ablation section, and adds dedicated explanation and annotation sections. The author list also changes. The new template introduces unfinished running headers, including 'F. Author et al.' and 'Abbreviated paper title'.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. V1's introductory figures are replaced by a redesigned comparison diagram, while its dataset and training pipelines are retained as v2 Figures 2–3. Generalization tables are reorganized, the backbone table is transposed, and numerous analysis displays and qualitative panels are added. Figure 5 receives new styling, axes presentation, and legends alongside its separately assessed numerical revisions.

R1.justification: The related-work framing remains largely intact. V2 adds references for DeepSeekMath, Qwen3-VL, FLUX2, Z-Image, and Qwen-Image, removes the VAR citation, and adds a limited contrast with interpretable rule-based classifiers. This updates supporting literature without substantially redefining the work's research positioning.

T1.justification: V2 substantively revises the mathematical definitions of the GRPO and R-GRPO objectives through probability-ratio clipping and a different KL direction and reference policy. The basic GRPO advantage also gains standard-deviation normalization and a denominator safeguard. These are non-equivalent mathematical revisions, unlike the simplification of already normalized R-GRPO advantages. The SFT factorization and loss remain, and no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's limited support for its generalization and explainability claims through recent-generator testing, controlled annotation and reasoning analyses, and an anonymized human preference study. Supplying previously unavailable training and expert details also materially improves auditability. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses, including unexplained Figure 5 revisions, unfinished presentation, and the new claim that alpha=0.1 prioritizes answers despite Equation 5 weighting reasoning by 0.9. The added evidence strengthens evaluation without establishing causal faithfulness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe REVEAL, and their supplied text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. However, v1 cites Appendices A–D but ends after its references; v2 includes Appendices A–I. This limits comparison of earlier supplementary details, while the main-text changes remain reliably comparable.

after.justification: V2 retains original detection results and reports additional generator evaluations, annotation ablations, human preferences, and qualitative analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original detection experiments, backbone comparisons, training ablations, and perturbation results in Tables 2–4 and Figure 5.

results.title: REVEAL: Reasoning-Enhanced Forensic Evidence Analysis for Explainable AI-Generated Image Detection

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims about metric-driven amortized attribution, dense maps, and optional refinement. Additional appendix evidence supports these claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: Section 3.2 adds an explanation linking score separation, decisive soft masks, and regularization to compact attributions. The appendix interprets complementary evaluations as evidence against optimization artifacts and transfer results as reducing retraining needs for related architectures. These extend the discussion, although Section 4.7 retains its original blanket retraining limitation.

D1.justification: v2 newly reports approximately 4.5 hours of training on four NVIDIA RTX 6000 GPUs for S=16 and approximately 2 hours for S=8, and identifies the used sorting temperature as 1.0. The abstract now advertises pretrained models alongside the already linked code. These are additional disclosures, not established changes to the original implementation.

E1.justification: v2 adds an ImageNet segmentation evaluation using ground-truth object masks to assess localization (Appendix A.7, Table 7). This is a limited task extension within the retained ImageNet domain; existing training, classification-attribution, and shortcut scenarios remain.

E2.justification: All seven original tables retain their comparator membership, including the ViT, ConvNeXt, and MDA-protocol comparisons. Added evaluations reuse existing comparators such as ViT-CX, TIS, and MDA; MAS and ROAD are evaluation metrics, not new attribution baselines.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends evaluation protocols: MAS and ROAD on the existing 5,000-image MDA subset; mask-based MAP, IoU, and F1 evaluation; cross-ViT transfer on correctly classified samples; and controlled grid-size and temperature sweeps. These are added experimental designs, while the settings of retained comparisons remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix A.2, A.8, and A.9 add training-cost break-even analysis, transfer between ViT-B/16 and ViT-B/32 with and without refinement, and grid/temperature sensitivity studies. A.6 additionally probes dependence on the optimized ranking metrics. Existing refinement, perturbation-step, and shortcut analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The existing runtime measurement over 100 iterations is unchanged; the added tables introduce no uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: All seven original tables retain identical numerical entries, but v2 adds substantial results in Tables 3 and 6–9. In Table 6, AHA's ROAD difference is 0.555 versus MDA's 0.498, while its MAS difference is lower, 0.471 versus 0.497. Table 7 reports segmentation IoU of 0.667 for AHA versus 0.702 for MDA. New cost, transfer, and sensitivity results further expand the evidence; these are additions, not improvements to retained benchmark scores.

M1.justification: The encoder-decoder architecture, Gumbel-Sinkhorn relaxation, deletion/insertion objectives, region perturbations, regularization, and optional refinement remain unchanged. The new transfer experiments apply the existing method; the expanded mechanism explanation does not introduce a component or procedural change.

P1.justification: v2 adds localized method explanations and experimental cross-references, rewrites the appendix roadmap, and reorganizes appendix subsections. Affiliations, contact information, and acknowledgements are also updated. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: Five new tables present amortization, complementary metrics, localization, transfer, and hyperparameter studies, substantially expanding the tabular presentation. Existing figures and tables are retained, with relocations and renumbering; for example, Figure 3 moves alongside Figure 4, and detailed Tables 5–7 become Tables 10–12.

R1.justification: Three references are added for ImageNet segmentation, ROAD, and magnitude-aligned attribution metrics. All 72 earlier references remain, and the related-work discussion and principal positioning are substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and Equations (1)–(11) are unchanged. The added discussion of score separation and compact attribution maps is a mechanism explanation, without a new formal result, derivation, or proof.

improvement.justification: v1's object-alignment evidence was principally qualitative, and its efficiency discussion did not quantify training overhead. v2 substantially strengthens these areas through ground-truth-mask localization, complementary MAS/ROAD evaluations, and amortization analysis. Transfer and sensitivity experiments further clarify practical applicability. The added evidence shows meaningful limits—MDA remains ahead on MAS and localization—while supporting AHA's strengths. Despite unchanged uncertainty-reporting gaps and imperfect reconciliation of the retraining limitation, the revision substantially improves validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AHA research work. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, support reliable comparison. Existing material can be matched despite appendix reorganization and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds complementary-metric evaluations, segmentation localization, cross-architecture transfer, hyperparameter ablations, and training-cost analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original attribution-quality and runtime experiments on ImageNet, refinement and perturbation-step ablations, ConvNeXt evaluations, and a controlled shortcut-detection experiment.

results.title: Learn to Rank: Visual Attribution by Learning Importance Ranking

C1.justification: v4 adds motion-frame scaffolding and its claimed fivefold distillation-convergence speedup as a central contribution. It strengthens the headline system claim from approximately 20 FPS to 45 FPS with 1.21-second TTFF and elevates the existing GenBench benchmark to a standalone contribution. The overarching 14B streaming and infinite-length generation claim is retained.

C2.justification: v4 expands the stability explanation with a static-scene assumption, noise-filtering arguments, and noisy-cache distribution-drift reasoning. It explicitly acknowledges reduced naturalness associated with accelerated motion in the distilled model. Its limitations now identify reliance on largely unchanged scenes and approximately three-second end-to-end latency that remains inadequate for bidirectional real-time interaction.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds detailed FP8 scaling and precision exceptions, attention-kernel selection, compilation, LoRA merging, streaming VAE caching, offloading, and memory information. v4 also specifies motion-frame noising and expands AAS/RoPE implementation details. E1.justification: Both versions use AVSpeech training and held-out evaluation, GenBench short and long videos with the same character and composition coverage, 10,000-second extrapolation, and human perceptual evaluation. The later ablations and hardware measurements vary configurations within this retained task coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated avatar-baseline memberships remain unchanged, including Hallo3, which already appears in v1's tables. v4 Table 6 adds fix-noisy-kv-cache at t=557 alongside the existing clean-cache comparator, providing a limited but substantive extension of the cache-scheduling comparison.

E3.justification: Stage 2 training changes from 2,500 to 500 steps, and v4 specifies an optimized FP8 inference configuration for its principal results. Table 3 revises non-TPP controls and GPU counts. New protocols vary denoising steps, latent-block size, and precision, and introduce T.Flicker evaluation and H20 runtime measurements. These changes preclude treating all revised scores as same-configuration improvements.

E4.justification: v4 adds controlled studies of motion-frame scaffolding convergence, 2–4 denoising steps, 1–4 latent frames per block, and FP8 versus FP16 inference. It extends the cache-noise analysis with fixed-noise and flicker measurements and adds visual stability ablations. The 10,000-second test already existed in v1; the earlier short-video cache comparison is no longer reported.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and mean normalized ratings from 20 participants without repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. The new convergence plot likewise provides no uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Results are extensively revised under the changed training and inference configurations. M1.justification: v4 introduces noisy motion-frame scaffolding in Stage 1 through a frozen FramePack encoder, then removes it for Stage 2; v1 explicitly removes FramePack and lacks this conditioning branch. Algorithm 4 also changes the AAS broadcast from decoded output to the generated latent. The underlying Self-Forcing, TPP, and Rolling RoPE framework remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, training explanation, stability discussion, and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten. Long-video generation now precedes TPP, the user study moves to the appendix, and references move before the supplementary material. These changes substantially reorganize the argument beyond accommodating new experiments.

P2.justification: The two-column main paper becomes a single-column layout. Figure 2 is redrawn to include scaffolding, new Figures 5–6 present stability examples and convergence, and new tables cover denoising steps, block size, and quantization. Table 3 becomes a component matrix, while existing user-study and supplementary displays are relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: v4 adds references supporting scaffolding, noise-based explanations, and evaluation, including History-guided Video Diffusion, VBench, DINOv2, and Z-image, while dropping Phased DMD and OmniHuman-1.5. It sharpens its criticism of Self-Forcing and LongLive. These are targeted changes within the retained positioning around large-model streaming, efficiency, and long-horizon stability.

T1.justification: The flow-matching equations, DMD gradient, and autoregressive formulation in Equations 1–5 remain substantively unchanged. v4 adds conceptual arguments about noisy caches and static scenes, but no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens validation of central design choices through the cache-scheduling, convergence, step-count, block-size, and precision controls, while documenting the optimized execution path in enough detail to make its efficiency claims more assessable. The explicit scene and interaction-latency limitations also improve claim calibration. Lower reported naturalness and conflicting default TTFF values in Tables 3/5 versus Table 10 remain weaknesses, but the gains in experimental support and implementation transparency provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Live Avatar, with matching research objectives and identifiable methods and experiments. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive revision and reformatting.

after.justification: v4 reports original benchmark and user-study results, together with additional experiments on training convergence, denoising steps, block size, cache-noise scheduling, and quantization.

before.justification: v1 reports original GenBench and AVSpeech evaluations, efficiency and stability ablations, 10,000-second generation results, and a 20-participant user study.

results.title: Live Avatar: Streaming Real-time Audio-Driven Avatar Generation with Infinite Length

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion newly claim that Pro-Pose provides a canonical intermediate that improves downstream VTO. They also assert full-body UV-based identity preservation, including visible skin details, whereas v1 leaves body-texture conditioning as future work. The original donor-reposing and hybrid-training contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the face-only-conditioning limitation with specific explanations of SMPL-X shape-estimation errors and unrecoverable self-occluded body regions. It newly attributes VTO improvements to removing source-clothing interference and interprets the BC-input control as evidence for methodological gains. Extreme-pose hallucination and the earlier identity-overfitting interpretation remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies the Gemini comparison prompt in Figure 12, explicitly labels main results as zero-shot, and discloses combining source-estimated body shape with target pose during evaluation. It also revises the garment-editing prompt. Backbone, optimizer, hardware, dropout, donor-pool, and few-shot training details are largely retained.

E1.justification: The existing training sources and evaluation datasets are retained. v2 adds distinct application tasks: downstream garment transfer through Google Virtual Try-On and controlled texture editing through a manually added tattoo (Sections 4.4–4.5). These are demonstrated qualitatively rather than through new quantitative benchmarks.

E2.justification: Gemini 2.5 Flash Image changes from a preprocessing tool into an evaluated comparator in Table 1, the facial-region table, and qualitative comparisons. The five existing pose-generation baselines remain. The new downstream comparison also evaluates Google VTO directly versus Google VTO using Pro-Pose preprocessing.

E3.justification: v2 introduces BC-preprocessed baseline-input controls, head-pose-change stratification using Euler-angle differences, and a FaceSim < 0.4 failure criterion. It also adds direct-versus-preprocessed VTO testing. Existing test-pair counts and training budgets remain unchanged. Appendix A revises Prompt V1 to specify 3-inch shorts; this documents a preprocessing revision without establishing dataset regeneration.

E4.justification: New analyses test identity robustness across pose difficulty (Figure 6) and whether clothing preprocessing explains the comparison advantage (Appendix D.3). v2 also adds texture-editing and VTO case studies and replaces the tattoo-loss failure example with a body-estimation failure. The earlier donor-mask, training-data, personalization, and identity-overfitting analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Figure 6 newly displays shaded ranges around pose-binned FaceSim curves. Their statistical meaning and construction are unspecified, so they cannot reliably be identified as confidence intervals or standard deviations. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts or seeds; the earlier identity-distribution plots are retained.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises Pro-Pose and training-variant scores: full-model DeepFashion FaceSim changes from 0.5919 to 0.6047, and WPose M-PSNR from 19.87 to 19.95. These accompany the method revision and do not isolate its effect. v2 adds Gemini results, BC-input results, pose-stratified findings, and application examples. Tables 2–3 remain numerically unchanged, as do existing facial-region entries relocated from Table 4 to Table 5.

M1.justification: v1 explicitly restricts UV conditioning to the face and personalization loss to a facial mask. v2 extends conditioning to full-body UV textures, illustrated in Figure 3, and changes the personalization mask to visible skin/foreground in Section 3.5. This materially expands the conditioning and optimization scope, while retaining the Flux backbone, donor-mask mechanism, and paired/unpaired training framework.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites emphasize full-body identity and downstream VTO, refine terminology, and clarify zero-shot evaluation. Most methodological and supplementary prose retains its sequence and substance. References move before the supplement, whose numbered sections become Appendices A–E.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a narrower single-column format with extensive resizing and repositioning. Figure 1 is redesigned around VTO; new displays cover pose difficulty, texture editing, VTO, and BC-input comparisons. Existing comparison grids gain Gemini panels and additional examples, Figure 3 shows body textures, and the limitations figure is revised.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Google Try-On tool reference and positions Pro-Pose as a preprocessing complement to existing VTO systems. The previous 57 references and the related-work taxonomy are retained, apart from ordering and bibliographic formatting changes.

T1.justification: Equation 9 retains its algebraic form but redefines its mask from the facial region to skin/visible foreground, changing the objective's mathematical support. The donor-mask reasoning, flow formulation, and supplementary UV-extraction derivation otherwise remain equivalent; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evaluation credibility: the new BC-input control addresses an important preprocessing confound in v1, and Gemini supplies a stronger additional comparison. The explicit body-estimation limitation also improves interpretation. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses: Figure 4 still describes a facial loss, Figure 6 leaves its bands undefined and overgeneralizes the failure-rate comparison, and downstream VTO claims rely on limited qualitative examples.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Pro-Pose and contain readable methods, equations, experiments, figures, references, and supplementary material. Retained content can be matched across the substantial formatting and numbering changes.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds Gemini comparisons, standardized-input controls, pose-stratified identity analysis, and qualitative application demonstrations.

before.justification: v1 reports original DeepFashion and WPose evaluations, training-data and personalization ablations, and supplementary identity-overfitting analyses.

results.title: Pro-Pose: Unpaired Full-Body Portrait Synthesis via Canonical UV Maps

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: donor-based UV self-supervision, joint paired/unpaired training, BC standardization, personalization, and identity-preserving portraits supporting VTO. Naming Gemini 3 in the evaluation contribution adds supporting evidence without redefining these claims.

C2.justification: v3 explains lighting behavior through BC standardization, argues for partial UV extraction over FreeUV, and interprets the UV ablation as locating the principal gains in unpaired-data learning. It also discusses the body-shape fidelity cost of inference fallbacks and attributes the VTO study's slight person-error increase to SMPL-X limitations.

D1.justification: New disclosures specify OminiControl-style token conditioning, LoRA masking and adapter locations, SMPLify-X estimation, original-image textures versus BC targets, and approximately 51-second inference. A project-page link is added. These are localized reproducibility additions; the PDFs do not establish a new code or data release.

E1.justification: The training sources, DeepFashion/WPose benchmarks, and supplementary in-the-wild and personalization coverage are retained. The new body measurements, UV ablation, and controlled VTO study evaluate existing data and tasks; they do not establish additional dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Gemini 3 Pro Image on both benchmarks while retaining Gemini 2.5 Flash Image. Figures 12 and 15 replace their Gemini 2.5 comparison columns with Gemini 3. The BC-input and face-region quantitative comparisons retain their previous comparator sets.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a pose-matched VTO study using 500 images, six garments, and ten raters, totaling 30K votes. It also adds segmented body-skin evaluation, SMPL-X shape-parameter distance/similarity metrics, and a paired-only training control without UV conditioning. Existing benchmark splits and main training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test whole-body preservation beyond facial identity (Appendix D.6), the contribution of UV conditioning alone (D.8), lighting behavior and Gemini failures (D.3), and VTO benefits with pose controlled (D.9). These substantially extend the retained donor-masking, training-data, personalization, and identity-overfitting analyses.

E5.justification: No new model-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. Existing shaded plots and distribution summaries are retained. The new VTO study supplies sample counts and aggregate percentages without introducing uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v3 adds Gemini 3 scores, body-preservation and UV-ablation results, and VTO preferences/errors, including 71.98% preference for Pro-Pose preprocessing. Existing Table 1 rows remain unchanged. The donor-ablation Ours row is revised from PSNR 19.87/FID 6.04 to 19.95/5.99 (v2 Table 3; v3 Table 4), without explaining whether experiments were rerun.

M1.justification: The core donor-masking, hybrid-training, flow-matching, and personalization procedures remain unchanged. Section 5 adds optional inference fallbacks for unreliable SMPL-X estimates: dropping pose conditioning or substituting a similar subject's shape parameters. The expanded conditioning-architecture description otherwise documents implementation rather than establishing a model redesign.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes comprise localized methodological explanations, additional appendix subsections, wording edits, and author-affiliation information rather than extensive rewriting or narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the displayed evidence with VTO-study, body-preservation, and UV-ablation tables (Tables 3, 7, 8), plus lighting and matched-pose VTO figures (Figures 16, 19). Comparison columns in Figures 12 and 15 are replaced, missing-image markers are clarified, and several existing displays are relocated. The underlying visual style is retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to Gemini 3 Pro Image, OminiControl, and FreeUV. It attributes the conditioning architecture to OminiControl and contrasts its full-body partial textures with FreeUV's facial generative recovery. The broader related-work organization and research positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: Equations 1–11 and the UV-visibility, flow-matching, personalization, and rasterization formulations remain mathematically unchanged. The added standard body-shape evaluation metrics do not introduce new theoretical results or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important validation gaps: the full-body identity claim gains direct skin/shape measurements, and the previously illustrative VTO benefit gains a pose-controlled human evaluation. The UV ablation clarifies the source of improvement, while implementation disclosures improve reproducibility. The VTO study also exposes a small person-error tradeoff. Together, these substantially strengthen support for the existing claims despite remaining reporting imperfections.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Pro-Pose and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices A–E. Content can be reliably matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original VTO user-study results, body-skin and body-shape measurements, and a UV-conditioning ablation.

before.justification: v2 reports original DeepFashion/WPose experiments, training-data and donor-masking ablations, personalization results, and identity-overfitting analyses.

results.title: Pro-Pose: Unpaired Full-Body Portrait Synthesis via Canonical UV Maps

C1.justification: The contribution list expands from one benchmark to two, making prompt-camera entanglement evaluation an explicit contribution. v1's conclusion claims the first absolute camera-control method for text-to-video; v2 drops that priority claim and positions the contribution around extreme and full-360-degree rotations. Gravity alignment and null-pitch conditioning remain central.

C2.justification: v1 attributes reduced CLIP and visual-quality scores primarily to training-data differences. v2 develops a substantive alternative interpretation: prompt-based CLIP can penalize correct camera views when requested content should be outside the frame. It also explains why null-pitch captions can induce capture artifacts and qualifies GEN3C comparisons because that method cannot generate scene motion.

D1.justification: v2 documents resolution and pose-quality filtering, retention of 4,798 of 7,797 training videos, 720-by-480 sampling, and variable prompt lengths. It adds camera-encoder initialization, AdamW settings, and a one-day training duration on eight H200 GPUs, replacing v1's four-A100 training description. Both still defer some implementation details to unavailable supplementary material.

E1.justification: v2 adds PolyHaven panorama evaluation with viewpoint-specific reference content for prompt-camera disambiguation, alongside the retained SpatialVID-extreme video benchmark. The reported training source changes from WEB360 to a filtered PanoVid YouTube subset. Figure 2 also introduces a full-rotation, return-to-start test scenario.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds UCPE and PreciseCam+GEN3C while retaining both AC3D variants and PreciseCam+WAN. The SpatialVID qualitative comparison replaces PreciseCam+WAN with PreciseCam+GEN3C and adds UCPE. UCPE also joins the prompt-camera entanglement comparison in Figure 6.

E3.justification: The reported training setup changes from a 2B backbone trained for approximately 8,000 iterations to a 5B backbone jointly finetuned for 30,000 iterations. SpatialVID evaluation now specifies ViPE-derived metric translations instead of reusing original translations. The new entanglement protocol evaluates 20 panoramas at 19 static pitches and computes CLIP against pitch-specific reference captions.

E4.justification: The existing null-pitch ablation is retained under the revised setup and incorporated into Table 1. Section 4.6 adds a systematic pitch-sensitivity analysis testing prompt-camera conflicts across 380 conditions, extending v1's qualitative illustration. Figure 2 adds a full-rotation case study comparing trajectory adherence and return-view consistency.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bars for the experimental results. The new aggregate curves in Figure 6 do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces numerical results for the proposed method and retained baselines, and adds comparator results. Reported pitch/gravity errors for Ours change from 23.79/27.06 to 9.35/11.67 under changed training and method conditions, not a controlled same-setting comparison. Unlike v1's ablation, v2 shows that null-pitch conditioning improves camera metrics but worsens CLIP, FID, and FVD relative to its ablated model. Figure 6 adds pitch-dependent findings.

M1.justification: The main model changes from CogVideoX-2B with an AC3D-style ControlNet to WAN-2.2 5B with a convolutional camera encoder and joint backbone finetuning. Section 3.2 adds gravity estimation from eight perspective views and changes pose composition. Section 3.3 adds downward-view captions and negative-prompt guidance to suppress tripods and other capture artifacts.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around extreme rotations and two evaluation goals. Related-work explanations are expanded and reorganized, gravity annotation precedes path sampling, and experimental exposition is reworked. The separate discussion and conclusion sections are merged into Section 5.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the teaser and reference-matching examples, redraws the pipeline, and replaces Euler-angle plots in the training examples with spatial camera trajectories. It redesigns the qualitative comparisons and expands Figure 6 into qualitative and quantitative panels. The ablation table is merged into a grouped Table 1; v1's distribution plot is absent from the supplied v2 pages.

R1.justification: Section 2 introduces UCPE as a concurrent gravity-aware alternative and substantially expands positioning against panoramic video generation and static novel-view synthesis. New discussions include GEN3C, ViewCrafter, PanoWAN, and PanFlow, with arguments about rotation diversity, cropped resolution, prompt visibility, and translation control. This changes the novelty argument beyond adding citations.

T1.justification: Equation (2) substantively revises the absolute-pose construction by introducing gravity alignment through psi and separate translation and rotation expressions. This is a focused change to the mathematical definition of pose composition; neither version contains a theorem or proof development.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important evidential gap by adding a controlled test of prompt-camera entanglement across pitches, beyond v1's general ablation and illustrative example. View-specific reference captions address a concrete metric mismatch, while UCPE provides a directly relevant gravity-aware comparator. Expanded implementation details also improve reproducibility. Changed backbones and data prevent controlled cross-version performance claims, and centered CLIP curves and visual-quality tradeoffs limit stronger conclusions, but the gains in mechanism testing and comparison relevance substantially improve the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GimbalDiffusion and provide readable text, equations, figures, and tables supporting comparison. Both end with references; neither includes the separately cited supplementary material, whose contents cannot be assessed.

after.justification: v2 reports revised SpatialVID-extreme experiments and ablations in Table 1, plus original prompt-camera entanglement experiments on PolyHaven panoramas in Section 4.6 and Figure 6.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation experiments on SpatialVID-extreme, quantitative baseline comparisons in Table 1, and a null-pitch ablation in Table 2.

results.title: GimbalDiffusion: Gravity-Aware Camera Control for Video Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contribution bullets and discussion retain the same central claims: gravity-aligned camera control through panoramic training data, null-pitch conditioning, and two evaluation benchmarks. The broader implementation evidence supports the existing framework claim without materially redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: V3 explains its UCPE default through better translation accuracy, qualifies look-down prompting as especially useful during full finetuning because of artifact overfitting, and attributes the relative-camera ablation's errors to missing absolute orientation information. The existing limitations concerning source-video translations and visual artifacts remain.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a 30k-iteration schedule, AdamW learning rate 10^-5, weight decay 0.01, one day on eight H200 GPUs, and camera-encoder construction details; these are absent from the supplied v3. V3 instead adds 49-frame sampling, more precise backbone/checkpoint descriptions, and AC3D's eight-layer ControlNet and 40% denoising-step details, while deferring further training information to an unavailable supplement. The documented reproducibility information changes substantially.

E1.justification: Both versions document PanoVid training, SpatialVID-extreme evaluation and the PolyHaven prompt-pitch task. V3 newly points to quantitative RealEstate10K results in supplementary material absent from the supplied PDFs. Consequently, whether that evaluation coverage was added cannot be reliably established. The SpatialVID-extreme sample-count revision is a protocol change.

E2.justification: The reported comparisons retain UCPE, AC3D with camera text, AC3D with camera text and absolute Plücker poses, PreciseCam+WAN-I2V-CC, and PreciseCam+GEN3C. Figure 6 retains PreciseCam and UCPE. Additional Table 1 rows are GimbalDiffusion variants and ablations, rather than new external comparators.

E3.justification: V3 adds comparisons using corresponding CogVideoX-2B and WAN-2.1 1.3B backbones and conditioning architectures, substantially changing the experimental controls. Section 4.3 also revises SpatialVID-extreme from 140 to 138 videos and replaces metric-scale conditioning translations with trajectories normalized to unit maximum translation magnitude. These reported setting changes prevent straightforward same-setting comparisons with v2.

E4.justification: Table 1 adds an absolute-versus-relative camera-conditioning ablation, labeled 'w/o absolute rotations', and extends the existing null-pitch ablation to the UCPE implementation. These are focused additions to component validation. The underlying prompt-pitch entanglement analysis remains, with revised examples and curves.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or run-to-run uncertainty estimates. Table 1 and Figure 6 retain point-result reporting without a newly documented uncertainty procedure.

E6.justification: Table 1 expands from one full GimbalDiffusion implementation to four, with additional ablation results. For the retained WAN-2.2 5B/Plücker variant, PitchErr changes from 9.35 to 8.36, GravityErr from 11.67 to 10.54, and FVD from 981.0 to 1014.4. Several baseline values and Figures 2, 5 and 6 also change. These are revised or newly reported results under changed settings, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V2 implements GimbalDiffusion through a Plücker camera encoder with full WAN-2.2 5B finetuning. V3 retains that variant but adds UCPE self-attention conditioning as the default, UCPE-module training, and a CogVideoX/ControlNet implementation. These substantially expand the implemented conditioning and training procedures; the gravity-alignment, trajectory-sampling and captioning pipeline remains.

P1.justification: Section 3.1 gains separate UCPE and Plücker explanations. The experimental narrative reorganizes model and baseline descriptions into Section 4.2 and separates metrics into Section 4.4. Local wording, captions and author information are edited, but most prose and the overall five-section narrative are retained.

P2.justification: The document changes throughout from two-column to single-column layout. Table 1 is rebuilt into backbone/conditioning groups with a Dynamic column and a grayed GEN3C row. Figures 2, 5 and 6 replace example imagery, Figure 4 drops one displayed training example, and Figure 6 changes its CLIP axis from mean-centered variation to raw scores. These substantially revise the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V3 adds citations including Spotlight, EscherNet, GTA and RoFormer, principally supporting lighting-control context and camera positional encodings. UCPE is additionally positioned as a conditioning component usable by GimbalDiffusion. Most related-work discussion and the central gravity-aware positioning remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 corrects the Plücker ray-direction expression by removing the added camera translation from R K^-1 [u,v,1]^T. V3 also supplies mathematical definitions for UCPE's block-diagonal encoding and attention transformation. The gravity-alignment equations and trajectory-sampling algorithm remain equivalent; no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: V2's main comparison uses a single WAN-2.2 5B implementation against methods with different backbones. V3's corresponding-backbone and conditioning comparisons in Table 1 substantially reduce this architecture confound and strengthen evidence that the pipeline's benefits generalize. The absolute-rotation ablation and corrected ray-direction formula add support and accuracy. Losing explicit optimizer, training-budget and hardware details weakens reproducibility in the supplied v3, but the stronger experimental controls provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs clearly describe GimbalDiffusion, and all supplied text, equations, figures and tables are readable. Neither contains appendices or the repeatedly referenced supplementary material, limiting comparison of supplementary training details and the RealEstate10K evaluation mentioned in v3.

after.justification: V3 reports original results for multiple GimbalDiffusion implementations and ablations in Table 1, alongside qualitative comparisons and the Figure 6 entanglement evaluation.

before.justification: V2 reports original camera-control experiments on SpatialVID-extreme in Table 1, a null-pitch ablation, and prompt-camera entanglement results in Figure 6.

results.title: GimbalDiffusion: Gravity-Aware Camera Control for Video Generation

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list make Optics-Aware Representation Alignment a new central contribution and explicitly claim to open-source ROSE++. The geometric-placement and dataset-construction claims remain. Calling ROSE++ a quadruplet dataset clarifies the four components already described in v1 rather than establishing a new dataset structure.

C2.justification: v1 attributes shadows outside the mask and lighting adaptation to ROSE++ LoRA fine-tuning. v2 argues that fine-tuning alone remains insufficient and attributes these effects to representation alignment, supported by new attention and regional-fidelity interpretations. It also adds an explicit limitation excluding complex physical interactions, such as a heavy object deforming a soft sofa.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds extended-mask cleanup instructions and B200 inference time and memory measurements. Reported training changes from 5,000 iterations/40 hours to 6,500 iterations/60 hours, while v1's 50-denoising-step disclosure disappears. Appendix D specifies inputs supplied to new baselines. v2 states ROSE++ is open source but supplies no dataset access link.

E1.justification: The VOI task and ROSE++/VOIBench remain. Appendix B adds a specifically selected shadow/reflection-rich evaluation population for the optics-focused study. The larger VOIBench sample and new held-out ROSE++ split are protocol changes rather than new datasets or general domains.

E2.justification: The main comparison expands from Pika-Pro and Kling to include AnyV2V, ReVideo, Señorita, and VACE with the proposed masks. Table 2 adds ROSE++-fine-tuned VACE controls. The general user study removes Pika-Pro and adds Señorita and VACE; the optics-focused study additionally includes fine-tuned VACE.

E3.justification: VOIBench's stated size changes from 50 to 200 clips, and training increases from 5,000 to 6,500 iterations. New protocols include a 25-sample ROSE++ holdout with region-specific LPIPS/PSNR/SSIM, controlled VACE fine-tuning, and a 30-participant study on 50 optics-rich clips. The existing 20-participant study changes from three to four alternatives.

E4.justification: v2 adds alignment-loss ablations, fine-mask versus extended-mask attention analysis, optical-region measurements, unedited-background fidelity checks, and an optics-focused perceptual study. The progressive ablation drops v1's initial camera-only configuration and adds alignment. Reference-crop and scene-flow analyses are retained; moving the latter into the main text is not a new analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v2 calls the motion-smoothness gap within per-clip noise but supplies no uncertainty estimate or statistical procedure supporting that statement.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the full model's CLIP-I/DINO-I/imaging-quality scores of 0.8122/0.5678/0.7101 with 0.8132/0.5669/0.7473, adds baseline results, and drops commercial multi-view entries. Commercial scores on retained metrics are unchanged. New Table 4 reports optics-region PSNR of 19.9065 without alignment versus 27.2362 with alignment. User-study and qualitative results also change substantially. Revised settings prevent interpreting cross-version differences as like-for-like performance gains.

M1.justification: v2 introduces Optics-Aware Representation Alignment, absent from v1: source–target differences generate extended masks, and intermediate features from ordinary-mask inputs are aligned to a stop-gradient extended-mask branch. This adds a substantive training component beyond v1's ROSE++ LoRA fine-tuning and first-frame conditioning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten around geometric grounding and optics-aware synthesis. ROSE++ construction moves inside the synthesis section, and the supplement gains explicit A–D organization. The title, terminology, author order, and equal-contribution designation also change.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation. v2 adds alignment-architecture, attention-map, and user-study displays; replaces many qualitative comparison panels; and restructures comparison tables. The existing scene-flow illustration and quantitative component-ablation table move from the supplement into the main text.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to OmniInsert, ReVideo, and Señorita-2M and removes several image-insertion and general-video references.
