Related work is refocused around mask-free versus mask-conditioned VOI, elaborating a distinction already present in v1's method overview rather than introducing an entirely new research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 adds a mathematical definition of the extended-mask feature-alignment loss with a stop-gradient target in Equation 7. Other equations largely expand or restate existing placement, scene-flow aggregation, reprojection, and reference-selection procedures. Neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central optical-effects claim through same-data VACE controls, held-out regional measurements, alignment ablations, and an optics-focused user study. These address v1's reliance on qualitative lighting examples and commercial-only comparisons. Clearer mechanism documentation and explicit limitations also help. Benchmark accounting remains unclear because commercial scores are unchanged despite the stated expansion, and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but these gaps do not outweigh the substantial gains in controlled evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe InsertAnywhere, ROSE++, and VOIBench. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete supplementary materials are readable and support comparison despite substantial rewriting and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark comparisons, alignment ablations, held-out optical-region measurements, qualitative results, and two user studies in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark comparisons, component ablations, qualitative insertion results, and a 20-participant user study, including supplementary Tables 3–4.

results.title: InsertAnywhere: Geometrically Grounded and Optics-Aware Video Object Insertion

C1.justification: The abstracts, introductions and conclusions retain the same central contributions: lifelong personalized head spaces, Dynamo, DNA-2DGS and TimeWalker-1.0, supporting identity preservation and controllable, realistic animation. The additional experiments and preliminary extensions do not redefine these main contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations of shared representations and temporal generalization, plus explicit limitations involving yaw angles beyond 45 degrees, lighting/lifestage entanglement, matting noise and inaccurate FLAME fitting. Appendix I also distinguishes the limited benefits of output refinement from targeted generative augmentation and expands misuse and access discussions. These extend the earlier FLAME-expression and incomplete-lifespan limitations.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies 512×512 evaluation inputs, revises reported training time from 3–4 to 3–5 hours, and documents the augmentation images, age/pose captioning and pretrained tools. It updates the listed project-page address and adds a proposed dataset usage-agreement requirement. The A100 hardware, 5,000-step warm-up, 30,000-step training and principal hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: TimeWalker-1.0, INSTA and the RenderMe-360/NerSemble animation examples are retained. Coverage expands within the existing head-avatar domain through explicit large-yaw and lighting-control scenarios, generative age/pose extrapolation attempts, and approximately 3,000 synthetic training images for Leonardo DiCaprio (Appendices F and I).

E2.justification: V2 extends the comparison scope to generalizable one-shot avatars by evaluating pretrained and finetuned GAGAvatar (Tables 15–16). It also adds an indirect GPHM score comparison, explicitly acknowledging different experimental settings. The earlier comparator set is retained; INSTA++ is newly positioned as a PAV reimplementation rather than being a newly added baseline.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include GAGAvatar testing on three different identities using each lifestage's first image as the source, pretrained-versus-finetuned comparisons, an ArcFace identity metric, and additional controlled component/training comparisons. The stated original holdout rule also changes from the last 10% capped at 150 frames per appearance to an unqualified last 10%; the retained scores do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds residual-embedding placement/removal ablations, a 20-hashgrid setting, training-cost and retained-basis analyses, single-versus-multiple-lifestage training, yaw robustness, lighting disentanglement, and generative-model failure/augmentation studies. However, the numerical loss-ablation rows from v1 Table 2 disappear, although their qualitative examples and discussion remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates or averages without specifying repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added experiments do not introduce uncertainty reporting; the dataset-distribution statistics retain their existing reporting approach.

E6.justification: The original benchmark values match between v1 Tables 5–7 and v2 Tables 11–13. Substantial new results include Table 16's mean identity scores of 86.8 for TimeWalker versus 83.7/80.7 for pretrained/finetuned GAGAvatar. New Table 4 reports single-/multi-lifestage PSNR of 23.69/27.22, but SSIM of 0.959/0.955. Additional robustness, timing and augmentation findings are reported, while the earlier numerical loss-ablation results are removed.

M1.justification: The core Dynamo, residual embedding, DNA-2DGS, Defer-Warping and losses remain unchanged. Appendix I.1.2 adds limited experimental pipeline extensions: LoRA-tuned Qwen-Image generates supplemental training images, and DouBao post-processes rendered outputs. V1 discussed generative priors only as future work.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: benchmark comparisons move into the main experiments, while detailed losses, age-progression related work, personalized-space visualizations and limitations move into reorganized appendices. The method exposition is compressed, the appendix is divided into thematic sections A–I, and v1's duplicated bibliography is consolidated.

P2.justification: V2 changes the page template and extensively resizes, relocates and restructures displays. It reformats benchmark and hashgrid tables, splits the existing mesh comparison and geometry-loss visualization into separate figures, expands the capability table, and adds tables and figures for the new analyses. Many retained illustrations are moved rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around PAV, one-shot head avatars and large pretrained models. PAV is now acknowledged as a closely related approach supporting multiple appearances, qualifying the earlier broad characterization of existing methods. New discussions of GAGAvatar, GPHM, Flux and Qwen extend the research comparison beyond the original reconstruction and personalized generative methods.

T1.justification: V2 omits the explicit Gaussian-kernel and covariance-matrix definitions, including the flattened covariance expression, from v1 Section 3.1. The neural combination, warping, rendering and loss equations remain equivalent, with several relocated to the appendix. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central personalized-space claim: v1 primarily supported identity preservation through image-quality metrics and illustrations, whereas v2 directly measures identity consistency and tests temporal diversity and residual-embedding design. The viewpoint and lighting studies also establish clearer applicability limits. Missing numerical loss-ablation rows, ambiguity about the test cap, and the indirect GPHM comparison weaken reporting completeness, but the targeted validation and more explicit failure analysis provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TimeWalker with the same authors, core framework and dataset. All 22 pages of v1 and 29 pages of v2, including appendices, were readable; visual inspection resolved interleaved table extraction. The substantial reorganization does not prevent reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds identity-consistency measurements, further ablations, robustness analyses and generative-model experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original rendering comparisons, component ablations, mesh reconstruction, reenactment and dataset analyses in Section 4 and Appendix A.

results.title: TimeWalker: Personalized Neural Space for Lifelong Head Avatars

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about reference-based temporal effect transfer, the large training dataset, joint conditioning, unseen-effect generalization, and superiority over baselines. The introduction clarifies the framework's components without changing these claims.

C2.justification: V4 newly interprets its bootstrap deviations as confirming statistical reliability and discusses the near-chance input-adherence result against No Ref. This reliability interpretation is stronger than near-chance entries warrant. The under-editing explanation and Appendix A limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: New Appendix C documents MTurk recruitment, randomized presentation, 30 distinct annotators per experiment, five practice trials, and the study interface. V4 also specifies Wan2.1 in the main implementation description and changes the project-page link target. Existing training, inference, hardware, and runtime details are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same LoRA-derived I2V, neural V2V, and programmatic V2V coverage. Section 4.1 retains 28 unseen LoRA effects, 56 reference videos, and the existing V2V scenarios. V4 clarifies their organization and use of real input videos without establishing newly added coverage.

E2.justification: V4 adds Lucy Edit to the code-based V2V human-preference and similarity comparisons in Tables 1 and 4, where v1 has dashes. The comparator sets in the other corresponding comparisons remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The primary human evaluation changes from five-level ratings to two-alternative forced choice and adds Overall Match alongside the existing adherence criteria. V1 reports 669, 455, and 252 annotations across its three tasks; v4 reports over 15,000 annotations from over 500 annotators. Training and automatic evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Tables 1–2 extend the existing No Ref ablation to Overall Match, adding evidence about reference conditioning's contribution to jointly transferring effects and preserving input content. The guidance sensitivity example in Figure 8 and failure analysis in Figure 9 remain unchanged.

E5.justification: V1 reports win rates and mean preference scores without uncertainty estimates. V4 reports bootstrap standard deviations throughout Tables 1–2; Appendix C specifies 10,000 iterations resampling annotators and trials. This adds uncertainty estimation to the primary evaluation, without establishing additional model-training runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 replace the human-study results and add Overall Match scores. For example, I2V preference against Wan2.1 changes from 74.7% to 57.1 ± 2.4% under the revised procedure, so this is not a same-setting performance decline. Table 4 adds Lucy Edit's code-based input/reference similarities of 0.8882/0.6539. Tables 3 and 10 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The data-generation pipelines, reference-latent concatenation, conditioning masks, training procedure, and inference guidance remain unchanged. References to an 'updated conditioning' scheme describe the architecture already documented in v1, rather than a new procedure.

P1.justification: V4 makes localized revisions to the introduction, method overview, dataset terminology, validation description, and user-study discussion. It inserts a user-study appendix, renumbers the subsequent appendix sections, and adds acknowledgments while retaining the overall narrative structure.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain Overall Match columns and revised captions, and Figure 10 newly illustrates the study interface. V4 also changes a Figure 3 transition label, identifies Table 5 as a subset, and relocates Table 4. Existing qualitative and architecture illustrations are retained.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive related-work discussion remain unchanged. The positioning against text-driven editing, static reference conditioning, and effect-specific finetuning is retained; reference back-reference changes reflect pagination.

T1.justification: The triplet construction definitions, guidance equations (1)–(5), and supplementary motion-quality expression (6) are retained. No mathematical assumptions, propositions, proofs, or substantive derivations are added or revised.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens the paper's primary empirical validation. It replaces a sparsely documented preference study without uncertainty reporting with a larger, explicitly specified study, adds joint assessment of effect transfer and content preservation, and reports annotator/trial bootstrap uncertainty (Section 4.3 and Appendix C). These changes address important weaknesses in assessing and reproducing the central evidence. The blanket reliability claim remains overstated for near-chance results such as 51.3 ± 3.1%, but the evaluation is materially more transparent and informative.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RefVFX research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including the expanded user study in v4.

after.justification: V4 retains original generation and quantitative results and reports a revised human study, including Overall Match judgments and bootstrap uncertainty.

before.justification: V1 reports original video-generation comparisons, human preference results in Tables 1–2, similarity measurements in Tables 3–4, and supplementary video-quality measurements in Table 10.

results.title: Tuning-free Visual Effect Transfer across Videos

C1.justification: v1 principally claims a unified staged-to-wild benchmark and identifies differences between frozen representations. v2 makes controlled synthetic data a central contribution and claims synthetic training can match or surpass staged training on wild transfer. The abstract and conclusion also expand the benchmark claim to three domains, 16 classes and privacy-amenable data generation.

C2.justification: v1 explains transfer through I3D's simpler motion representations and transformer overfitting. v2 emphasizes demographic/environmental diversity, synthetic appearance versus staged motion, and differences in recovery coverage. Its limitations newly discuss generator-induced biases and incomplete synthetic realism, extending the retained concerns about wild coverage and deployment privacy.

D1.justification: v2 documents generation prompts and attributes, annotation tooling and review, source permissions, feature extraction, four H100 GPUs and extraction time. Some precise v1 classifier and loss details disappear. Access wording changes from direct dataset/code links to a project page and an Appendix A.5 release-on-acceptance statement; actual availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

E1.justification: The eight staged datasets and OOPS-derived wild corpus are retained under revised names. v2 adds 12,000 synthetic videos with demographic and environmental variation, expands the taxonomy from 10 to 16 classes, reports full-taxonomy wild evaluation beyond v1's binary wild labels, and evaluates cross-age and cross-BMI scenarios.

E2.justification: v1's classification comparison among I3D, VideoMAE-Pre and VideoMAE-K400 is replaced by VideoMAE-K400 training-source comparisons. SigLIP2 enters the feature comparisons, ASQuery replaces MS-TCN++ for supervised segmentation, and Appendix Table 8 adds evaluated TW-FINCH and KMeans baselines.

E3.justification: The staged CS/CV partitions are retained in Appendix A.2. Reported classification settings change from 150 epochs, batch size 256 and learning rate 5e-4 to 50 epochs, batch size 32 and 1e-5. v2 adds single-source, synthetic and combined-source controls and demographic protocols; embedding smoothing changes from 18-feature averages to five-frame means.

E4.justification: v2 adds training-source ablations, cross-age/BMI robustness tests in Figure 7, and temporal trajectory and recovery-completeness analyses in Appendix A.5.1 and Figure 8. Existing domain-shift analyses incorporate synthetic data and SigLIP2. Conversely, v1's qualitative segmentation prediction example becomes an annotation-only illustration in v2 Figure 3.

E5.justification: Appendix A.3.5 newly documents deterministic, hash-based seeding for synthetic attribute selection. This is limited seed information, not evidence of repeated experimental runs. Neither supplied PDF reports confidence intervals, significance tests or run-to-run variability for the benchmark scores.

E6.justification: v1 reports wild Fall F1 of 0.76/0.82 for I3D and 0.34/0.26 for VideoMAE-K400 under CS/CV training. v2 replaces these comparisons with scores of 52.3% for CMDFall training, 61.2%/60.5% for OF-Staged, 64.2% for synthetic and 65.6% for combined training. These are different experimental conditions, not same-setting improvements. New segmentation, demographic and temporal-analysis results further expand the evidence.

M1.justification: v2 introduces controlled Wan 2.2 synthetic-video generation and reports end-to-end VideoMAE-K400 classification, replacing v1's frozen-backbone approach. Supervised segmentation changes from MS-TCN++ to ASQuery. However, v2's end-to-end description is not clearly reconciled with Appendix A.5's classifier operating on extracted features.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten around three domains. Experiments are reorganized around training sources, and dataset splits, search details and limitations move into a substantial appendix. This changes the narrative and document organization beyond simply inserting new results.

P2.justification: v2 changes the single-column layout to two columns, introduces a three-domain overview, redraws distribution and embedding plots, and reorganizes result tables with colored rankings. It adds demographic and trajectory figures and appendix tables. Figures 9–20 enlarge the existing embedding analysis rather than constituting separate experiments.

R1.justification: The review of existing fall datasets remains largely intact. v2 adds references supporting Wan, SigLIP2, ASQuery, VIA and demographic attribute design, while removing the class-balanced-loss and MS-TCN references. These are targeted additions supporting the expanded benchmark rather than a comprehensive restructuring of the prior-work landscape.

T1.justification: v1 Section 4.2 explicitly defines capped dataset weights as w_i = min(max_j |D_j| / |D_i|, 20); v2 omits this mathematical specification. Neither version develops theorems or proofs, so the change is limited to removal of a formal training rule.

improvement.justification: Shared 16-class wild timelines, direct training-source controls and demographic/recovery analyses substantially strengthen the benchmark's ability to investigate generalization beyond v1's backbone-focused evaluation. Generation and annotation documentation makes the expanded benchmark more auditable. These gains outweigh reduced classifier-backbone coverage, although implementation and access descriptions remain unclear. v2 also overstates universal SigLIP2 superiority: Table 6 gives staged-to-wild F1@50 of 20.26 for SigLIP2 versus 26.37 for I3D. The improvement rests on stronger benchmark design and evidence, not cross-version performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OmniFall, and their supplied pages, tables and figures are readable. However, v1 references supplementary backbone settings, a VideoMAE-Pre table and numerical distance tables that are not included in its PDF. v2 includes Appendix A. This limits comparison of those supplementary details, while the principal revisions are directly assessable.

after.justification: v2 reports original training-source comparisons, demographic generalization tests, supervised and unsupervised segmentation results, and temporal-completeness analyses in the main text and appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original domain-shift analyses, backbone classification experiments in Tables 2–3, and MS-TCN++ segmentation results in Table 4.

results.title: OmniFall: From Staged Through Synthetic to Wild, A Unified Multi-Domain Dataset for Robust Fall Detection

C1.justification: The satellite-only, domain-independent, curriculum-refinement contribution remains. v2 recasts the abstract/introduction's broad priority wording as a hybrid reconstruction-and-generation framework while retaining qualified first-method claims elsewhere. Its conclusion additionally claims operation without human intervention.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning fixed-camera blind spots, dependence on off-nadir imagery, and coverage estimates that cannot detect missing surfaces. It interprets weaker performance on relatively flat scenes, discusses competing LPIPS/SSIM results, and explains prompt robustness, transient-object handling, and seed-dependent textures. These substantially expand the applicability boundaries and mechanism discussion beyond v1.

D1.justification: v2 documents appearance fusion for standard renderers, memory and Gaussian counts, detailed runtime profiling, approximation procedures, prompt variants, and multi-block settings. Conversely, it omits v1's densification-threshold and extended CoR-GS-training details, Zenodo example-data notice, and code/full-data release promises. These are substantial documentation changes; actual external resource availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

E1.justification: The original DFC2019 and GoogleEarth scene coverage is retained, including v1's additional Jacksonville AOIs. v2 adds Neuschwanstein Castle and Wells Cathedral examples and jointly reconstructs adjacent JAX_214/JAX_260 blocks, extending architectural and spatial-scale coverage within the existing synthesis task.

E2.justification: v2 adds Mip-Splatting to the reported GoogleEarth comparisons, DFC2019 per-scene table, and both user studies. Although v1 already mentions evaluating it on both datasets, these corresponding comparisons omit it. Table 4 also introduces an evaluated SDEdit replacement control; the established comparator suite is otherwise retained.

E3.justification: The reported user-study cohort changes from 89 to 44 participants per study, with expanded comparator choices. New protocols include LiDAR-based DSM evaluation using MAE/RMSE, matched-schedule SDEdit testing, and multi-block training with a 6-by-3 look-at grid. Appendix B.1 also specifies disabling GoogleEarth opacity regularization, revising v1's unqualified regularization setting without establishing whether experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Tables 3–4 extend perceptual ablations with geometric validation, sample counts of 1/2/3/5, timing, prompt controls, and SDEdit replacement. Appendix D adds prompt sensitivity, transient-object handling, bridge and irregular-geometry cases, multi-block consistency, episode-versus-coverage analysis, and seed-dependent appearance comparisons. These substantially broaden tests of mechanisms, robustness, and applicability.

E5.justification: Appendix D and Figure 23 newly report varying diffusion random seeds while holding geometric initialization fixed. This adds qualitative seed-sensitivity information; neither version supplies quantitative uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the main comparisons.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 2, 8, and 9 revise numerous scores: Skyfall-GS FIDCLIP changes from 27.35 to 27.03 on DFC2019 and 9.91 to 10.29 on GoogleEarth. User-study percentages are replaced under changed study conditions. New results include reconstruction MAE/RMSE of 2.250/3.483 meters, refinement-control results, coverage curves, and scalability findings; these are additions or revisions, not uniformly comparable performance gains.

M1.justification: Equation 3 changes the stated depth objective from |PCorr| to 1 - |PCorr|, correcting its optimization direction. The reconstruction-plus-curriculum-refinement pipeline otherwise remains intact. This establishes a written objective correction, without establishing whether the implementation changed.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, experimental discussion, and conclusion receive substantial rewriting. The appendix is reorganized into implementation, main-experiment details, and additional experiments; performance/scalability gains a dedicated subsection. The ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-disclosure sections are removed. This extends well beyond renumbering or added scientific content alone.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a substantially different page format, expands ablation tables, adds ranking colors and comparator columns, and redraws the user-study charts. New figures display refinement progression, scalability, complex geometry, prompts, embeddings, coverage, and seed variation. The earlier pseudo-camera sampling scatterplot is removed, while many original figures are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially revises positioning around satellite reconstruction, urban synthesis, and diffusion editing. It adds works including Horizon-GS, Sat2City, Sat3DGen, Sat2RealCity, WonderWorld, and RealmDreamer, while removing some earlier citations. New comparisons emphasize preserving observed facade appearance versus unconstrained inpainting, beyond bibliographic or citation-style changes.

T1.justification: Equation 3 corrects the mathematical definition of the depth loss to 1 - |PCorr|. Appendix B.2 additionally states the weak-perspective assumption Z much greater than depth variation and explains the projection-matrix approximation. No substantial theorem or proof framework is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's central geometric and refinement claims through LiDAR validation, SDEdit and sample-count controls, and multi-block/coverage analyses. It also corrects the depth objective and states concrete applicability limits. These gains outweigh lost reproducibility disclosures and remaining reporting problems: notably, Section C.3 claims three GoogleEarth CMMD wins, whereas Table 9 shows two. The improvement rests on better validation and qualification, not higher scores or greater length.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Skyfall-GS and provide readable methods, equations, experiments, figures, tables, and appendices. Corresponding content can be matched despite substantial reformatting and supplementary additions.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and reports additional geometry validation, refinement ablations, scalability experiments, and qualitative robustness analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original DFC2019 and GoogleEarth experiments, component ablations, qualitative reconstructions, and two user studies.

results.title: Skyfall-GS: Synthesizing Immersive 3D Urban Scenes from Satellite Imagery

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same contribution: diagnosing static-background geometric inconsistency through disagreement among local camera poses while avoiding penalties for valid foreground motion. The introduction makes this existing scope more explicit; the added validation does not redefine the central claims.

C2.justification: New Appendix A explicitly discusses estimator domain shift, tracking failures, and the absence of absolute calibration separating estimator noise from generated-video corruption. Sections 4.2 and 4.5 add interpretations of Cosmos's metric disagreement and estimator-independent ranking stability, while Appendix E interprets human alignment. These materially expand the discussion of validity and applicability.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds reproducibility information for human-label collection and processing, including annotation priorities, randomized presentation, half-credit ties, and aggregation across 11 entities. Existing implementation algorithms, hyperparameters, baseline preprocessing details, PCA weights, and the stated code-access link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same 1,296-video corpus, ten generators spanning T2V/I2V/V2V, and nuScenes, RT-1, and OpenVid. The new human and estimator analyses evaluate the existing static-background stability target; their sampling and grouping changes do not establish new video-domain or task coverage.

E2.justification: Main Table 1 retains the same metric comparators. New Table 3 adds SGC comparison variants using Any4D and Page4D, alongside a variant without the VGGT global-pose component. These extend the evaluated alternatives within a focused robustness comparison.

E3.justification: Appendix E introduces a substantial new evaluation design: 150 blinded video pairs, seven annotators, randomized A/B ordering, background-specific instructions, tie-aware scores, and Spearman/Kendall correlations across 11 entities. Section 4.5 also introduces estimator substitutions and a subset excluding nuScenes. Existing benchmark protocols are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds two important validation analyses absent from v1: whether rankings survive replacing or removing the geometry estimator, and whether metric rankings agree with human judgments. Existing geometric perturbations, component ablations, PCA cross-validation, segmentation sensitivity, and qualitative cases are retained, including material moved through appendix renumbering.

E5.justification: The ten-fold PCA means and standard deviations and existing correlation-significance reporting are retained. Table 3 adds significance outcomes for new comparisons, while Appendix E reports point correlations. Neither introduces a new uncertainty-estimation practice, run/seed disclosure, or confidence-interval treatment.

E6.justification: Original benchmark and ablation values remain unchanged. New Table 3 reports ranking correlations of 0.993 without VGGT, 0.860 with Any4D, and 0.937 with Page4D. Appendix Table 5 adds human agreement results: SGC achieves Spearman 0.945 and Kendall 0.818, versus MEt3R's 0.864 and 0.745. These are new validation outcomes, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The proposed pipeline, five score components, normalization, and PCA weighting remain unchanged in Section 3 and Algorithms 1–2. Pose and angular-distance symbols are simplified. Alternative estimators and removal of VGGT are experimental variants, not revisions to the default method.

P1.justification: Targeted edits revise the title, affiliations, pose notation, related-work wording, and experimental explanations, and add acknowledgements and explicit appendix cross-references. New limitations and human-study sections shift appendix lettering, but most prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds main Table 3 and appendix Table 5 while retaining the existing figures and tables. The larger page canvas introduces wider margins and reflow, including changed algorithm placement; Figure 3's caption updates notation. There is no substantial redesign of the retained visual evidence.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Any4D, Page4D, and a study of Sora's geometric consistency. Related work distinguishes reconstruction-based analysis of Sora from an automated model-agnostic metric and qualifies the criticism of VBench's consistency dimensions. The broader research positioning is retained.

T1.justification: The rigid-background premise and mathematical definitions in Equations 1–8 are retained. Renaming pose variables and angular distance changes notation only. The human-study scoring formula is an evaluation-protocol addition, not a new theoretical result or derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses two important validation gaps in v1: absent human agreement evidence and untested dependence on the geometry estimator. Appendix E and Table 3 substantially strengthen the metric's empirical justification, while Appendix A clarifies unresolved calibration and tracking limitations. Human correlations cover only 11 aggregate entities without uncertainty for comparative superiority, and estimator tests exclude nuScenes; these constrain the conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SGC research, despite the revised title and formatting. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, algorithms, and figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds geometry-estimator robustness experiments and a blinded human study with 1,050 judgments.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on 1,296 videos, controlled geometric perturbations, component ablations, motion analyses, PCA cross-validation, and segmentation-sensitivity experiments.

results.title: Measuring 3D Spatial Geometric Consistency in Dynamic Video Generation

C1.justification: The central training-free, plug-and-play contribution remains. v3 corrects the abstract's 'over 5%' improvement claim to +4.47–+7.48 percentage points and replaces the introduction's cross-backbone Watch & Learn superiority claim with a same-backbone style control and an explicit WAA transfer contribution.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 substantially expands attribution: v3 credits structured decomposition over raw trajectories, separates visual annotation from transcript-only guidance, and qualifies OmniParser's contribution as modest under GPT-5.2. It also explains demonstration-count saturation and interprets Windows transfer. The original retrieval-mismatch limitations and failure mechanisms remain in Appendix F.

D1.justification: v3 adds a project-page pointer announcing code, dataset, and additional results, plus technical details for the new controls, including trajectory limits and the component-study annotator. Existing integration prompts, default pipeline settings, and detailed API cost accounting remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates task execution only on OSWorld. v3 adds 154 WindowsAgentArena tasks across six domains, introducing native Windows widgets and a different action interface (Table 2). The original OSWorld coverage remains.

E2.justification: v3 removes the published Watch & Learn-on-Jedi comparison from Table 1 and introduces a distinct Watch & Learn-style raw-trajectory control using Qwen3-VL-8B and GUIDE's retrieved videos (Table 3). It also adds grounding-only and title-only/random retrieval comparators (Tables 3 and 6).

E3.justification: New protocols include a balanced 120-task component study with 12 tasks per domain and a GPT-5.2 annotator, a separate 50-task Qwen3-VL-8B study varying retrieved demonstrations from one to three, and Windows evaluation including Qwen3-VL-32B. The raw-trajectory control specifies two demonstrations, 12 steps each, and a 24K-character cap. Existing OSWorld settings are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds tests of raw versus decomposed knowledge, grounding alone, subtitle-only annotation, removal of OmniParser, demonstration count, and retrieval ranking alternatives (Tables 3–6). The original grounding-element and annotator-model ablations remain in Appendix C, Table 7, corresponding to v1 Table 3; the failure cases are also retained.

E5.justification: v3 Table 4 newly reports averaging over three random seeds. v1 contains no corresponding seed-averaging statement. This does not establish increased runs for retained experiments; neither version reports dispersion estimates, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: The retained GUIDE OSWorld scores are unchanged. New WAA baseline/GUIDE scores are 49.00/59.21 for Agents3+GPT-5.2 and 31.70/44.16 for Qwen3-VL-32B (Table 2). New OSWorld controls score 31.96 for raw trajectories and 34.31 for grounding alone (Table 3). Component, demonstration-count, and retrieval-control results are also added; the original published Jedi comparison is removed.

M1.justification: The retrieval, keyframe extraction, OmniParser processing, frame-pair annotation, knowledge decomposition, and agent integration procedures remain unchanged. Section 3 renames inverse dynamics annotation as VLM pairwise video annotation without changing its inputs, outputs, or operational steps.

P1.justification: v3 systematically revises annotation terminology, condenses parts of the method, quality evaluation, and conclusion, and reworks Section 4.3 around additional controls. It adds acknowledgments and a Supplementary Material heading, while preserving the overall section sequence and most existing prose.

P2.justification: New Tables 2–6 substantially expand the experimental presentation. v3 removes the external comparison rows and the original main-text ablation summary while retaining detailed ablations in Appendix C. The eight figures retain their substantive content with label, caption, size, and placement changes; Figure 5's reduced layout crowds its bottom labels against the caption.

R1.justification: v3 adds WindowsAgentArena, Mobile-Env, and three agent-training/tool-use references, and removes the Jedi reference. Its empirical positioning against Watch & Learn becomes a clearly identified style control. The related-work organization and principal distinctions concerning live retrieval, subtitles, and annotation remain.

T1.justification: Equation 1 retains the same annotation function arguments and output, with fIDM renamed fVPA. The revised pairwise-annotation explanation introduces no substantive mathematical definition, assumption, derivation, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important validation gaps in v1 through Windows transfer and same-backbone, component, and retrieval controls (Tables 2–6). These strengthen evidence for generality and identify which parts of GUIDE contribute, while replacing the earlier cross-backbone superiority assertion and retaining the detailed appendices. Limited uncertainty reporting, terse documentation of some new settings, and small presentation regressions remain, but the validation gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GUIDE and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–F. Retained material can be matched reliably across terminology changes, renumbering, and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds WindowsAgentArena evaluation and new OSWorld and retrieval controls in Tables 2–6.

before.justification: v1 reports original OSWorld agent evaluations, component ablations, human evaluations of the retrieval and annotation pipelines, and execution case studies.

results.title: GUIDE: Resolving Domain Bias in GUI Agents through Real-Time Web Video Retrieval and Plug-and-Play Annotation

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the framing from comprehensively covering all relevant sound events to authoring multiple complementary tracks. The central claims about NAG, training with single-reference datasets, separability, and composite quality remain; the new contribution list largely consolidates them.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive explanations of shared acoustic context and avoidance of waveform copying, and clarifies why visually plausible captions need not reproduce recorded audio. New discussions interpret event-dependent gains, source-separation failures, and the text-alignment versus audiovisual-alignment tradeoff. The original base-model and mixing limitations are retained in Appendix M.

D1.justification: v4 adds a project-page URL, replacing the local supplementary demo instruction, and discloses AudioSep's default configuration, caption reuse, and GPT-5 label assignment. It also clarifies that the sensitivity sweep shares a random generation order. Existing architecture, optimizer, training-budget, hardware, and timing details are retained.

E1.justification: v4 expands evaluation beyond Multi-Caps VGGSound to human, audio-aware captions in VGGSounder, the AudioCaps test set, and Movie Gen Audio Bench (Section 5.3; Appendix J). AudioCaps was already a training source in v3, but its evaluation use is new. Training dataset coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The original comparator sets remain in Tables 1-2. v4 adds fused-caption MMAudio followed by AudioSep, independent AudioX text-to-audio generation, and ControlFoley evaluated with and without NAG (Tables A2, A3, A7). These introduce substantially different comparison approaches.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs separate VGGSounder videos into subsets with 2-5 captions and aggregate separability by 309 event labels. The original eight-second, five-track evaluation, metrics, training settings, and human-study sample sizes remain unchanged. These are additional protocols, rather than revisions demonstrating reruns of existing experiments.

E4.justification: Section 5.3 newly examines effectiveness across caption-count subsets. Appendix E tests whether separability gains extend across event categories, and Appendix K examines dependence on the MMAudio backbone. These substantially extend the retained guidance-strength and generation-order analyses.

E5.justification: v4 replaces rating standard deviations with 95% confidence intervals and adds Wilson preference intervals with evenly split ties (Appendix A; Tables 3-4), without increasing the reported responses. However, the preference widths are inconsistent with the stated calculation: 50 responses imply approximately ±11.97 percentage points for audio quality, versus the reported ±7.71.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1-2 and sensitivity scores are retained. v4 adds caption-count and category findings, derived preference summaries, and results for new datasets, comparators, and ControlFoley. For example, Table A7 reports ControlFoley CLAP A-A of 60.67 without NAG and 53.81 with it. The existing random-order DeSync entry changes from 0.42 to 0.43 (v3 Table A3; v4 Table A4).

M1.justification: The NAG equation, MMAudio/ControlNet architecture, flow-matching objective, non-overlapping training pairs, and sequential generation procedure remain unchanged. The ControlFoley experiment applies NAG to another backbone without documenting a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: v4 edits the abstract and introduction, adds contribution bullets and explanatory paragraphs, swaps the model and dataset appendices, and moves limitations to the end. Much existing prose and the main narrative order remain recognizable. Appendix B also introduces incorrect main-equation references.

P2.justification: v4 changes document-wide typography, margins, headers, table formatting, and caption placement, while adding several result tables and the caption-count plot. v3 Figure 5 moves to v4 Figure A1, and rating Table A1 becomes main Table 4. Existing method diagrams and spectrogram examples retain their substantive content.

R1.justification: Related work adds focused comparisons with ReWaS, SelVA, and SonicVisionLM, alongside references supporting new benchmarks and comparison methods. These extend the existing positioning around negative audio conditioning and generative addition without fundamentally redefining the claimed novelty. Publication variants of existing references are not distinct new works.

T1.justification: The concept-negation assumption, probability factorization, guidance equations, and Appendix B derivation retain the same mathematics. Added training explanations are conceptual. Incorrect equation cross-references introduced in v4 do not constitute a substantive change to the derivation.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v3's narrow validation on one automatically captioned benchmark and one proposed-method backbone. Human-captioned evaluation, additional datasets, alternative generation comparisons, and ControlFoley tests strengthen evidence for generality and the practical value of sequential generation. Clearer task framing also helps interpretation. Sparse details for some new experiments, incorrect cross-references, and inconsistent preference confidence intervals limit the gains, but do not outweigh the substantially broader empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NAG research. Their complete main texts and appendices are available, and visual inspection resolves equation-extraction artifacts. Figures, tables, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds caption-count, event-category, cross-dataset, alternative-baseline, and ControlFoley evaluations.

before.justification: v3 reports original benchmark evaluations, a human preference and rating study, guidance-coefficient sensitivity experiments, and generation-order comparisons.

results.title: Step-by-Step Video-to-Audio Synthesis via Negative Audio Guidance

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow broad references to scene layout and diverse control scenarios to depth-guided scene structure and reference/depth/pose conditioning. The central MMCU, dual-stream bypass, guidance-scaling, and state-of-the-art claims remain.

C2.justification: Appendix C adds interpretations connecting component removals to synchronization, speaker similarity, and structural errors. Appendix D explains the loudness-versus-timbre distinction limiting the AVControl comparison and acknowledges its pose-aesthetics advantage. Section 4.3 also qualifies VACE comparisons and separates visual structural evaluation from joint audio-video capability.

D1.justification: Appendix C specifies the six ablation modifications and exact guidance values, including fixing the other scale at 1. These add limited reproducibility information. The original backbone, optimizer, training budget, hardware, preprocessing, and audio-evaluation tools remain unchanged; no new code or data access information appears.

E1.justification: Both versions train on 30,000 Hallo3 samples and cover reference-image/audio, depth, and pose conditioning. Pose control already appears in v1 Figure 6. Its new quantitative evaluation and the added appendix experiments do not introduce a new dataset, domain, or task.

E2.justification: v3 adds AVControl as a comparator for depth and pose control in Table S5. Existing comparator sets are retained; Text2Video-Zero, ControlVideo, and VACE already participated in v1's qualitative pose comparison.

E3.justification: v3 extends evaluation with quantitative pose MAE and temporal consistency, component comparisons on 90 paired samples, an AVControl comparison on 60 samples, and guidance sweeps over 0.5, 1.0, and 1.3. The original training settings, 200-sample audio/depth benchmarks, human-study design, and 150-case audio evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained qualitative guidance study in Figure 7, Appendix C adds substantial quantitative validation. Table S3 tests masks, projector initialization, unified attention, removal of each bypass branch, and added cross-attention across audio/depth/pose tasks. Table S4 adds guidance-strength sensitivity analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new 90- and 60-sample counts describe evaluation samples, not repeated runs or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 2, S1, and S2 retain their values. Substantial new results include pose MAE ×100 of 3.07 versus VACE's 3.29 in Table 3, component and guidance results in Tables S3–S4, and AVControl comparisons in Table S5: depth MAE 11.49 versus MMControl's 4.52 and pose MAE 7.57 versus 3.07. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 under matched settings.

M1.justification: The MMCU inputs and masks, dual-stream bypass architecture, modality-specific guidance, and two-stage inference remain unchanged in Section 3. The new ablation variants test the existing method rather than revise the proposed model.

P1.justification: v3 tightens wording throughout the method, experiments, and conclusion while retaining the main section sequence and narrative. It adds a main-text summary of existing human/audio results, expands the appendix outline, and changes citation style and author/header presentation.

P2.justification: The document is comprehensively reformatted with different typography, text width, running headers, and figure/table placement. Four tables are added: Table 3 and Tables S3–S5. The seven existing figures retain their illustrated content but are resized or relocated, with several captions revised.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for AVControl and Text2Video-Zero. Appendix D positions AVControl as concurrent work using task-specific IC-LoRA adapters and distinguishes its acoustic control target. The main related-work discussion otherwise retains its existing positioning.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5 retain the same task mapping, conditional representations, masks, projection, and residual guidance formulation. No new theorem, proof, derivation, or substantive mathematical revision appears.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked component ablations and supported pose control only qualitatively. v3 substantially strengthens evidence for its central contributions through quantitative pose evaluation, component and guidance studies, and a relevant concurrent baseline comparison. Narrower scope statements and more careful comparison language also improve precision. The added studies still lack uncertainty estimates and detailed protocols, but they address important gaps in the original empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MMControl research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison. v3 retains Appendices A–B and adds C–D.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds quantitative pose evaluation, component and guidance-scaling ablations, and an AVControl comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation experiments, quantitative baseline comparisons, qualitative control studies, human evaluation, and audio-quality measurements.

results.title: MMControl: Unified Multi-Modal Control for Joint Audio-Video Generation

C1.justification: The central contributions remain automated large-scale affordance annotation and unified 2D/3D grounding. v2 explicitly extends the pretraining-benefit claim to prior architectures and emphasizes gains on unseen categories. It drops v1's explicit claim of being the first to integrate the separate 2D and 3D research streams.

C2.justification: v2 interprets filtered-pretraining gains as evidence beyond category overlap, attributes cross-domain asymmetry primarily to training volume, and explains early 2D saturation through the synthetic-to-real domain gap. It adds substantive CoT, mask-selection and error-propagation explanations. v1's frozen-encoder rationale, detailed critique of prior heatmaps and partial-view robustness discussion are removed. Existing background and action-detail limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents smallest-mask selection, category-filtering instructions, explicit instance/view/query separation, and interpolation when training and test resolutions differ. It adds a project-page link while retaining the dataset URL. Model checkpoints, hardware, training budgets and most implementation recipes remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds qualitative zero-shot evaluation on cluttered Open X-Embodiment robot-workspace images (Figure 7) and removes the Affogato-Partial evaluation of partially observed furniture objects (v1 Appendix C). The principal Objaverse-derived, LASO and AGD20K coverage remains. Affogato-750K renames the existing annotation collection rather than introducing another dataset.

E2.justification: The LASO comparison expands beyond OpenAD and PointRefer to include Referring Transformer, 3D-SPS, ReLA and IAGNet (v2 Table 2). AffordanceNet, associated with RAGNet, is added to both zero-shot and supervised AGD20K comparisons (Table 4). These are substantive additions to the reported comparator sets.

E3.justification: v2 replaces direct LASO–Affogato transfer comparisons with LASO seen/unseen comparisons using pretraining followed by target-dataset fine-tuning. It adds category-filtering, training-volume and point-resolution controls. Human validation now describes disjoint annotator assignments and removal of incorrect queries. The reported 2D image count falls from 300,208 to 150,104, consistent with retaining only the most visible viewpoint instead of also sampling a neighboring view.

E4.justification: v2 adds held-out-category filtering, pretraining-scale and volume-matching analyses, training/test resolution sensitivity, qualitative CoT and mask-selection ablations, and stage-specific failure analysis (Section 5.4; Appendix C). These investigate overlap, scaling, design choices and error mechanisms previously untested. The partial-view robustness study is removed; the background-augmentation ablation remains.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or error bars. The added scores and failure percentages do not introduce uncertainty estimation or change the reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for pretraining, new comparators and controls; its new LASO comparison reports Espresso-3D unseen aIoU of 18.7 without versus 20.8 with pretraining. Human validation changes from 72.3% good, 12.3% ok and 15.4% not good to 84.8% success with an error breakdown. Direct cross-dataset and partial-view results disappear. Retained Affogato and Espresso-2D scores match after accounting for percentage rescaling.

M1.justification: The documented Espresso-3D objective changes from equally weighted Focal and Dice losses to BCE and Dice losses (v1 Appendix A.2; v2 Appendix B.2). Section 4 also changes frozen encoders to fine-tuned encoders, although v2 Appendix B.2 still states that the vision backbone is frozen, leaving the actual policy unresolved. The core architectures and three-stage annotation pipeline remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Separate 2D/3D related-work discussions are consolidated, Affogato becomes the framework name and Affogato-750K the dataset name, a dedicated analysis subsection is introduced, and the appendices are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: The overview and pipeline diagrams are redrawn, the prior-dataset failure figure is replaced by human-validation and pipeline-error displays, and several analysis tables and figures are added. Tables are reorganized around pretraining comparisons. The former zero-shot Figure 7 moves to Appendix Figure A4, selected supervised examples move into Figure 9, and partial-view displays are removed. Typography and page layout also change throughout.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of 2HandedAfforder, RAGNet, LMAffordance3D and recent 2D-to-3D transfer work. It acknowledges automated large-scale 2D datasets and contrasts their single-view supervision with multi-view aggregation. These update the competitive context while retaining the underlying positioning around affordance-data scarcity and open-vocabulary coverage.

T1.justification: Neither version provides theoretical propositions, proofs or substantive derivations. The coverage and diversity definitions remain equivalent, and the added empirical analyses introduce no new formal theory.

improvement.justification: v1's main 3D evidence for dataset utility relied on cross-dataset performance gaps. v2 directly tests pretraining benefits across architectures and checks held-out-category overlap (Tables 2 and 5), substantially strengthening the central empirical argument. Scaling, volume controls and pipeline-error analysis further improve validation. The contradictory encoder-training descriptions in Section 4 and Appendix B.2 impair reproducibility, and partial-view validation is lost, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the stronger evidence for the dataset's principal contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Affogato dataset, annotation pipeline and Espresso models. Their main text, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial restructuring and renaming.

after.justification: v2 reports original grounding experiments, human validation, pretraining comparisons, filtering controls, scaling and resolution analyses, and qualitative robot-scene evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original annotation-quality evaluation, quantitative 2D and 3D grounding experiments, background-augmentation ablations and partial-view experiments.

results.title: AffoGato: Open-Vocabulary Affordance Grounding with Automated Data Generation at Scale

C1.justification: The central diffusion, SAT and RMML contributions remain. v2 narrows broad state-of-the-art claims to superiority over reimplemented baselines under matched conditions and explicitly claims the first application of masked diffusion to HMER. Its abstract also more clearly identifies CROHME as held-out cross-dataset evaluation.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning repeated-pass latency, dependence on large training datasets and fixed-resolution inputs. New analyses interpret complementary SAT/RMML effects, refinement convergence and recovery failures at intermediate timesteps, including higher recovery CER with SAT despite improved SER. These substantially expand the account of mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies PyTorch/DINO, encoder dimensions, decoder depth, attention heads, dropout, sequence padding, epochs, batch size, AdamW settings and V100 timing hardware. It also details modifier alignment and loss computation over masked and unmasked positions. These are primarily disclosures, not demonstrated setting changes. Conversely, v1's explicit 626K training count and parameter-count columns disappear.

E1.justification: MathWriting and CROHME 2014/2016/2019/2023 remain the benchmark coverage. v2 Section 4.9 adds a distinct recovery scenario initialized with operator-deleted expressions, extending evaluation from recognition from fully masked sequences to correction of partially corrupted symbolic inputs.

E2.justification: v2 adds matched TAMER and PosFormer comparisons on both benchmarks, Mask-Predict decoding on MathWriting, and literature-only NAMER scores on CROHME. It removes CTC, PaLI and PaLIGemma from MathWriting and replaces the extensive literature-comparison block on CROHME. BTTR, CoMER, ICAL and Google OCR, renamed OCR, remain.

E3.justification: The main training dataset, held-out CROHME evaluation, rasterization and core metrics remain. v2 expands the latency study from T={2,10,50} to {1,2,5,10,20,50} and introduces timestep-controlled recovery tests that retain arguments and braces while removing operators. Reported near-match thresholds are reduced to ≤1 rather than including ≤2 and CROHME 2023's ≤3/≤4.

E4.justification: v2 adds an RMML-only control, step-wise CER/EM/SER trajectories and targeted structural-error recovery, and expands latency and diversity analyses. These substantially strengthen investigation of component effects and refinement behavior. Conversely, v1's test-set component-ablation table and two of its three qualitative cases are removed.

E5.justification: v1 specifies ten-run averaging for Proposal in the main comparison captions. v2 Section 4.1 explicitly extends the statement to all results and identifies these as inference runs. This broadens reporting without establishing additional training runs; neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests or seed-based uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Proposed-method scores, ablations and throughput are extensively revised, with additional diagnostic results. MathWriting's headline changes from 5.56% CER/60.42% EM for SAT-only Proposal to 5.51%/59.9% for GryphOne with RMML; v1's corresponding RMML row reports 5.55%/59.60%. Reported T=50 throughput changes from 0.62 to 21.2 FPS, but v1 lacks hardware details needed to establish a comparable speedup.

M1.justification: The core encoder–decoder, SAT and RMML remain. Algorithm 2 makes a limited procedural correction: v1 remasks predictions at time t, whereas v2 explicitly predicts the clean sequence and remasks at t−1, leaving the final output unmasked. Expanded architecture and loss descriptions otherwise primarily disclose existing components.

P1.justification: Beyond naming the method GryphOne, v2 extensively rewrites existing prose, moves related work before methodology, separates training and inference explanations, and organizes components into Method/Effect discussions. Experimental reporting is reorganized into substantially more focused subsections.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. Architecture/refinement and SAT illustrations are substantially redrawn, the separate RMML diagram is removed, and new trajectory/recovery plots appear. CROHME tables are merged, benchmark columns are streamlined, and component ablations and latency results receive separate displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds explicit positioning against confidence-guided Mask-Predict and references for DINO, AdamW and Transformers. It removes the large-scale-data subsection and references to PaLI, PaLIGemma, MMHMER, Tex80M and Sahoo et al.'s masked diffusion work. Most of the HMER research lineage and its relationship to AR, NAR and syntax-aware models remain.

T1.justification: Algorithm 2 corrects the reverse-time specification by remasking at t−1 instead of t, ensuring zero masking at termination. The newly written embedding sum, expanded two-view loss and factorized corruption equation otherwise formalize operations already described in v1. No theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves reproducibility through previously missing implementation and training specifications. Mask-Predict comparisons, an RMML-only control and targeted refinement analyses provide stronger evidence for the central mechanism, while matched-setting claims and explicit limitations improve interpretation. These gains outweigh the loss of test-set component ablations and some broader comparisons. The large throughput revisions remain insufficiently explained for cross-version speed claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same masked-diffusion HMER work, renamed GryphOne in v2. Their text, equations, tables and figures are readable and support comparison. Both were inspected through their references; neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations and ablations, plus refinement trajectories, structural-error recovery and accuracy–latency experiments in Tables 1–4 and Figures 3–6.

before.justification: v1 reports original MathWriting and CROHME evaluations, component ablations, inference measurements and output-diversity analyses in Tables 1–4 and Figures 6–7.

results.title: GryphOne: Symbol-Aware Masked Diffusion for Structural Refinement in Offline Handwritten Mathematical Expression Recognition

C1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions, and conclusion expand the central claim from synchronized video-audio generation to a single framework for generation and editing. The approximately 3M-pair corpus, editing-data synthesis pipeline, and generation/editing benchmarks become central contributions, replacing the earlier emphasis on mouth supervision as a separate headline contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving preservation of pretrained priors and avoidance of cascading editing errors, and qualifies editing comparisons by noting baselines receive ground-truth audio. It newly identifies fast-hand artifacts, failures to preserve background text, and human-speech-only editing coverage caused by limited paired data. v1's RoPE trade-off and small-model deployment interpretations are removed.

D1.justification: v2 documents an editing-data pipeline using GPT-4o, FLUX.1-Kontext-dev, Wan2.2 control, Qwen3, and Higgs-Audio, alongside conditioning-mask conventions and detailed editing-task distributions. These substantially expand implementation information. Conversely, explicit mouth-box mapping formulas and v1's total-parameter accounting are omitted. The project-page access information remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's natural-scene and human-speech generation coverage, v2 trains on video editing, audio editing, joint editing, and reconstruction tasks. It adds JoVABench-Edit evaluations covering background, style, and local modifications, plus VBench video-generation evaluation. The corresponding generation comparison appearing as JoVABench-Gen is not counted as new coverage merely because its name changes.

E2.justification: JavisDiT enters both generation comparisons; LTX-2 and UniAVGen enter JoVABench-Gen. The editing comparison adds Ditto, ICVE, InsViE, Lucy, and OmniVideo, each combined with Diff2Lip or Wav2Lip. Appendix A additionally compares against video generators using borrowed baseline scores. These are substantial additions to actual comparisons, including methods only cited in v1.

E3.justification: Reported joint training changes from 50K steps at 5e-5 to 100K steps at 3e-5 and includes editing. New evaluations introduce LSE-D, FC, IB-TV, and DeSync; IS is now specified on video frames rather than described as an audio metric. Appendix B adds blind 1–5 MOS evaluation with 21 participants and 50 samples per task.

E4.justification: v1's temporal-RoPE ablation and smaller-backbone scaling study are removed. v2 adds an Ovi-style sequential cross-attention variant to the fusion ablation and editing case studies examining instruction following and unintended changes. The mouth-loss ablation remains, and the existing mouth-mask validation moves from Appendix A to Appendix E.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, uncertainty intervals, dispersion estimates, or significance tests. The new human-evaluation tables report mean scores only; their participant and sample counts describe the new evaluation protocol rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: JoVA's reported Verse-Bench results change, including LSE-C 6.51 to 6.65, FD 1.10 to 0.82, and MS 0.80 to 0.75. These accompany changed training and are not controlled same-setting gains. v2 adds editing results, including LSE-C 5.88 and LSE-D 1.66, VBench total score 82.61, and human ratings. Generation and ablation entries are also revised, while RoPE and smaller-model results disappear.

M1.justification: v2 extends generation to joint editing through reference-audio token concatenation and reference-video/image conditioning with a binary mask, channel concatenation, and a projector (Section 3.2). These change the supported inputs and procedure beyond v1's text/image-conditioned generation. Joint attention, flow matching, and the mouth-area loss remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions, and related-work discussion are extensively rewritten. The method is reorganized around architecture, conditioning, and objectives; dataset composition receives a separate section; and the appendix expands into sections A–F. The former 'Quantitative Results' heading for qualitative examples is also corrected.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the opening architectural comparison with a capabilities montage, redraws the main architecture and data pipelines, and adds dataset charts, editing comparisons, training examples, and new tables. The fusion table changes structure, while existing generation and mouth-mask illustrations are relocated. The new Figure 2 reverses the generation/editing labels on its example prompts.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially reframed around joint generation and joint editing. v2 adds positioning against unified video editors and audiovisual editing systems, including VACE, UniVideo, OpenVE-3M, Object-AVEdit, and lip-sync methods, as well as newer generation work such as LTX-2. The claimed distinction now concerns unified generation/editing rather than primarily simpler synchronized generation.

T1.justification: v2 omits v1's explicit floor/ceiling spatial-coordinate mapping and min/max temporal bounding-box definition (Section 3.2.2, Equation 5), retaining only a higher-level description. The transformer, flow-matching, joint-attention, and mouth-loss mathematics otherwise remain equivalent; neither version provides theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 turns v1's largely prospective task-extensibility claim into an implemented editing capability supported by comparative experiments. Broader generation baselines, the added Ovi-style attention control, and blind human evaluation substantially strengthen the evidence beyond v1's automatic metrics and selected examples. Specific failure conditions also clarify applicability. These gains outweigh the removed RoPE/scaling analyses and reduced mouth-mask implementation detail, although uncertainty estimates remain absent and some presentation errors persist.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe JoVA and retain identifiable architecture, losses, experiments, and appendix validation material. Their complete text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison despite v2's substantial extension to editing.

after.justification: v2 reports original generation and editing experiments, architecture ablations, JoVA's VBench results, and a human evaluation with 21 participants.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation comparisons, mouth-loss and attention ablations, model-scaling experiments, and appendix mouth-mask validation.

results.title: JoVA: Unified Multimodal Learning for Joint Video-Audio Generation and Editing

C1.justification: V1 centers its contributions on HoMi's single-codebook reconstruction and SOTA performance in completion, interaction generation and comprehension. V2 centers FlowVQ, generalist-to-specialist training and standardized MotionHub benchmarks, claiming SOTA on seven of nine tasks. This substantially redefines the principal methodological contributions and performance claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations linking generalist pretraining to benefits on data-scarce interaction tasks and linking quantizer effectiveness to encoder quality. It discusses computational tradeoffs behind tokenizer choices. Appendix F newly acknowledges that caption granularity is not explicitly exploited and that arbitrary-agent architectural support has only been validated on two-person interactions.

D1.justification: V2 Appendix A adds detailed architectures, optimizer settings, GPU resources, training times, precision, distributed-training tools, flow-sampling steps and missing-hand loss handling. However, v1's explicit repository link and inference temperature/top-p settings disappear; v2 describes the MMotion codebase without providing its access link. Documentation is substantially expanded but retains gaps.

E1.justification: MotionHub substantially expands its training coverage with sources including NTU-RGBD-120, UESTC and TED (v1 Table 10; v2 Table 2). V2 also evaluates combined audio/text conditioning qualitatively in Figure 5. The nine core benchmark task families remain, and empirical multi-agent evaluation still concerns two people.

E2.justification: V2 adds Lodge to music-to-dance comparisons and MDM to multi-agent text-to-motion, while removing MCM from single-agent text-to-motion. Its main reconstruction comparison adds Motion FSQ-VAE and drops MoVQ and standalone RVQ rows; RVQ remains evaluated in appendix ablations. These alter comparator membership across several retained experiments.

E3.justification: Reported training budgets change from v1's 500-epoch pretraining/instruction-tuning setting to 30 pretraining, 30 generalist-tuning and 100 specialist-tuning epochs in v2 Appendix A. V2 adds controlled 10-epoch initialization comparisons across 1B–8B backbones. Reconstruction tables also report PA-MPJPE instead of N-MPJPE. These are substantive reported setting changes.

E4.justification: V1 already studies motion representations, codebook size and HoMi components. V2 replaces the HoMi-component ablation with FlowVQ reconstruction/downstream ablations and adds training-stage and initialization/scale analyses. Appendices B–C greatly expand tokenizer investigations, including standardization, dilation, quantizer choice, depth, causal convolutions, patchification and training-clip length.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. V2's standard-deviation formulas concern input normalization, not uncertainty in experimental results.

E6.justification: Benchmark results are extensively replaced and supplemented with generalist, specialist and FlowVQ rows. For example, v1 Table 3 reports T2M FID 0.0268 versus MCM's 0.0179; v2 Table 4 reports 62.8245 for specialist+FlowVQ versus MoMask's 76.0154, the best listed external comparator. These are results under revised conditions, not a same-setting performance gain. Numerous new ablation results also appear.

M1.justification: HoMi's separate hand/body encoders and Fourier gating are replaced by FSQ-based FlowVQ with an iterative Flow Matching decoder. V2 also introduces sequential generalist pretraining, reply-only generalist tuning and specialist tuning, replacing v1's two-stage strategy. Optional compound conditions extend the motion-message procedure.

P1.justification: The paper is renamed, and the abstract, introduction, contribution narrative and method description are extensively rewritten around FlowVQ and generalist/specialist training. MotionHub moves from the appendix into a dedicated main-text section, implementation details move into Appendix A, and the appendices are substantially reorganized and expanded.

P2.justification: V2 adopts an ACM journal layout, adds a new teaser, redraws the framework/tokenizer diagrams and introduces baseline-comparison and compound-conditioning visuals. Tables gain generalist/specialist/FlowVQ rows, and music-to-dance and dance-to-music comparisons are merged. V1 Figure 1 is retained as v2 Appendix Figure 6, while the codebook-utilization plot disappears.

R1.justification: V2 expands positioning around quantization bottlenecks, scalable motion models and reconstruction versus generation quality. Newly incorporated works include ScaMo, Finite Scalar Quantization, The Language of Motion, MotionGPT-2, Cosmos and the optimization-dilemma study. These support a substantially revised methodological framing rather than merely updated bibliography formatting.

T1.justification: V2 Section 4.2 adds mathematical definitions of noisy motion, conditioned velocity prediction and the residual-field loss in Equations 3–5. These formal additions are localized to the new decoder. Existing R-precision, BAS and F1 definitions are retained in the relocated metrics appendix; neither version develops theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the unified-training contribution: Tables 11–12 isolate training-stage effects that v1 did not test, while tokenizer ablations establish which design choices matter. Appendix A greatly improves implementation documentation, and Appendix F clarifies applicability limits. These gains outweigh the removed repository link and MCM T2M comparison. Unspecified benchmark splits and remaining overstatements, such as the S2G FGD claim despite MCM's better value in Table 9, still limit confidence in some conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same unified motion synthesis/comprehension research, renamed from MotionLLaMA to VersatileMotion. The complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables and equations, support comparison despite substantial methodological revisions.

after.justification: V2 reports original VersatileMotion and FlowVQ results, generalist/specialist comparisons, initialization experiments and extensive tokenizer ablations in Section 5 and Appendices B–C.

before.justification: V1 reports original MotionLLaMA benchmark results, tokenizer reconstruction experiments and ablations in Section 4 and Appendix C.

results.title: VersatileMotion: A Unified Framework for Motion Synthesis and Comprehension

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from broadly reusable pathology embeddings and PMEB to defining expanded Pathology Composed Retrieval and adapting MLLMs through a two-stage HOMIE framework. The abstract, introduction and conclusion now emphasize interleaved modalities, task/domain mismatch and retrieval as a clinical computational consult.

C2.justification: v2 emphasizes data efficiency, modality alignment and the adequacy of sampled evaluation. v3 introduces stronger explanations based on morphology-first learning and claims that every adaptation component is essential. It attributes CONCH's Pubmedset advantage to likely training/test overlap without reporting an overlap audit, and identifies genomics integration as future work.

D1.justification: v3 documents stage-specific corpus sizes, trained modules, batch sizes of 576/384, learning rates of 4e-5/1e-4, two-epoch schedules and eight H100 GPUs instead of six. Earlier QLoRA, checkpointing, DeepSpeed and temperature disclosures are no longer stated. The new filtering threshold remains unspecified, and referenced benchmark-construction prompts are unavailable.

E1.justification: v3 adds multi-image-to-text, image-text-to-image and video-to-text evaluation, plus Educontent and MMUpubmed simple retrieval. DigestPath's two classification tasks and Wsss4luad disappear. Training adds MedNLI/MedMCQA text pairs and PathGen-1.6M. Bookset/Pubmedset retain the cited sources of Arch-book/Arch-PubMed; those name changes alone are not new coverage.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained E5-V, PLIP, PathCLIP and QuiltNet, v3 evaluates PubmedCLIP, BiomedCLIP, Pathgen-CLIP variants, Patho-CLIP variants, MUSK, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, LamRA and GME. CONCH expands from classification-only comparison in v2 to retrieval comparisons. Conversely, QuiltNet is no longer included in the fusion ablation.

E3.justification: Evaluation sizes change substantially: LCcolon increases from 1,000 to 10,000 samples, and Bookset from 1,306 to 2,688. Retrieval reporting changes from R@5/10/50 to R@1/5/10; classification changes from wF1 and accuracy to an undefined 'weighted accuracy.'
